title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 358 époux , ou les époux eux-mêmes , soient obligés, avant de s'unir , de déposer dans la caisse, que nous nommerons matri moniale , une somme proportionnée à Fétat des contractans , depuis dix mille jusqu'à dix francs pour les plus pauvres. Ce revenu , considérable sans doute , ser vira à pourvoir à F éducation des enfans délaissés après la séparation des époux ; ils seront, comme à Sparte , les enfans de la patrie , et sans doute leur éduca tion sera préférable à celle qu'ils rece vroient de leurs pères et mères séparés, désordonnés et souvent ruinés. Ne crai gnons pas que la dépense qu'exigeront ces enfans , surpasse les fonds de cette caisse ; quand cela seroit , doit - on déli bérer lorsqu'il s'agit du bonheur de tous? Mais ne le craignons point , se priver de ses enfans est le dernier effort des pères et des mères ; la nature leur ordonne de les aimer , et l'ordre civil doit se rassurer quand la nature commande. Enfin, nous ne devons pas nous dissimuler que , si les liens du mariage contraignoient les époux
name: Grétry, André-Ernest-Modeste

title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 359 à vivre ensemble lorsqu'ils ne se con viennent plus , toutes les ressources de la morale la mieux raisonnée, seroient imu tiles au bonheur des hommes. En France, on a d'abord laissé la plus grande facilité aux époux malheureux qui soupiroient depuis long-temps après leur séparation ; quelques-uns ont abusé des bienfaits de la loi ; des femmes ont divorcé plusieurs fois après s'être fait avantager dans leurs contrats en cas de divorce ; des hommes ont épousé plusieurs femmes de suite , et n'ont paru contracter les nœuds du mariage que pour assouvir leurs passions. Ces abus sont grands sans doute , mais qae sont-ils en comparaison du malheur général dont l'humanité est accablée par des liens indissolubles ? Reposons - nous sur la société des gens honnêtes qui punit tous les crimes que la loi ne peut attein dre ; elle repousse le libertin déhonté , comme elle bannit de son sein le fripon et l'escroc qui , après s'être enrichis , ne peuvent obtenir l'honneur de voir assis à leur table splendide l'honnête honim*

C'est là leur ver ron geur , leur punition éternelle ; ils vou draient , après avoir, volé une fortune immense , se rapprocher , se confondre parmi les honnêtes gens ; vain espoir , la tache est empreinte sur leur front, elle est ineffaçable. Que d'efforts ne font pas , chaque jour, les femmes suspectes pour entrer dansl'intimité des femmes honnê- tes ! jamais elles n'ont pu y parvenir. La pauvreté vertueuse les visite quelquefois , mais la femme perdue sait bien que la misère, dans ce cas, contraint la vertu de s'humilier , et que telle femme , aussi vertueuse qu'indigente , rougiroit de pa roître en public avec la femme qu'elle courtise dans ses foyers. Au reste, ne craignons pas que dans une république , les entraves au divorce soient jamais trop multipliées ; le législateur républicain ne sort de la classe du peuple que pour y rentrer bientôt. text: 361 empestée par le scélérat libertin ; il plaide sa propre cause en plaidant celle de tous. II n'appartient qu'au despote immoral , aux suppôts qu'il favorise, de ne pas obéir aux lois faites pour tous, de vivre sans mœurs et d'en exiger du reste des hommes soumis à leur empire tyrannique. §, XVI. L'homme protégé par F Amour jusque dans sa vieillesse. Nous venons de montrer l'homme protégé , dirigé par l'amour dans les trois premiers âges de sa vie : il nous reste à voir si , même dans sa vieillesse , il ne reçoit pas de l'amour ses plus douces consolations. Oui, n'en doutons pas; de .méme qu'à son berceau , les tendres réac tions amoureuses de ses générateurs étoient ses titres les plus surs ; parvenu à la vieillesse, aux approches du tombeau-, ses enfans lui rendent le tribut de ten dresse qu'il leur a prodigué dans le temps de l,eur enfance. title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 362 ne s'efface jamais de la mémoire de l'homme ; mon père m'aimoit , dit-il , il me consacroit tous ses soins ; aujour d'hui que je suis à la fleur de l'âge , et lui dans la vieillesse, qui n'est que l'en fance de la vie à venir, je veux lui rendre les mêmes soins dont il a protégé ma foi blesse ; ma vie, alors, n' étoit qu'une étin celle, il daigna la conserver ; la sienne n'est plus qu'un souffle , c'est à moi de le ranimer. Où l'homme trouve-t-il encore quelque joie dans son âge avancé ? où le vieillard se sent-il encore ragaillardir un instant ? C'est lorsqu'il retrouve la femme qu'il aima et dont il fut aimé. Quels souvenirs pour tous les deux ! que de plaisirs , mais que de regrets ! aussi ces deux sensations marchent-elles souvent ensemble chez le vieillard ; des larmes accompagnent pres que toujours le moindre épanouissement de sa joie. Bacchus , en ranimant sa vieille existence , le favorise encore par des réminiscences de sa tendresse passée et des souvenirs d'un plaisir qui n'est plus.
name: Grétry, André-Ernest-Modeste

title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 363 Voltaire, dans sa vieillesse , veut encore baiser le sein d'une femme qui lui fut chère. — Quoi , lui dit-elle , vous aimez encore ce que vous appeliez vos petits fripons ? — Ils sont devenus de grands pendards , répond le poète qui saisit tou jours les contrastes. Jean - Jacques , aurois-tu fait cette réponse cruelle à celle qui t'avoit jadis charmé? Non, la tendre reconnoissance eût remplacé le feu de Famour éteint par le temps et par l'âge. Nous venons de montrer que l'homme à tout âge est vivifié ou récompensé par Famour , mais l'amour honnête qui res pecte les mœurs. Le plus inconstant des dieux , lorsque les hommes sont dans le bel âge , est peut-être le plus reconnois sant envers ceux qui ont sacrifié sur ses autels. — Mais , dira - 1 - on , vous nous montrez l'amour bienfaiteur de l'homme, plus que régulateur des mœurs. — Oui , mais à mon tour , je demande si l'on peut être heureux , sans être bon ? ou bon , sans être heureux ? et si l'on peut être mal heureux, sans, presque toujours, être

text: 365 NOTE DU SEIZIEME CHAPITRE. (1) Les théologiens , les philosophes , ont beaucoup discuté pour et contre l'existence des idées innées. N'auroient-ils pas du dire , pour être d'accord , que les sentimens innés , tels que celui de l'amour , la conservation de son être , et par suite l'amour-pro pre , doivent produire les idées innées relatives aux sentimens innés qui les font naître ? Nieront-ils que ces trois sentimens soient naturels et innés dans l'homme ? Alors il faut renoncer à ses perceptions les plus sensibles.

text: 366 CHAPITRE XVII. Continuation du méme sujet ; nouvel examen sur les sources du mensonge, et sur les moyens d'en préserver la jeunesse. XLn approfondissant bien Fétat politique de l'homme en société, remarquons qu'il a renoncé à presque toutes ses propriétés naturelles dont il ne lui est plus permis de jouir que d'après la modification des lois ; et qu'il ne cesse de revendiquer tacitement ses droits primitifs en bouleversant -les mœurs. Nous ne parlons maintenant que de ses propriétés physiques. Ces anciennes et principales propriétés sont les produc tions de la terre et les femmes. La femme est la propriété de l'homme , mais il est aussi la propriété de la femme , après avoir contracté alliance avec elle. text: 369 mutuellement, comme un million d'ames que renferme une enceinte telle que celle de Paris, doivent se leurrer de fausses ca resses en se mangeant Fherbe sous le pied. L'atmosphère d'une grande ville est un nuage que le mensonge a formé. Dans les grandes villes , les enfans mentent pour avoir du sucre , les hommes pour avoir de l'argent , de la considération et des fem mes, et les femmes ne s'y occupent qu'à tromper les hommes. D'autres s'y débat-» tent pour acquérir de la gloire , de la repu- tation, et ceux-là ne sont pas les plus petits menteurs. Le lit de la mort, pas plus que la couche matrimoniale , n'est exempt de supercherie; on meurt comme on a vécu : peu sûr de ses principes et de l'avenir, On y est tremblant et l'on veut encore faire le brave pour tromper les spectateurs , les hommes de son siècle et la postérité (*). Quant aux moralistes, je le répète, ils (*) Au sein des malheurs , combien de fois ne dit on pas , j'en mourrai ! sachant très-bien qu'on n'en mourra pas ; et cela m'en égal , quand il n'en est rien. i //. 24

title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 370 nous invitent à nous rapprocher de la nature , c'est là le grand mot ; et ils n'osent pas avouer qu'il faut renoncer à presque tous nos droits naturels pour ne pas violer les lois civiles , sans lesquelles la société ne seroit qu'un repaire de bri gands. Oui , les lois naturelles sont divines et peuvent se pratiquer dans les forêts presque désertes ; mais puisque Dieu rap proche les sexes , il ordonne les sociétés : alors aucun droit naturel n'est légitime s'il n'est autorisé par la loi. Nous le savons : certains animaux vi vent en société , et n'ont d'autres législa teurs que leur instinct et leur force ; mais ils ont le bonheur d'être bêtes , c'est-à dire , d'obéir ponctuellement à leur ins tinct sans pouvoir y déroger. Ils sont privéa de cet amour - propre , de cet instinct personnel qui détruit et fait tout dans l'homme : mais qu'il est petit dans son orgueil ! O sublime et premier de tous les polypes que produisit la nature, que tu es lâche, quand tu crois pouvoir mentir im punément !
name: Grétry, André-Ernest-Modeste

title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 371 - Combien ce dédale a besoin d'être en core expliqué à l'avantage des mœurs ! c'est un labyrinthe affreux pour tout homme qui l'observe de sang-froid. Ce pendant nous ne pouvons nous choisir et nous quitter comme des sauvages. Loin de moi Fidée de flétrir les mœurs , lorsque je fais des efforts pour les établir d'une manière solide ; pour que 1 homme puisse enfin lever le masque et vivre sans mentir dans la grande société la plus policée (i). title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 372 perfection de Fentendement humain ne peut être autre chose que la connoissance intime de la vérité universelle : une fois reconnue généralement, le respect qu'elle impose , précipitera Fodieux mensonge au fond de ce même puits , d'où l'au guste vérité sortira rayonnante de gloire. Non , ne nous décourageons pas ; faisons de nouveaux efforts pour régénérer son empire et ramener les hommes au seul principe qui puisse les rendre heureux, je veux dire la vérité de toutes choses. Avant d'examiner d'où nous vient la foiblesse de notre caractère et notre pen chant à la dissimulation , répondons aux questions que nous nous sommes faites précédemment. i.° Par quel moyen peut on établir plus de sincérité en amour ? II n'y en a qu'un ; c'est de permettre aux époux de rompre les nœuds qu'ils con tractent imprudemment. On se trompe quand on se recherche , la passion de l'amour nous abuse , et les époux qui se détestent , sont plus vrais que les amans qui se jurent un amour éternel.
name: Grétry, André-Ernest-Modeste

title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 373 z.° Verrons- nous encore long -temps des époux qui feignent de s'aimer encore, et qui se trompent mutuellement pour ne pas , soi - disant , blesser les bonnes mœurs ? 3. ° Verrons-nous toujours des femmes ( avons - nous dit ) qui pleurent , qui se meurent, parce qu'on ne les aime plus ; et des hommes qui n'adorent que les femmes qui les repoussent et les mépri sent ? — C'est le manège des amans , c'est le jeu de l'amour-propre , de la coquet terie, de la fatuité, de la sottise les faire, ils se punissent tous réciproque ment de leurs ruses et de leurs perfidies. Du reste, en substituant la vérité au men songe dans nos mœurs politiques et do mestiques; en dégradant le préjugé du faux honneur et faisant régner à sa place celui du véritable honneur, je veux dire la véracité, les mœurs mêmes des boudoirs se régénéreront. Suivons , je le répète , l'usage des Grecs et des premiers Ro mains : respect profond et religieux aux femmes honnêtes, sous peine d'infamie.
name: Grétry, André-Ernest-Modeste

text: 374 Laissons les jeunes gens s'amuser des Lais , comme de leurs chevaux de course. De même qu'à Athènes , estimons les Aspasies qui élèveront Famé de leurs amans ; punissons sévèrement et publi quement les courtisanes déhontées. Voilà ce qui nous manque pour être plus heu reux. title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être
text: 377 nous-mêmes , et ne nous en rapportons qu'à nos jouissances réelles. La dissimulation qui , depuis la chute des Grecs et des Romains , déshonore presque toutes les parties du monde connu, est, je crois, Fouvrage des prêtres. Je ne dis pas que leur intention fut de nous rendre dissimulés et menteurs ; mais ils nous y ont forcés par leurs ins titutions et leur doctrine trop opposées au vœu de la nature. Dans leurs vues étroites ils ont fulminé Fanathême contre ceux qui , hors du mariage, se livreroient à leur penchant amoureux ; ils ont cou vert la terre d'asyles destinés à protéger la chasteté des deux sexes , et toutes ces victimes de Ferreur ont passé leur triste vie dans le mensonge , en opposition à leurs vœux , que leur conscience et leurs sens démentoient à chaque moment. Les vœux mêmes des prêtres non cloîtrés , of ferts en exemple au monde, étoient chaque jour démentis par leurs mœurs. Le visage rubicon du moine , sa voix de stentor qui préchoit la chasteté, effrayoient la pudeur.
name: Grétry, André-Ernest-Modeste

title: De la Vérité. Ce que nous fumes, ce que nous sommes, ce que nous devrions être

On you a poet calls, you, rich in lands, Of treasures various, to call forth the bands Of youthful heroes, to the post of fame ; Each stripling glowing at a warrior's name : Do you their breasts inspire, their bosoms warm, With these high words Britons for freedom arm ! After what manner, therefore, are they generated r For it cannot be said that the generation of these is from chance; since neither nature nor divinity makes any thing in vain. As the generation of men, therefore, is not from chance, it is evidently from seed. Let it, then, be admitted that man is from seed; but seed possesses produc- tive powers in capacity, and not in energy. For since it is a body, it is not naturally adapted to possess productive poAvers impartibly and in energy. For every-where a subsistence in energy precedes a subsist- ence in capacity ; since the latter being imperfect, requires the assist- ance of something else endued Avith a perfective power. This some- thing else, you Avill say, is the nature of the mother; for this perfects and fashions the offspring by its productive powers. For the apparent form of the mother does not make the infant, but nature, which is an incor- poreal power and the principle of motion. If, therefore, nature changes the productive powers of seed from capacity to a subsistence in energy, nature must herself possess these productive powers in energy. Hence being irrational and Avithout imagination, she is at the same time the cause of physical productive poAvers. As the nature of man, there fore, contains human productive powers, does not, also, nature in a lion contain those of the lion; as, for instance, the productive poAvers of the head, the hair, the feet, and the other parts of the lion ? Or whence on shedding a tooth does another grow in its place, unless from an inherent power Avhich is able to make the teeth ? How, like- Avise, does it at the same time make bone and flesh, and each of the other parts ? For the same thing energizing according to the same would not be able to fashion such a variety of organization. But does not nature in plants, also, possess productive powers as well as in animals ? Hence the generation of things from putrefaction, and the growth of different kinds of plants in the same place Avithout human care and attention, originate from the whole nature of the earth containing the productive poAvers of all these in herself. If, also, from the celestial spheres we ascend to the nature of the universe itself, We may, also, enquire respecting this, Avhether it contains forms or not, and we shall be compelled to confess, that in this, also, the productive and motive powers of all things are contained. For thus nature, merged together with and dwelling in cor poreal masses, inspires them with her productive powers and with mo tion ; since things which are moved by others require a cause ofthis kind, a cause which is properly irrational, indeed, that it may not de part from bodies, which cannot subsist Avithout a cause continually residing with them, but containing the productive powers of bodies, that it may be able to preserve all things in their proper boundaries, and move every thing in a convenient manner. Nature, therefore, belongs to other things, being merged in or co-ordinated with bodies. But it is requisite that the most principal and proper cause should be exempt from its productions : for by how much the maker is exempt from the thing made, by so much the more perfectly and purely will he make : and, in short, if nature is irrational it requires a leader. There is, therefore, something prior to nature Avhich, contains productive powers, and from Avhich it is requisite that every thing in the Avorld should be suspended. Hence a knoAvledge of generated natures Avill subsist in the cause of the Avorld more excellent than the knoAvledge Ave possess, so far as this cause not only knoAvs but gives subsistence to all things ; but Ave possess knowledge alone. But if the fabricating cause of the universe knows all things, if he beholds them externally, he will be ignorant of himself, and will be subordinate to a partial soul such as our's; but if he beholds them in himself, he Avill contain in him self all forms both fabricative and gnostic. text: BOOK I. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 22 CHAPTER XIII. After the thorax, in the anterior parts is the belly; and the root of this is the navel. The part under this root, and Avhich is twofold, is the ilia ; and the single part which is under the navel is the abdomen. At the extremity of this are the pudenda or privities ; but the part above the navel is the hypochondrium. The part common to the hypochondrium and ilia, is called cholas. But in the posterior parts, those parts Avhich are opposite to the hypochondria at the cincture, are called the loins, (o<r<pus), whence also the name is derived ; for it appears to be, as it were, ta-otfvs, i. e. endued with an equal breadth. The part through Avhich the dry excrement is emitted, is subdivided into tAvo parts, of Avhich the fleshy part, subservient to sitting, is called nates ; but the part in Avhich the thigh is turned, is the acetabulum. The part peculiar to the female is the vulva; and to the male, the penis, Avhich extends outAvardly to the end of the thorax. And the extremity of it indeed is fleshy, and, as I may say, equally smooth, and is called glans penis ; but the skin which surrounds it is anonymous ; Avhich if it is cut off does not regenerate, as neither does the skin of the cheek, nor of the eyelids. To this penis and its glans the prœpuce is common ; but the remaining part is carti laginous, is easily increased, and has an egression and ingression con trary to that of beasts of burden or animals that have a tuft of hair on the forehead. Beneath the penis are the two testicles, Avhich are sur rounded Avith a skin called the scrotum. But the testicles are neither of the same nature with flesh, nor yet very remote from it. With re spect to the manner, hoAvever, in which they subsist, and in short, con cerning all such parts, Ave shall speak more accurately hereafter. C H A P.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK I. 24 Man, however, has the parts of his body distinguished by the supe rior and inferior, the anterior and posterior, and the right and the left. The right and left parts, therefore, are nearly similar and the same, ex cept that the left parts are more imbecile ; but the posterior are disi milar to the anterior, and the inferior to the superior parts; except that the inferior correspond in a certain proportion to the superior. Thus the lower belly corresponds to the face in corpulency, or gracility, and the legs to the arms. Hence those Avhose arms are short, have also for the most part, short thighs ; and those whose feet are small have like- Avise small hands. Of the superior extremity, however, there is a tAvo fold part, the arm ; and the arm is divided into the humerus, the lacertus, the cubitus, or the cubit, the ulna, and the hand '. But the parts of the hand are the palm and the five fingers. And of the finger indeed, that part which can be inflected is the joint, but that which cannot be in flected is the part between the joints. The great finger also, or the thumb, has only one joint; but the other fingers have two joints. The inflection, hoAvever, both of the arm, and all the fingers, is inward ; and the arm is inflected towards the gibbous part of the cubitus. The in terior part of the hand, the palm, is fleshy, and is distinguished by lines, in those that are long-lived indeed, by one or two lines which extend through the whole of the palm ; but in those that are short-lived, by two lines, Avhich do not extend through the whole. But the joint by Avhich the hand is connected with the arm, is the wrist. And the ex ternal part of the hand is nervous, and Avithout a name. Another twofold division of the inferior extremity consists of the legs. BOOK I. 26 pect to the other part of the body ; but man alone, as Ave have just observed, being fashioned conformably to the order of the universe, has this part corresponding to the heavens. After the head is the neck, then the breast and the back, the former having an anterior, but the latter a posterior position ; and to these succeed the belly and the loins, the pudendum, and the hip ; afterwards the thigh and the tibia ; and, in the last place, the feet. With respect to the legs, hoAvever, they are inflected toAvards the anterior part, tOAvards Avhich part also they are moved ; and the more motive part of the foot and its flexure, are also anterior. But the heel has a posterior position. And each of the ankles has the same position in the tibia, as the ears have in the head. The arms hang from the right and left side of the body, and have their flexure inward ; and are so inflected, especially in man, that the incur vation of the legs and the arms have a position opposite to each other. With respect to the senses, however, and the sensoria, viz. the eyes, the nostrils, and the tongue, man has them situated in the same, i. e. in the anterior part ; but he has the hearing, and its sensorium, the ear, in a lateral position indeed, but in the same circumference Avith the eyes. Man likewise has his eyes proportionally less distant than other ani mals. But of the senses, the most accurate in him is the touch, the next to this in accuracy is the taste, but in the other senses he is ex celled by many animals. CHAPTER XVI. Thus, therefore, the parts in the external superficies of the human body are arranged, and, as we have said, they are especially denomi nated and known from custom. The brain there- fore occupies the first situation in the head, and is posited in the an- terior part of it ; and this similarly takes place in other animals that have this part. But all sanguineous animals have it, and besides these the mollia. Man, hoAvever, in proportion to the magnitude of his body, has the largest and the moistest brain. Two membranes like- Avise contain it ; one about the bone, Avhich is the stronger of the two ; but the other about, the brain itself, Avhich is less strong. The brain how- ever in all animals is twofold, and to the posteriorpart of it, that which is called the cerebellum, is joined, Avhich has a different form * from the brain, both according to the touch and the sight. But the posterior part of the head in all animals is [partially at least] empty and holloAv, according as the head is larger or smaller. For in some animals that have a larger head, the part of the face Avhich is subjected to the head is small ; as is the case Avith those animals that have a round face. Other animals, on the contrary, have a small head but long cheeks, such as all the genus of labouring cattle, or animals that have a tuft of hair on the forehead. The brain however in all animals is exangui- ous, has no veins, and is naturally cold to the touch ; and in the middle of it, in most animals, there is a small cavity ; but the membrane Avhich surrounds it is veiny, and of the nature of skin. Above the brain also, there is a bone which is the thinnest and weakest of all the bones of the head, and is called the sinciput. But their avenues, or ducts, tend from the eyes to the brain ; the largest indeed, and the mid- dle, tend to the cerebellum ; but the smallest tends to the brain itself. And the smallest of these ducts, is that which especially verges to the nose. The greatest ducts, therefore, are parallel to each other, and never coincide; but the middle ducts coalesce. Within the neck are what is called the oesophagus, which has its de- nomination from its narrowness and length, and the aspera arteria. The aspera arteria, however, is prior in position to the oesophagus in all animals that possess it ; and all animals have it that have lungs. But this artery is indeed naturally cartilaginous, has but little blood, and is surrounded by many thin veins. It is also placed in the supe- rior part towards the mouth, opposite to the ducts Avhich extend from the nostrils to the mouth. Hence it happens, that if Avhen we are drinking, the liquor enters into the aspera arteria, and is throAvn upAvard, it departs through the nostrils. The head of the aspera arteria, in the superior part in Avhich it extends to the mouth, has, Avhat is called the epiglottis, which is in the middle of the tAvo avenues that reach from the nostrils to the mouth. The aspera arteria, therefore, in the superior part is conjoined Avith the tongue, but Avith the other extremity it descends into the middle of the lungs ; aftenvards from this it is divided into each part of the lungs. For the lungs are bipar- tite in all the animals that have them. In viviparous animals, however, the separation is not similarly apparent, and it is in the smallest degree apparent in man. But the lungs of man are not multifidious, as they are in some viviparous animals, nor are they smooth, but anomalous. In oviparous animals, however, as in birds, and such quadrupeds as are oviparous, the two parts of the lungs are very much separated from, each other, so that they seem to have two lungs. Since the lungs therefore are bipartite, the aspera arteria which is one, Avhen it arrives at the lungs is divided into two canals, as it were, and insinuates itself into each part of the lungs ; it is also connected Avith the great vein, [or vena cava] and Avith another vein which is called the aorta. When in respiring, however, we inflate the aspera arteria, then the breath enters into the hollow parts of the lungs. But the cavities of the lungs have certain little pipes inserted in them Avhich are always narrower and narrower, till at length they end in a sharp point ; and from these pipes certain cavities are deduced, Avhich so extend through the Avhole substance

The heart also is conjoined Avith the aspera arteria by fat, cartilaginous, and fibrous bonds, and in that part in which it depends from the aspera arteria, it is holloAv [and sinuous]. But though in some smaller animals it is not manifest, whether Avhen in respiring they inflate the aspera arteria, the breath not only enters the lungs, but likeAvise the heart, yet in larger animals it is evident that the breath insinuates itself through the aspera arteria into the heart likewise. The aspera arteria therefore subsists after this manner, and its office consists in alone receiving and emitting the breath, but it does not receive any dry or liquid nutriment. Indeed, if food, either liquid or dry, happens to fall into the aspera arteria, the animal is in pain till it is ejected. The stomach however, [or oesophagus] depends in the superior part of it from the mouth, adheres to the artery, and is conjoined both with the spine and the artery by membranaceous ligaments. But it passes through the transverse septum, [by which the breast is divided from the belly] and ends in the ventricle. It has also a fleshy nature, and is adapted to be extended both according to length and according to breadth. The human, however, is similar to the canine ventricle; for it is not much larger than the intestine, but resembles, as it Avere, a broader intestine. Under the ventricle the intestines are situated, one of which is simple and winding, but the other is broad; and the Ioav er cavity, [or the alvus, which contains the intestines] is similar to that of a soav ; for it is broad, and the part under the alvus, Avhichis extend ed to the seat, is short and thick. From the middle of the alvus the omentum depends ; Avhich is naturally a fat membrane, in the same manner as in all other animals which have only one ventricle, and teeth on each side of the mouth. Above the intestines is the mesentery, which is membranaceous, broad and fat. But from the great vein and the aorta many veins are deduced, Avhich are diffused through the me sentery in that part by Avhich it is connected Avith the intestines, and beginning from the summit of the mesentery, they are diffused as far as to its lowest parts. It has also a fat and thick membrane, through Avhich it is conjoined both to the great vein and the aorta. But the cuspis or point of the heart in all animals that have a breast, is si milarly directed towards the breast ; and in those animals that are Avith out a breast, the cuspis of the heart verges to the anterior part. This however is frequently latent, because during the dissection of the ani mal, the heart is removed from its natural situation. But the convex and curved part of the heart is upward ; the cuspis of it is for the most part fleshy and dense; and nerves are inherent in the cavaties them selves. In other animals, hoAvever, that have a breast, the heart is situ ated in the middle of the breast, but in man it verges to the left side, a little inclining from the division of the mammæ, in the upper part of the breast. Nor is it large, and its whole form is not oblong, but has something of rotundity, yet so as to end in a point, It has also, as we have said, three cavaties, the greatest indeed in the right, but the least in the left parts, and the middle in magnitude has an intermedi ate situation. Avenues also tend to the lungs from the heart, which are divided after the same manner as the aspera arteria, and follow the canals of the artery through the Avhole of the lungs. These avenues however are in the superior part of the heart; nor do they accord in any com mon avenue, but they are severally conjoined to the lungs, and from this conjunction receive hot air, and transmit it to the heart. For one of the avenues leads to the right, but the other to the left cavity of the heart. Concerning the great vein, however, and the aorta, Ave shall separately speak in common hereafter. But in animals that have lungs and are viviparous, so that they not only produce, but also conceive an animal in themselves, there is no member Avhich contains so much blood as the lungs. For the Avhole of them indeed are spongy, and re ceive in their several canals blood from the great vein. Those however who think that the lungs are empty are deceived, in consequence of surveying the lungs taken from dissected animals, Avhich in that state are wholly destitute of blood. But of the other viscera the heart alone contains blood ; for the lungs contain blood, not in their own essence but in the veins ; but the heart contains blood in itself. For in each of its cavaties it has blood; but the most attenuated blood is in its middle cavity. Under the lungs is the transverse septum, through which the breast, or the superior part of the thorax, [in Avhich the heart and lungs are contained,] is separated from the belly [in Avhich the liver, spleen, &c. are contained]. The septum transversum is also called the diaphragm, præcordia, and cinctura : The diaphragm is connected Avith the spine of the back, and also Avith the ribs and hypochondria. But the mid- dle part of the diaphragm is thin and membranaceous ; and [many] veins are extended through it. The veins of a man however are thick, considered Avith reference to the magnitude of the human body. Un- der the transverse septum in the right-hand parts, the liver is situated, but the spleen is in the left-hand parts ; and the liver and spleen are similarly disposed in all animals that have these parts naturally, and not

Both the liver and the spleen, however, are in the loAver belly, near to the omentum [by which the intestines are covered.] The spleen hoAvever of a man is narrow and long, and resembles that of a hog. But the liver for the most part in most ani- mals is Avithout the gall, but in some animals it is connected Avith the gall. The liver of a man also is round, and resembles the liver of an ox. It happens however in some victims that there is a privation of the gall. Thus, for instance, in a certain place of Chalcis in Eubœa, the cattle have no gall ; but in Naxus nearly all the quadrupeds have so large a gall as to astonish the strangers that sacrifice there, Avho fancy that this circumstance is prognostic, and that it is not natural to these animals. The liver also is connected Avith the great vein, but has no communication Avith the aorta. For a vein Avhich proceeds from the great vein passes through the liver, in that part of it Avhere Avhat are called the gates of the liver are situated. The spleen likeAvise is con joined with the great vein alone ; for a vein extends from the great vein to the spleen. After these, the reins or kidneys are situated near the spine of the back [under the liver and spleen] which [in men] are of a nature similar to the reins of oxen. But in all animals that have reins, the right is higher than the left, but it is less fat and more dry than the left. This like wise similarly takes place in all other animals. Avenues, however, or ducts, lead to the reins from the great vein and the aorta, except that they do not reach to the cavity [which is in the middle of the reins.] For the reins have a cavity in the middle, some a large and others a less cavity, except the reins of the phoca or sea-calf; and these resem bling the reins of an ox, are the most solid of all. The avenues, how ever, Avhich extend to them, are consumed into the body of the reins. But that these avenues do not terminate in the cavity of the reins, is indicated by their having no blood, either fluid or congealed. They have therefore, as we have said, a small cavity ; but tAvo solid avenues lead to the bladder from the cavity of the reins, and other strong and continued avenues tend also from the aorta. WITH respect, hoAvever, to the parts of other animals, some are com mon to all animals, as Ave have before observed, but others are peculiar to certain genera. But they are the same with or different from each other, in the way we have frequently mentioned. For nearly all ani mals Avhich are of a different genus, have most of their parts specifically different. And some indeed have their parts only analogously the same, but generically different ; but others have them generically the same, and specifically different ; and there are many parts Avhich some animals have, but others have not. Viviparous quadrupeds therefore [accord with man, and Avith each other, in this, that they] have a head and neck, and all the parts in the head. But the several parts differ from each other in their form. And the neck of the lion indeed, consists of one bone, but has no verte brae. All the interior parts however of a lion are similar to the inte rior parts of a dog. Viviparous quadrupeds also have the fore legs in- f 2 stead

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 36 stead of arms ; but those fore legs Avhich have multifidous feet, are especially analogous to hands ; for they use them for many purposes instead of hands. The left legs, hoAvever, of quadrupeds, except those of the elephant, are less agile and expedite than the left hands of men. But the elephant has the division of the five toes in the foot, indistinct, and has the fore much larger than the hind legs. In his hind legs also, he has small mallets. He has hoAvever a nose of such a kind and so large, that it serves him instead of hands. For he both eats and drinks extending his nose [or proboscis] to his mouth. He also ex tends this to his keeper Avhen riding on his back, tears up trees Avith it, and respires by its assistance when he Avalks through the Avater. The extremity likeAvise of the proboscis may be bent, but cannot be fold ed; for it is cartilaginous, [though the other parts of it may also be folded.] Man hoAvever is the only animal that is ambidexter, or has the use of both his hands. With respect to the breast, hoAvever, all animals have this part ana logous, but not similar to the breast of man ; for the human breast is broad, but that of other animals narroAV. But no other animal besides man has mammæ in the anterior part; for the elephant has two mam mæ indeed, yet they are not in the breast, but near [i. e. a little below] the breast. The legs hoAvever of other animals, as well the fore as the hind legs, have flexions contrary to each other, and to the flexions of the legs and arms of man, the elephant being excepted. For viviparous quadrupeds have their fore legs bent towards the fore part, but their hind legs bent towards the hind part, and they have the cavity of one flexion opposite to the cavity of the other. What is asserted of the elephant, hoAvever, by some, is not true [i. e. that he cannot bend his legs, nor sit] for he can do both, except that he cannot on account of his weight at one and the same time bend each fore leg, and recline on each side, but he can alone bend one leg, either the right or the left, and alone recline on one side, and in this manner he sleeps, [leaning against some, wall :>r tree.] But he bends his hind legs in the same manner as men. For, being bipeds, they bend their legs towards the posterior part ; but instead of arms and fore legs, they have Avings, the flexion of which is toAvards the anterior part. ■ The sea-calf however is, as it were, a mutilated quadruped ; for im mediately after the shoulder-blade it has [two fore] feet similar to hands, such as are the [fore] feet of bears. Such parts, hoAvever, as in man are anterior, are inferior in quadru peds, and turned toAvards the earth ; and the parts which in man are posterior, are superior in quadrupeds, and directed towards the ' hea vens. All such animals likewise as are quadrupeds and viviparous are, as I may say, hairy, and in this respect they do not resemble man, who, ex cept in his head, has but feAv and short hairs, but in his head is the most hairy of all animals. In other animals hoAvever that have hairs, the prone parts are more hairy, but the supine parts are either entirely smooth, or less hairy. But the contrary takes place in man. The tails also of quadrupeds, Avhen they have any magnitude, follow the condition of the body, Avith respect to abounding with or being deprived of hairs ; for some have so little hair that it can scarcely be perceived. Camels, however, differ from other quadrupeds in this, that they have what is called a tuber or swelling on the back. But the Bactrian differ from the Arabian camels. For the Bactrian camel has two swel lings on the back, but the Arabian has only one. Each camel also has another swelling in the inferior similar to that in the superior part, by which the rest of the body is supported when they bend their knees. It also has but one knee in each leg, and not many flexions as some say ; but through the form of the belly [which is very small and drawn up] it ap pears to have many knees or flexions. And it has indeed an ankle bone similar to that of an ox, but a small thigh in proportion to the magnitude of its body. It is also bisulcous, and has no teeth in the up per jaw. But it is bisulcous in such a Avay, that in the inferior part of the foot it is bipartite, as far as to the second flexion of the toes, but in the superior part it is quadripartite, as far as to the first joints of the toes. The intervals of the fissures also are covered with a certain membrane, similar, as it Avere, to that Avith Avhich the intervals of the fissures in geese are covered. The sole too of the foot is fleshy, like that of a bear; and on this account when they lead camels to battle, to

All quadrupeds, hoAvever, have bony, nervous and fleshless legs ; and, in short, this is the case Avith all other animals that have feet, except man. They are also Avithout hips, and especially birds. On the con trary, man has hips that are very fleshy Avith respect to the other parts of his body, and his thighs and tibiæ are very fleshy ; for that part of the tibia Avhich is called sura, is very fleshy. But of sanguineous and viviparous quadrupeds, some are multifidous, as the hands and feet of man ; for some have feet with many fissures, as the lion, the dog, and the panther ; but others have bifidated feet, and instead of nails have hoofs, as sheep, goats, stags, and the hippo potamus. Others have their feet without fissures, such as those that have solid hoofs, as the horse and the mule. The genus of swine, hoAV ever, is ambiguous ; for in Illyria, Pœonia, and other places, the swine have solid hoofs. Bisulcous animals, therefore, have tAvo fissures behind and before ; but animals that have solid hoofs -have feet Avith out fissures. Some animals likewise have horns, but others are Avithout horns. Most of those therefore that have horns are naturally bisulcous, as the ox, the stag, and the goat ; but Ave have seen no animal that has solid hoofs, and is bicornous. There are hoAvever a few animals that have one horn and solid hoofs, as the Indian ass. But the oryx • has one horn, and is bisulcous. The interior and concave part of the horn there fore seems to be naturally formed from skin ; but the exterior and solid part is formed from bone, and appropriately surrounds the interior part ; and such are the horns of oxen. But the stag is the only animal that casts off its horns annually, beginning to do so at the age of tAvo years ; and other horns groAv in their stead. Farther still, quadrupeds differ from each other, and also from man, both in the mammæ, and in the organs subservient to generation. For some animals have the niammæ in the anterior part of the body, i. e. in the breast, or a little under the breast; and they have also two mam mæ and two papillæ or nipples, as man, and the elephant, as Ave have before observed. In addition to this also, man when he has acquired his proper mag nitude, has his superior less than his inferior parts ; but in other san guineous animals, the contrary takes place. We call hoAvever the supe rior part that which extends from the head as far as to the part in which there is an egress of the excrements-, and Ave denominate the inferior part, that which remains of the body from the places through Avhich the excrements are emitted. In those animals, therefore, that have feet, the hind legs determine the magnitude of the inferior part ; but in those that have no feet, the magnitude of the inferior part is deter mined by the tail, and whatever is instead of a tail. Such, therefore, are animals when they have arrived at perfection. For man in his in fancy has the superior larger than the inferior parts ; but the contrary takes place as he increases through age. Hence man alone has not the same progressive motion when he is an infant, and Avhen he has ar rived at perfection ; but at first he creeps on the ground with his hands and feet, like a quadruped. Some animals also have an analogous in crease of the superior and inferior parts, as the dog. But in others, the superior parts are at first less, and the inferior larger, but as they advance to perfection, the superior parts become larger, as animals which have a tuft of hair on their forehead. For these receive no in crease in the inferior part Avhich extends from the hoof to the hip. There is however much difference in the teeth of other animals, both with respect to each other, and those of man. For all such qua drupeds as are sanguineous and viviparous have teeth ; but in the first place, some have teeth on both sides, and others have not.' And some animals indeed have teeth projecting beyond the mouth, as male swine, but in others they do not project. Again, some animals have serrated teeth, as the lion, the panther, and the dog ; but others have them in a continued series, as the horse and the ox. For those animals have serrated teeth, Avhich have at the same time the order of the sharp teeth changed, [so that the space intercepted betAveen the tAvo inferior teeth is occupied by the superior tooth, and the space intercepted between the two superior teeth is occupied by the inferior tooth.] No animal, however, has at one and the same time projecting teeth and a horn ; nor is there any animal Avhich has serrated teeth, and is horned, or has projecting teeth. But most animals have the fore teeth sharp, and the inward teeth broad. The sea-calf, hoAvever, has all its teeth serrated, as being an animal allied to fishes; for nearly all fishes have serrated teeth. None also of these genera of animals have double rows of teeth ; though if we may believe Ctesias, there is a certain animal which has. For he says, that in India there is a savage animal, the name of which is Martichora, that has a triple row of teeth in each jaAv. He adds, that this animal is equal in magnitude to a lion, that it is similarly hairy with, and has feet resembling those of a lion, but that its face and ears are like those of a man, and that its eyes are azure, and its colour resembling that of cinnabar. It has also a tail armed with a sting, and resembling the tail of the land scorpion- It is likewise furnished with certain native darts, which it hurls forth ; and it utters a sound resembling that of a pipe and a trumpet. But it runs with no less swiftness than the stag, and is savage and feeds on human flesh. Man, therefore, sheds his teeth, and also other animals, such as the horse, the mule, and the ass. It is reasonable also to suppose that the like takes place in other savage animals, since they are said to shed only their canine teeth. The age of dogs, hoAvever, is known from their teeth; for those that are young have white and sharp teeth; but those that are elderly have black and obtuse teeth. CHAPTER III. The contrary, however, takes place Avith respect to teeth in other animals and in horses ; for other animals as they advance in age have blacker teeth, but the horse as he grows old has whiter teeth. But the teeth Avhich are called canine separate the sharp from the broad teeth, participating of the form of both ; for beneath indeed they are broad, but above they are sharp. In the human species, however, the last maxillary teeth, which they call genuini, [or the innermost cheek teeth] grow about the twentieth year, both in men and Avomen. CHAPTERS VIII. and IX. Some animals hoAvever have an ambiguous nature, because they partly imitate man and partly quadrupeds, such as apes, the coebi [a kind of apes] and the cynocephali. But the cœbus has the tail of an ape ; and the

Their manners also are more savage, and they have teeth more canine and strong. Apes, hoAvever, as being quadrupeds, are hairy in the prone part of their body ; and in a similar manner, in their supine parts, as having in these the human form. For hairiness, as we have before observed, subsists contrarily in men and quadrupeds ; except that apes have very thick and dense hairs, both in the prone and in the supine part. But the face of the ape has many similitudes to that of man ; for it has si milar nostrils and ears; and both its fore and maxillary teeth resemble those of man. And farther still, since other animals have not hairs on both eye-lids, the ape has, though they are very thin, especially on the inferior eye-lid, and very small ; for other quadrupeds are deprived of these. The ape also has tAvo papillæ of small mammæ in the breast. It has likeAvise arms in the same manner as man, except that they are hairy : and they bend these and their legs in the same way as man, viz. so that the curvatures of the arms are contrary to the curvatures of the legs. Besides this also, apes have hands, fingers and nails, similar to those of the human species, except that all these are of a more brutal form. They have however feet peculiar to themselves ; for they are as it were large hands; and Avith respect to their toes, in the same manner as in the fingers of the hand, the middle is longer than the rest; and the sole of the foot resembles the palm of the hand, except that it extends itself as far as to the extremity, or heel. But the last part of their foot is callous, and rudely and obscurely imitates the heel of the human foot. They likeAvise use their feet, both as hands and feet, and bend their [fore] feet in the same manner as hands. The cubit how ever and thigh of apes are short in proportion to the other part of the arm and the tibia. They likewise have not a prominent navel, but a certain hard substance in the place of the navel. The superior part of the body also of these animals is much larger than the inferior part, in the same manner as in quadrupeds ; for in quadrupeds the length of the superior is to the length of the inferior part, nearly as five to three. They

All quadrupeds however Avhich are oviparous and sanguineous, (and no terrestrial and sanguineous animal is oviparous, Avhich is not a qua druped or without feet) have a head, neck, back, and the prone and su pine parts of the body. The chamæleon has the whole figure of its body resembling a lizard, but its sides tend downward, and are conjoined under the belly, in the same manner as in fishes, and the back bone rises above the other parts in a manner similar to that of fishes.
