The first part of the foot therefore corresponds to a thumb, but the second part, to the rest of the hand, and is therefore divided into many other fingers. The second part hoAvever of the forefeet, is not divided in the same Avay as the second part of the hind feet, but the second part of the fore feet is divided imvardly, i. e. toAvards the sole, into three parts, and as it were fingers, but outwardly it is divided into two parts only. But the second part of the hind feet, is divided towards the sole into two fin- gers as it Avere, and outAvardly, i. e. in the superior part, it is divided into three parts resembling fingers. These parts also are covered Avith crooked nails. The Avhole body however of the chamæleon is rough, in the same manner as that of the crocodile. But its eyes are situated in a cavity, are very large and round, and are covered with a skin si- milar to that of the rest of the body ; and in the middle of the skin that covers the eye there is a small avenue, through which it sees, which avenue is never covered with any skin. The motion also of its eye is circular, and it transfers its sight to all places, and thus sees Avhat it Avishes to see. But the mutation of its colour takes place when it is inflated. It has also a black colour, not very remote from that of the crocodile, and a pale colour like lizards, variegated with black spots like the panther. A mutation likeAvise of this kind takes place through the Avhole of its body ; for its eyes and its tail are changed in a manner similar to the rest of the body. But its motion is very slow like that of the tortise. When it is dying also it is of a pale colour, and it has a colour of this kind Avhen it is dead. But the parts about the stomach, and the aspera arteria, are situated similarly to those in the lizard. It has, however, no flesh, except in the head, the jaws, and the extremity of the tail, and these parts have a little flesh. It like wise has blood only about the heart, the eyes, the parts Avhich are above the heart, and such veins as extend from these parts. But in these there is very little blood. Its brain also is placed a little above the eyes, but in continuation with them. And if the skin which covers the eyes is taken away, the eyes will be found to contain a shining h 2 substance
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 52 substance resembling a thin brazen ring. Many strong membranes likewise are extended nearly through the whole of its body, and which are much superior in strength to those which cover the rest of its body. And when it is Avholly dissected, it breathes for a long time, a small motion strenuously yet remaining in it about the heart. It is likewise capable of contracting all the parts of the body, and especially the parts about the sides. It has not however any Avhere the spleen ap parent ; and it conceals itself in caves in the same manner as lizards. CHAPTER XII. In like manner birds also have certain parts in common Avith the above-mentioned animals. For all of them have a head, neck, back, the supine parts of the body, and that which is analogous to the breast. They differ likewise from other animals in this, that they are bipeds in the same manner as man, except that their legs are bent like those of quadrupeds, in a way contrary to those of man, as we have before ob served. They have, hoAvever, neither hands nor fore-feet, but [instead of them] they have Avings, Avhich are peculiar to birds. Farther still, they have a hip similar to a thigh, Avhich hip is long, and extends as far as to the middle of the belly, to which it is affixed, so as to appear when divulsed to be a thigh. But the thigh in the other part is joined to the tibia. Birds, however, that have crooked nails have the largest thighs, and their breast is more robust than that of other birds. But all birds have feet armed with many nails, and all of them are after a manner multifidous ; for the feet of the greater part of birds have toes. Those birds also which seek their food by sAvimming, though they have broad feet, and which are covered with a skin, yet they have perfect and distinct toes. All such birds, however, as fly high have four
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 53 BOOK II. four toes ; for they have three for the most part in the anterior part of the foot, and one in the posterior part, in the place of the heel. But some few have tAvo toes indeed in the anterior part, and tAvo in the posterior part, as is the case with the bird called jynx. This bird, how ever, is a little larger than the chaffinch, and its plumage is various. But it has something peculiar in the disposition of its toes, and its tongue is similar to that of serpents ; for it can extend this to the length of four fingers out of the mouth, and again draAv it Avithin its, beak. Farther still, it can also turn its neck round to the hind part of it, the rest of the body being quiescent, in the same manner as ser pents. It has also large nails, and Avhich are naturally similar to those of a jack-daAV ; and it emits a shrill voice. Birds, however, have indeed a mouth, but one peculiar to them selves ; for they have neither lips nor teeth, but a beak ; nor have they cars or nostrils, but they have the avenues of these senses ; of the nos trils indeed, they have the avenue in the beak, but of the hearing in the head. All of them, however, have tAvo eyes, in the same manner as other animals, but Avithout eye- lids. Heavy birds also [i. e. those which do not fly high] wink, that is, shut and open the eyes Avith the inferior eye-lid ; and they likewise cover the eyes Avith a certain mem brane emitted from the corner of the eye. Nocturnal birds, however, wink with the superior eye-lid. Animals also that are covered Avith scales do the very same thing, such as lizards, and others that are of a kindred nature to these animals. For all of them wink with the in ferior eye-lid, though all of them do not cover the eyes with a mem brane emitted from the corner of the eye. Again, birds have neither scales, nor hairs, but feathers. But all feathers have a quill. And they have not indeed a tail like that of quadrupeds, but their tail consists of feathers. Those birds also which have long legs and broad feet, have a short tail, but those which have short legs and not a broad foot have a longer tail. Those birds too, which have a longer tail, when they fly have their legs contracted to their belly ; but those that have a short tail, when they fly have their iegs extended to their tail. All birds likewise have a tongue, but this is
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II 54 is dissimilar; for some have a long, others a short, others a broad, and others a narrow tongue. Some genera of birds also, beyond all ani mals after man, utter the sound of our letters; and this is especially the case with those birds whose tongue is broad. No oviparous ani mal, hoAvever, has the epiglottis on the aspera arteria, but they are able to contract and dilate the avenue of the aspera arteria, so as to prevent any weight from falling on the lungs. Some genera of birds also have a spur ; but there is no bird Avhich has at the same time crooked nails and a spur. Some birds, however, that are armed with crooked nails fly high ; but those birds that have spurs are heavy [and fly near the earth]. Again, some birds have a comb, or crest, consist ing of raised feathers j but the cock alone has a peculiar crest, which is neither flesh, nor very remote from the nature of flesh. CHAPTER XIII. Among aquatic animals, however, the genus of fishes alone is di- vided into many species. For they have a head, and the prone ' and supine parts ; and in the supine part of the body their belly and in- testines are contained. In the last part of the body also they have a tail, which is in continuity Avith, and is not divided from, the rest of the body ; and this tail is not similar in all fishes. But no fish has a neck, or hands, or feet, or in short testicles, either internally, or externally ; nor have they any mammæ. To be deprived of mammæ, however, is not peculiar to fishes, but is common to them Avith many other ani mals, since all animals that are not viviparous are Avithout mammæ, 1 The prone parts in fishes have a direction towards the heavens, and the supine parts to wards the earth. and
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 55 and of viviparous animals, those only have them which do not first conceive an egg in themselves, but an animal. For the dolphin is vi viparous ; and hence it has two mammæ, yet not in the superior, but in the inferior part, and near the organs of generation. It has not, however, like quadrupeds, apparent papillae, but in the place of these it has as it were two orifices, one on the right, and the other on the left side, from which the milk flows. From these it is sucked by its young that follow it ; and this by certain persons has been evidently seen. Fishes, therefore, as we have said, have neither mammæ, nor any exterior and apparent genital member. They have, however, certain peculiar members, viz. gills and fins, by Avhich they return the water which they receive through the mouth. Most fishes likewise are furnished with four fins, yet there are some that have only tAvo ; for certain long fishes, such as eels, ha\*e only tAvo, near the gills. In a si milar manner also, the mullets have only tAvo fins, Avhich are produced in the lake in Siphæ [in Tuscany] ; and this is likewise the case with the fish called tœnia. But some of the long fishes, such as lampreys, have neither fins nor gills entire and perfect like other fishes. Of those, however, that have gills, some have them concealed and others ap parent; but all the cartilaginous kind have them apparent. And all those, indeed, that have their gills concealed, have them obliquely situated. But of cartilaginous fishes, those that are broad, as the torpedo and the ray, have their gills in the inferior and supine part ; but those that are long have them in their side, as is the case Avith all the genera of lampreys. The frog fish, however, has them obliquely and concealed, yet not with a thorny covering, like those fishes that are not cartilaginous, but with a skinny covering. Farther still, of some fishes the gills are single, but of others two-fold ; but that part of the tAvo-fold gills Avhich is turned towards the body of the fish is not tAvo-told but single. And some fishes indeed have feAv gills, but others many. In either case, hoAvever, they have as many on one side as on the other. But those that have the fewest gills, have one on each side ; and this is tAvo-fold, as in the fish called the boar. Others again, have
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 56 have tAvo on each side, the one simple, but the other double, as the conger and the scarus; but others have four simple gills on each side, as the ellops or sturgeon, the synagris or denticus, the lamprey, and the eel. Others have four gills indeed, but they are in a tAvo-fold order, except the last, as the sea-thrush, the perch, the glanis, and the carp. All those, however, that are of the nature of lampreys have two-fold gills, and five on each side ; but the sword-fish has eight tAvo fold gills. And thus much concerning the multitude of gills in fishes. Farther still, fishes differ from other animals, not only in their gills, but also in the covering of their body. For they neither have hairs in the same manner as terrestrial viviparous animals ; nor have they scales l like some oviparous quadrupeds ; nor are they covered with feathers, as the genus of birds ; but most of them, indeed, have thin scales, a feAv of them are rough, and a very few of them are smooth. Of the cartilaginous kind, therefore, some are rough, but others are smooth ; but the conger, the eel, and the tunny, are among the num ber of the smooth. All fishes, likewise, have serrated teeth, except the scarus. All of them too have their teeth sharp, and some of them have many rows of teeth, and inserted in the tongue. They have also a hard and thorny tongue, and so adherent and fixed, that sometimes they seem not to have a tongue. With respect to the mouth, in some fishes it is very open, in the same manner as in some viviparous quadrupeds. But with respect to the sensoria or organs of sensation, they neither have the sensoria of hearing or smelling, nor the avenues of these apparent ; but all of them have eyes without eye-lids, though their eyes are not hard. The Avhole genus of fishes, therefore, is sanguineous ; but some of them are oviparous, and some of them are viviparous. All those indeed that are covered with thin scales are oviparous ; but all the cartilaginous kind are viviparous, except the frog-fish. * i. e. Scales resembling those of a serpent. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 57 CHAPTER XIV. Of sanguineous animals, however, there remains the genus of ser pents. But they partake of the nature both of terrestrial and aquatic animals. For most of them are terrestrial, and but a few of them are aquatic, and which live in potable Avater. There are also marine ser pents similar in form to the terrestrial genus, except that their head more resembles that of the conger. There are, however, many genera of marine serpents, and they have an all-various colour; but they are not generated in very deep places. Serpents, also, are Avithout feet, in the same manner as the genus of fishes. There are, likewise, marine scolopendra, resembling the terrestrial in their form ; but their magnitude is someAvhat less. These marine sco lopendra are generated in rocky places [of the sea] ; but their colour is more red, they have a greater number of feet, and their legs are thin ner, than those of terrestrial scolopendra. These, likewise, are not ge nerated, as neither are serpents, in very deep places of the sea. There is, also, a certain little fish found on rocks, which some call echeneida, or the sea lamprey, and some use it as a philter, and for the purpose of obtaining victory in judicial processes ; but it is useless for food. Some also say that it has feet, but it has not. It appears, how ever, to have them, because it has fins resembling feet. And thus avc have shoAvn Avhat and how many the external parts of animals are, and what their differences are Avith respect to each other. i CUAf
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 58 CHAPTER XV. In the first place, therefore, avc must [next] shoAv how the internal parts subsist in sanguineous animals. For the greatest genera of ani mals differ from the rest in this, that the one are sanguineous, but the other exanguious. Sanguineous animals, hoAvever, are man and vivi parous quadrupeds ; and besides these, oviparous quadrupeds, birds, fish, cetaceous animals, and others Avhich are not contained in these greatest genera, but are signified by the name of species, as serpent and crocodile. All such animals, therefore, as are quadrupeds and viviparous, have a stomach and aspera arteria, and these are situated in the same man ner as in men. This is also the case Avith such quadrupeds as are ovi parous, and Avith birds ; but they differ in the form of these parts. In short, all such animals as by receiving the air respire and expire have lungs, the aspera arteria, a stomach ; and the position of the stomach and aspera arteria is similar, though these parts differ in species from those of other animals. On the contrary, the lungs are not only spe cifically different in different animals, but have also a different posi tion. Farther still, all sanguineous animals have a heart, and a transverse septum or diaphragm ; but in small animals, the blood is not similarly apparent, on account of its tenuity and paucity, except in the heart. It is also peculiar to a certain genus of oxen, but not to all oxen, to have a bone in the heart ; and the heart of horses, likewise, has a bone. All sanguineous animals, however, have not lungs. Thus, for instance, fishes, and all animals that have gills, are without lungs. ,A11 such animals
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANTMALS. 59 animals, too, as have blood have a liver; yet not all, but the greater part of them, have a spleen. Many animals, likewise, that are not vivi parous, but oviparous, have a spleen so small that it can scarcely be perceived, as is evident in most birds ; as in the dove, the kite, the haAvk, and- the owl. But the bird called Ægocephalus, [i. e. having the head of a goat] is entirely Avithout a spleen, she like also takes place in oviparous quadrupeds ; for these have a very small spleen, as is evi dent in the tortoise, the rubeta or land toad, the lizard, the crocodile, and the frog. Again, of those animals that have a liver, some have the gall annexed to the liver, but others have not. Of viviparous quadrupeds, indeed, neither the stag, nor the fallow-deer, nor the mule, nor the ass, nor the sea-calf, has the gall ; and this is also the case with some rats. With respect to stags, however, those which are called achaini, seem to have the gall in their tail ; but they have, indeed, a colour in their tail resembling gall, yet it is not fluid like gall, and in the interior part is similar to the spleen. All these stags, too, have in their head living, Avorms ; and these are generated under the concavity of the tongue, about the vertebra, by Avhich the head is connected with the neck. They are also not less in magnitude than the largest Avorms. But they are generated at once, and in continuity, and they are about twenty in number. Stags, therefore, as avc have said, are Avithout a gall, but their intestine is so bitter, that the dogs are not willing to eat it, un less the stag himself is very fat. The liver of the elephant also is with out a gall, yet if it is cut in that part to Avhich the gall usually adheres, a liquor Aoavs from it which is more or less bilious. But of animals which receive the sea water, and have lungs, the dolphin alone has no gall. All birds, and other fishes, however, have a gall, and all oviparous quadrupeds, in short, have it more or less ; but some fishes have the gall in the liver, as the sea-dog, the glanis, the skate, the smooth ray, and the torpedo ; and among long fishes, the eel, the acus or needle fish, and the zagœna or libella. The fish also which is called callionymus has the gall in the liver, and larger than in other fishes, in proportion to the magnitude of its body. Other fishes I 2 have
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II, 60 have the gall, not in the liver, but in a certain intestine depending from the liver, which intestine has very slender avenues. The fish, therefore, called hamia has the gall in a certain intestine, Avhich is extended in an equal length, and which is frequently redoubled ; but others have the gall at the intestines, some more remote from, and others nearer [to the liver], as the frog-fish, the ellops or sturgeon, the synagris, or dentex, the lamprey, and the sword-fish. It frequently happens, how ever, that the same genus of fishes is seen to have the gall in both situations, as the conger ; and some indeed have it at the liver, but others at the intestines. The like also takes place in birds. For some of these have the gall joined to the belly, but others to the intestines; as the dove, the croAv, the quail, the swalloAv, and the sparrow. Some birds, likewise, have the gall at the same time, both at the liver and at the belly, as the ægocephalus; but others have it, at the same time, at the liver .and the intestines, as the haAvk and the kite. CHAPTER XVI. All viviparous quadrupeds, likewise, have the kidneys and the blad^ der; but among oviparous animals, both birds and fishes are Avithout kid neys and a bladder. And of oviparous quadrupeds, the marine tortoise alone has kidneys proportional in magnitude to the rest of the body, but they are similar in proportion to the kidneys of oxen. The kid neys, however, of the ox are composed as it Avere from certain small kid neys. The bonasus also has all the interior parts similar to those of an ox. Such animals, likewise, as have these parts, have them in a similar situation. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 61 CHAPTER XVII. The heart, too, is in the middle of the breast in all animals except man ; for he has it rather in the left side, as Ave have before observed. But the point of the heart in all animals is towards the anterior part, except in fishes, in which it is not turned towards the breast, but to the head and mouth. The extremity of the heart also, in fishes, is sus pended from that Avhich conjoins the right and left gills Avith each other. But there are other tubes, or avenues, Avhich tend from the heart of fishes to the several gills, which are greater or less, according to the greater or less magnitude of their bodies. In large fishes, however, the tube Avhich has its egress from the point of the heart is very thick and Avhite. Very few fishes also have a stomach ; such as the conger and the eel, and in these it is very small. Those animals, likewise, that have a liver, Avhich is not divided but continued, have the Avhole of it in the right side ; but those that have it divided from the beginning, have not the Avhole liver, but the greater part of it in the right side. For some animals have the two parts of the liver not conjoined, but divided from the beginning; and of this kind, among fishes, is the sea-dog, and a certain genus of hares, Avhich are found elsewhere, and about the lake Bolba, in what is called Sycina. These hares have the liver so divided, that some one might think they had two livers, because the avenues, [and fibres] of the tAvo parts of the liver are conjoined at a distance from each other, in the same manner as in the lungs of birds. The spleen, also, is naturally in all animals in the left side. A certain quadruped, however, on dissection, has been found to have the spleen Mi
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: 62 THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. in the right side, and the liver in the left ; but things of this kind must be considered as prodigies. The aspera arteria also in all animals extends to the lungs, but in what manner we shall afterwards explain. But the stomach, in such animals as have it, extends to the belly, through the diaphragm ; for fishes, for the most part, as we have already observed, have no sto mach, but the belly in these animals is immediately connected Avith the mouth. Hence it frequently happens, that Avhile some of the larger fishes pursue the less the belly falls into the mouth. All the above-mentioned animals, hoAvever, have a belly, and simi larly situated. For it is directly situated under the transverse septum, and the intestine adheres to the belly, and ends at the egress of the food ; which part is called the anus. They have, however, bellies of a various form. For, in the first place, such viviparous and horned qua drupeds as have not teeth in both jaAvs, have four such avenues, or ducts ; and these quadrupeds are said to ruminate. For the stomach, beginning from the mouth, extends dowmvard to the lungs, from the diaphragm, and ends in the [first, Avhich is called] the great belly, the internal parts of which are rough and wrinkled. To this first belly, in that part in Avhich it is joined to the stomach, a second cavity and belly are united, Avhich form a similitude to the fillets of Avomen they call reticula ; for this fillet is externally similar to the first belly, but internally resembles folded fillets. This reticulum also is much less than the first belly. After the second sinus, or belly, folloAvs the third, which is called omasum ; which in the interior part is rough, and dis tinguished by certain cells after the manner of a sponge, and is similar in magnitude to the second belly, or reticulum. After this follows the fourth belly, which is called abomasum ; which is of a more ample mag nitude than the omasum, but its figure is more oblong; and inwardly it contains many large and smooth cells. This also is followed by the intestine. Horned quadrupeds, therefore, and Avhich have not teeth in both jaws, have such a belly as Ave have explained. They differ, however, from each other in the figure and magnitude of the belly, and also
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 63 also because the stomach in some extends to the middle belly, but in others to the side of the belly. On the contrary, animals Avhich have teeth in both jaws, as man, the dog, the lion, the Avolf, the SAvine, and the bear, have but one belly [to which the intestine is joined]. But the thos [an animal generated from a hind and a wolf], has all the internal parts similar to those of a wolf. All animals, therefore, that have teeth on both sides, have one belly, and after this the intestine ; but some have a larger belly, as the swine and the bear, the belly of the former of Avhich has a few smooth cells ; and others have a much less belly, and which is not much larger than the intestine, as the dog, the lion, and man. But other animals differ in the form of the belly ; for some have it similar to that of the swine, and others to that of the dog. These bellies, also, differ according to magnitude and figure, thickness and thinness, and also in the position in which the stomach is connected Avith the belly. The nature of the intestines also differs in each of the above-men tioned animals, (viz. in those Avhich have not teeth on both sides, and in those that have), in magnitude, thickness, and reduplications. In all animals, hoAvever, that have teeth only on one side, the intestines are larger ; for these animals also are larger ; since but feAv animals that have teeth only on one side are small ; for they are horned, and no horned animal is entirely small. Some animals, also, that have teeth only on one side, have certain appendices of intestines. But the intestine of an elephant is so sinuous, that it seems to contain four bellies. In this, also, the food is received ; for separate from this it has no other recep tacle. The elephant likeAvise has viscera, similar to the viscera of swine, except that its liver resembles that of an ox, but it is quadruply larger ; just as the other parts of the elephant are much larger than the parts of the ox. The spleen, hoAvever, of the elephant is much less than its proportion Avith the rest of the body seems to require. Oviparous quadrupeds, also, viz. both the land and sea tortoise, the lizard, the river crocodile, and the crocodile Avhich is not fluviatic, and in short all such animals, have the belly and intestines after the same manner as quadrupeds Avhich have teeth on both sides. For they have
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IL 64 have one simple belly, and in some it resembles the belly of swine,. but in others that of dogs. The genus of serpents, hoAvever, resembles, and has nearly every part similar to, lizards, Avhich are terrestrial and oviparous animals, if Ave give length to the lizard, and deprive it of feet. For serpents are covered with scales, and have both the prone and supine parts similar to those of the lizard ; except that they have no testicles : instead of Avhich they have tAvo avenues in the same .manner as fishes, Avhich con cur in one place, and a small and bifidated vulva. But their other in ternal parts are the same as those of lizards, except that all their vis cera, on account of the length and narrowness of their bodies, are long and narrow, and can scarcely be distinguished from those of the lizard. For they have the aspera arteria very long, but the stomach in them is . even longer than the artery. But the beginning of the artery is so near to the mouth, that the tongue seems to be under it. The artery, how ever, appears to be above the tongue, because the tongue is contracted and subsides, and does not remain in the same manner as in other ani mals. But the tongue of serpents is thin, long, and black, and Avhen it is draAvn out may be extended farther. This, however, is peculiar to serpents and lizards, that the extremity of their tongue is bifidated • and this is especially the case Avith the tongue of serpents ; for the ex tremities of their tongues are as thin as hairs. The tongue of the sea calf also is bifidated. The serpent also has a belly, which is as it Avere a more broad intes tine, resembling the belly of the dog ; and after the belly, they have a long and thin intestine, which is uniform to the end. But a small and long heart, and having the form of the kidneys, adheres to the pha rynx ; on which account it may sometimes seem that the point of the heart is not towards the breast. In the next place the lungs follow, which are simple, fibrous, replete with pipes or little tubes, very long, and very distant from the heart. The liver also of serpents is long and simple ; but their spleen is small and round, in the same manner as the spleen of the lizard. Their gall, however, resembles that of fishes ; for aquatic serpents, indeed, have the gall at the liver; but other ser- pents
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 65 pents have it for the most part at the intestines. All serpents, however, have serrated teeth. But they have as many sides as the month has days ; for they have thirty. They also say that a circumstance hap pens to serpents, which happens to the young of SAvallows ; for they report that if their eyes are dug out, they will be re-produced. The tails also of serpents and lizards Avhen cut off are re-produced. After this manner, therefore, these parts of the great vein are divided. The vein, however, which extends from the heart through the spine of the back, and the vertebrae of the neck, not only sends various ramifi cations of itself to the ribs and vertebrae, but, in its superior part, the whole of it is again divided into two places. For some of these ramifi cations tend to the sides and shoulders, and afterwards are diffused through the arm-pits ; in men into the arms, in quadrupeds into the anterior legs, in birds into the wings, and in fishes into the superior fins. These veins, however, when they first begin in the throat to be divided into many branches, towards the throat and shoulders, are called jugular veins; but after the great vein, being divided in the throat, has ascended through the neck to the head, two of its branches proceed near that artery of the lungs which is called the aspera arteria. And if any one externally compresses these two veins, which proceed from the neck to the head, those in whom they are compressed will fall down, without suffocation, indeed, yet they will become senseless3, and will close their eye-lids. These veins, therefore, extend through the neck to the head, so that the artery comes between them, and they proceed as far as to the ears, i. e, to that part in which the jaws are conjoined to the head. BOOK III. 80 divided into four veins [or branches], one of which, passing through the neck and shoulders, is conjoined in the curvature of the arm with the other branch of the greater vein, which, as was before observed, proceeds through the arm-pits to the arms. But the second vein, or branch, descends from the interval of the ears as far as to the hand and fingers, and in them is terminated. And the third branch tends from each seat of the ears to the brain, and to the membranes which cover the brain, and which are called by the Greeks the meninges, and is then divided into many thin branches. [Though the membranes of the brain, however, are full of many little veins], yet the brain itself is en tirely exanguious, and neither a small nor a large vein terminates in it. But of the remaining ramifications which proceed from this vein, some circularly surround the head, but others end in the sensoria and the teeth, in small and very thin veins. CHAPTER IV. After the same manner, also, the parts of the less vein, which i* called the aorta, are diffused, since the branches of the aorta are the attendants of the branches of the greater vein ; except that the avenues of the aorta are less than the avenues of the greater vein. The veins, therefore, from the heart, are propagated after this manner to the superior parts of the body. But the part of the great vein which is under the heart, extends directly through the transverse septum or diaphragm, by which the thorax is separated from the belly, and adheres both to the aorta and spine by membranous and pliant avenues. This vein, also, having passed through the transverse septum, is divided into two branches, one of which tends to the liver, which is in

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 81 in the right, but the other to the spleen, which is in the left part. The branch, likewise, which extends to the liver, is short but broad ; from which many thin veins, extending to the liver, are obliterated. But two larger branches proceed from the vein of the liver, of which one ends in the transverse septum, and what are called the præcordia, but the other returning upward, and descending through the arm-pit to the right arm, concurs in it with other veins, near the interior curvature of the arm. Hence this vein of the arm is cut by physicians, that, by taking blood from it, certain diseases of the liver may be cured. Another branch, likewise, of the great vein, which is also short but broad, tends to the spleen, which is in the left part, and being diffused in the spleen into small veins, becomes no longer apparent. But another branch of the great vein ascends to the left arm. Yet though the vein which passes through the liver ascends to the right arm, yet the vein which passes through the spleen does not ascend to the left arm, but the vein which ascends to the left arm is different from the vein which passes through the spleen. Again, from the greater vein, which proceeds from the inferior part of the heart, two other veins are derived, one of which. tends to the omentum or caul, but the other to what is called the pan creum, [which is so denominated because the whole consists of a cer tain glandulous flesh j. But from the vein which tends to the pancreum. many veins are scattered through the mysentery ; and all these end at length in one large vein, which is extended through the whole intestine and belly as far as to the stomach. From this vein, also, many branches are diffused about the parts through which it is extended. Both the aorta and the great vein, therefore, proceed as far as to the kidneys, and here they rather adhere to the spine. Both of them, like wise, are divided into two parts, after the manner of the letter V, and the great vein verges to the posterior part of the body, somewhat more than the aorta. The aorta, however, especially about the heart, adheres. to the spine by nervous and small veins. But the aorta in its first egress from the heart is very ample and capacious ; but in its progress. it becomes narrower and more nervous. Veins, also, extend from the aorta to the mysentery, in the same manner as the branches from the great vein, except that they arc much less ; for they are narrow and m fibrous;

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 82 fibrous ; since they terminate in thin, hollow, and fibrous little veins. No vein, however, tends from the aorta to the liver and the spleen. But those branches into which each vein is divided extend to the hip, and both of them insert themselves into the bone of it. Veins, also, tend to the kidneys, from the great vein and the aorta, except that they do not insinuate themselves into the cavity of the kidneys, but into the body of them. From the aorta, therefore, two other strong and con tinued avenues tend to the bladder, and others proceed from the cavity of the kidneys, but have no communication with the great vein. From the middle, also, of each of the kidneys a hollow and nervous vein is suspended, and which extends, near the spine itself, through the [ramifications of] veins ; then, in the first place, they enter each hip, and are no longer apparent; but afterwards being extended to the hip, they become again visible. The extremities of them, however, in males are connected with the bladder and the penis, but in females with the vulva. And from the great vein, indeed, no vein extends to the womb, but many and large veins tend to the womb from the aorta. Other less branches, likewise, are derived from the branches of the great vein and the aorta; of which, in the first place, some that are large and capacious tend to the groin, and afterwards through the legs, and in the feet and fingers. Others, again, proceeding through the groin and thigh, change their course, so that the right proceed to the left part, and the left to the right, and conjoin themselves with other veins at the concave part of the knee. After what manner, therefore, the veins subsist, and whence they originate, is from hence evident. All sanguineous animals, however, accord in the principles of the veins, and in the greatest veins ; ! but they do not accord in the multitude of the other veins. For the same number, and the same mode of the subsistence of the veins, is not in all animals, or at least is not apparent in all : but their progress is especially apparent in very sanguineous and the largest animals. For in small animals, and which are not very sanguineous, either naturally, For all of them, according to Aristotle, have the cavities of the heart as the principles of the veins ; and they have, likewise, the great vein, and the aorta, or artery. or.

text: BOOK III. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 83 or from the fatness of their body, the secondary veins and their mode of subsistence can scarcely be perceived. For, on account of the fat, the avenues of the veins are confused, and resemble rivulets which contain a great quantity of mud. But very small animals have fibres instead of veins, [and therefore they can scarcely be distinguished]. The great vein, however, in all animals, and even in those that are small, is very conspicuous. CHAPTER V. The nerves, however, subsist in animals after the following manner: The principle of these, indeed, is from the heart ; for the heart con tains nerves in its greatest cavity ; and what is called the aorta is a nervous vein, and its extremities are perfectly nervous, since they are not hollow [like the Veins], but have an extension like nerves, and end in the flexions of the bones. The nature of the nerves, however, is not derived from one principle [i. e. from one principal nerve] with which it is in continuity, in the same manner as the veins. For the veins are distributed through the whole body, so as to resemble the painted streams of a fountain, and hence, in emaciated bodies, all the parts are seen to be full of veins. For the same place in those that are ema ciated is veiny ; but in those that are corpulent is fleshy. But the nerves are divulsed about the limbs and the flexions of the bones. If, however, the nature of them was continued, the continuity of all of them would become apparent in emaciated bodies. But the principal nerves are about that part of the body to which the province of leaping is assigned; and this partis called the ham. In the next place, there is a certain double nerve, which is called a tend.on. In the third place, there is a nerve which is an auxiliary to m 2 the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 84 the strength of the body, and which in Greek is denominated epitonos, and omoiaia, or pertaining to the shoulders. But the other nerves, which are about the flexion of the bones, are anonymous. For all the bones, whether they touch each other, or so subsist that the one is inserted in the other, are bound together by nerves; and there is a multitude of nerves about all the bones, except the bone of the head, in v/hich there is no nerve, but the head is connected by the sutures of its bones. The nature of nerve, however, is divisible according to length, but is indivisible according to breadth, and possesses much tension. A mucous moisture, likewise, white and glutinous, is pro- duced about the nerves, by which they are nourished, and from which they appear to be generated. A vein, therefore, may be burnt [with- out being destroyed] ; but every nerve is destroyed when burnt ; and if it is cut off it will not be reproduced ; nor does any part of the body experience a numbness where there is no nerve. Most of the nerves, likewise, are about the feet and the hands, the shoulders, neck, and arms. All sanguineous animals, too, have nerves ; but those animals that are without flexions or curvatures of the members, and are de prived of feet and hands, have thin and immanifest nerves. Hence, in fishes, the nerves near the fins are especially conspicuous. CHAPTER VI. The fibres, however, have a nature between nerve and vein ; but some of them have the moisture of lymph, and tend from the nerves to the veins, and from them to the nerves x. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS, 85 of fibres, which subsists, indeed, in blood, yet not in the blood of every animal ; and the blood cannot be congealed if these fibres are taken from it, but if they are not taken from it it can be congealed. Fibres, therefore, are inherent in the blood of most animals ; but there are no fibres in the blood of the stag, the deer, the buffalo, and certain other animals. Hence, their blood is not congealed in a manner similar to that of other animals ; but the blood of stags is congealed similar to that of hates. The congelation, however, of the blood of both these is not of a firm consistence, like that of other animals, but is fluid, so as to resemble milk without the coagulum. But the blood of the buffalo is congealed in a greater degree ; for it is similar, or not much less congealed than the blood of sheep. After this manner, therefore, vein, nerve, and fibre, subsist. CHAPTER VII. All the bones, likewise, in animals, depend from one bone, and are in continuity with each other, in the same manner as the veins ; but there is no bone which subsists itself by itself. The spine of the back, however, is the principal in all animals that have bones. But the spine is composed from vertebrae, and extends from the head as far as to the hips. All the vertebrae, therefore, are perforated. But the bone of the head, which is called the cranium, is in continuity with the last vertebrae ; and the place in which one part of the cranium is inserted in the other is called the suture. The cranium, however, does not subsist similarly in all animals ; for in some, as in the dog, the cranium consists of only one bone [without any sutures] ; but in others, as in man,

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 86 mali, it is composed from many bones : and the female, indeed, in the human species, has the parts of the cranium conjoined by a circular suture ; but the male has three sutures, which are conjoined trian o-ularly at the vertex. The head of a man, however, has been seen without sutures. But the head is composed, not from four, but from six bones ; and two of these, which are small when compared with the rest, are about the ears. The bones of the jaw, however, are extended from the head ; and in all other animals the lower jaw is moved ; but the river crocodile is the only animal that moves the upper jaw. The genus of teeth, also, is inherent in the jaws ; and consists of bones, which are partly solid and partly perforated, and the bone of the teeth is the only bone which it is impossible to carve. From the spine, the fibula, the clavicles, and the ribs, originate. The breast, also, is placed in the ribs; and of these, some are conjoined, but others are unconjoined. For there is no animal which has a bone about the belly. Farther still, there are also the bones in the shoulders, and what are called the scapulae, or shoulder-blades, and the bones of the hands and arms, which are annexed to them. These bones, however, subsist after the same manner in animals which have fore legs, as in man. But beneath, where the spine of the back ends, and after the hip, is the cotyloid cavity, and the bones of the legs, from which the thighs and tabiae consist, and of which the ankle bones are a part, and of these what are called spurs in animals that have an ankle bone. In continuity with these, also, are the bones of the feet. I he bones, therefore, of such sanguineous and pedestrious animals as are viviparous are not very different, but rather differ analagously in hardness, softness, and magnitude. Again, of the bones in the same animal, some have marrow, but others have not. Some animals, how ever, do not in short appear to have any marrow in their bones, as is the case with the lion, because it has but very little and thin marrow, and but in few of its bones; for it alone has it in its thighs and fore feet. But the lion, beyond all other animals, has its bones solid ; for they are so hard, that from the attrition of them, in the same manner as from flints, fire is excited. The

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 87 The dolphin, also, has bones, but not a spine. But other sanguineous animals either have bones not very different from those of the animals hitherto enumerated, as birds; or, though they are without bones, they have something analagous to them, as fishes. For, of fishes, such as are viviparous have a cartilaginous spine, as is the case with the fishes called selache, or of the cartilaginous kind ; but such of them as are oviparous have a thorn, which subsists in them in the same manner as the bone of the back in quadrupeds. It is, however, the peculiarity of certain fishes, that within the flesh they have separate thorns. Ser pents, also, accord with fishes in this, that in the place of bones they have the spine of the back. With respect, however, to oviparous qua drupeds, the larger among them [as the crocodile] have in the back something which is more similar to bone than a thorn, but the less [as the lizard] have in the back something which more resembles a thorn than bone. But all animals that are sanguineous have a spine, which is either bony or thorny ; and the other bones that have been enumerated are inherent in some animals, and in others not, just as they have certain members, or are deprived of them. For such animals as have not legs and arms, are also deprived of the bones of the legs and arms ; but those which have these parts, or what are ana logous to them, have also bones corresponding to such parts, which differ in the more and the less, or in the analogous. The particulars, therefore, respecting the bones, subsist after this manner in animals. CHAPTER VIII. Cartilage, however, is of the same nature with the bones, but differs from them in the more and the less ; and as a bone when cut off is not increased, this is also the case with a cartilage. But the cartilages in sanguineous
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 88 sanguineous animals that are terrestrial and viviparous are not hollow, nor have they marrow within them, in the same manner as there is in bones. In cartilaginous aquatic animals, however, the cartilage which is under the back, in the place of the spine, is hollow, and full of a certain moisture which is analogous to marrow. But in viviparous and pedestrious animals there are cartilages about the ears and the nostrils, and about certain extremities of the bones. CHAPTER IX. Again, there are other genera of parts, which have neither the same nature with these, nor are remote from them ; such, for instance, as nails, the horn of the foot, whether the foot is one entire hoof, or is cloven, the horns of the head ; and, besides these, the beaks of birds. For these are flexible and fissile, but no bone is either of these, but is alone frangible. The colours, likewise, of horns, nails, and hoofs, follow the colour of the skin and the hair. For the horns and hoofs of animals that have a black skin are black, but of those that have a white skin are white ; and the like takes place in the intermediate co lours. The nails, also, subsist after the same manner. But the teeth are of the nature of the bones ; and hence in black men, such as Ethio pians, and the like, the teeth and the bones are white; but the nails are black, in the same manner as the whole of the skin. Of horns, however, the greater part is hollow from the root, which is at the mouth, and inwardly proceeds from the head; but the extre mity of the horn is solid and simple. And the horns of stags alone are solid throughout, and multifidous. Other horned animals, likewise, do not change their horns ; but the stag alone changes them every year, unless he is castrated. We shall, however, afterwards speak about
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK III. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 89 about castrated animals. But the horns rather adhere to the skin, than to the bone ; and hence in Phrygia, and elsewhere, there are oxen which move their horns in the same manner as some animals move their ears. Of those animals, however, that have nails, (but all ani mals that have toes have nails, except the elephant, and this animal has undivided toes, indistinct, and imperfect, and has no nails,) some have straight nails, as man ; but others have crooked nails, as of pedes trious animals, the lion, and of winged animals, the eagle. CHAPTER X. With respect to hair, however, and what is analogous to hair, and also with respect to the skin, they subsist in the following manner. Such animals, indeed, have hair as are pedestrious and viviparous ; but those viviparous fishes alone, that bring forth a friable egg, have scales; for of long fishes, neither the conger, nor the lamprey, have an egg of this kind ; but the eel, in short, produces no egg. The thick ness, thinness, and magnitude of hair, however, differ according to the situation of the parts in which they are, and the quality of the skin. For it happens for the most part, that harder and thicker hairs grow in thicker skin; and that more abundant and longer hair grows in the more hollow, and more moist parts of the body, if these parts are adapted to the production of hair. The like, also, takes place in the scales of terrestrial animals, and of fishes. Such animals, there fore, as have soft hair, through the use of better food acquire harder hair ; but those that have hard hair, have through this mean fewer and softer hairs. In the third place, hairs differ according as places are hotter or colder. Thus, for instance, human hair is hard in hot, but soft in cold, regions. And again, straight hair is soft, but curled hair is hard. N CHAP.

text: THE, HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK Til. 90 CHAPTER XL The nature of the hairs, however, is fissile. But hairs differ from each other, in the more and the less ; and some are so gradually in durated, that they no longer resemble hairs, but thorns, such as the hairs of the land hedge-hog. The like, also, takes place in nails ; for the genus of nails in some animals is so hard, that it does not in any respect differ from bones. Man, however, has the thinnest skin of all animals, in proportion to the magnitude of his body. But in all skin there is a mucous vis cosity ; in some, indeed, less, but in others more. Thus, for instance, in the skin of oxen there is a mucous moisture, from which they make glue ; and in some places, glue is made from fishes. The skin, also, when cut off, is of itself deprived of sense ; and this is especially the case with the skin of the head, because, between this and the bone, [or cranium,] nothing of flesh intervenes. But, whenever the skin is by itself, if it is cut, it does not coalesce ; as in the thin parts of the cheek, prepuce, and the eye-lids. In all animals, likewise, the skin is continued through the whole of the body, so that its continuity is not interrupted, except where there is a natural evaporation through the pores, and where the mouth and nails are situated. All san guineous animais, therefore, have skin, but all have not hairs, but those only of whom mention has been already made. The hair, however, changes its colour in old age, and in men be comes whiter ; but in other animals it becomes whiter indeed, yet not very apparently so, except in the horse. Hair, also, becomes white at the extremity, [which is the most distant from the skin ;] but most hair that is hoary becomes white immediately ; from which it is evi- dent.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 91 BOOK in. dent, that hoariness is not, as some say, a dryness of the hair, since nothing grows immediately dry. But in that disease of the skin, which is called the white leprosy, all the hairs become white. It happens, likewise, that some when they are ill become hoary ; but, the hair fall ing off, when they recover their health black hair grows in its stead. Hair, too, becomes more swiftly hoary when covered than when ex posed to the air. But in men, the temples first begin to be hoary; and the anterior parts of the head become hoary prior to the posterior parts ; and the hairs about the private parts become white in the last place. In man, however, alone among all animals, some of the hairs are connascent, and others are produced afterwards, as he advances in age. The connascent hairs, indeed, are those in the head, in the eyebrows, and eyelids ; but those of posterior origin are first the hairs on the private parts, in the next place those of the arm-pits, and in the third place those of the chin. For the places are equal in number in which the connascent hairs and those of posterior origin grow. But the hairs of the head especially fail, and fall off, and the first of all the hairs ; and this is confined to the hairs in the anterior part of the head : for no one becomes bald in the posterior part of the head. The smoothness, therefore, [or defluxion of the hairsj of the head, is called baldness, but that of the eyebrows depilation; and neither of these happens to any one prior to the age adapted to copulation. Baldness, however, neither happens to a child, nor to a woman, nor to those who are castrated ; but if any one is castrated prior to the emission of the hairs of posterior origin, he will not emit them ; and if he is castrated after the emission of these hairs, such hairs will fall off, except those on the private parts. Hairs, however, do not grow on the chin of a woman, some few women excepted; and this takes place when the menses stop, and resembles that which hap pens to the priestesses in Caria, which is considered as a sign of divina tion. Hairs, too, grow about the private parts and under the arm pits of women, but they are few. There are, likewise, both men and women, who from their birth are deprived of hairs of posterior origin ; a 2 and

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 92 and those, also, are impotent who are without hairs on the private parts. Other hairs, therefore, are increased by a certain law of nature, either more or less, especially those in the head ; in the next place, those in the beard, and particularly those that are more thin. In some persons, likewise, the eyebrows are so thick with hair, when they be come old, that they ought to be shaved ; and this is because the mois ture, from which the eyebrows are produced, proceeds from the com missures of the bones, which commissures in old age are loosened, and, therefore, a greater quantity of moisture pervades through them. But the hairs of the eyelids are not increased ; and they fall off Avhen ve nery begins to takes place, and are more abundant in those that are more addicted to venery. They also become hoary very slowly. While we are growing, also, the hairs, if they are plucked out, are re-produced, but when we no longer grow, they are no longer re-pro duced. All hair, too, has a viscous moisture at the root, and there fore, if the hair, as soon as it is plucked out, touches any thing light by its root, it adheres to, and draws it. But animals, which are covered with hairs of many colours, have also a variety of colour in their skin, and in the skin of their tongue. With respect to the beard, however, it happens that some have the chin and upper lip hairy, but others have these parts smooth, and have the cheeks covered with thick hair ; and those that have a bipartite chin and lip, are less accustomed to become hoary. The hair, likewise, is increased in certain diseases, and especially in those of the consumptive kind, in old age, and in dead bodies, and instead of being soft becomes harder. The very same things, also, happen with respect to the nails. In the libidinous, how ever, the connascent hairs more rapidly fall off, but those of posterior origin are more swiftly produced. Those, likewise, whose veins are more tumid than is proper, are less subject to baldness; and some when afflicted with this disease have abundance of hair. Hair, how ever, when cut off, is not by this mean increased, but growing from the root becomes longer. The scales, also, of fishes become harder and thicker ; and in those that are slender and old, they become more hard.

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK III. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 93 hard. Of quadrupeds, likewise, when they grow old, the hair and the wool become thicker, but less in multitude. The horns, too, and hoofs of pedestrious animals, and the beaks of birds, become larger in old age ; and hoofs are increased in the same manner as nails. CHAPTER XII. With respect to the feathers of birds, they suffer no change from age, except those of the crane ; and this bird has been found when it becomes old to have blacker feathers. In consequence, however, of the passive qualities produced by the different seasons, as when the weather happens to be very cold, sometimes the feathers of birds that are of one colour, such as black or a dark brown, become white, as is the case with the feathers of the crow, the sparrow, and the swallow ; but white birds are never seen to become black. Indeed, many birds change their colours at stated times of the year ; so that one, who is not well acquainted with this circumstance, would be unconscious of the change. Some animals, likewise, change the colour of their hairs, from changing the water which they drink ; for by one kind of water they become white, and by another black. The like, also, takes place with respect to their copulations ; for there are in many places waters, which when the sheep have drank, if they copulate immediately after, they produce black lambs ; and such is the water called Psychrus, a river of Assyria, in the country of Chalcis in Thrace. In Antandria, also, there are two rivers, one of which causes the sheep that drink it to be white, and the other to be black. 'I he river Scamander, likewise, is seen
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 94 seen to make the sheep that drink of it yellow ; and on this account they say that Homer calls this river Xanthus, instead of Scamander. Other animals, therefore, have hair alone in the prone part, [i. e. in the back,] but they have not any in the supine part, [i. e. in the breast and belly,] and they have also hairs externally, and not internally; but the hare alone has hairs within the mouth, in the cheek, and under the feet. Farther still, the fish called mysticetus has no teeth in its mouth, but has hairs similar to those of a swine, in the place of teeth. Hairs, therefore, when they are cut, grow from the root, and not from the place where they are cut ; but feathers if they are cut? neither grow from the root, nor from the part where they are cut, but fall off. Those animals, also, that have continued wings, and not com posed from many feathers, as bees, and the like, have not their wings re-produced if they are plucked out ; nor is the sting of the bee re produced when it is ejected ; but bees when they loose their sting shortly after die. CHAPTER XIII. There are, likewise, membranes in all sanguineous animals. But a membrane is similar to a strong and thin skin; and it is also of a dif ferent genus from skin, since it is neither fissile, nor capable of being stretched. About each of the bones, however, and each of the vis cera, there is a membrane, both in larger and smaller animals; but the membranes are immanifest in smaller animals, because in these they are very thin and small. The largest, however, of the mem branes are the two which are about the brain; of which the superior, and

text: BOOK HI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 95 and harder membrane adheres to the bone of the head, [and is called dura mater,] but the other which is softer, and is in contact with the substance of the brain, [is called pia mater.] The next to these, in magnitude, is the membrane which covers the heart. But a mem brane when cut does not coalesce and become reunited ; and bones when deprived of their membranes mortify. CHAPTERS XIV. and XV. The epiploon, or caul, is also a membrane. And all sanguineous animals have an epiploon ; but in some, indeed, it is fat, and in others lean. In animals, likewise, that are viviparous, and have teeth on both sides, the epiploon originates, and depends from the middle belly, where a certain suture, as it were, exists of the epiploon with the belly ; and in animals which have only teeth on one side, the epiploon in a similar manner depends from the greater belly. The bladder, likewise, is indeed membranous, but it is a membrane of a different genus, since it can be extended. All animals, however, have not a bladder, but all viviparous animals have it; and of ovi parous animals the tortoise alone. The bladder, likewise, when cut, does not coalesce, except in that part which is called the neck of the bladder, unless very rarely ; for a thing of this kind has happened. In the dead, indeed, no moisture pervades to the bladder; but in living animals, not only moisture, but also dry substances, descend into the bladder, from which the disease called the stone is produced. And in some persons there is such a concretion of dry matter in the bladder, that

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III 96 that it does not appear to differ in any respect from shells. After this manner, therefore, vein, nerve, skin, fibre, and membrane subsist, and also hair, nails, hoofs, horns, teeth, beaks, cartilage, and bones, and parts analogous to these. CHAPTER XVI. Flesh, also, and that which has a nature similar to flesh, subsists in all sanguineous animals, between the skin and the bone, and the parts analogous to the bones. For as spine is to bone, so is that which is fleshy to flesh, in animals which have bones and a spine. Flesh, how ever, can be divided every way, [i. e. according to length, breadth, and depth,] and not like the nerves and veins, according to length only. When animals, therefore, become thin, the flesh is consumed, and the veins and fibres become apparent ; but by good nutriment and in great abundance, the flesh is changed into fat. In those, also, that have much flesh, the veins are smaller, the blood is redder, and the viscera and belly are small ; but in those that have large veins, the blood is blacker, the viscera are large, and the belly is great, but the flesh is in a small quantity. But fat is produced about the flesh of those that have a small belly. chap.

text: BOOK III. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 97 CHAPTER XVII. Fat, however, and suet differ from each other. For suet, indeed, is entirely fragile, and is congealed by cold ; but fat is fluid, and not adapted to be congealed. The broth, also, which is made of the fat of the horse, and the swine, does not coagulate ; but the broth which is made from the suet of a sheep, or a goat, does coagulate. Fat and suet, likewise, differ from the places in which they are produced. For fat is produced between the skin and the flesh, but suet is produced in the extremity of the flesh. The epiploon, also, or caul, is fat in animals that are fat ; but is suety in animals that have suet. And ani mals that have teeth on both sides [as the swine] have fat; but those that have not [as sheep] have suet. With respect to the viscera, however, in some animals the liver is fat, as among fishes, in those of the cartilaginous kind ; for, from the colliquation of their liver they make oil. The flesh of the selache, however, [or of a cartilaginous kind of fishes,] is without fat; but they have fat separately in the belly. The suet, also, of fishes is fat, and does not congeal. With respect to all animals, however, some have fat about the flesh, but others have it separate from the flesh. But such animals as have not fat separate from the flesh are less fat in the belly and epiploon ; and this is the case with eels, for they have but little suet about the epiploon. Most animals, however, become fat in the belly, and this is especially the case with animals that are not in motion. Of fat animals, also, such as the swine, the brains are fat; but of animals that are suety, the brains are dry. o With

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 98 With respect to the viscera, likewise, animals are especially fat aboufe the kidneys. But the left kidney is always more fat than the right ; and though the kidneys should be very fat, yet there is always some part in the middle of them which is not fat. The kidneys, however, of animals which have suet, are more fat than the kidneys of those that have fat, and this is especially the case with the kidneys of sheep ; for when the kidneys are entirely covered with fat this animal dies. Sheep, however, become fat about the kidneys through feeding abun dantly, as is the case with the sheep in Sicily, about Leontium; and, on this account, the shepherds in that country lead the sheep to pasture late in the day, in order that they may take less nutriment. CHAPTERS XVIII. and XIX. The part, however, about the pupil of the eye is common to all ani mals; for all such as have the pupil in the eyes, and have not hard eyes, have it composed from suet, and not from fat. Fat animals, also, both male and female, are less prolific ; and they become more fat when they are elderly than when they are young, but this is especially the case when the body, having obtained its proper length and breadth, begins to be increased in depth. With respect to the blood, also, it subsists as follows ; for this is most necessary, and most common to all sanguineous animals, and is not adventitious, but is inherent in all animals whose body is not in a cor rupted state. All the blood, however, is contained in what are called the veins, as in a vessel, but in nothing else, except in the heart alone. The blood, also, does not in any animal perceive the touch, as neither does
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK III. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 99 does the excrement in the belly, nor the brain, nor the marrow. But wherever the flesh is divided in a living body, the blood flows, unless the flesh is in a corrupt state. The blood, however, if it is sane, has naturally a sweet taste and a red colour ; but if it is vitiated, either naturally, or by disease, it is of a blacker colour. The best blood, like wise, is neither very thick nor very thin, if it is not vitiated, either naturally, or from disease. And in the animal, indeed, it is always hot and moist ; but when it proceeds forth externally, it is congealed : the blood of the stag, and the deer, and any other animal of a similar nature, excepted. The blood, however, of all other animals, when separated from the animal, is congealed, unless the fibres are taken out of it. But the blood of the bull is congealed the most rapidly of all blood. Of sanguineous animals, also, the viviparous have more blood than the oviparous. Those animals, too, whose body is in a good con dition, either naturally, or from health, have neither very much blood, as is the case with those that have been recently drinking, nor blood in a small quantity, as is the case with those that are very fat. For those that are fat have, indeed, pure, but little blood-, and the less blood animals possess the fatter they become; for the fat is exanguious. And fat, indeed, does not become putrid ; but blood and sanguineous sub stances rapidly putrify, and this is especially the case with the parts about the bones. Man, however, has the most attenuated and the purest blood ; but the bull an d the as have the thickest and the blackest blood of all animals ; and the blood becomes thicker and blacker in the inferior than in the superior parts. In all animals, like wise, the blood palpitates, and has at the same time a pulsation in the veins in all directions ; and it is the only humour that is dispersed through the whole body in animals, and this perpetually as long as they live. The blood, however, is first produced in animals in the heart, and before the whole body is organized. The loss, also, of much blood is attended with swooning, but of a very great quantity with death; and when it becomes very liquid, the animal is diseased. For some times it becomes lymphatic, and is so serous that some persons emit a sanguineous sweat. It also happens, that the blood of some persons is o2 . so
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 100 so liquid, that it will not congeal, or that only a certain part of it will congeal separate from the rest. In those that arc asleep, likewise, there is a less quantity of blood in the external parts ; so that if an aperture is made in the body of these, less blood will flow from it than if they were awake. From lymph, however, when concocted, blood is produced, and from blood fat. But when the blood is vitiated, a flux is produced called an hcemorrhois, either from the nostrils, or from the fundament, and which produces inflated veins. Pus, also, is generated from the blood when putrid; and from this a white and thick substance is produced, called porus. But the blood of females differs from that of males ; for it is thicker and blacker in females, if both are similar in health and age. Females, likewise, have less blood in the external parts of the body, but more in the internal parts. A woman, also, has the most blood of all female animals ; and what are called the menses are more abundant in women than in other animals. The blood, also, of the menses, when vitiated, is called a flux. Women, however, have less of other diseases which originate from the blood than men. For few women are afflicted with a flux of blood from the hœmorroidal veins, or with an inflation of the veins, or with a flux of blood from the nose ; and if any one of these happens to them, the menses are not in so good a condition. The blood, likewise, differs according to age in multitude and form [i. e. in quantity and quality]. For, in those that are very young it is lymphatic, and abundant ; but in those that are old it is thick, black, and in a small quantity ; and in those that are in the acme of life it has a middle mode of subsistence. The blood, also, of those that are old is congealed rapidly, and even in the superficies of the body ; but this does not happen to young persons. Lymph, however, is unconcocted blood, either because it is not yet concocted, or because, through a defect of heat, it has degenerated into a serous and aqueous matter! CHAP,
