text: BOOK HI, THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 101 CHAPTER XX. In the next place, it follows that we should speak concerning the marrow ; for this, in some sanguineous animals, is one of the liquid parts. All such liquid parts, however, as are naturally inherent in the body are contained in vessels, just as the blood is contained in the veins, and the marrow in the bones ; but the other liquid parts are contained in membranes, and skins, and bellies. In young animals, however, the marrow is entirely sanguineous ; but when they become older, in those that are fat the marrow is fat, but in those that have suet instead of fat the marrow is suety. All the bones, however, do not contain marrow, but only those that are hollow, and even in some of these there is no marrow. For of the bones of the lion some have marrow, and others contain so small a quantity of it, that, as we have before observed, some assert that they are entirely without marrow. In the bones of swine, likewise, there is but little marrow ; and in some of them there is none at all. These, therefore, are nearly the humid parts of animals, which are always connascent with them ; but milk, and the genital seed, are things of posterior origin. Of these, however, that which is secreted from all animals when it is inherent is milk ; but genital seed is not secreted in all animals, but instead of it, in some, as in fishes, there is what is called the soft roe. All such animals, however, as have milk have it in the mammae; and those animals have mammæ that generate an animal in themselves, and bring it forth externally ; such as ani- mal
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK nr. 102 mals that have hair, as man, and horse ; and likewise cetaceous ani mals, such as the dolphin, the sea-calf, and the whale ; for these have mammæ and milk. But such animals as alone generate an animal, or an egg, externally, have neither mammae nor milk ; as, for instance, fishes and birds. All milk, however, has an aqueous lymph, which is called whey ; and it has also a certain corpulent substance, which is called cheese. The milk, therefore, of animals which have not teeth on both sides coagulates ; and, on this account, front the milk of tame animals cheese is made; but the milk of those animals that have teeth on both sides does not coagulate, as neither does the fat ; and it is thin and sweet. The milk, however, of the camel is the thinnest of all milk; the second in thinness is the milk of a mare, and the third is that of the ass, but that of the cow is more thick. Milk, therefore, is not coagulated by cold, but becomes through it more serous ; but it is coagulated and thickened by fire. Milk, however, for the most part, is not produced in any animal prior to copulation ; but when conception takes place milk is produced indeed, yet so, that both at first and at last it is use- less. Certain food, also, will cause animals that are not pregnant to have milk; and these have been elderly women, from whose mammae when sucked milk has flowed, and in such abundance as to nourish the infant with it. In mount Oeta, likewise, the shepherds rub the udders of the she-goats that have not copulated with a nettle so ve- hemently as to cause pain, by which it comes to pass, that in the first place a sanguineous moisture is induced, after which a purulent humour follows, and at last milk is produced, and in no less abundance than from those that have copulated. For the most part, however, milk is not produced in the males of other animals, nor in those of the human species, though it sometimes happens that males also have milk. Thus, in the island of Lemnos, so much milk was induced from the two mammæ of a he-goat, which were situated near the penis, that little cheeses were made from it, and the same thing also happened to the male offspring of this goat. Things of this kind, however, are considered as prodigies ; since the Lemnian deity [Vulcan] said that it
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 103 it was an indication of the acquisition of wealth. In some men, also, after puberty, a small quantity of milk is induced, and from some by sucking a great quantity has been produced. A fatness, likewise, is inherent in milk, which in coagulation becomes of an oily nature, [and is called butter.] In Sicily, however, and other regions, where there are a great quantity of she-goats, they mingle the milk of goats with that of sheep, [for the purpose of making cheese.] But milk is espe cially coagulated, not only that which contains the greatest quantity of cheese, but also that which contains the driest cheese. Some ani mals, therefore, have more milk than is sufficient to nourish their off spring. The milk, also, of sheep and goats is most useful for the purpose of making cheese and reserving ; and next to this, the milk of the cow. But the milk of the mare and the ass are mingled in order to make Phrygian cheese. There is, however, more cheese in the milk of the cow than in the milk of the she-goat. For shepherds say, that from an amphora of goat's milk twenty cheeses wanting one are made, for an obolus a piece; but that thirty were made from an amphora of cow's milk. The milk, however, of those animals which have as much as is sufficient to nourish their offspring is useless for the pur pose of making cheese ; and of this kind are all those animals that have more than two mammæ ; for the milk of none of these is either abundant or adapted to make cheese. But the juice and coagulum of the fig coagulate milk. Wool, therefore, imbued with the juice of the fig is washed with a little milk; for this milk, being mingled with a greater quantity of milk, coagulates the whole. CHAP.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. JJOOK HI. 104 CHAPTER XXI. This coagulum, however, is milk; for it is contained in the belly of those that suckle. Coagulum, therefore, is milk, containing a fire" in itself, which is produced from the heat of the animal, in conse quence of the milk being concocted. But all ruminating animals have a coagulum ; and among animals that have teeth on both sides, the hare has it. Coagulum, also, is better in proportion as it is more old ; for a thing of this kind, and also the coagulum of a hare, are useful in the cure of a diarrhœa. But the best coagulum is that of the fawn. More or less milk, however, is emulged from animals that have milk, according to the magnitude of their bodies, and the diversity of their food. Thus, in Phasis, though the cows are small, yet they give a great quantity of milk, because they are nourished with the best food ; but each of the large cows of Epirus only gives an amphora and a half of milk from its two mammæ. The cows, however, of Epirus are so large, that they cannot be milked by the shepherds, ex cept when they stand, or are a little inclined ; because when they sit they cannot reach to their mammæ. Except the ass, other large qua drupeds also are produced in Epirus; but the largest among them are the oxen and dogs. Since, also, the oxen are large, they require a greater quantity of pasture; but the region abounds with a pasture of this kind, for it has places adapted to the feeding of cattle in every season of the year. As the oxen, likewise, in Epirus are very large, so also are the sheep, called Pyrrhic, from Pyrrhus the king. With respect to nutriment, however, one kind extinguishes, [i. e. diminishes] milk,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK III. HIE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 105 milk ; such, for instance, as the Median grass, and especially in rumi nating animals; but another kind of nutriment increases the milk, such as the cytisus, and theorobus ; except that the cytisus, when it is in blossom is of no use, for it inflames ; and the orobus is not useful to pregnant animals, because it renders their delivery more difficult. In short, of animals that are able to eat, as the possession of them is ad vantageous, so likewise they afford a greater quantity of milk,, if they are well fed. Certain flatulent substances, also, when given as food produce much milk; such, for instance, as beans, when largly given to sheep, she-goats, cows, and young goats ; for it causes the udders to be distended with the quantity of milk* It is an indication, however^ that there will be abundance of milk,, when the udder, prior to the time of parturition, is pendent towards the earth. But in all animals milk endures for a long time, if they continue without copulation, and have appropriate food ; and this is especially the case with sheep, be yond all other quadrupeds; for they are milked during the space of eight months. In short, ruminating animals have much milk, and which is useful to the making of cheese. The cows, however, about Torona, a few days prior to their delivery, are without milk, but at every other time they have milk. But with respect to the milk of wo men, the milk which is of a livid colour is better for the nourish ment of infants than that which is white ; and the milk which is of a dun is more salubrious than that which is of a white colour. That milk, therefore, is most nutritious which contains the greatest quan tity of cheese ; but that is most salubrious to infants which contains the least. . All sanguineous animals, however, emit seed ; but what seed con tributes to generation, and how it contributes, will be shown else where. Man, however, in proportion to the magnitude of his body, emits the most of all animals. But the seed of animals that have hair is viscous, but of other animals is not viscous ; and the seed of all animals is white. The assertion, therefore, of Herodotus is false, that the Ethiopians emit black seed. Seed, also, in its egress, if it is sane, is white and thick, but after its egress it becomes thin and black. VtE have, therefore, already discussed such parts of sanguineous animals as are common, and also such as are peculiar, and have con sidered the dissimilar and the similar parts, and such as are internal, and such as are external ; hence it remains, that we should now speak concerning exanguious animals. There are, however, many genera of these; one, indeed, being the genus of what are called the mollia; and these are such as, being exanguious, have a fleshy substance ex ternally, but a solid substance internally, in the same manner as sangui neous animals, and of this kind is the genus of cuttle-fishes. But another genus of this kind is that of crustaceous animals ; and these are such as have a solid substance externally, but a soft and fleshy substance inter- p 2 nally
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 108 naliy. Their hard covering, however, is not brittle, but is capable of being bruised ; and of this kind are the genera of locusts and crabs. Another genus is that of testaceous animals ; and these are such as have a fleshy substance internally, but externally a solid substance, which is brittle, and may be broken, but cannot be bruised ; such as is the genus of snails and oysters. The fourth genus is that of insects, which comprehends many and dissimilar species of animals. Insects, how ever, are, as the name implies, such animals as have certain incisures cither in the supine or prone parts, or in both ; and they neither con sist of a body partly bony, and partly fleshy, but of a body which is between both ; for their body both internally and externally is simil arly hard. Of insects, also, some are winged, and others are without wings; such as the iulus, and the scolopendra. But the winged are such as bees, beetles, and wasps. And insects of a doubtful genus are ants, and what are called glow-worms; for some of these are winged, and others are without wings. Of those animals, therefore, which are called mollia, the external parts are these; one indeed, what are called the feet; the second, the head, which immediately adheres to the feet ; and the third, the cavit}r, [or belly and alvus,] which contains all the rest of the body, and which some improperly denoninate jceAupas, a shell'. And besides these are the fins, Avhich are circularly disposed about the cavity. It hap pens, however, in all the mollia, that the head is between the feet and the belly. All the mollia, likewise, have eight feet, which, according to length, in the bottom part, are furnished with a twofold order of ace tabula2, one genus of the polypus excepted. It is the peculiarity, however, of the cuttle-fish, and the small and large calamary to have two long trunks, which in their bottom part are rough, with a twofold series of acetabula ; and by these they take their food, and convey it to their mouth. By these, also, in stormy weather adhering to rocks, 1 In the original xtQaiw, a head ; but, I have no doubt, it should be komQov, as in the transla tion ; for a shell is hard, but the cavity or belly of the mollia is soft. a The acetabula are knots and joints, within which the parts of the leg or arm enter without intermission they
