text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 109 they fix themselves as by an anchor. But they swim by the fins, which they have about the cavity. The polypus, therefore, uses its flagella, or arms, as feet and hands ; for it uses the two arms, which are above the mouth, for the purpose of taking the food and conveying it to the mouth ; but it uses the last of its arms for the purpose of coition. And this last arm is the sharpest, is alone of a whitish colour, and in its extreme part is bifurcated, and annexed to the back. That smooth part, however, of the polypus is called the back, from which the order of the acetabula commences. The polypus, also, before the cavity or alvus, and above the arms, has a hollow pipe for canal] by which it returns the sea-water it has received in its cavity, when it happens to have this water in its mouth. But it moves this pipe, at one time to the right, and at another to the left ; and by this, also, it ejects its ink. The polypus, likewise, swims obliquely, extending its feet above what is called its head ; and it happens that, swimming in this manner, it sees what is before it ; for its eyes are above, but its mouth is behind. Its head, however, as long as it lives is hard, and is as it were inflated. It touches, also, and holds with its arms incur vated from the supine part ; and a membrane is extended through all the space which is between the feet. But if it falls on the sand, it is no longer able to hold any thing. The polypi, however, and the above-mentioned mollia differ [in many respects.] For the polypus has a small cavity, or belly, but its feet are long; but the other mollia have a large belly, and short feet, so that they are unable to walk with them. When, however, the other mollia are compared with each other, the small calamary is longer, but the cuttle-fish is broader. But of the two calatnaries, those that are called teuthoi are much the larger, for they grow to the magnitude of five cubits. Some cuttle-fish, also, grow to the size of two cubits. The arms, likewise, of the polypus become two cubits, and even more, in length. The genus, however, of the great calamary is but few in number. But the small and large calamary differ in figure from each other, for the point of the large calamary is broader. Again, a fin circularly surrounds the whole cavity of the larger calamary, [and this fin
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 110 fin is very continued,] but the cavity of the small calamary is sur rounded with a less continued fin. The small, however, as well as the large calamary, lives in the sea. After the feet in all the mollia is the head, which is in the middle of the feet that are catted jiagella. But of the head one part is the mouth, in which there are two teeth. And above these are two large eyes, between which is a small cartilage, which contains in itself a small brain. But in the mouth there is a small fleshy substance, which serves the purpose of a tongue, for no one of these animals has a tongue. After the head is the cavity, or belly, the external parts of which are obvious to the sight. The flesh, however, of it is divided, not indeed in a right line, but in a circle. And all the mollia have a skin about this. After the mouth, also, they have a long and narrow oesophagus ; and adhering to this they have a large avenue of the throat, similar to the craw of a bird. In continuation with this is the belly, which resembles one of the ventricles of ruminating animals ; and the figure of it is similar to the spirals of a horn. But after the belly a thin in testine succeeds, which again tends upward to the mouth. The intes tine, however, is thicker than the stomach. No one of the mollia, likewise, has any viscera, but they only have what is called mytis, in which their ink is contained. This ink, also, is possessed in the great est quantity by the cuttle-fish. All the mollia, therefore, when they are terrified, and especially the cuttle-fish, emit this ink. The mytis, also, is placed under the mouth, and through this the stomach ex tends ; but in the inferior part, by which it is joined to the intestine, it contains the ink, and the avenue of the mytis is closed by the same membrane as the avenue of the intestine. By the same avenue, also, the ink and the excrement are ejected. All the mollia, likewise, have certain capillaments in their body. The cuttle-fish, therefore, and the large and small calamary, have internally certain solid parts, under the back. And of these, the solid part of the cuttle-fish is called sepium, or a cuttle-bone, but the solid part of the large and small calamary is called gladhts, or a sword. These
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 111 These, however, differ from each other ; for the sepium is strong and broad, and has a nature between bone and spine, and a certain fun gous and friable corpulency; but the gladius of the calamary is thin, and more cartilaginous. The sepium and gladius, also, differ in figure, in the same manner as the abdomen or cavity differs, into which they are received. The polypi, however, are without this solid part [which is analogous to bone,] but they have a cartilaginous substance about the head, which becomes hard when any one of the polypi becomes old. The females, likewise, among the mollia, differ from the males; for the males have an avenue under the stomach, which extends from the brain to the inferior part of the abdomen, and the part to which it tends is similar to a papilla. The females, however, have, as it were, two papillae in the superior part of the abdomen. And under the pa pilla, both of the male and female, certain red corpuscles are seen. The egg, also, of the polypus is externally anomalous and large, but inwardly it contains a moisture, the whole of which is of a uniform white colour, and smooth ; and the quantity of this moisture is so great, that it can fill a vessel larger than the head of the polypus. On the contrary, the cuttle-fish has two cavities or abdomens ; and there are many eggs in these, which are similar to white hail-stones. The manner, however, in which each of these parts is situated may be seen from anomatical figures. But all these males differ from the fe males, and this is especially the case with the cuttle-fish. For the males have the prone part blacker than the supine part; they have, likewise, all the parts rougher than the females, and variegated with rods ; and the extremity of their body is more acute. There are, also, many genera of the polypi : and one genus of these is frequently seen to swim on the surface of the water, and is the largest of all of them. Those, however, that live near shores are much larger than those that live in the sea. Besides these, also, there are other small polypi, of a various colour, and which are not eaten. There are, likewise, two other genera, one of which is called h&ledane, and differs from the rest in the length of its feet, aud in only having one series of acetabula or joints in its legs; for all the others have two series
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 112 series of acetabula. But the other genus is what some call bolitcena, and others ozolis. There are, also, two other genera of polypi, which are in shells, one of which is called by some nautilus, and by others nauikus. This genus, however, resembles a polypus, and the shell of it is similar to a hollow comb, but does not so naturally adhere to the polypus that it cannot be separated from it. This polypus, likewise, frequently feeds near the land, but afterwards is thrown by the waves on the sand, and falling from its shell is caught, and dies on the land. These polypi, also, are small, but in their form resemble the bolitanœ. But there is another polypus, which is covered with a shell like a snail, so that it never leaves its shell, but sometimes outwardly extends its arms. And thus much concerning the mollia. CHAPTER II. With respect to crustaceous animals, however, one genus is that of locusts; and another genus, similar to this, is that of lobsters, which differ from locusts in having claws, and certain other differences which are not numerous. A third genus is that of squills, and a fourth is that of crabs. There are, however, many genera of squills and crabs. For of squills there are those that are crooked, and the crangones, and a small kind of squills, which never become larger. But the genus of crabs is all various, and cannot be easily enumerated. The greatest, therefore, is that which they call maia; but the next to these are the paguri, and heracleotic crabs ; and besides these are those which live in rivers. The rest are less than these, and are more anonymous. In the stores about Phœnicia, however, there are certain crabs which they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 113 they call troopers, because they run so swiftly that it is not easy to catch them ; but when opened, they are found to be empty from the want of food. There is, also, another genus, which is as small indeed as crabs, biit in form resembles lobsters. All these, therefore, as we have before observed, have externally that which is solid and testa ceous in the place of skin ; but internally that which is fleshy. They have the supine part of the body, however, [i. e. the belly] distin guished by certain tablets, into which the females deposit their eggs. With respect to feet, indeed, locusts have five on each side, together with their ultimate claws ; and, in a similar manner, crabs have ten feet, together with their claws. But of squills, those that are crooked have five feet on each side, which verge to the head, and are acute. They have, also, five others on each side, at the belly, the extremities of which are broad. They have not, however, tablets in the supine parts ; but in the prone parts [i. e. in the back] they resemble locusts. But the contrary takes place in the crangones ; for they have on each side four feet, near the head, and three other thin feet consequent to these, and the rest of the body, which in the greater part is without feet. The feet, likewise, of all the above-mentioned animals, are bent obliquely [i. e. towards the body of the animals ;] in the same man ner as the feet of insects ; and those which have claws bend them in wardly, [so that the cavity is towards the body.] The locust, also5 has a tail, and five fins on each side ; but the squills which are called crooked, have a tail, and four fins on each side. The crangones, like wise, have a tail, and fins on each side of it. But the middle fins of the squills of each genus are thorny ; except that the middle fins of the cr6bked squills are broad, but those of the crangones acute. The crab, however, alone, of animals of this kind, is without a tail ; and the body, indeed, of locusts and squillæ is long, but that of crabs is round. The male locust, however, differs from the female [in many re spects.] For the first foot of the female is bipartite, but that of the male is simple. With respect to the sins, also, in the supine part 01 the body, the female locust has large fins, but they diminish as they q approach
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 114 approach to the neck : but the male has all the fins equally less, and not dissimilar by diminution. Farther still, in the last feet of the male there are, as it were, large, 'and sharp spurs ; but in the last feet of the female these are small and smooth. In a similar manner, also, both the male and female locust have two large and rough horns before their eyes, under which there are other less and smooth horns. But the eyes of all these are hard, and are moved inwardly, outwardly, and obliquely. This is, also, similarly the case, and even in a greater de gree, with the eyes of most crabs. The lobster, however, is wholly of a splendid colour, but variegated with black spots. In the inferior part of its body, also, it has eight feet [orderly] disposed as far as to two large feet. But its two great feet are much larger than the rest; and in their extremities are much broader than the extremities of the feet of the locust. Its two large feet, like wise, are anomalous. For the right foot has its extremity broad. oblong, and thin ; but the left foot is thick and round. Each foot, however, is bipartite, and resembles a jaw, with teeth above and below; except that the right foot has, as it were, small, serrated teeth, but the left foot has serrated teeth in its extremity, and within, as it were, maxillary teeth. In the inferior part, also, it has four continued teeth ; but in the superior part three, which are not continued. Each foot, likewise, moves the superior part, and by it binds the inferior part. In the inferior part, too, each foot is distorted [i. e. inflected]; because each is naturally adapted, to lay hold of, and compress. Above these large feet, also, there are two other hairy feet, a little below the mouth; and a little below these there are many hairy gills, about the mouth, which the lobster continually moves. It, likewise, bends and moves to the mouth these two hairy feet ; and the feet which are near the mouth have thin beards adhering to them. The lobster, also, has two teeth in the same manner as the locust; but above these it has horns, which are shorter and thinner than those of the locust ; aiyl, besides these, it has four other horns, which are similar in form to these, but are shorter and thinner. Above these, too, it has small and short eyes, and has not, like the locust, large eyes. Again
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 115 Again, above the eyes there is, as it were, a sharp and rough forehead, larger than that of the locust. And, in short, the face of the lobster is sharper, but the thorax is much broader than the thorax of the locust, and the whole body is more fleshy and soft. But of its eight feet, four of them are bifidated ; and four of them are not. And, with respect to what is called the neck, it is divided, indeed, externally into five parts, and the sixth and last part is broad, and is divided into five ta- blets; but the internal parts, into Which the females deposit their eggs, consist of four hairy tablets. And in each of the above-mentioned tablets there is a short and erect spine, which extends outwardly. The whole body of the lobster, likewise, about the thorax is smooth, and is not rough, like that of the locust ; yet lobsters, in the external parts of the two large feet, have large thorns. There does not, however, ap- pear to be any difference in the male with respect to the female ; for both the male and the female have one claw, just as it may happen, larger than the other ; but they never have both of them equal. All crustaceous animals, however, receive the sea- water in their mouth; but crabs return the water which they receive by a narrower part of the mouth ; and locusts transmit the received water to the gills ; for locusts have many gills. But it is common to all these animals to have two teeth. For locusts have two primary teeth ; and in the mouth they have a fleshy substance instead of a tongue. The belly, also, in these animals immediately follows the mouth, except in locusts, which have a small stomach before the belly ; and after this the intestine im mediately follows. But this in locusts, in lobsters, and in squills, ends in a right line at the tail, where they emit the excrement, and bring forth their eggs. In crabs, however, [which are without a tail,] the intes tine ends where there is a certain covering, which is opened when the excrement is emitted, and shut after it is emitted ; from which part crabs, also, bring forth their eggs, since female crabs have a recep tacle of eo-gs near the intestine. All crustaceous animals, likewise, have that moisture which is called mytis or mecon, in a greater or in aless degree. It is, however, necessary, that we should now survey the several dis- ci 2 ferences
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 116 ferences of crustaceous animals. Locusts, therefore, as we have be- fore observed, have two large and hollow teeth, in which there is a juice similar to the moisture called mytis; and between the teeth there is a small piece of flesh, which is a species of tongue. After the mouth, also, there is a short oesophagus, and a membranous belly, adhering to this ; and in the mouth of this belly there are three teeth, two of which are opposite to each other ; but the third is below the other two. But the intestine, beginning and proceeding from the side of the belly, is simple, and of an equal thickness throughout, as far as to the egress of the excrement. Locusts, squills, and crabs, therefore, have these parts. Farther still, locusts have, also, an ave nue, which depending from the breast is extended, as far as to the egress of the excrement. But this, indeed, is the matrix of the female locust, and in the male is the receptacle of the genital seed. This avenue, however, is situated near the cavity of the flesh, so that the flesh is between this cavity and the intestine. For the intestine is constituted in the convex part, but the avenue is near the cavity; just as they subsist in quadrupeds. Indeed, this avenue in the male differs in no respect from that of the female ; for both are thin and white, and contain in themselves a pallid moisture, and both, also, are suspended from the breast. But after this manner squills have eggs, and certain spirals. The male, however, differs from the female in having in the flesh of the breast two white parts, which in colour and figure resemble the proboscis of the cuttle-fish. But these white parts are contorted in the same manner as the trumpet called mecon, and they derive their origin from the acetabula or joints, which are under the last feet. The breast, however, contains, also, red flesh, and is of of a sanguineous colour; but it is viscous to the touch, and does not resemble flesh [in general.] Near those two white parts, also, which are contorted like a trumpet, there is another spiral of the thickness of a string, under which there are two sandy substances, adhering to the intestine, and destined to the reception of the genital seed. These parts, therefore, the male possesses ; but the female squill lays eggs of a red
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 117 red colour, which are involved in a thin membrane, and are annexed to the belly, and each side of the intestine, as far as to the fleshy parts. These, therefore, are the parts as well internal as external of crustaceous animals. CHAPTER III. It happens, however, that the internal and external parts of sangui neous animals have [appropriate] appellations, [but the genus of exanguious animals wants many of those parts with which sanguine ous animals are indued.] For all sanguineous animals have viscera, but this is not the case with any exanguious animal. A belly, however, mouth, and intestine, are common both to exanguious and sanguine ous animals. With respect to the claws and feet of crabs, indeed, we have already shown the manner in which they subsist. For the most part, however, all of them have the right claAV larger and stronger than the left. We have, also, before spoken about the eyes of crabs, and shown that most of them look obliquely. But with respect to the mass of the body, the head, and the other parts of the trunk, are one indistinct whole. The eyes, however, are not in all of them in the same position ; but some of them have the eyes obliquely situated under the prone part of the back, and very much distant from each other; and others, as the he racleotic crabs, and those called maiœ, have the eyes in the middle, and near to each other. Under the eyes is the mouth, and in it there are two teeth, in the same manner as in locusts, except that the teeth of the crab are not round, but long. The teeth, also, of crabs are co vered with two valves, as it were, between which there is a certain fleshy part
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 118 BOOK IV part, which is used by them instead of a tongue, in the same manner as in locusts. They receive water, therefore, in the mouth by removing those valves, and return it by the superior avenues of the mouth, shut ting the valves through which it entered. These avenues, however, are immediately under the eyes; and when the water is received, they shut their mouth with both the valves, and thus afterwards eject the water they had received. After the teeth a stomach follows, so very small that the belly seems immediately to succeed after the mouth. But from the middle of the belly an intestine originates, which is simple and slender; and the intestine is terminated under the external part of the covering, as was before observed [in Chap. 2.] Within the cavity, also, or alvus of the crab, there is a pale [excrementitious] liquor, and toge ther with this certain small, oblong, white substances, and other red substances, variegated with spots. The male, however, differs from the female crab in magnitude, thickness, and covering. For the fe male has a covering [at the avenue of the intestine] larger, more dis tant, and more hairy, as is, also, the case in female locusts. After this manner, therefore, the parts of crustaceous animals subsist. CHAPTER IV. With respect to testaceous animals, however, snails, whether of the land or the sea, and all such as are called shell-fish, and besides these, the genus of sea hedge-hogs, if they have a fleshy substance have it similarly to crustaceous animals, for they have it inwardly ; but they have the shell externally, and inwardly they contain nothing hard [and analogous to bones.] They have, however, many differ ences with respect to themselves, both as to their shells, and the inter- nal
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 119 nal flesh. For some of them have not any flesh, as the sea hedge-hog; but others have flesh, indeed, yet have it perfectly inclosed in the shell, so that no part is apparent except the head, as is the case with land-snails, and the shell-fish, which are called by some cocalia, the buccina1, the murex3, and others of the turbinated kind. But of other testaceous animals, some are bivalves, and others univalves. I call, however, bivalves, those that are contained in two shells; and univalves, those that are contained in one shell, and of which the fleshy part is uncovered ; such, for instance, as the lepas. But of the bivalves, some can be opened [and shut,] as cockles and muscles ; for all such as these adhere to one shell, but do not adhere to the other, and can be opened and shut ; but others are bivalves, indeed, and ad- here to each shell, yet not so that they cannot be opened and shut, as the fishes called solenes. There are, also, some that are wholly con tained in the shell, so that no part of the flesh is externally naked, as those that are denominated in Greek tethya, [and in Latin are called vertibula, tubera, and calli.'] Again, in the shells of testaceous animals there is a difference with respect to each other. For some of them are smooth, as is the case with the solen, muscles, and certain shell-fish, called by some galades ; but others are rough, as oysters, the pinna, certain genera of shell-fish, and the buccina. And of these some, indeed, are striated, as the cockle, and a certain genus of shell-fish ; but others are not striated, as the pinnae, and a certain genus of shell-fish. Shells, likewise, differ in thickness and thinness, as well in the whole as in a part, as for in stance, about the lips or extremities. For some have thin lips, as mus cles ; but others thick, as marshy oysters (Ai^oT^a). Farther still, some testaceous animals move themselves, [and change their places] as the cockle ; for some say that scallops fly, since they frequently leap from the iron instrument by which they are caught. But other testaceous animals are immoveable, and are so fixed to a ■ Shell-fish, resembling a horn. ' A shell-fish, from the liquor of which the ancients made purple. place.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 120 place, that they can only be removed by force, as the pinna. All the turbinated kind, however, are moved, and creep ; and the lepas searches after nutriment when detached from the place to which it adheres. It is common, however, to these, and to other testaceous animals, to have a shell internally smooth. The flesh, also, as well of the univalves as the bivalves, so adheres to the shell, that it can only be divulsed from it by violence ; but the flesh of the turbinated kind is less adherent. It is peculiar, however, to the latter to have the shell turbinated from the head, and to have a spiral inflexion as far as to the bottom. AU testaceous animals, likewise, are covered with a shell from their birth. And farther still, all the turbinated kind are moved according to the right-hand part, not towards the spiral, but in an opposite direction. Such, then, are the differences of the external parts of these animals; but the nature of the internal parts, and especially in the turbinated kind, is after a manner similar in all of them. For they differ from each other in magnitude, and in the passive qualities pertaining to excess. The univalves, however, and shut bivalves do not much differ; for they have a small difference with respect to each other, but they have a great difference with respect to those testaceous animals that are im moveable. This, however, will be more evident from what will after wards be shown. But the nature of all the turbinated kind is similar; yet differs, as we have before observed, in excess. For some of them have larger and more manifest parts, but others have parts which are less and more obscure. They, likewise, differ in hardness and softness, and other such like passive qualities. For all of them have the flesh which is most external in the mouth of the shell firm, some, indeed* more, but others less ; but from the middle of the shell are the head and two horns. These, however, in larger testaceous animals, are large j but in those that are less, are very small. All of them* likewise, raise the head out of the shell after the same manner ; and when they are terrified, again draw it within the shell. Some of them, however, as the snail, have a mouth, and sharp, small, and thin teeth. They have, also, a proboscis, in the same^ manner as flies ; and this proboscis is in the form of a tongue. This proboscis, however, in the purple and buccina is
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 121 and hard. And as ox-flies, and horse-flies, pierce with their proboscis the skin of quadrupeds, in like manner these testaceous animals perfor ate the shells of others on which they feed. After the mouth immediately follows the belly, which resembles the craw of a bird, and is similar to the belly of the sea-snail. But in the inferior part they have two white and firm substances, similar to mam mæ ; such as are, also, found in the cuttle-fish, except that these are of a firmer consistence. After the belly, however, there is a long twofold stomach, which is extended as far as to the mecon [i. e. to the mem brane containing the excrements;] which membrane is in the bottom [of the navel.] These things, therefore, are manifest in the purple, and buccina, in the spiral of the shell. But the intestine follows the stomach, the whole of which is simple as far as to its egress. The be ginning, however, of the intestine is about the spiral of the mecony than which it is broader. For the mecon is as it were, for the most part, in all testaceous animals, full of an excrementitious matter. But after wards, the intestine being inflected upward, tends again to the fleshy parts, and terminates near the head ; from which place all turbinated testaceous animals, as well terrestrial as marine, eject their excrements. In large sea-snails, however, under the belly, a membrane is annexed to the stomach, from which a long and white avenue extends, and which is similar in colour to those fleshy parts which have the form ol mammæ. This avenue, also, has incisures similar to those which are in the egg of the locust, except that the colour of this avenue is white. but the egg of the locust is red. This avenue, however, has no egress, but is contained in the narrow cavity of a thin membrane. From the intestine, also, certain black and rough parts extend downward in a continued series, such as are in the tortoise, except that they are less black. Other snails, however, have these parts white, except that they are less in smaller snails. The univalves, also, and bivalves, are partly similar to snails, and partly dissimilar. For they have a head, horns, and a mouth, and a certain part which has the form of a tongue ; yet in less animals of this kind these parts, on account of their smallness, are immanifest ; and in 11 such
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK rv 122 such of them as are dead, or which are not moved, they cannot be perceived. All of them, however, have the mecon, yet not in the same place, nor of an equal magnitude, nor similarly manifest; but the lepas has it downward in the bottom, and the bivalves in the cavity next to the commissure of the two shells. All these, likewise, have certain capil laments circularly disposed, in the same manner as in cockles. And with respect to what is called an egg, it is contained, when they have it, in one side of the periphery of the circle, in the same place in which snails contain their white substance; for in them this has a similar sub sistence. All such parts, however, as we have mentioned, are indeed manifest in large testaceous animals ; but in those that are small they are either not at all, or scarcely visible. Hence, these are especially apparent in large cockles; and these are such as have one of the valves broad, and which serves them as a covering. With respect, however, to the egress of the excrement, in others it is obliquely; but what is called the egg [though it is a certain excrement], yet there is no avenue for its egress in any of these animals, but it comes forth from the flesh in the form of a swelling. Hence it is not in the same part in which the intestine is, but the egg, indeed, is in the right-hand, and the intes tine in the left-hand, parts. Such, therefore, in other testaceous animals, is the egress of the excrement; but in the savage lepas, which some call the marine ear, [because it resembles the human ear], the avenue through which the excrement is ejected is in the bottom part of the shell. It is, however, evident that the belly in this animal is immediately after the mouth, and, also, those substances in the form of an egg, [which we have before mentioned.] But the situation of the parts in all these animals must be surveyed from dissections. With respect, however, to what is called the small crab, it accords in some things with crustaceous, and in others with testaceous, animals. For ithas a nature similar to that of locusts, and is born unconnected with any shell ; but in consequence of entering into, and living in a shell, it resembles testaceous animals; so that it seems to partake of the nature both of testaceous and crustaceous animals. And, in short, the form of ithese animals resembles that of spiders, except that the part under the head
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 123 head and thorax is larger than in the spider. Thevhave, also, two slender red horns, and two small eyes under these, which do not recede inwardly, nor incline, like the eyes of crabs, but are direct. Under the eyes, like- wise, is the mouth, which is surrounded, as it were, with numerous capil- laments. And consequent to these are two bifurcated feet, by which they convey food to their mouth. There are, also, two other feet on each side, and a third small foot. The inferior part, however, of the thorax, is wholly soft, and within it a certain matter of a pale colour is contain- ed. One avenue, likewise, extends from the mouth to the belly ; but the avenue by which the excrementis emitted is not apparent; and the feet and the thorax are hard, indeed, but less so than in crabs. They do not, how- ever, adhere to the shell in the same manner as the purple and the buc- cina, but they easily liberate themselves from it. Those small crabs, also, that dwell in turbinated shells are longer than the neritæ, i.e. than those that dwell in sea-shells (ev roa vngnatf.) Though, however, the small crabs called neritæ are different from the turbinated kind, and, also, differ from them in length, yet in other respects they are not dissimilar to them. For in the neritæ, of the bifurcated feet which are under the mouth, the right foot is small, but the left is large ; and, therefore, in walking they more frequently use the left than the right foot. Among the shell-fish, however, which after the manner of testaceous animals adhere to the shell, there is one which they call the little lame fish. But the neritæ have a smooth, large, and round shell, and a form simi- lar to the buccina, except that they have not the mecon black, like the buccina, but red- They, also, firmly adhere to the middle of the shell. In fair weather, therefore, they leave their shell, and search for food ; but when the wind blows [violently] the small crabs betake themselves to rocks, and there quietly remain. But the neritæ adhere to rocks after the manner of the lepas, and the aporrhais, and others of the like kind. AU these, however, adhere to rocks, by removing the shell which serves them for a covering. For what both shells are to the bivalves that one shell is to those of the turbinated kind. Within the shell, however, there is a fleshy substance, and in this there is a mouth. The like, also, takes place in the aporrhais, in the purple, and all such r 2 like
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK TV. 124 like animals. Such of them, however, as have the leftfoot larger than the right, these never dwell in the shells of the turbinated kind, but dwell in the shells of the neritæ. But there are certain snails which contain in their shells animals similar to the small lobsters which are produced in rivers. They differ from them, however, in having the inward part of the shell soft. But the nature of their form must be surveyed from dissections. CHAPTER V. The sea hedge-hogs, however, have not a fleshy substance inter nally, like other testaceous animals ; for all of them are deprived of this, and instead of it, they have a certain black substance. But there are many genera of sea hedge-hogs ; one of which, indeed, is esculent. And these contain within themselves what are called eggs, which are large, and fit to be eaten, and are both in the larger and smaller sea hedge-hogs ; for they have these immediately from their birth. But what are called the spatages and brysses form the two other genera of sea hedge-hogs. These, however, dwell in the deep sea, and are rarely seen. Besides these, also, there are what are call ed echinometræ, or hedge-hog-mothers, and these are in magnitude the greatest of all the sea hedge-hogs. And, in addition to these, there is another small genus, which are covered with large and hard prickles; but these are produced at the depth of many fathoms in the sea, and are used by some as a remedy in stranguries. About Torone, how ever, there are white sea hedge-hogs, which have shells, prickles, and eggs, but they are greater in length than other sea hedge-hogs ; though their prickles are neither large nor strong, but soft. From the mouth, however,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 125 however, there are a great number of black parts, which are extended as far as to the external avenue, [or excretory duct], but are uncon joined with each other, and are separated by certain limits. Those sea hedge-hogs, likewise, that are esculent, are moved more frequently, and more rapidly, which is always indicated by their bristles, [to which some extraneous matter constantly adheres.] All of them, therefore, have eggs, but some are very small, and not sit to be eaten. It happens, however, that what are called the head and mouth in the hedge-hog are in the bottom part; but the part through which the excrement is emitted is upward ; and the very same thing happens in all testaceous animals of the turbinated kind, and in the lepas. For these animals search for their food in the ground, so that their mouth is towards the earth, where their nutriment is ; but the excrement is in the upward part, and in the prone parts of the shell, [i. e. in the parts directed towards the heavens.] The hedge-hog, also, has five teeth, which are inwardly hollow ; and in the middle of these there is a fleshy substance, which performs the office of a tongue. After this follows the stomach, and then the belly, which is divided into five parts, and is full of excrement. All the cavities of the belly, likewise, unite in one at the egress of the excrement, i. e. at the avenue where the shell of the hedge-hog is perforated. What are called eggs, how ever, are contained under the belly in another membrane, and these are equal in number in all of them; for they are five, and are, there fore, an odd number. But above the eggs are those black parts, which depend from the root of the teeth, and ape bitter, and not fit to be eaten. In many animals, however, a thing of this kind, or that which is analogous to it, happens ; for it happens in tortoises, in the hedge frog, in the common frog, in turbinated shell-fish, and in the mollia. But eggs of this kind differ in colour, and are either entirely unfit to be eaten, or more so than others. The body of the hedge-hog, therefore, is continued from the beginning to the end, but resembles a lamp, which is without a circular covering.. The hedge-hog, also, uses his prickles instead of feet for supporting himself, and being moved on these, he clianges his place. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV, 126 CHAPTER VI. Those animals, however, which are called tethya, [and in Latin are by some denominated vertibula, or calli, and which, by following the etymology of the Greek word, may be called mammillae,] have a cer- tain most peculiar nature ; for the whole body of these animals alone is concealed in a shell ; but the shell is of a substance between skin and shell, and on this account may be cut like a hard hide. This ani- mal, therefore, adheres by its shell to rocks. But it has two avenues, distant from each other, very small, and not easily seen, through which it emits and receives moisture ; for it has no apparent excrement, like other testaceous animals, such as that which is in the hedge^hog, or in that animal which is called mecon. When, however, they are opened, in the first place, they are found to have a nervous membrane about the shelly part, and in this the fleshy substance of this animal is con- tained, but it does not resemble the flesh of other animals. This flesh however, is similar in all the tethya. This flesh, also, adheres in two places to the membrane and the skin obliquely ; and where it adheres, it is in each place narrower. In these places, likewise, there are two avenues, through which these animals receive and eject nutriment and moisture, just as if one of these avenues was a mouth, but the other the passage through which the excrement is emitted. And one of these avenues, indeed, is thicker, but the other thinner, but within these is a cavity on each side, between which a certain small conti- nued substance intervenes, and in one of the cavities moisture is pro duced. They have not, however, any other part, either organic, or destined
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 127 destined to sensation, nor is any excrement found in them, as it is in other testaceous animals, as we have before observed. The colour, also, of this animal is partly pallid, and partly red. The sea-nettle, also, constitutes a peculiar genus of animals. It ad heres, however, to rocks in the same manner as some testaceous ani mals, but is sometimes liberated from them. It, likewise, has no shell, but the whole of its body is fleshy. But it is sensitive, and seizes the hand, to which also it adheres, [of any one that touches it,] in the same manner as the polypus with its arms, so as to cause the flesh of the hand to swell. It has, also, a mouth in the middle of its body, and lives in a rock just as testaceous animals live in a shell. It, likewise, takes, as if it were a hand, any little fish that may fall in its way; and if it meets with any thing esculent it eats it. A certain genus, also, cf the sea-nettle is liberated from rocks, and eats the hedge-hogs and cockles that may fall in its way. These animals, however, do not appear to have any excrement, but in this respect they resemble plants. There are, also, two genera of sea-nettles ; one of which, indeed, is less, and more eatable; but the other is large and hard, such as are those which are produced about Chalcis. In winter, therefore, their flesh is firm, and on this account they are then sought after, and are eatable ; but in summer they are dissolved. For then they become fluid, are rapidly dispersed by the touch, and in short cannot be pluck ed. But when they suffer very much from the heat, they betake themselves into the more interior parts of rocks. And thus much con cerning the parts, as well exterior as interior, of the mollia, and of crustaceous and testaceous animals. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV» THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 128 CHAPTER VII. Let us, however, after the same manner, speak concerning insects;, But this genus contains many species in itself; though to some, which are allied to each other, no common name is assigned; as, for instance, to the bee, the drone, the wasp, and others of the same kind. fThh is, also, the case with such as have wings inclosed in a sheath, as the green beetle, the beetles called pilularii, [who make a ball from dung] the cantharides, and the like. Of all insects, therefore, there are three common parts, viz. the head, the cavity about the belly, and the third, that which is between these, which corresponds to the breast and back of other animals. This middle part, however, which is be tween the head and the belly, is in most insects one, [and is not dis tinguished by any incisures] ; but in insects that are long, and have many feet, the intermediate parts are nearly as numerous as the incis ures. All insects, likewise, wdien divided have life, except those which are very cold, or which on account of their smallness are soon refri gerated [when divided,] since wasps, also, live when they are divided. The head, therefore, and the belly live together with the middle part, [when the insect is divided,] but without this part the head does not live. But such insects as have a long body, and many feet, live for a long time when divided, and the part which is cut off is moved to either extremity, for it moves both towards the head, and towards the tail, as is evident in what is called the scolopendra. All insects, likewise, have eyes, but no other organ of sense is appar ent; except that some have a tongue, which all testaceous animals have,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 129 have, and this they employ both for tasting their food, and drawing it to them. The tongue, however, in some insects is soft, but in others. as in the purple, is very hard and strong. The ox-fly, also, the horse fly, and nearly most other insects, have a strong tongue. For in all in sects that have not a sting behind, the tongue is as it were a weapon ; but such as have a sting have no teeth, a certain few excepted ; since flies by inserting this [i. e. their tongue] draw blood, and gnats pierce with this. Some insects, however, have stings. But some, indeed, contain the sting in themselves, as bees, and wasps ; and others have it externally, as the scorpion, which is the only insect that has a long tail. This insect, also, has claws ; and, likewise, the little kind of scor pion, which is engendered in books. Insects that fly, however, in addition to other parts, have wings. And some of them, indeed, have two wings, as flies ; but others have four wings, as bees. No flying insect, however, that has a sting be- hind has only two wings. Farther still, some flying insects have their wings enclosed in a certain sheath, as the beetle; but others have them uncovered, as the bee. But no flying insect steers its course by its tail, and the wing has not any stem, or scissure. Again, some insects have small horns before their eyes, as the butterfly, and the grasshopper; but in such of them as are formed for leaping, the hind are larger than the fore legs, and the legs by which they leap are con- cave before, and convex behind, in the same manner as the legs of quadrupeds. All insects, however, have the prone different from the supine parts, in the same manner as other animals ; but the flesh of their body is neither testaceous, nor such as that which is contained under the shell of testaceous animals, but has a middle nature be- tween these. Hence they have neither spine nor bone, nor any part analogous to bone, such as that is which is called sepium in the cuttle- fish ; nor are they surrounded by a shell. For their body on account of its hardness preserves itself, and docs not require any other support. They have, however, a skin, but this is very thin. Such, therefore, are the external parts of insects, and after this manner they subsist. But inwardly, immediately after the mouth is s the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 130 the intestine, which in most insects is straight and simple, as far as to its exit; but in some few it has convolutions. No insect, however, has either viscera, or fat, as neither has any other exanguious animal. But some, of them have a belly, and from this the remaining intestine is either simple, or convolved, as in the locust. The grasshopper, also, is the only insect, and, indeed, is the only animal, that has not a mouth; but, instead of a mouth, has along, compact, and undivided part, simi lar to that tongue-like substance which is in animals that have a sting behind. Through this part the grasshopper is alone nourished with dew ; but it has no excrement in the belly. There are, however, many species of these insects, and they differ in magnitude and parvitudc. The grasshoppers, also, which are called canorous, are divided under the transverse septum, in which they have a visible membrane, which small grasshoppers have not. There are, however, certain peculiar animals in the sea which, be cause they are rare, cannot be referred to any certain genus. For now some experienced fishermen say, that they have seen in the sea ani mals resembling black and round pieces of wood, of an equal thick ness; and also other animals resembling shields, of a red colour, and furnished with numerous wings. They, likewise, report that they Jhave seen some animals similar in form and magnitude to the puden dum of a man, except that, instead of testicles, they have two wings ; and that such an animal was once caught by the top of the instru ment [used by fishermen,] which consists ,of many hooks. After this manner therefore, the external and internal parts of all animals in each genus, as well peculiar as common, subsist. chap.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 131 CHAPTER VIII. Let us, however, now speak concerning the senses. For they are not similarly present with all animals, but some have all the senses, and others not all. But the greatest number of the senses, and be sides which there does not appear to be any other sense, is five ; viz. the sight, the hearing, the smell, the taste, and the touch. Man, therefore, and terrestrial viviparous animals, and besides these, san guineous viviparous animals, are seen to possess all these senses, except some mutilated genus, such as that of moles ; since this is deprived of sight. For the mole has not eyes externally apparent ; but if a thick skin is taken off from the head, and which is in the place of the eyes, certain corrupted eyes will be seen within, which have all the parts of perfect eyes. For they have the black part of the eye, and within the black what is called the pupil, and the white circle, [which is called the white of the eye.] These, however, are less than in animals which have eyes [externally] apparent. But no one of these parts is exter nally visible, on account of the thickness of the skin with which the eyes of moles is covered from the first, as if nature was mutilated in their generation. For their eyes originate from the brain ; and from that part in which the brain is conjoined with the optic nerve two nervous and strong avenues extend to the seat of the eyes, and are ter minated in the upper teeth of the mole, which project beyond the mouth. Other animals, however, have a sensible perception of co lours and sounds, and besides these of odours and sapours. All other animals, likewise, have that fifth sense which is called the touch. s 2 In
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV 132 In some animals, therefore, the sensoria are most apparent, and espe cially the sensorium of vision. For they have the place of the eyes and the hearing definitely assigned ; since some of them have ears, and others [instead of ears] have visible avenues. The like, also, takes place with respect to the smell ; for some, indeed, have nostrils, but others, as the genus of birds, have the avenues of smelling. In a simi lar manner, also, they have a tongue, as the sensorium of sapours. Aqua tic animals, however, which are called fishes, have indeed a tongue, the sensorium of sapours, but they have it obscurely; for it is bony, and not detached, [but adhering to the inferior part of the mouth]. In some fishes, also, the palate is fleshy; as, of river fishes, in the carp ; so that to those who have more accurately surveyed these fishes, the palate has appeared to be a tongue. That fishes, however, have the sense of taste is evident; for they are very much delighted with peculiar sapours, and they are especially caught by the bait of the fish hamia, and by the fat of fishes, as delighting in a taste of this kind, and in food formed from such like baits. But they have not any apparent sensorium of hearing and smelling. For though, about the place of the nostrils, they have certain avenues which to some may appear to be the organs of smelling, yet such avenues do not extend as far as to the brain, but in some they are blind, and in others extend as far as to the gills. But that fishes hear and smell is evident. For they are seen to fly from very loud sounds, such as those which are made by the rowing of the three-ranked gallies ; so that, in consequence of their flight, they are easily taken in their caverns. For a sound which out of the water is but little, yet to all those that hear it in the water is found to be vio lent, loud, and oppressive; which also takes place in fishing for dol phins. For fishermen, when they have collected the dolphins about their boats, by making a noise in the sea cause the affrighed dolphins to leap on shore, where they are taken, their head being oppressed by the sound; though neither have dolphins any apparent sensorium of hear ing- Farther still, fishermen in catching fish are especially careful not to make any boms with their nets or oars. Hence, when they understand that
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 133 that many fishes are collected together in a certain place, they drop their nets at such a distance as they think is sufficient to prevent the fishes from hearing them, being cautious lest any sound should arrive at that place, either from the oars, or the motion of the boat. They, likewise, admonish all the sailors to row with the greatest silence, till the fishes are entirely surrounded with the nets. Sometimes, also, when they wish the fishes to assemble together, they adopt the same method as in fish ing for the dophin. For they make a noise by throwing stones, that the fishes being terrified may assemble in one place, and that thus they may surround them with their nets. And before they enclose them, as we have said, they forbid the sailors to make a noise; but when they have surrounded them with their nets, they order the sailors to make a loud noise ; because the fishes, hearing the noise and the tumult, fall into the net through fear. Again, when fishermen see from a great distance a collected multi tude of fishes feeding and swimming on the surface of a tranquil sea, and when they are likewise desirous to perceive their magnitude, and of what kind they are, if they sail near to them without any noise, they latently catch them, while they are yet swimming on the surface ; but if prior to this any noise happens to have been made, their visible flight is the consequence. Farther still, in rivers there are little fishes under rocks, which some call xoiToi, gulls ; and these are caught by certain persons through strik ing the rocks in which they are concealed with stones; for these fishes on hearing the sound come forth, having their head oppressed with the noise. From particulars of this kind, therefore, it is evident that fishes hear. There are, however, some who assert that fishes hear the most acutely of all animals; and this they confirm by the authority of those who dwell near the sea, and who assert that they have found this to be true by repeated experiments. But the fishes which excel in acuteness of hearing are the mullet, the chremps, the sea- wolf, the stock-fish, the chro mis, and others of the like kind. Other fishes, however, hear less acutely than these and hence they principally live near the bottom of the sea. In a similar manner, also, it may be proved that fishes have the sense
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 134 sense of smelling. For the greater part of them is only to be caught with a recent bait ; and all fishes are not caught with the same baits, but with particular baits, which they know by the smell. Some, indeed, are caught by fetid baits; as, for instance, the stock-fish by dung. Again, many fishes live in caverns ; and fishermen when they wish to catch them anoint the mouth of the cave with briny odours, by which the fishes are soon allured [and taken]. After this manner, also, eels are caught. For fishermen, in order to catch them, use a certain vessel con- taining brine, in the mouth of which they place the collar of a bow-net. In short, all fishes are allured by the smell of roasted flesh ; and hence fishermen roasting the flesh of the cuttle-fish, use the smell of it as a bait -, for fishes are thus more easily caught. They also say that fishermen put into their nets roasted polypi, on no other account than for the sake of the smell. Farther still, the fishes called ruades, when the lotion or the filth of fishes is discharged, fly from it, in consequence of smelling the fetid odour. They, likewise, say that fishes quickly smell the blood of those of their own species. This, indeed, is evident by their flying to distant places when the blood of fishes is poured forth. And, in short, if putrid baits are put into the nets, fishes will neither be will ing to enter into nor approach the nets; but if the bait consists of fresh roasted meat, they will immediately tend to it, though at a dis tance, and enter into the nets. What has been said, however, is especi ally evident in dolphins. For these have no apparent sensorium of hearing, but they are caught in consequence of being oppressed with a heaviness in the head from sound, as was before observed. Neither, likewise, have they any apparent sensorium of smelling ; and yet they smell acutely. That these animals, therefore, have all the senses is evident ; but the remaining genera of animals have a fourfold division, which compre hends the mollia, crustaceous and testaceous animals, and besides these insects. Of these, however, the mollia, crustaceous animals, and insects, have all the senses ; for they have sight, the smell, and the taste. For insects, as well those that have as those that are without wings, perceive at a distance. Thus, for instance, bees, and the cnipes [a kind of gnats have
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 135 have a sensible perception of honey ; for they perceive it at a distance, as knowing it by the smell ; and many insects perish from the smell of sulphur. Farther still, if the powder of sulphur and wild marjoram is sprinkled over the habitation of ants, they leave their holes ; and the greater part of such kind of insects fly from the odour of the burnt horn of a stag ; but they especially avoid the fume of storax. The cuttle-fish, likewise, the polypi, and the lobster, are caught by baits ; and the polypus so pertinaciously adheres to a bait, as to suffer himself to be cut in pieces rather than be divulsed from it. If, however, any one presents to him the herb flea-bane, it is said, that as soon as he smells it, he will drop the bait. The like, also, takes place with respect to the taste. For sometimes insects pursue a different food, and all of them are not delighted with the same sapours. Thus, for instance, bees do not approach to any thing fetid, but to what is sweet ; and the conops, or gnat, does not fly to any thing sweet, but to what is acid. To have a sensible perception, nowever, by the touch is, as we have before observed, common to all animals. But testaceous animals have, indeed, the smell and the taste ; and this is evident from the baits by which they are caught ; as, for instance, in the purple fish. For this animal is allured by putrid substances, and approaches to a bait of this kind, as having a sensible perception of it at a distance. That testaceous animals, also, have a sensation of sapours is evident from the same arguments ; for each of them is de lighted with the sapour of those substances to which it is allured by the smell. And again, such as have a mouth receive either pleasure or pain from the contact of sapours. With respect, however, to the sight and hearing of testaceous ani mals, nothing stable nor very apparent can be asserted. But the so lenes are seen to withdraw themselves, and to subside lower, when they perceive the iron instrument by which they are caught ; for a small part of their body only is seen, but the rest is as if it were in a place of retreat. And with respect to cockles, if any one presents his finger to them they open and shut themselves, as having the sense of sight. Aad
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 136 And those who catch the shell-fish called neritæ do not approach them with a bait when the wind blows, nor speak, but are silent, because these animals both smell and hear ; for if those that are employed in catching the neritæ speak, it is said they withdraw themselves. Of tes taceous animals, however, which have a progressive motion, the hedge hog, but of those that are without motion the tethya, and the sea acorns (Qatevu), appear to have the sense of smell in the smallest degree. After this manner, therefore, the sensoria subsist in all animals. CHAPTER IX. Voice, however, differs from sound ; and the third of these is speech. No animal, therefore, is vocal by any other part than the pharynx; and hence such animals as are without lungs are not vocal. But speech is the articulation of voice by the tongue. The voice, therefore, and the larynx emit what we call vowels, but the tongue and the lips conso nants ; from which two speech consists. Hence such animals as have not a tongue, or have it adhering to the inferior part of the mouth, do not speak. But the other parts of the body are capable of producing a sound. Insects, therefore, have neither voice nor speech. They produce a sound, however, by the internal, but not by the external, air* For no insect respires ; but some of them utter a humming sound, as bees, and winged insects ; and others are said to sing, as grasshoppers. All these, however, produce a sound by the attrition of the internal air, which subsists within a membrane under the division called the trans verse septum, as, for instance, the genus of grasshoppers; and this is, likewise,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 137 likewise, the case with flies, bees, and all the rest, in consequence of raising and depressing that membrane when they fly. For [such] sound is produced by the attrition of the internal air. But crickets pro duce a sound through the attrition of the legs by which they leap. Neither any one of the mollia, however, nor any crustaceous animal has a voice, or produces any natural sound. Fishes, also, are without voice, since they have neither the trachea nor the pharynx. Those, however, that are said to be vocal emit certain sounds and noises, as the fish called the lyre and the chromis; for they emit as it were a certain grunting ; and this is, also, the case with that fish, in the river Achelous, called the wild-boar ; and with the chalcis and cuckow. For the first of these fishes produces a kind of whistling ; but the second emits a sound similar to that of the bird called a cuckow ; whence, also, it derives its name. All these fishes, however, that appear to utter a voice, pro duce it either by the attrition of the more rigid gills which they possess, or of the air which they contain in the cavity of their belly. For in each of these there is a hot air, the attrition and motion of which pro duce sounds. Those cartilaginous fishes, also, called the selache ap pear to produce a stridulous sound. These, however, cannot be properly said to have a voice, but to produce a sound. For cockles Avhen they are seen floating on the surface of the water, which they call flying, make a crashing noise ; and this is, also, the case with the swallows of the sea: For these fly high, and do not touch the sea, their wings be ing broad and long. As, therefore, the sound produced by the wings of flying birds is not voice, so neither is the sound produced by any thing of the above-mentioned kind. The dolphin, likewise, produces a stri dulous sound, and murmurs when he comes into the air, yet not in a manner similar to the before-mentioned fishes. For the sound emitted by the dolphin is voice ; since he has lungs and a trachea, but his tongue is not loose, and he has no lips, so that he cannot produce articulate voice. But of those animals which have a tongue and lungs, such as are oviparous and quadrupeds, emit a voice, which is, however, feeble. And some, indeed, produce a hissing sound, as serpents ; but others a slender and feeble voice ; and others a small hissing, as tortoises. The t frog,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 138 frog, however, has a peculiar tongue. For the anterior part, which is detached from the other parts of the tongue, adheres after the manner of the tongue of fishes; but the parts of the tongue near the pharynx, by which the frog emits his peculiar voice, are detached and expanded. The male frogs, also, produce a croaking in the water when they call females to coition. For all animals have peculiar voices significant of the desire of coition, as is evident in swine, goats, and sheep. Frogs, however, produce that [venereal] croaking by making the lip of the lower jaw to be equally under the water, and extending the upper jaw above the water. But their jaws becoming luminous from the exten sion, their eyes have the appearance of lamps ; for they are seen to copulate for the most part by night. The genus of birds, however, is vocal ; and such as have a moder ately broad tongue, and, also, such of them as* have a thin tongue, have especially the faculty of speech. Some of them, therefore, as well male as female, have the same voice ; but others have a differ ent voice. Less, also, have a louder voice, and are more loquacious than larger birds ; and every bird at the time of coition is more loqua cious than at any other time. Some birds, likewise, as the quail, are vocal when they fight ; others, prior to the combat, call on their oppon ents to engage, [as the partridge]; and others are vocal when they have conquered, as the cock. And with some genera of birds, indeed, the males sing as well as the females ; as for instance, both the male and female nightingale sing; except that the female nightingale ceases to sing during the time of her incubation, and while she rears her young. But in some genera of birds, as cocks and quails, the power of voice belongs rather to the males, and the females do not sing. Different viviparous quadrupeds, however, have a different voice, yet none of them has the faculty of speech; but this is the peculiarity of man. For such animals as have the faculty of speech are also vocal ; but not all such as are vocal have the faculty of speech. All such, too, as are deaf from their birth are likewise dumb ; and though they are vo cal, yet are entirely deprived of speech. But children as they cannot at first manage the other parts of the body, so neither can they use the tongue.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 139 tongue. The tongue, also, at first is imperfect, and it is some time before it is detached ; so that children, for the most part, lisp and stutter. Voice and speech, also, differ according to places. Voice, there- fore, is, indeed, especially manifest by acuteness, and gravity ; nor is there any specific difference in [inarticulate] voices of the same genera. But the difference in articulate voice, which may be called as it were speech, differs according to places in different animals, and, also, in animals belonging to the same genus. Thus, with respect to partridges, the voice of some of them repeats the syllables cac, cac, but of others tri, tri. And some small birds, if they are taken from their parents, so that they cannot be educated by them, do not emit the same voice as their parents, but become accustomed to the manners and singing of other birds. A nightingale, also, has been seen instructing her young in singing ; so that speech and voice are not similarly natural, but the former may be acquired by instruction. Men, likewise, have, indeed, the same voice, but not the same speech. The elephant, how ver, is vocal, not through the nose [or proboscis], but emits a windy voice through the mouth, such as men emit when they breathe, and at the same time speak ; but with his proboscis he emits a hoarse sound, which resembles the sound of a trumpet. CHAPTER X. With respect, however, to the sleep and wakefulness of animals, it is obvious to sense that all such as are pedestrious, and sanguineous sleep, and are wakeful ; for all such as have eyelids sleep by closing them. Again, not only men are seen to dream, but, also, horses, dogs, T 2 and
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 140 and oxen ; and besides these, sheep, and goats, and every genus of viviparous quadrupeds. Dogs, also, evince this by barking when they are asleep. With respect, however, to oviparous animals, it is immani fest whether they dream ; but that they sleep is evident. In like man ner aquatic animals sleep, such as fishes, the mollia, crustaceous ani mals, locusts, and others of the same kind. All such animals, there fore, though they are seen to sleep, yet sleep but for a short time. But an indication of this cannot be obtained from their eyes, for they have no eyelids, but from the quiet state of their bodies. For fishes are easily caught with the hand while they are asleep, unless they are roused by certain animals, which are called pulices and pediculi. Now, however, if fishes sleep for a long time during the night, they are devoured by these animalcula, which are very numerous. They are, likewise, produced in the profundity of the sea, and are so numer ous that the bait made from a fish is consumed by them, if it con tinues for any length of time on the land. And it frequently happens that fishermen, when they draw the bait out of the sea, find these ani malcula collected about it, so as to form as it were a sphere. It may, however, in a greater degree be inferred that they sleep from such circumstances as the following ; For fishermen frequently attack fishes so latently as to take them in their hand, or strike their harpoon into them, without their being conscious of it. But during the time of their sleep they are very quiet, and only gently move their tails. Their agitation, also, if any thing is moved while they are quiet evinces that they sleep ; for they shake, as if roused from sleep. Farther still, fishes are likewise taken in rocks, in consequence of being asleep in them. Frequently, also, fishermen enclose the tunny in their nets while they are asleep ; but it is evident that they are asleep from their being taken in a state of rest, and gently disclosing the white of their eyes. The tunny, however, sleep by night rather than by day, and so profoundly as not to be moved by the throwing of the harpoon. For the most part, also, fishes sleep either on the sand, or on the land, or adhering to some stone in the profundities of the sea, or concealing themselves under a rock or bank ; and flat fishes conceal
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 141 conceal themselves while they sleep in the sand. They are detected, however, by the figure of the sand, and are caught by striking them with a trident. With this instrument, likewise, the sea-wolf, the gold fish, the mullet, and others of the same kind, are caught in the day, in consequence of being asleep ; but it does not appear that any of these are caught with the trident, unless they are asleep. But those cartilaginous fishes called selache sometimes sleep so profoundly as to be caught by the hand. The dolphin, however, the whale, and such fishes as have a pipe [through which they eject the water], sleep, ele vating this pipe, through which they respire, above the sea, and gently moving their fins. Some, also, assert that they have heard the dolphin snore. The mollia, likewise, sleep after the same manner as fishes ; and similarly with these, crustaceous animals. That insects, also, sleep, is evident from such indications as the fol lowing : For they are sometimes manifestly quiet and without motion, and this is especially evident in bees ; for by night they are still, and cease to hum. And this is manifest in those insects with which we are especially conversant, [viz. in flies.] For they are quiet by night, not only because they do not then acutely see, for all animals that have hard eyes see obscurely, but when near the light of a lamp they are nevertheless seen to be quiet. Man, however, dreams the most of all animals. And infants, in deed, and very young children do not dream ; but, for the most part, children begin to dream about the fourth or fifth year of their age. There are, also, some men and women that have never known a dream. Some of these, however, as they have advanced in years have begun to dream, after which a change has taken place in their body ; in some, indeed, the change terminating in death, but in others in disease. Ajid thus much concerning sense, and sleep, and wakefulness. CHAP
