text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS, BOOK IV, 142 CHAPTER XL The male and female, however, are inherent in some animals, but not in others ; though, according to a certain similitude, they are said to bring forth and to be pregnant. There is, indeed, no distinction of male and female in stable animals, [i. e. which are fixed to one place,] nor, in short, in testaceous animals. But in the mollia, and in crusta ceous animals, there is the distinction of male and female, and also in pedestrious animals, in bipeds and quadrupeds, and in all such as from coition produce an animal, or an egg, or a worm. In other ani mals, therefore, this is either simple or not simple. Thus, for instance, in all quadrupeds there is the distinction of male and female, but in testaceous animals there is not; but as in plants, some are prolific, and others are sterile, so likewise in these. In insects, however, and fishes, there are some which are so deprived of this distinction of sex that they cannot generate an offspring, and therefore are neither male nor female, and such are eels. But those who assert that eels are sometimes seen to have capillaments and worms adhering to them, [internally] speak inconsiderately, not having previously surveyed where these worms subsist. For no animal of this kind contains with in itself an animal, unless it has first conceived an egg; but no eel has ever been found to have an egg. Such animals, also, as are vivipar ous, contain the foetus in the womb, and not in the belly ; for if it were contained in the belly, it would be concocted in the same man ner as nutriment. But the difference which they speak of between the male and female eel, viz. that the male has a larger and longer head.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK rv. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 143 head, but the female a more depressed head, is not to be ascribed to the difference of sex, but of genus. There are, however, certain fishes which are called epitrageæ, [from the sterility of a goat,] and such among river fishes are the carp, and the baris ; but such fishes have neither an egg, nor any prolific seed, and such of them as are solid, and fat, have a small intestine, and are excellent food. Farther still, as in the genus of testaceous animals and plants, so in the genus of fishes, there are some which bring forth of themselves and generate, though they do not copulate ; and of this kind are place, the roach, and cockles, and all such as these are seen to have eggs. In pedestrious and sanguineous animals, therefore, which are not oviparous, the males are for the most part larger, and live longer than the females, the mule excepted ; for among mules, the females live longer, and are larger than the males. But in oviparous and vivipar ous animals, as in fishes and insects, the females are larger than the males, as is evident in serpents, in the spiders called phalangia, in liz ards, and frogs. The like, also, takes place in fishes, as in the small selache, in the greater part of fishes that live in shoals, and in all that are called saxatiles, [or living among rocks.] That among fishes, how ever, the females live longer than the males is evident from the females that are caught being older than the males. The males, however, in all animals, have the superior and anterior parts better, stronger, and more vigorous ; but the females, those parts which may be called posterior and inferior. And this is the case, not only in the human species, but also in other pedestrious and viviparous animals. The female, likewise, is less nervous and more infirm than the male, and the hair in such females as have hair, or that which is analogous to hair, is thinner. The flesh, also, of females is more humid, their knees are more liable to crack, and their legs are thinner; but their feet are more elegant, viz. in such animals as have these parts. With respect to voice, too, the voice of all females, except that of the cow, is more slender and acute : for the cow has a graver voice than the bulL But with respect to the parts which nature has given to animals for
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 144 for their defence, such as teeth, fangs, horns, spurs, and other such like parts, in some genera, indeed, the male has these, but the female has not. Thus for instance, the female stag has no horns ; and among such birds as have spurs, the females of some of them are entirely with out spurs. In a similar manner, also, the females among swine have no fangs. In some genera of animals, however, these parts exist both in the male and female, but they are more excellent in the former than in the latter. Thus, the horns of bulls are stronger than those of cows. THE

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. CHAPTER I. IN the preceding books, therefore, we have spoken concerning the in ternal and external parts of animals ; and farther still, concerning their senses, voice, and sleep, and the difference between the males and the females. Hence it remains, that we should now direct our attention to their generation, and in the first place discuss such particulars as are first. The generations, however, of animals are many, and possess much variety ; being, indeed, in one respect dissimilar, but in another similar, to each other. Since, also, the genera of animals was first di vided by us, we must now endeavour that the speculation shall be formed after the same manner ; except that, then, in speculating about the parts, we made the beginning from man, but now we shall speak u about
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V 146 about man in the last place, because the generation of man requires the most ample discussion. But we shall first begin from testaceous animals ; afterwards speak of such as are crustaceous ; and then dis cuss the rest after this manner, in an orderly series. And these are the mollia and insects. After these, we shall direct our attention to the genus of fishes, both the viviparous and the oviparous ; and then con sider the genus of birds. And, in the next place, we shall speak con cerning the generation of pedestrious animals, as well viviparous as oviparous. But some quadrupeds are viviparous, and man is the only biped that is viviparous. A common circumstance, therefore, happens in the generation of ani mals, as well as in the generation of plants. For of plants some are generated from the seed of other plants, but others are generated spon taneously from analogous causes. And of these some receive their nutriment from the earth, but others are ingenerated in other plants, as we have shown in the speculation concerning plants. Thus, also, with respect to animals, some indeed are generated from animals, ac cording to an alliance of form ; but others have a spontaneous origin, and not from kindred natures. And of these some are generated from putrid earth and plants, as happens to be the case with many insects ; but others are generated in animals themselves, and from the excre ments in the parts of animals. Animals, however, which are generated from kindred animals, if there is the distinction in them of male and female, are generated from coition. But in the genus of fishes, some are generated neither male nor female, and though they accord in genus yet differ in spe cies from other fishes, and some are entirely peculiar. There are, also, some fishes, among Avhich there are females without males, and from which, in the same manner as in birds, windy eggs are produced. All such eggs of birds, however, are unprolific, but the nature of these birds is able to accomplish the generation of an egg, unless some other mode of communication with the males happens to them ; which particulars, however, will be more acurately discussed hereafter. But it happens to certain fishes, when they generate spontaneous eggs, that animals
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 147 animals are produced from them, except that some produce these ani mals from themselves, but others not without the co-operation of the male. The manner, however, in which this is effected will be evident in what follows ; for nearly the same thing takes place in birds. But from such animals as are generated spontaneously either in the earth, or in plants, or in the parts of these, if they have the distinction of male and female, from the copulation of these something is produced, from which, however, nothing else can be generated. Thus, for in stance, from the copulation of lice what are called lendes are gener ated ; from the copulation of flies certain worms are produced ; and from the copulation of fleas, worms in the shape of eggs. From these, however, neither any other animal, nor any thing else, but things of this kind alone are generated. In the first place, therefore, we must speak of coition, and of the animals which generate from coition ; and afterwards discuss other particulars, which follow in an orderly series, and the accidents both peculiar and common which pertain to their generation. CHAFsER II. Those animals, therefore, copulate in which there is a distinction of male and female. The copulations, however, are neither similar in all animals, nor have they a similar mode of subsistence. For in all san guineous animals that are viviparous and pedestrious, the males have organs adapted to such a generative act, yet all of them do not simil arly approach to the female ; but those that discliarge the urine back- u 2 ward,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 148 ward, as lions, hares, and lynxes, copulate backward*; and with re spect to hares, the female frequently gets on the back of the male. The mode of copulation, likewise, is the same in the greater part of other animals. For the usual mode of copulation with most quadru peds is for the male to get on the female ; and this mode is adopted by the whole tribe of birds. There are, however, certain differences with respect to birds. For with some, while the female sits on the oround, the male gets upon her, and this is the case with the bustard, and the cock ; but with others, as with cranes, the female does not sit on the ground, during the act of coition ; for among these the male leaping is conjoined with the female, and the copulation is rapidly ac complished, in the same manner as with sparrows. Of quadrupeds, however, bears lying on the ground copulate in the same manner as other animals who rest on their feet during the act, the supine parts of the male being in contact with the prone parts of the female ; but land hedge-hogs copulate erect, having the supine parts in contact with each other. Among large viviparous animals, however, the female stags do not suffer the males to have connexion with them, unless rarely, nor the cow the bull, on account of the stiff ness of the penis, but as they withdraw themselves from the male they receive the genital seed ; for this has been seen to happen in tame stags. But wolves copulate after the same manner as dogs ; and cats do not copulate backward, but the male is erect, and the female places herself under him. Females, however, are naturally libidin ous, incite the males to copulation, and cry out during the act of coi tion. But camels copulate the female sitting, and the male covers her, not having his buttocks in an opposite direction, but in the same manner as other quadrupeds. They continue, likewise, in the act for a whole day ; but when they copulate withdraw into solitude, and it is not then safe for any one but the herdsman to approach them. The penis also of the camel is so nervous that the string of a bow may be made from it. Elephants, likewise, copulate in solitary places, and i. e. The buttocks of the one being in an opposite direction to the buttocks of the other. especially
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 149 especially near rivers, and where they are accustomed to dwell. But the female elephant copulates lowering her body, and removing her legs ; and the male gets upon her back. The sea-calf, also, copulates after the same manner as animals that discharge the urine backward, and, as well as dogs, are a long time in the act of coition. The males, likewise, have a large penis. CHAPTER III. Among pedestrious animals, also, oviparous quadrupeds copulate after the same manner. For, just as with viviparous animals, the males of some of these get on the back of the female, and this is the case with the land and sea tortoise. But the avenues have something with which they are conjoined, and to which they approximate in coition, as is evident in the turtle-dove, the frog, and every such like genus of animals. CHAPTER IV. But animals without feet, and which have a long body, as the ser pent and the lamprey, copulate by enfolding the supine parts with the supine, [i. e. the belly with the belly.] And serpents are so closely en- folded
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 150 folded in the embraces of each other, that the whole body appears to be one serpent with two heads. This is, also, the case with the genus of lizards; for they copulate with a similar circumplication. CHAPTER V. Ali, fishes, however, except the broad selache, copulate by uniting the supine parts [i. e. the belly] with the supine. But the broad se lache, and which, also, have a tail, such as the thornback, the pas tinaca, and others of this kind, not only copulate by uniting the su pine parts, but by the supine parts of the male being placed on the back of the female, unless the tail is an impediment on account of its thickness. The skate, however, and such as have a thick tail, copu late by the attrition alone of the supine with the supine parts. There are, also, some who report, that they have seen certain selache copu late behind, in the same manner as dogs. But in every class of the selache the female is larger than the male ; and nearly, also, in other fishes, the females are larger than the males. The fishes, however, above-enumerated are comprehended among the selache, and also the sea-ox, the lamia, the eagle, the torpedo or cramp fish, the sea frog, and all the species of sea-dogs. All the selache, therefore, have been clearly seen by many to copulate after this manner. For the connexion of all viviparous is of a longer duration than the con nexion of oviparous animals. Dolphins, likewise, and all animals of the cetaceous kind, copulate after the same manner; for the male co pulates by uniting his supine parts with those of the female, and is ■neither a short nor a very long time in the act. But the males of some
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 151 some of the selache differ from the females, because in the males two appendices hang from the orifice through which the excrements are discharged, and of which the females are deprived ; as may be seen in the sea-dog. Neither fishes, therefore, nor any other animal without feet, have testicles, But serpents and male fishes have two avenues, which be come full of genital seed about the season of coition, and all of them emit a milky moisture. These two avenues, however, unite in one, in the same manner as in birds. For birds have testicles internally, and every thing, also, which is possessed by oviparous animals that have feet. This, therefore, is inclosed, and extends to the place and recep tacle of the female. But the same avenue of the seed and of the moist ex crement exists externally in viviparous and pedestrious animals ; and in ternally there is another avenue, as we before observed in explaining the difference of the parts of animals. In those animals, however, that have no bladder the same avenue of the dry excrement exists externally, and internally there is another avenue, both which are near to each other. These, also, subsist similarly both in the males and females of this genus of animals. For, except the tortoise, these animals are without a bladder ; and the female tortoise has one avenue, though she has a bladder. But with respect to tortoises, they rank among oviparous animals. The copulation, however, of oviparous fishes is less manifest, and on this account many are of opinion that the females become prolific by swallowing the genital seed of the males; since they are frequently seen to do this. For about the season of copulation, the females, fol lowing the males, do this, and strike their belly with their mouths ; but the males in consequence of this emit their seed, and in greater abun dance. At the time of delivery, however, the males follow the females, and devour the eggs which they lay ; and from those that are left fishes are generated. But about Phœnicia fishes are caught through the assistance of each other. For the fishermen take the male and present them to the female mullets, and the females to the males. In consequence?
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 152 consequence, therefore, of this being frequently seen, an opinion has been formed that the females become pregnant from swallowing the seed of the males. This very same thing is, also, done by quadrupeds. For about the season of copulation, both males and females dis charge a seminal moisture, and smell the private parts of each other. But with respect to partridges, if the females stand opposite .to the males when the wind blows, they become pregnant ; and they frequently become pregnant even from the voice of the male, if they happen to be enflamed with the desire of coition. The same effect is also pro duced from the male flying above the female, in consequence of her inbibing the odour which then proceeds from the male. Both the male and female, likewise, during the act of coition have their mouths open, and their tongues hanging out. The true copulation, however, of oviparous fishes is seldom seen, because they do not continue long in the act ; since their copulation has been seen to be effected after this manner. CHAPTER VI. The mollia, also, the polypus, the cuttle-fish, and the calamary, after the same manner copulate with each other ; for they are con nected with each other by the mouth, at the same time adapting their arms to each other. The polypus, therefore, when it has fixed what is called its head against the earth, and has unfolded its arms, another polypus adapts itself to the extension of the arms, and they make the acetabula to be in continuity with each other. Some, also, say that the male
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 153 male has a kind of penis in one of its arms, in which there are two of the largest acetabula ; that a thing of this kind is as it were nervous, and is extended as far as to the middle arm ; and that the whole of it enters into the nose of the female. But the cuttle-fish and the cala mary swim at the same time that they are connected with each other; and coadapting their mouths and arms, they swim in a direction oppo site to each other. The nose, likewise, as it is called, of the one adheres to the nose of the other. And with respect to the swimming, that of the one is in a backward direction, but that of the other is towards the mouth. But they bring forth in that part of the body which is called the fistula, by which part, also, it is said by some that they copulate. CHAPTER VII. Crustaceous animals, however, such as locusts, lobsters, squills, and others of the same kind, copulate after the manner of quadrupeds that discharge the urine backward, the female causing her tail to be supine, and the male placing his tail upon it. They copulate, also, near the land, at the beginning of the spring ; for the copulation of all such animals has been detected. Sometimes, also, they copulate when figs begin to be ripe. After the same manner, likewise, lobsters and squills copulate. But crabs copulate by their anterior parts, adjusting to each other their envelopments, which consist of many folds. In the first place, therefore, the less gets on the larger crab from behind, and afterwards the larger crab turns himself obliquely. Hence the female differs in nothing else from the male, except that the envelop ment of the female is more ample, detached, and hairy, in which she x brings
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 154 brino-s forth her eggs, and discharges the excrement. Their copulation, however, is not attended with the insertion of one member into ano- ther. CHAPTER VIII. But insects approach to each other behind, and afterwards the less gets on the larger insect; -and the less is the male. The female, however, from beneath, extends an avenue to the male, who is above her ; but not the male t© the female, as is the case with other animals. And this part, indeed, in some insects is seen to be larger than the proportion of the whole body requires, and is, likewise, very small ; but in others is less than the proportion of the body demands. This, however, will be evident, if any one dissects flies when in the act of copulation. Insects, also, are with difficulty liberated from the embraces of each other ; for the copulation of animals of this kind continues for a long time. This is evident in insects with which we are familiar, as in flies and beetles. For all these copulate after the same manner, viz. flies, beetles, sphondyles, the spiders called phalangia, and every other insect of this kind which copulates. But the phalangia that weave copulate as follows: when the female has drawn one of her extended threads, the male again draws it in an opposite direction ; and when they have frequently done this, they come together, and are united in their posterior parts; for in consequence of the roundness of their belly, this mode of copulation is adapted to them. After this manner, therefore, the copulation of animals is effected. The time, also, of the copulation of animals, and the age at which they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 155 they copulate, are definite. For the intention of nature is, that this connexion should take place with most animals about the same time, viz. during the change from winter to summer. And this is the season of the spring in which most animals, the winged, the pedestrious, and those that swim, are impelled to copulation. Some animals, however, copulate and bring forth in autumn and winter ; as, for instance, certain genera of aquatic and winged animals. But man especially, and many animals that live with man, copulate at every season of the year, in consequence of having at all times sufficient warmth and abundant nutriment. The time, also, of the gestation of these animals is short* and this is the case with the swine, the dog, and such winged animals as bring forth frequently. Many animals, likewise, directing their attention to the nurture of their offspring, copulate in that season of the year which is best adapted to this purpose. But in the human spe cies, the male is more impelled to coition in the winter, and the female in the summer. With respect, however, to the genus of birds, the greater part, as we have already observed, except the halcyon, copulate and bring forth at the commencement of the summer; but the halcyon brings forth about the winter solstice. Hence when the winter solstice is tranquil, the days are called halcyon. Halcyon days, however, are fourteen, seven before, and seven after, the solstice; as, also, Simonides sings, when he says, " As when Jupiter in the winter month produces fourteen mild days, which mortals call the period in which the winds are still, the sacred nurse of the variegated halcyon." But these tran quil days take place when the winter solstice happens to be southern, and the [setting] of the pleiades northern1. It is, also, said that the halcyon in the first seven days builds her nest ; but in the remaining seven brings forth and nurtures her young. About these places, there fore, [i. e. in Greece] it does not always happen that the halcyon days are at the time of the winter solstice; but about the Sicilian sea, it nearly always happens. The halcyon, likewise, lays about five eggs. 1 i. e. They happen in November, X 2 CHAP.
name: Aristotle

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 156 CHAPTER IX. But the plungeon and sea-gull bring forth their eggs in the rocks about the sea ; and the multitude of them is two or three. The sea gull, however, lays its eggs in summer, but the plungeon at the begin ning of the spring, immediately after the winter solstice, and their incubation is the same as that of other birds. Neither of these birds, however, hides itself. But the halcyon is seen the most rarely of all birds; for it is scarcely ever seen except about the setting of the pleia des, and the winter solstice. When, likewise, it enters a port, and has flown about as much space as a ship occupies, it immediately disap pears ; as, also, Stesichorus the poet sings in his verses. The nightingale, also, lays her eggs at the beginning of the summer; but she lays five or six eggs. And she hides herself from the autumn to the spring. But with respect to insects, those which do not hide themselves copu late in the winter, and are produced when the weather is tranquil, and the wind southern ; such, for instance, as flies and ants. Most wild animals, however, which have no superfetation bring forth once in the year, as for instance hares. In a similar manner most fishes bring forth but once in the year, as the ckutoi, which are so call ed because they are caught in nets in great abundance ; such, for in stance, as the tunny, the pilcher, the mullet, the chalets, the colias, the chromis, and the like, except the sea- wolf, who is the only one among these fishes that brings forth thrice in one year. The posterior progeny, however, of this fish is more imperfect. The trichias, also, and

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 157 and the fishes that live among rocks, bring forth twice in a year; the baTbel alone brings forth thrice in a year. But this may be inferred from its progeny; for in some places it is seen to have offspring thrice. The marine scorpion, however, brings forth twice ; and the sargus, likewise, brings forth twice, viz. in spring and autumn ; but the stock fish brings forth only once, and that in autumn. The tunny, also, brings forth once in a year, but because she emits into light one part of her offspring maturely, and another part late, she appears to bring forth twice. But her first delivery is in the month of December, in the winter solstice, and her second in the spring. The male tunny, how ever, differs from the female in this, that the female has under its belly a fin which they call aphareus, but the male has not. CHAPTER X. Of the selache, however, the lima or Jik alone brings forth twice ; for she brings forth at the beginning of autumn, and about the setting of the pleiades, [i.e. about the autumnal equinox;] but she brings forth more successfully in the autumn. Each time, also, she is deli. vered of seven or eight offspring. Some of the sea-dogs, howevei, the star-fish for instance, bring forth twice in a month ; but this happens because the eggs of this fish are not all of them perfect at once. Some fishes, also, bring forth at every season of the year; as, for instance, the lamprey. But this fish brings forth many eggs, which rapidly in crease from a small to a large size, in the same manner as the eggs of that kind of lobster called hippurus ; for these from being very small become rapidly very large ; except that the lamprey brings forth at all time

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 158 times of the year, but the hippurus in the spring. The murus, how ever, differs from the muræna or lamprey. For the lamprey, indeed, is variegated, and is more imbecil ; but the murus is of one colour, is strong, and its colour is similar to that of rosin. It has, also, teeth externally and internally. They, likewise, say that the murus is the male, and the muræna the female ; there being this distinction of sexes in them, in the same manner as in other fiches. Each of these fishes, however, comes on dry land, and is frequently caught. It happens, therefore, that nearly all fishes rapidly increase, and particularly the little fish called the small crow. But this fish brings forth near the land, in such places as are shady and abound with plants. The fish, likewise, called orphus, from being small becomes rapidly large. The pilcher and the tunny bring forth in the Euxinus Pontus, or black sea, and no where else ; but the mullet, the gold-fish, and the sea-wolf, principally bring forth at the mouths of rivers. The orcines, however, the scorpiones, and many other genera, bring forth in the deep sea. CHAPTER. XI. Most fishes, likewise* bring forth in the three months of March, April, and May ; but a few, such as the stock-fish, the sargin, and others of this kind, bring forth in the autumn, a little before the au tumnal equinox; and this is, also, the case with the torpedo and the file. Some fishes, however, as was before observed, bring forth both in winter and summer ; as, for instance, in winter, indeed, the sea wolf, the mullet, and the needle-fish ; but in summer, the tunny, in the month

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 159 month of June, about the solstice. The offspring of this fish, however, resembles a sack, in which many small eggs are contained. The ruades, also, [or fishes that go in band J bring forth in summer. Of mullets, likewise, those that are called labeones, sargones, mucones, and capitones, begin to be pregnant in the month of December, and their pregnancy con tinues for thirty days. Some mullets, however, are not generated from copulation, but originate from mud and sand. Generally, therefore, most fishes are pregnant in the, spring, though some, as we have said, are pregnant in summer, autumn, and winter; yet this does not similarly happen to all of them, nor simply, nor according to each genus, nor to most, nor in those other seasons are they pregnant with such a numerous progeny as in the spring. In short, it is necessary not to be ignorant that as places produce a great difference in plants and quadrupeds, not only as to the good condition of the body in other respects, but, also, as to their greater or less fecundity; so, likewise, with respect to fishes, places produce a great difference in them, not only as to their magnitude and proper nourishment, but, likewise^ as to their pro geny and copulation, so that the same fishes in one place generate more and in another less frequently. CHAPTER XII. The mollia, also, bring forth in the spring, and rank among the first of marine animals that spawn ; but the cuttle-fish brings forth in every season, and continues laying her eggs for fifteen days. As soon, how ever, as the female has laid her eggs, the male following pours his se minal liquor on the eggs, which renders them firm. But the male cuttle-

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK -*, 160 cuttle-fish is more variegated than the female, and his back is blacker. The polypus, however, copulates in winter, but brings forth in the spring, and is concealed for about two months. The egg, also, which it lays is as it were a tuft of hair, and resembles the fruit of the white poplar. This animal, however, is very politic ; for from the egg of the polypus an infinite multitude of pelypi are produced. But the male differs from the female, both in having a longer head, and because it contains that white substance in its arm which fishermen call the puden dum. The female, also, incubates the eggs which she brings forth ; and hence the polypi at that time are in an ill condition of body, because they do not then take any nutriment. The purples, likewise, are generated about the spring, and the buc cina at the end of the winter ; and, in short, testaceous animals appear in the spring and autumn to have what are called eggs, except those sea hedge-hogs that are fit to eat ; for these though they have eggs especially in spring and autumn, yet they are at no time without eggs, and they particularly abound with them during the full moon, and in warm days. Those hedge-hogs, however, must be excepted, that live in the Pyrrhæan straits ; for these are better in winter. And they are, indeed, small, yet full of eggs. In a similar manner, likewise, all snails are seen to be pregnant in the same season of the year [the spring]. csiaf

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 161 CHAFFER XIII. Or birds, however, those that are wild, as we have before observed, for the most part copulate and bring forth once. But the swallow and the blackbird bring forth twice. The first progeny, therefore, of the blackbird are destroyed by the winter; for she brings forth the first of all birds ; but she nurtures her second progeny, and causes them to arrive at perfection. With respect, however, to domestic birds, or such as can be domesticated, these bring forth frequently. Thus, for instance, pigeons and hens bring forth during the whole of the sum- mer. For cocks and hens copulate perpetually, and the latter bring forth at all seasons of the year, except during the winter solstice. Of pigeons, however, there are many genera. For one kind is of a livid colour, and this is the stock-dove, or wood pigeon. The wood-pigeon, therefore, is less than the pigeon, and is, also, less capable of being domesticated. But the wood-pigeon is black, small, and has red and rough feet ; and hence no one rears a wood-pigeon. The ring-dove, therefore, is the largest of pigeons; but the next to this is the vinous pigeon ; and this is a little larger than the pigeon properly so called ; but the turtle-dove is the smallest of birds of this kind. Pigeons, how- ever, properly so called, bring forth and rear their young at all sea- sons of the year, if they have a warm place and proper food ; but if not, they are pregnant in summer only. The offspring of the pigeon, also, that are produced in spring are better than those that are pro- duced in autumn ; but those are the worst of all that are produced in summer, and in very hot weather. v c If A P,

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 162 CHAPTER XIV. Animals, also, differ with respect to copulation, according to age. In the first place, therefore, most animals do not at one and the same time begin to emit their seed, and possess a generative power, but the latter of these is posterior to the former. For the young of all ani mals are at first unprolific ; and if they happen to be prolific, their offspring are smaller and more infirm. This, however, is especially evident in men, quadrupeds, and birds. For the two former, when they are young, produce smaller children, and young birds lay smaller eggs. In the next place, animals of the same species are, for the most part, adapted to copulation at the same age, unless some premature circumstance prevents them, either arising from something prodigious and monstrous, or from their nature having sustained some injury. In the human species, therefore, the aptitude to copulation is indicated by the mutation of the voice, and the pudenda, not only in magnitude, but also in form, and in a similar manner in the mutation of the mammæ, and especially by the hairs of the private parts. But man begins to have seed about the fourteenth year of his age, and possesses a [perfect] generative power about the age of twenty-one. Other animals, however, have no hairs in the private parts. For some, in short, have no hair, but others have no hair in the supine parts, or have less than in the prone parts. The change of the voice, also, is in some animals manifest ; but in others, other parts of the body in dicate the commencement of the seed and prolific power. With respect to voice, also, that of the female in most animals is more
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 163 more acute, and of the younger than that of the older. For among stags, the males have a graver voice than the females ; and the males, indeed, are vocal at the season of copulation, but the females when they are terrified. The voice of the female, however, is short, but that of the male is long. The voice, likewise, of dogs is more grave when they become old. The voices, also, of horses differ. For as soon as they are born, in deed, the females emit a slender and small voice, but the males a small voice, yet louder and graver than that of the female ; and in progress of time they have a still louder voice. But when they become two years old, and begin to copulate, the male, indeed, emits a loud and grave voice, but the female a louder and clearer voice than she emit ted before, and this is the case, for the most part, till the twentieth year of their age. After this period, however, the voice both of males and females is weaker. For the most part, however, as we have said, the voice of males dif fers from that of females, as being more grave, in such animals as have an extension of voice. Yet this is not the case in all animals ; but in some, as in oxen, the contrary takes place. For in these the voice of the female is graver than that of the male, and the voice of calves than that of perfect oxen. Hence, bulls when they are castrated change their voice into that of the female, since through this their voice becomes more acute. The times, however, of copulation, according to age, subsist in ani mals as follows: Female sheep and goats, therefore, eopulate and are pregnant at the age of one year ; but this is more especially the case with goats. And the males, also, copulate at the same age. But the offspring of sheep and goats differ in these and other respects; since the males are better when they are produced in the second year, or when they are produced by a male and female of an advanced age. Both the male and female swine, however, begin to copulate in the eighth month of their age ; but the female brings forth at the age of one year ; for thus the time of her pregnancy happens to take place. The male, also, generates in the eighth month of his age, but Y 2 the

As we have observed, however, the ages of the copulation of animals are not every where similar. Fc-r in some places, both male and female swine copulate when they are four months old ; so as to produce and nurture offspring in the sixth month. But in other places, boars begin to copulate in the tenth month of their age, and for three years retain a perfect generative power. Dogs, however, both male and female copulate, for the most part, when they are one year old ; but it sometimes happens that they co pulate in the eighth month of their age ; though this rather takes place with the females than with the males. The females, also, are preg nant during sixty-one, or two, or three days at farthest ; but they are not pregnant for a less time than sixty days. And if they happen to be delivered prior to this period, the progeny never arrive at perfec tion. After they are delivered, likewise, they copulate again in the sixth month, and not before. With respect to horses, also, both the male and female begin to co pulate when they are two years old, and at this period are able to ge nerate ; yet the offspring which at that time they produce is small and feeble. For the most part, however, they copulate when they are three years old, and every succeeding continues to be more excellent than the preceding offspring, till they are twenty years old. But the male copulates till he is thirty three years old ; and the female till she is forty ; so that horses copulate nearly during the whole of their life. For the male, for the most part, lives thirty-five years, and the female more than forty years. A horse, also, has been known to live seventy five years. With respect to the ass, however, both the male and female copu late in the thirtieth month of their age ; yet they do not for the most part generate at this period, but when they are three years old, or three years and six months. There has, however, been an instance of an ass which has conceived when but a year old, and has reared her progeny. This has, also, been the case with a cow, the progeny of which has been reared, and arrived at its proper magnitude. The

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 165 The principles, therefore, of generation in these animals subsist after this manner. But with respect to the human species, the male generates till he is seventy years old ; and the woman till she is fifty. This, however, is rarely the case ; for few have offspring at these ages; but, for the most part, men cease to generate in the sixty-fifth year, and women in the forty-fifth year of their age. But sheep bring forth till the eighth year of their age ; and if good care is taken of them, they bring forth till they are eleven years old; for it happens that they copulate nearly through the whole of their life. Goats, however, when they are fat are less prolific ; on which account vines, also, when they are barren, are said to be goatish. But when goats become lean, they are able by copulation to generate. Rams, however, first copulate with older sheep, and afterwards with those that are young ; but, as we have before observed, young sheep produce fewer offspring than those that are more advanced in age. The wild boar, also, is good for the purposes of copulation till the third year of his age. But the progeny of those that are older than this are of an inferior kind. For the wild boar after this period re- ceives no increase, and becomes destitute of strength. It is usual, also, with this animal to copulate when he is full, and when he has not recently copulated; for, if this is not the case, his connexion with the female continues but a short time, and the offspring which he begets are small. The sow, however, at the first birth brings forth a very few offspring ; but the second birth is more abundant ; and when she becomes old she brings forth in a similar manner, but copulates more slowly. When, however, they are fifteen years of age they no longer generate, but become wild. If they are well fed, likewise, they are more rapidly impelled to copulation, both when they are young and when they become old But when the sow is pregnant, if she is very fat, she has less milk after her delivery. And with respect to her progeny, they are then the best when she is in the acme of her age, and when they are begot at the beginning of winter; but those that are begot in sum mer are the worst, for they are small, thin, and moist. But the male swine, if he is well fed, is able to copulate at all seasons, and both day and
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 166 and night ; but if he is not well fed, he principally possesses the power of copulating in the spring. And when old, as we have before observed, he is always less able to copulate. Frequently, however, such of them as are unable to copulate rapidly, through age or imbecility, approach ing to each other, copulate reclining, through the infirmity of the fe male. The sow, however, then, especially becomes pregnant, when, being furiously eager for copulation, she hangs her ears ; for if this is not the case, she does not become pregnant, but the seed is ejected by the womb. Dogs, however, do not copulate through the whole of life, but only as far as to a certain acme of their age ; but, for the most part, their copulations and pregnancies continue till they are twelve years of age. Some dogs, however, have been known to possess the power of gener ating, and some bitches of being pregnant, even at the ages of eighteen and twenty ; though these, as well as other animals, are deprived by old age of the ability of generating and bringing forth. But the camel discharges its urine backward, and copulates in the manner before explained. The time, however, of its copulation, in Arabia, is in the month of September. This animal, also, is preg nant during the space of twelve months, and only brings forth one at a birth ; for it is uniparous. Both the male and female, likewise, be gin to copulate when they are three years old ; and the female again copulates in one year after her delivery, f The female elephant, however, begins *o copulate at the earliest pe riod, indeed, in the tenth year of her age, and at the latest period, when she is fifteen ; but the male copulates, when he is five or six years of age. The time, also, of their copulation is the spring. The male, likewise, again copulates after an interval of three years, but is never a second time connected with a female that he has made pregnant. The time, however, of the gestation of the female is two years, and she brings forth only one offspring ; for she is uniparous. The em bryo, also, of this animal is about the size of a calf of the age of two or three months. And such are the particulars concerning the copu lation of animals. CHAP.

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS, 167 CHAPTER XV. We must now, however, discuss the generation both of animals that are produced by copulation, and of those that are produced without it, and in the first place the generation of testaceous animals ; for the whole of this genus is, as I may say, produced without copulation. The purples, therefore, in the spring, collecting together in one place, make what is called their wax. But this is, as it were, the honey-comb of bees, except that it is not such an elegant production, but resem bles a multitude of the shells of white peas collected in one heap. No one of these shells, however, has any avenue ; nor are the purples gener ated from these, but both the purples and other testaceous animals are generated from putrefaction and mud. This wax, therefore, or honey-comb is, as it were, a certain purgation both of the purples and buccina ; for the buccina, also, make wax. Hence those testaceous animals that make wax are generated after the same manner as other testaceous animals, and, indeed, they are more easily generated this way, when homogeneous substances pre-exist [in the putrid matter.] When the purples, therefore, make their wax they emit a certain mu cous viscosity, from the concretion of which those substances resem bling the shells of white peas are formed. But these shells, being analyzed by putrefaction, the putrid mucus contained in the shells is diffused into the earth, and in the place into which it flows small pur ples are formed, which are found when they are caught adhering to larger purples, and some of them which thus adhere are not yet per fectly formed. If, however, the larger purples are caught before they have
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V 168 have produced that mucus from which the small purples originate, they do not bring forth in any casual place, but in mats and hurdles, in the same manner as they bring forth in the sea, and from the narrowness of the hurdle in which they are delivered, their foetus resembles a grape. There are, however, many genera of purples ; and some of them indeed, are large, a those aobut Sigeum and Lectum; but others are small, as those in the Euripus, and about Caria. And those, indeed, which are found in gulfs are large and rough, and most of them have a black flower, but some of them have a red and small flower. Some of them, likewise, are large, and weigh twelve ounces and a half. The small purples, however, are found in shores, and about coasts, and have a red flower. Again, in the northern parts, they are for the most part black, but in the southern parts red. They are, likewise, caught in the spring, when they make their wax; but during the dog-days they are not caught, for then they are not fed, because they retire and con- ceal themselves. But that part of them which is called the flower, [and with which wool is dyed] is between the neck and the mecon, [or papaver ] That, likewise, which unites these two parts is compact, and the colour of it resembles a white membrane, which is taken off. When the flower, also, is pressed it tinges and dyes the hand, and extends through it like a vein. This, however, appears to be the flower ; but the remainder of that which unites the neck and the mecon resembles alum, 'she flower, likewise, of the purples is then in the worst condition when they make their wax. But [in order to collect the flower of the purple] they bruise the small purples together with their shells ; for it is not easy to collect the flower in any other way. They divest, however, the larger purples of their shells, and then take away the flower, on which account the neck and the mecon are, also, separated ; for the flower is between these, above that part which is called the belly. The flower, therefore, being taken away, the neck and mecon are necessarily divided. But those that collect the flower of the purples endeavour to bruise them while they are alive, for if they should die before they are bruised, they cast out the flower together with their life ; on which account they are preserved in bow-nets, till
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 169 till they are collected and quiet. The ancients, therefore, together with a bait did not employ nets in catching the purple, and, therefore, it fre quently happened that the purples escaped ; but fishermen of the pre sent time fasten the bait to a bow-net in order that if the purples should drop off, they may not escape. Then, however, they especially drop off when they are saturated ; but if they are empty, they are with difficulty divulsed from the bait. These, therefore, are the peculiari ties which happen to the purple. The buccina, also, are generated after the same manner as the pur ples, and at the same season of the year. Both the buccina and pur ples, likewise, and other turbinated animal, are from their birth covered with a shell which adheres to them after the same manner and in the same position ; but they are fed by stretching out what is called their tongue, under the shell. And with respect to the magni tude of the tongue in the purples, the tongue is longer than finger, by which they are fed, and by which they pierce shell-fish, and their shell. Both the purple, however, and the buccinum live long ; for the purple lives about six years, and every year the increase of them is evident by the intervals of the spiral in the shell, [i. e. by the increase of the number of the spirals.] Muscles, also, make wax. But with respect to what are called marshy oysters (Aydo^ed'), wherever there is mud there the origin of them consists. And periwinkles, the chames, the solenes, and cockles, receive their formation in sandy places. But the erect pinnae [which are testaceous immoveable animals] are formed in the bottom of the sea in sand and mud ; and they contain within their shell, as a guar dian, a small crab, or squill, of which when they are deprived they soon perish. In short, all testaceous animals are generated spontane ously in the matter which is at the bottom of the sea, and are different according to the difference of this matter ; oysters, indeed, being gener ated in mud, but periwinkles, and the above-mentioned genera, in a sandy matter. The tethya, likewise, and the balani or glandes, and those which appear on the surface of the water, such as the lepas, and the neritæ, are generated in the hollows of rocks. All such testaceous animals, therefore, have a rapid increase, and especially purples and •1 cockles ;
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 170 cockles ; for these become perfect in one year. In the shells, how ever of certain testaceous animals very small white crabs are formed ; most of them, indeed, in broader muscles [which are called foliati, because they have a broad shell like a leaf,] and in the next place those crabs which are called the guardians of the pinnæ are produced in the shells of the pinnæ. They are, likewise, produced in cockles, and in marshy oysters; but they do not receive any apparent increase. Fishermen, however, say that these guardians of the pinnæ are gener ated together with the pinnæ. But cockles, in the same manner as pur ples, disappear for a time in the sand. After this manner, therefore, testaceous animals are formed. But some of them are formed in shallow water, others in shores, and others in muddy places. Some, likewise, are produced in hard and rough, but others in sandy, places. And some, indeed, change the places of their abode, but others do not. And of those which do not change their habitation, the pinnæ are rooted to a place ; but the solenes and peri winkles remain fixed, without being rooted ; yet when they are divulsed are no longer able to live. The testaceous animal, however, which is called the star- fish, is naturally so hot as instantly to burn and consume every thing which it touches. But they say that the species of this animal which is found in the Pyrrhæan straits is of the most destructive nature ; and that its form resembles that of a painted star. Those marine animals, also, that are called pulmones or lungs, are spontane ously produced. But the shell-fish used by painters is very thick, and the flower is external to the shell, [and not like that of the purple with in it.] Shell-fish of this kind, also, are principally found in the places about Caria. The small cancer, however, derives its origin from the earth and mud ; and afterwards enters into empty shells. When it has increased, likewise, it again enters into another larger shelf; as, for in stance, into the shell of the neritus, or trumpet, or some other of this kind ; but it frequently enters into the shells of the small buccina. When, however, it has entered any shell, it carries it about, and in this is again nourished. When, also, it is again increased, it betakes itself to another larger shell. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 171 CHAPTER XVI. Animals, also, that have no shell, such as the sea-nettle, and the sponge, are generated after the same manner as testaceous animals, in the caverns of rocks. There are, however, two genera of sea-nettles ; for some of them adhere to the cavities of rocks, so that they cannot be liberated from them ; but others adhere to smooth and broad places, so that they can be liberated from them, and change their habita tion. In the second place, sponges have certain cavities. And in these cavities certain animalcula are generated, which have the same analogy to the sponges as the guardians of the pinnæ [above-mention ed] to the pinnæ, from which guardians deriving their appellation they are called pinnophylaces. But these animalcula dwell in the cavities of the sponges, just as small spiders dwell in their cavities. They, likewise, cause the sponge to open when small fishes are about to enter into it, and to shut when they have entered, these little fishes being their prey. There are, however, three genera of sponges ; one of which is thin, the second dense, and the third, which is called Achillœan, is most thin, dense, and strong. Sponges, also, of the last kind are put under the helmets and greaves of soldiers, and cause a blow to produce a less sound ; but they are very rare. Of sponges, however, those that are very hard and rough are called goats. All sponges, likewise, are either produced near rocks or shores ; but they are nourished in mud, of which this is an indication, that when they are taken they are found to be full of mud. For other animals that adhere to any substance derive their nutriment from that to which they adhere. The dense, z 2 however,

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 172 however, are more imbecil than the thin sponges, because the adherence of the former is not so tenacious as that of the latter. The sponge, also, as they say, is sensitive; of which this is an indi cation, that it contracts itself at the approach of the person who plucks it, so that the divulsion of it is difficult. It, likewise, does the very same thing when there is much wind, and the weather is tempestuous, in order that it may not be removed from its situation. There are, however, some who are dubious with respect to this circumstance, as for instance, the inhabitants of Torona. For they say that the sponge nourishes certain animals within itself, such as worms and the like ; which, when the sponges are divulsed, are devoured by the fishes that live in rocks, together with the remaining roots of the sponges, but that if the sponges are not radically extirpated, they grow again from what remain, and are again filled. The largest sponges, therefore, are those that are thin, and of which there are a great number about Lycia; but the dense sponges are most soft ; for the Achillœan sponges are more compact than these. In short, the sponges which are found in places where the water is deep, and of a mild temperature, are most soft, for wind and cold harden them, in the same manner as other productions of the earth, and pre vent their increase ; on which account, the sponges in the Hellespont are dense and rough, and, in short, those which are beyond and within the promontory of Malea differ in softness and hardness. Sponges, however, will not bear immoderate heat, for they become putrid through it in the same manner as plants. Hence the sponges which are found near shores where the sea is deep are the best ; for they acquire a proper temperament, on account of the depth of the water. But while they are unwashed and alive they are black. They adhere, how ever, to rocks, neither by one part only, nor by all their parts ; for between the parts which adhere there are certain void spaces, and a membrane, as it were, is extended about the roots ; but they adhere by many of their parts. But the other void spaces in the upper part are closed. Four or five of them are, however, apparent ; on which account some assert that these are the avenues by which they receive their food. There

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 173 There is, also, another genus of sponges which they call aplysia, because it is incapable of being washed. These sponges have, indeed, large avenues, but all the rest of their body is dense. And when they are dissected they are found to be more dense and viscous than other sponges, and the whole of their substance resembles the lungs. It is, however, universally acknowledged that this genus of sponges is sensi tive and lives for a long time. They are, likewise, easily distinguished in the sea from other sponges, because others are found to be white when the mud subsides, but these are always black. And thus much concerning sponges, and the generation of testaceous animals. CHAPTER XVII. Of crustaceous animals, however, locusts are pregnant after copula tion, and carry their eggs during the three months of May, June, and July ; after which they deposit them in the folds under their belly, and in these the eggs increase in the same manner as worms increase. The same thing, also, takes place in the mollia, and in such fishes as are oviparous ; for the eggs of all these are increased. The egg, therefore, of locusts is friable, and is divided into eight parts. For to each of the covers which exist at the side of the locust a certain cartilaginous sub stance is united, to which the eggs adhere, and the whole resembles a grape; for each of these cartilaginous substances is divided into many branches. And these, indeed, when divided are apparent; but when they are beheld undivided, they seem to form one mass. The largest eggs, however, of the locusts are not those which are near to the avenue of their egress, but those which are situated in the middle ; and the least
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 174 least are those which are situated in the last place. The size of the small eggs, also, is that of a grain of millet ; and the eggs do not imme diately adhere to the avenue, but there is something between them and the avenue. For the eggs on each side, i. e. as well from the supe rior part of the breast as from the inferior part of the tail, are divided by a certain interval ; since the covers are thus naturally disposed. They are not, therefore, able to enclose the eggs laterally, and hence the intervals in the extremities of the eggs are so disposed as to cover all the eggs. The locust, also, when it brings forth its eggs places them in the cartilaginous folds, at the same time expanding its tail, and com pressing and bending itself. At the time of its delivery, likewise, the car tilaginous folds are increased, and become the recipients of the eggs ; for the locust then depositits eggs in these folds, in the same manner as the cuttle-fish deposits its eggs near the branches of vines, and other sub stances which it meets with in the sea. After this manner, therefore, the locust brings forth. The locust, however, after it has brought forth its eggs, concocts them in its cartilaginous soldo for the space of twenty days, and afterwards ejects them into a fit place ,so as th t they are seen to be conglomerated in a heap ; and from these eggs locusts are produced in about fifteen days, and they are frequently less than the length of a finger. Locusts, therefore, bring forth their eggs before, but eject them after, the rising of Arcturus. But the pregnancy of crooked squills continues about four months. And locusts, indeed, are produced in rough and rocky, but lobsters in smooth, places. Neither of them, however, are produced in muddy places. Hence lobsters are produced in the Hellespont, and near the island of Thasus ; but locusts about Sigœum and Athos. But fisher men, from the shores and adjacent coasts, conjecture whether the places in which they intend to fish are rough or muddy. In the spring and winter, however, locusts and lobsters are found near the land; but in summer they live in the deep sea. For at one time they are in search of heat, and at another of cold. Those crustaceous animals, also, which are called bears bring forth in a manner similar to locusts. Hence, in winter, and before they begin to lay their eggs in spring, they are the best as food ; but when they have brought forth they are the worst. Locusts

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 175 Locusts and crabs, also, put off their shell in the spring soon after they are born, and during every succeeding year, in the same manner as serpents put off their skin, which is called their old ao-e. But all locusts are long-lived. CHAPTER XVIII. The mollia, however, from copulation have a white egg. But this in process of time becomes friable, in the same manner as the eggs of crustaceous animals. And the polypus, indeed, brings forth either in caverns, or shells, or other hollow places, and its progeny resembles the tufts of the wild vine, or the fruit of the white poplar, as was ob served before. The eggs, also, which the polypus lays depend from the walls of the cave in which they dwell in such abundance, that when collected, they fill a vessel* much larger than the head of the polypus, in which these eggs are contained. Polypi, therefore, are produced from the bursting of these eggs, in about fifty days after they are brought forth, and they creep on the ground very numerous, like the spiders called phalangia ; in which, though the nature of the seve ral members cannot be distinguished, yet the whole form is sufficiently apparent. This great multitude, however, of polypi perishes, on ac count of their smallness and imbecility ; and some of them are so small, that no parts can be distinguished, though from the touch it is evident that they move. The cuttle-fish, also, brings forth, and its eggs resemble large and black myrtle-berries ; for she sprinkles them with her ink. These eggs, likewise, adhere to each other in the form of a grape, and the whole !!■

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 176 is so connected by one certain substance, that the eggs cannot easily be separated. For the male pours on the eggs a certain mucous mois- ture, by the viscosity of which they adhere to each other, and in- crease. And these eggs, indeed, as soon as they are emitted are white, but when the cuttle-fish sprinkles them with her ink, they be- come larger and black. But when a little cuttle-fish is generated, it is wholly formed within the egg from the white of it, and the mem- brane of the egg bursting, it comes forth. When, however, the female has sprinkled the egg with her ink, the interior white part of the egg be- comes like a drop of hail ; and from this the little cuttle-fish is produced, the head being first formed, in the same manner as birds, and the belly being connected with the head. The mode, however, in which the navel of the cuttle-fish is connected with that part of the egg from which the little cuttle-fish originates has not yet been discovered, except that as the little cuttle-fish increases the white of the egg always becomes less; and at length, in the same manner as the yellow in the eggs of birds, this white entirely disappears. But, as inother animals, so likewise in these, the eyes at first are seen to be large. As for instance, let A be the egg, B C the eyes, and D the little cuttle-fish1. The cuttle-fish, also, is pregnant in the spring; but she brings forth in fifteen days [after conception]. And when she is delivered of her eggs, in the space of another fifteen days they become like the small stones of a grape ; on the bursting of which little cuttle-fish come forth. If, however, any one cuts the mem- brane of the eggs before they spontaneously burst, the little cuttle-fish, being not yet completely formed, emit dung, and change their colour through fear, so that from being white they become red. Crustaceous animals, therefore, differ from the mollia in this, that the former hatch their eggs conjoined to themselves ; but the polypus, the cuttle-fish, and other animals of the like kind, hatch their eggs separated from themselves, wherever they may be, and this is especially the case with the cuttle-fish, whose belly during her incubation is frequently seen near the ground. But the female polypus at one time hatches her eggs-by incubation, and at another time, placing herself at 1 See the figure in Scaliger's edition of this work. the

The cuttle-fish, however, brings forth near the earth, among weeds, branches of trees, reeds, heaps of stones, or any other accumulation of this kind. Hence fishermen deposit, in opportune places, bundles of twigs, [in order that they may allure the cuttle-fish to bring forth in them] ; for the cuttle-fish in these bundles lays that long series of eggs, adhering to each other, which resembles a lock of hair. The cuttle-fish, also, when she lays her eggs, after some respite, sprinkles them with her ink, because the act of bringing them forth is painful. But the calamaries bring forth in the deep sea; and their eggs are in a connected series, like those of the cuttle-fish. Neither the calamary, however, nor the cuttle-fish live long ; for except some few of them, they do not live the space of two years. This is, also, the case with the polypi. But from one egg one small cuttle-fish is produced ; and the like, also, takes place with the calamaries. The male calamary, however, differs from the female ; for if the belly of the female is dissected, it will be seen that she contains in it two red substances, which resemble small mammæ, and which the male has not. The * cuttle-fish, also, has this difference ; and besides this, the male is more variegated than the female, as was before observed. CHAPTER XIX. With respect to insects, also, we have before shown that the males are less than the females ; that in copulation the male gets on the back of the female, and that they are a long time before they are separated. Most, however, of those insects that generate from coition bring forth 2 a very

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 178 very soon after copulation. All insects, likewise, bring forth worms, except a certain genus of butterflies, and these bring forth a hard sub stance resembling a grain of bastard saffron, but which internally is liquid. An animal, however, is not generated from a certain part of worms, in the same manner as it is from a certain part of eggs ; but the whole is increased, and becomes a distinctly formed animal. Some insects, also, are generated from kindred animals. Thus, for instance, the spiders called phalangia, and other spiders, are generated from phalangia and spiders, and the attelabi(a. species of locusts), crickets, and grasshoppers. But other insects are not generated from animals, but are produced spontaneously. And some, indeed, are generated from the dew which falls on leaves ; and these insects are naturally gener ated in the spring, but they are likewise frequently produced in winter, when for a long time the weather has been mild, and the wind southern. Others, again, are generated in putrid mud and dung, but others in wood ; some, indeed, in the wood of plants, and some in dry wood. Some, likewise, are generated in the hairs, but others in the flesh, and others in the excrements, of animals. And of these, some are generated when the excrements are ejected, but others, as what are called lumbrici, or belly-worms, while the excrements are yet in the animal. There are, however, three genera of these ; those which are denominated broad, and the round, and the third kind, what are called ascarides. From the round, therefore, and the ascarides, nothing else is generated ; but the broad kind, which alone adhere to the intestines, produce something similar to the seed of a cucumber ; by the emis sion of which, physicians conjecture that this broad worm is latent in the intestines. What are called butterflies, however, are generated from caterpillars; but caterpillars are generated from green leaves, and especially from raphanos, which some call cabbage. And at first, indeed, something less than a grain of millet is produced ; afterwards small worms origin ate from this ; and these increasing, in the space of three days are formed into small caterpillars. Such caterpillars, also, when increased, cease from motion, change their form, and are called chrysalides, or aureliæ.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 179 aureliæ. In this state, likewise, they are enclosed in a hard shell ; but move if they are touched. The chrysalides are, also, enclosed in cavi ties, which resemble the webs of spiders, but they neither have a mouth, nor is any other part apparent. In a short time, too, the shell bursts, and winged animals fly out of it, which we call butterflies. At first, therefore, while they are caterpillars, they are nourished and emit excrement ; but when they become chrysalides, they neither taste any thing, nor emit any excrement. After the same manner, also, that but terflies are generated from caterpillars other animals are generated from worms, whether such worms originate from the copulation of ani mals, or are produced without copulation. For the worms which are afterwards changed into bees, drones, and wasps, when they are recently produced are nourished, and are seen to have dung ; but when from worms they pass another form, they are called nymphs, indeed, but in that state neither receive any nutriment, nor have any dung ; and being enclosed, they remain without motion, till they are formed into another animal. For then the substance in which they are enclosed bursting, they come forth [changed into bees, drones, or wasps.] The penies, also, and the hyperes, are produced from certain cater pillars which have an undulating motion in their progression. For as the sea during its fluctuation alternately raises and depresses the water, so these caterpillars, as they move along, raise their body in a bow-like manner, and afterwards, as they proceed farther, depress it. But every genus of animals which is produced from caterpillars has the colour of the caterpillars from which it originates. From a certain large worm, also, which has, as it were, horns, and differs from other worms, in the first place, indeed, the worm being changed, a caterpillar is produced, afterwards a bombylius, and from this the necydalus;i but the worm undergoes all these metamorphoses in the space of six months. From this animal, also, certain women unfolding silk draw it out into a thread, and afterwards weave it. But Pamphyle, • A worm, which in the space of six weeks is changed into a silk-worm. the 2 a 2

From the Avorms, likewise, which are in dry wood beetles are gener- ated, after the same manner. In the first place, indeed, the worms being immoveable, a certain membrane is produced ; afterwards, the shell in which they are enveloped bursting, beetles come forth. But from bee-hives the prasocourides l are generated, and these also have wings. And from the broad little animals which swim on the surface of rivers horse-flies (015001) are produced ; and hence there is a great quantity of these flies about rivers, where such animals are generated. But from black and hairy, though not large caterpillars, in the first place glow-worms, which do not fly, are produced ; and these again change, and winged animals are generated from them, which are called locks of hair. The empis, however, or gnat, is generated from the ascarides ; but the ascarides are worms which are produced in the mud of wells, and wherever there is a conflux of water in which there is an earthy sedi- ment. At first, therefore, the mud itself becoming putrid receives a white colour, afterwards it is black, and last of all it acquires the colour of blood. When, however, this is the case, substances resembling sea- weeds, very small and red, are produced. These, after a time, begin to move, adhering to the mud from which they originate ; but afterwards, being freed and separated from the mud, they move on the water, and are called ascarides. After a few days, also, they stand erect on the water, and become immoveable and hard. In the next place, the shell in which they are enclosed bursting, a gnat emerges, and sits on the water, till the sun or the wind moves him ; for then he flies away. The principle, however, of the generation of all other zvorms, and of animals which burst forth from, worms, appears to be derived from the sun or the wind. But the ascarides are generated more rapidly and in greater abundance in water, the sediment of which is various and promiscuous, such as is the sediment with which the land of Megara is manured ; 1 The frasocouris is an insect which feeds on lettuces in gardens, and particularly on leaks. for

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 181 for a substance of this kind becomes rapidly putrid. The ascarides, also, are more numerous in autumn, for then there is less moisture, [by an abundance of which they are destroyed.] The ticks, however, [or lice of dogs and sheep] are generated from putrid grass ; but green beetles are produced from the worms which are found in the excrements of the ox and the ass. And the beetles called pilularii, who make certain balls from dung which they roll, in winter hide themselves in these balls, and bring forth worms, from which beetles are generated. In leguminous substances, also, worms are generated, from which winged animals are produced, similar to those above-mentioned. But flies are generated from the worms found in the excrement which is separated from straw i; on which account, also, those who are employed in this work endeavour to separate the different parts of the dung, and then say they have rendered it fit for use. The principle, however, of these worms is small. For at first, indeed, a little red spot is seen, and from being immoveable, it begins to be moved, as it were, adhering to the dung; afterwards it becomes an immoveable little worm ; then being moved, it again becomes immoveable. But from this state it becomes a perfect fly, and is moved when excited by the wind or sun. Ox-flies, however, are generated from [putrid] wood ; but the orso dacnæ mordellæ, or blister-flies, from transformed worms ; and these worms are produced in the stalks of cabbage. The cantharides are generated from caterpillars in the fig-tree, the pear-tree, and the pine tree ; for in all these worms are produced. The cantharides, also, are generated from the worms in the sweet-brier. They, likewise, are impelled towards fetid substances, because they originate from a matter of this kind. But the conops, or gnat, is produced from worms which are generated in the dregs of vinegar ; for animals are generated in substances which appear to be most free from putrefaction. Thus, for 1 i. e. They are generated from the dung employed by husbandmen in dunging land, after they have separated it from the straw, not yet become putrid, with which it is mixed on dunghills. instance
