text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 186 But in the first place bees form their hive, and afterwards place their offspring in them; as some say, emitting their progeny from their mouth ; and this is the opinion of those who assert that they bring their offspring from a different place than the hive. Afterwards they make honey, for the purposes of nutriment, both in summer and autumn; but the honey is better which is made in autumn. The hive, also, is constructed from flowers ; but they derive their wax from the tears of trees ; and their honey is that which falls from the air, and especially during the rising of the stars, and when the rainbow is extended over the earth. And, in short, honey is not produced before the rising of the pleiades. The wax, therefore, of bees is from flowers ; and that they do not make the honey, but carry away that which falls from the air, is indicated by this circumstance, that the keepers of bees find their hives full of honey in the space of one or two days. And farther still, flowers, indeed, are produced in autumn; but honey is no longer produced, if, during that season, it is taken from the hives. The honey, therefore, which is now made being taken away, and no nutriment, or but little, remaining for the bees, they would again make it, if it were produced from flowers. Honey, also, [is at first liquid, but afterwards] becomes thick, and acquires a consistence ; for at first it is like water, and for some days is in a fluid state. Hence, if during these days it is taken from the hive, it is not thick, but in twenty days especially acquires a consistence. It may, also, be immediately known by the taste whether the honey is perfectly concocted ; for if it is, it is thicker and sweeter. Bees, however, collect honey from all plants that have flowers in a cup, and, also, from other things which are sweet ; nor do they injure any fruit, but receiving the juices of flowers by an organ resembling a t®ngue, they carry them to their hives. The time, also, of taking the honey from the hives is when the wild fig-tree begins to exhibit its fruits ; but bees produce the best offspring at the time in which they collect theirboney. They, also, carry the wax and erithace [ which is the thicker part of the wax] with their legs, but they put the honey from their mouth into the cells. And they sit upon their
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 187 their offspring when they are delivered of it, in the same manner as birds. This offspring, also, is at first a little worm, which lies at the side of the hive ; but afterwards it raises itself, and is nourished, and so adheres to the hive as to seem to be detained by it. The seed, how ever, both of the honey-bees and drones, from which little worms are produced, is white, and these worms, when increased, become honey bees and drones ; but the seed of the kings is of a reddish colour, and its consistence resembles that of thick honey. Its bulk, also, is imme diately similar to that which is produced from it. A worm, however, is not first produced from the seed of the kings, but a honey-bee is immediately seen. When bees, also, bring forth, the honey is disposed in the opposite part of the hive. Sometimes, likewise, the foetus of bees is not perfected, and then mutilated bees are produced, viz. such as are without legs and wings ; but when the foetus is perfect, then the membrane bursting in which they are enclosed, [perfect] bees come forth, which immediately fly. As long, also, as they are in the form of a little worm bees emit excrement, but not afterwards ; unless, as 1 have before observed, they have not come out of the membrane in which they are enclosed. But if any one amputates the head of the foetus before it has wings, the bees themselves devour it ; and if any one plucks off the wings of a drone bee, and sends it into the hive, the bees will eat off the wings of the other drones. The extent, also, of the life of bees is six years, though there are some that live seven years. But when a hive of bees has continued nine or ten years, those that keep bees consider themselves as fortunate. In Pontus, however, there are very white bees, which make honey twice in every month. But the bees in Themiscvra, near the river Thermodon, make their honey-comb as well in cavities of the earth as in hives. These hives, however, do not contain much, but very iittle wax, but the honey in them is thick, and the honey-comb is smooth and equable. Yet these bees do not make honey at all times of the year, but in winter only ; for there is much ivy in this place, which flourishes in the winter; and from the flowers ot the ivy they collect 2 c 2 their
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 188 their honey. White and very thick honey, also, is brought to Amisum from mountainous places; and this honey is made by bees, without hives, in the cavities of trees. Honey, likewise, of this kind is made in Pontus. There are, also, bees that construct triple hives, [i. e. dis tinguished by a triple order of cells,] in the cavities of the earth ; and these hives, indeed, contain honey, but have no worms [from which bees are produced]. Neither, however, are all hives such as these, nor do all bees make such hives. CHAPTER XXIII. But hornets and wasps make hives for their offspring, when they are without a leader, and when they wander and cannot find one. The hornets, indeed, construct their hives in some elevated place, but wasps in a hole. But when hornets and wasps have a leader, they build their hives under the earth. All the hives, therefore, of these, in the same manner as those of bees, are hexagonal ; but they are not composed from wax, but from a matter which is of the nature of bark and sand. The hive, also, of hornets is much more elegant than that of wasps. But they deposit their fœtus or seed, which is of the size of a drop of liquor, in the same manner as bees, in one side of their cells, to the wall of which it adheres. The fœtus, however, is not of the same size in all the cells, but in some it is so large as to be able to fly ; in some, also, there are nymphæ, [i. e. fœtus enclosed in mem branes] ; and in others there are worms. Among the fœtus, also, of hornets and wasps, the worms alone emit excrement, in the same manner as among bees; and as long as the fœtus are nymphs, so long they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 189 they remain immoveable and enveloped in membranes. Opposite, likewise, to the cell of the fœtus, as much honey as is equal in size to a drop of liquor is produced in the hives of hornets. The offspring, however, of hornets and wasps are not generated in the spring, but in the autumn, and they especially receive an apparent increase during the full moon. The fœtus, also, and the worms of these insects do not lie at the bottom of the cell, but adhere to the side of it. CHAPTER XXIV. Some silk-worms, also, in a stone, or something of this kind, con struct nests of mud or clay, which terminate in an acute angle, and which they cover with plaster, so as to give them the appearance of salt. And these nests are so thick and hard, that they can scarcely be perforated with a lance. In these, likewise, they bring forth white worms, involved in a black membrane. But, separate from the mem brane, wax is produced in the clay. And this wax is much paler than the wax of bees. CHAP
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 190 CHAPTER XXV. Ants, also, copulate and bring forth; but the little worms which are their offspring do not adhere to any thing when they are born. These worms, however, as they increase, from being at first small and round, become long and distinctly formed ; but the generation of these is in the spring. CHAPTER XXVI. Land scorpions, likewise, bring forth many little worms in the form of eggs, which they incubate. But the little scorpions, when they are perfect, expel and destroy their parents ; which is, also, the case with spiders. And frequently about eleven in number are produced. ciiaf
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 191 CHAPTER XXVII. With respect to spiders, all of them, indeed, copulate in the manner already explained [in Chap. VIII.] At first, however, they generate small worms ; for the whole of these worms, and not a part, is changed into spiders [though animals which are produced from an egg are not produced from the whole egg, but from a part of it.] But these worms are round at first; and when the spiders bring them forth, they incu bate them, and in the space of three days the worms become distinctly formed. All spiders, likewise, bring forth in a web; but some in a thin and small, and others in a thick, web. And some, in short, bring forth in a round cavity ; but others contain their offspring in their web, to a certain extent. Spiders, however, are not all generated at once ; and as soon as they are born they leap, and begin to form a web. But if the worms of spiders are bruised, a thick and white moisture is found in them, such as is in spiders when they are just born. The spiders, however, which live in meadows bring forth in a web, the half of which is within, and the other half without the spiders themselves, and in this they incubate and produce animals. But the spiders called pha langia weave a thick web, in which they bring forth and incubate their offspring. And such spiders, indeed, as are less hideous bring forth a less numerous progeny ; but the offspring of the phalangia are very numerous ; and when they are adult surround their mother, kill and cast her out of the web. Frequently, also, they kill the male, if they can catch him ; for the male, sometimes, incubales together with the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 192 the female. From one of these spiders, likewise, a hundred small phalangia are produced. But spiders, from being small, become per fect in about the space of four weeks. CHAPTER XXVIII. Crickets, also, copulate after the same manner as other insects, the less getting upon the larger, for the male is less than the female. But the female brings forth on the ground, fixing in it the tube which she has at her tail, and which the males have not. A multitude of crickets, likewise, assembling together, bring forth at once, in the same place ; so that there is, as it were, a hive of them. Afterwards, when they have brought forth, worms in the form of eggs are produced in the place of their delivery, which are enveloped in a certain thin earth, as in a membrane ; and from this, when it bursts, they come forth, and fly. The fœtus, however, of the cricket is so soft that it is crushed even if it is touched. But they do not deposit their offspring on the surface of the earth, but a little below it. And when the offspring have arrived at maturity, small and black crickets come forth from that terrene substance in which they are enclosed ; and afterwards, the skin burst ing, they immediately become larger. They, likewise, bring forth at the end of the summer ; and when they have brought forth, die. For, at the time of their delivery, worms are produced about their neck [which strangle them ;] and the males die about the same time. But they come forth from the earth in the spring. Crickets, however, are not generated in mountainous places, nor in barren ground, but in plains,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 193 plains, and crevices of the earth ; for they bring forth their offspring in crevices. Their eggs, also, remain during the winter in the earth ; but, together with the summer, crickets are produced from the fœtus of the former year. CHAPTER XXIX. In a similar manner, also, the attelabi [grass- worms, or a kind of locusts] bring forth, and having brought forth, die. But their eggs are destroyed by the autumnal rains, when they are abundant ; though, if it happens to be a dry autumn, a greater number of attelabi are gener ated, because they are not similarly destroyed. For the destruction of these insects appears to be without order, and their generation to be casual. CHAPTER XXX. Of grasshoppers, however, there are two genera; some, indeed, being small, which are the first that are seen, and the last that perish ; but others are large, which also sing, and these are produced last, and are 2 c the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 194 the first that perish. The grasshoppers, however, that sing, whether they are small or large, have similarly an incision at the transverse septum ; but those that do not sing have not this incision. Some, also, call the large and singing grasshoppers achetæ, but those that are small cicadulæ. Some of these small grasshoppers, also, that have an incision at the transverse septum sing a little. Grasshoppers, however, are not produced where there are no trees, on which account they are not generated in the plains of Cyrene, but there are many of them in the environs of the city ; and they are especially numerous where there are olives, because these trees are not the occasion of much shadow. For grasshoppers are not produced in cold places, and hence neither are they produced in shady thickets. The large and small grasshoppers, also, similarly copulate with each other, in a supine position. And the male inserts a part of himself into the female, in the same manner as other insects ; but the private parts of the female have a fissure. Grasshoppers, likewise, bring forth in uncultivated land, excavating it with the sharp point which they have behind, in the same manner as the species of locusts called at telabi; for the attelabi, also, bring forth in uncultivated ground ; and, on this account, they abound in Cyrene. Grasshoppers, likewise, bring forth in the reeds with which they support vines, for this purpose per forating the reeds ; and, also, in the stalks of the squill. These fœtus, however, fall to the ground. But they are numerous in rainy seasons. When, also, the worm of the grasshopper increases in the earth, it is called tettigometra, or the matrix of the grasshopper, and then the grass hoppers are most pleasant to the taste, before they burst through the bark or matrix in which they are enclosed. But about the time of the summer solstice they come forth by night, the matrix then immedi ately bursting, and grasshoppers are produced from the tettigometra. They immediately, however, become black, more hard and large, and begin to sing. But in both genera of grasshoppers, [i. e. both in the larger and less kind] the males sing, and not the females. And at first, indeed, the males are sweeter food, but after copulation, the females ; for they have white eggs. When grasshoppers, however, at the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 195 the approach of any one, fly away, they emit a liquid like water, which husbandmen say is their urine ; and they also assert, that, as they are fed with dew, they emit excrement analogous to dew. If any one, however, bending and unbending his finger, gradually approaches to grasshoppers, they will remain where they are sooner than if he imme diately extends his finger. They will, also, get upon his finger ; for, in consequence of seeing obscurely, they conceive the finger to be a leaf agitated by the wind. CHAPTER XXXI. All such insects, however, as are not carnivorous, but feed on the juice of living flesh, such as fleas, lice, and bugs, generate from coition what are called lendes, from which nothing else is again produced. But of these insects, fleas, indeed, arc generated from the least putridity ; for they are formed where there is dry dung ; bugs are generated from the vapour which arises from the skin of animals; and lice are gener ated from flesh. For when lice are nearly generated, certain pustules without pus are formed, and if these are opened with a needle lice come forth. Some men, also, are aflicted with disease when there is an abundance of humidity in the body, and some have after this man ner perished, as they say was the case with the poet Alcman, and Phe recydes of Syria. And in certain diseases great quantities of lice are produced. There is, likewise, a kind of lice which are called fierce. These are harder than the common sort, and are with difficulty separ ated from the body. Lice, therefore, are produced in the heads of children ; but in a less 2 c 2 quantity
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: igg THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. quantity in the heads of men. Women, also, are more subject to lice than men ; but those that have lice in the head are less afflicted with a pain in the head. Lice, likewise, are generated in many other ani mals. For birds have them, and what are called pheasants are destroy ed by them, unless they roll themselves in the dust ; and other birds whose wings have a quill have lice. Other animals, also, that are hairy have lice, except the ass, who has neither lice, nor ticks ; but oxen have both. Sheep, however, and goats have ticks, but not lice ; and swine have large and hard lice ; but in dogs, what are called cynoræstæ, or dog-flails, are generated. All lice, however, are generated from those animals that have them. But animals that wash themselves, and produce lice, then generate a greater quantity of them when they change the water in which they wash. In the sea, also, lice are ge nerated in fishes ; not, however, from the fishes themselves, but from the mud. These lice too, in their form resemble wood-lice, except that they have abroad tail. There is one form, however, of marine lice, and they are generated every where, but especially in caverns. But all these animals have many feet, are exanguious, and insects. About the fins, however, of some of the tunny a horse-flie is produced, which resembles a scorpion, and is as large as a spider. But in the sea which lies between Cyrene and Egypt, there is a certain fish about the dol phin which they call a louse; and this fish is the fattest of all lice, in consequence of its being furnished with abundance of nutriment from the hunting of the dolphin. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 197 CHAPTER XXXII. Other small animals, likewise, are generated, as we have before observed, some, indeed, in wool, and in such substaaces as are formed from wool; as, for instance, moth-worms, which are principally produced in dusty woollen substances, but especially if a spider is enclosed in them ; for if there is any moisture in the wool, the spider absorbs it, and renders the wool dry, [which in this state is adapted to the genera- tion of moth-worms.] This worm, also, is produced in garments. In lod wax, also, in the same manner as in old wood, an animal is gener- ated, which appears to be the smallest of all animals, is white, and is called acari. In books, likewise, other animals are generated ; some of which, indeed, are similar to those in garments, but others to very little scorpions, without a tail. And, in short, in all dry substances when they become moist, and in all moist substances when they become dry. little animals are generated [on account of the change of the tempera ment, from which corruption follows.] There is, likewise, a small worm, which is called xylopthorum, or the wood-destroyer, which is no less singular than any of the before-men tioned insects. For a variegated head comes forth from the shell in which it is enclosed, and its feet are at one extremity of its body [i. e. near the head], like those of other worms. But the rest of its body is enclosed in a garment of the nature of a spider's web, which is surrounded with sprigs, so that it seems to adhere to this garment when it walks. These sprigs, however, are connascent with the garment, in the same manner as the shell in which snails are enclosed naturally adheres to the snails ; nor
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. " 198 nor do they fall off, but, as being connascent, can only be separated by divulsion; and if any one takes away the garment of this insect it becomes useless and dies, in the same manner as a snail when divested of its shell. In the course of time, also, this worm becomes a chrysalis, in the same manner as caterpillars, and lives without any [visible] motion. But the winged animal which is generated from it has not yet been seen. The wild fig-tree, also, produces an insect which is called psen. This insect is at first a small worm; but, afterwards, the skin in which it is enclosed bursting, the psen leaving it flies away, enters into the fruit of the wild fig-tree, and opening it, is the cause that the fruit does not' fall off. Hence, husbandmen append branches laden with wild figs near to those that are fit to eat, and plant the wild in the neighbour hood of domestic figs. CHAPTER XXXIII. With respect, however, to sanguineous and oviparous quadrupeds, their generations, indeed, are in the spring ; yet they do not all co pulate at the same season ; but some in the spring, others in the sum mer, and others in autumn, according as each finds the following sea son is adapted to the generation of its offspring. The tortoise, there fore, brings forth eggs enclosed in a hard shell, and distinguished by a twofold colour, in the same manner as the eggs of birds ; but, having brought them forth, she digs a hole in the earth, in which she buries them, and having made the surface of the ground smooth, she then incubates her eggs, and in the following year discloses them. But the water
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 199 water- tortoise, coming out of the water, excavates in the earth a ditch in the form of a tub, in which she brings forth, and leaves her eggs. After thirty days, however, have elapsed, she again digs up the earth, rapidly discloses her eggs, and immediately brings her young into the water. The marine tortoises, also, bring forth in the earth eggs si milar to those of tame birds ; and, burying them in the ground, incubate them at night. But they bring forth a great multitude of eggs ; for they bring forth a hundred. Lizards, also, and both land and river crocodiles, bring forth in the earth. But the eggs of the lizard are spontaneously disclosed in the earth. For the lizard does not live the space of a year ; since the pe riod of its existence is said to be six months. The river crocodile, however, brings forth many eggs, at most about sixty, and of a white colour; she also incubates them for sixty days ; for the life of this animal is long. But from the very small eggs of the crocodile a very large animal is produced ; for the egg is not larger than that of a goose, and the little crocodile which is born from it is in proportion to the size of this egg. It increases, however, to the magnitude of seventeen cubits. Some, likewise, say that it increases as long as it lives. CHAPTER XXXIV. Of serpents, however, the viper produces an animal external to her self, having first produced an egg within herself. But the egg, in the same manner as that of fishes, is of one colour, and the shell of it is soft. The young viper, also, which is not enclosed in a hard shell, as
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 200 as neither are the young of fishes, is contained in the superior part of the womb. But the viper brings forth small vipers, which are enve loped in membranes, which burst on the third day, [and the young vipers come forth.] Sometimes, however, it happens that the little vipers eat through the mother, and come forth. The viper, likewise, brings forth one at a time in one day ; but she brings forth more than twenty little vipers. Other serpents, however, produce their eggs ex ternally, and these eggs are connected with each other, like the neck laces of women. But when they bring forth, they deposit their eggs in the earth, and there incubate them. These eggs, also, they disclose in the following year. THE
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. CHAPTER I. AFTER this manner, therefore, the generations of serpents and insects, and besides these of oviparous quadrupeds, subsist. With respect to birds, however, all of them are oviparous, but the season of their copu lation and bringing forth their young is not the same in all. For some, as I may say, copulate and bring forth at all times, such as the hen and the pigeon. The hen, indeed, during the whole year, except two months in the winter solstice, [i. e. in December and January]. But some hens, that are of a generous breed, are so prolific, that they lay sixty eggs before they begin to incubate them ; though hens of a gener ous breed are less prolific than those of a common breed. The hens, however, which are called Adrinnic, are, indeed, of a small size, but 2 d they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 202 they bring forth every day ; but they are choleric, and frequently de stroy their young. They have, likewise, all various colours. Domestic hens, also, bring forth twice in the same day. And some of them on account of their very great fecundity soon die. Hens, therefore, bring forth, as I have said, continually ; but the ring-dove, the turtle dove, and the vinous pigeon [or stock-dove], bring forth twice every year, and not ten times, like domestic pigeons. Most birds, however, bring forth in the spring, and some of them, indeed, are multiparous. But they are multiparous in a twofold re spect; some, indeed, because they bring forth frequently, as pigeons; but others because they bring forth many at a time, as hens. All birds, however, with crooked claws are pauciparous, except the kes trel. And this bird is the most prolific of all those that have crooked claws ; for she has been seen to lay four eggs, and she has brought forth more than four. Other birds, indeed, bring forth in nests ; but those which do not fly much, as partridges and quails, do not bring forth in nests, but in the earth, collecting together twigs in which they deposit their eggs. This is, likewise, the case with the lark, and the tetrix, [which, according to some, is a species of larks.] These birds, therefore, build their nests in the open air; but the bird which the Bœotians call merops is the only bird that builds its nest in caverns of the earth. Thrushes, how ever, form their nests from mud, in the same manner as swallows, in lofty trees, and they frame them in such successive connexion Avith each other, as to resemble from their continuity a chain of nests. But the lapwing is the only bird of its kind which does not build a nest ; but entering into the hollow trunks of trees, it there brings forth with out any preparation. And the cuckoo builds its nest both in edifices and in rocks. But the tetrix, which the Athenians call ourax, neither builds its nest in the earth, nor in trees, but in low plants. CHAF.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 203 CHAPTER II. The egg, however, of all birds has a hard shell, if it is produced from seed, and is not corrupted ; for some hens bring forth soft eo-gs. The eggs, also, of birds have a twofold colour ; being, indeed, externally white, but internally yellow. But the eggs of birds which dwell in rivers and marshes differ from those which dwell on dry land; for in the eggs of aquatic birds there is a much greater proportion of the yellow than of the white. And the colours, also, of the eggs differ according to the genera of the birds. For of some, as of the pigeon and the partridge, the eggs are white ; of others they are yellow, as of the birds that dwell in marshes; and of others, as of the turkey-hen and the pheasant, they are marked with points. But the eggs of the kestrel are red, like vermilion. There is, also, a difference in the parts of the egg ; for in one part it is acute, but in the other more broad ; and on its egress from the bird the broad part takes the lead. Small and acute eggs, likewise, are those from which females are produced ; but males are produced from such as are round and circular towards the acute part. Though eggs, therefore, are naturally disclosed by the incubation of birds, yet they are sometimes disclosed spontaneously, as in Egypt; where from eggs buried in the earth in dung chickens are hatched. And in Syracuse, they say that a certain toper, having put eggs under a mat in the earth, continued drinking without intermission till the eggs were hatched. Eggs, also, placed in warm vessels have been so con cocted that chickens have been spontaneously disclosed from them. 2 d 2 The
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 204 The genital seed, therefore, of all birds is white, in the same manner as the seed of other animals. But the female having by copulation received the seed in the superior part of the womb, which is near the transverse septum, conceives an egg, which at first appears to be small and white, but afterwards is red and sanguineous ; and when in the course of time it is increased, the whole becomes red and yellow. When, also, it becomes more thick it is distinguished by two colours ; and the yellow is inward, but the white externally surrounds it. But when it becomes perfect, it is liberated from the womb [to which it was fixed], and comes forth into the light. At that time, likewise, the shell from being soft becomes hard ; so that the egg in proceeding from the womb has not a firm consistence, but when it has proceeded from it, it imediately becomes firm and hard, unless it is diseased. An egg, also, has been seen to come forth entirely yellow, so as to resemble the young bird which is afterwards produced from it. Such eggs, likewise, are found in a hen, when she is dissected, under the transverse septum ; for in that place, to which the eggs usually adhere, eggs are seen having the magnitude of a perfect egg, but entirely of a yellow colour ; which is considered as a prodigy. Those, however, who assert that windy [or addle] eggs are the relics of preceding eggs which were produced from copulation, do not assert what is true ; for it has been sufficiently ascertained, that the young of hens and geese that have not yet copulated have brought forth windy eggs. But windy eggs are not so large as, are less sweet, and moister than, those that are prolific, but they are more numerous. These windy eggs, how ever, if they are put under the incubating bird, are not thickened in their moist part, but both the yellow and the white remain as they were before. Windy eggs, also, are produced from many birds, viz. from the hen, the partridge, the pigeon, the peacock, the goose, and the goose-fox. The young of birds, however, are more rapidly hatched by incuba tion in summer than in winter ; for hens in summer disclose their young in eighteen days ; but in winter they are sometimes five-and-twenty days before they are disclosed. Birds, also, differ from birds in this, that
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 205 that some are more adapted to incubation than others. But if it hap pens to thunder during the incubation of a bird the eggs are corrupted. The eggs, however, which are called by some cynosura [or the urine of a dog] and urina, are produced in summer more than in winter. But windy eggs are denominated by some zephyria, [or the eggs of zephyr,] because birds in the spring are seen to receive the western gales. A like effect, however, is produced by titillating the vulva of birds with the hand. Windy eggs, also, may become prolific, and those which have been now produced from coition are changed into another genus, if before the yellow is separated from the white the female which has windy eggs copulates with the male, or is pregnant from the seed of another bird ; for then the windy eggs become prolific, and the mat ter which was formed by the prior male subsists according to the nature of the male with which the female afterwards copulated. But if the female copulates after the yellow is separated from the white, then the copulation contributes nothing to the fecundity of the windy egg, or to that which was conceived by a prior copulation, passing into the genus of the other male with which the female is afterwards con nected. If, also, coition is intermitted when the eggs have begun to be formed, they do not at all increase ; but if copulation again takes place, they rapidly arrive at their proper magnitude. The yellow and the white of an egg, however, have a nature con trary to each other, not only in colour, but, also, in power. For the yellow acquires a firm consistence by the cold, but the white does not, but is rather liquefied by cold. By fire, however, the white acquires a firm consistence, but the yellow does not, but continues to be soft, unless it is burnt ; and it acquires a firmer consistence, and becomes more hard when boiled, than when exposed to a naked fire. The yellow and the white, also, are separated from each other by a membrane. But the globules which are seen near the beginning of the yellow do not contribute any thing to the generation of the young, as some are of opinion they do. These globules, also, are two ; one, indeed, in the in ferior, but the other in the superior, part of the egg. It happens, like wise, with respect to the vellow or yolk and the white of an egg, that if
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 206 if any one takes several of these out of the shell, and boils them in a saucepan over a gentle sire, all the yolks will come together into the middle, and the whites will surround them in a circle. The young, however, of hens first bring forth immediately on the commencement of spring ; and they bring forth a more numerous pro geny than older hens, though the offspring of the younger are o f a less size than those of the older. In short, if birds do not incubate, they die or become diseased. Among birds, also, the females after copu lation are seized with terror, shake their feathers, and frequently scat ter small pieces of straw; and sometimes they do the very same thing when they bring forth. But the female pigeon at that time [i. e. after copulation] raises her tail ; and geese plunge themselves in the water. Most birds, however, are rapidly pregnant, both with windy and pro lific eggs, as is particularly evident in the partridge, when she is stimu lated to copulation. For if she snuffs the male she becomes pregnant, and is immediately useless for fowling ; since the partridge appears to possess the sense of smelling in an exquisite degree. The generation of the egg, however, after coition, and again the genera tion of the infant bird from the egg when concocted, are not in all birds accomplished in an equal space of time, but the times differ according to the magnitude of the generating birds. The egg of the hen, indeed, acquires a consistence after copulation, and is for the most part per fected in ten days ; and the egg of the pigeon is completed in a some what less time. The female pigeon, also, has the power of retaining the egg in the womb, even at the time of parturition. For if she experi ences any disturbance, either with respect to her nest, or from the loss of a feather, or is afflicted from any other circumstance, she retains her egg, and defers her delivery to a more convenient time. Pigeons, like wise, have this peculiarity with respect to copulation, that the male will not get on the female unless they have first mutually kissed each other. The senior pigeon, indeed, at first copulates, having previously kissed, but afterwards he is connected with the female without kissing ; but younger pigeons never copulate without a kiss preceding. This, therefore, is their peculiarity ; and still farther, when the male is not present,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 207 present, the female pigeons get on each other, in the same manner as the males get on the females ; and though the one emits nothing into the other, yet they conceive and bring forth more eggs, from which, indeed, no young one is produced, but all such eggs are windy. CHAPTER III. The generation, however, from an egg, as has been before observed, happens, indeed, to all birds after the same manner, but the times of its arriving at perfection differ. In hens, therefore, after three days and three nights have elapsed, indications of the future bird present themselves; but in larger hens these indications appear more slowly, and in those that are less more swiftly. In this time, therefore, the yellow ascends to the acute part of the egg, where the principle of the egg subsists, and the egg is disclosed ; and then, in the white of the egg, the heart, like a sanguineous point, presents itself to the view. But this point, as if animated, leaps and is moved ; and from it, when it is increased, two veiny avenues, sanguineous and convolved, tend to each of the surrounding tunics. About the same time, also, a certain mem brane appears, distinguished by sanguineous fibres, and which arising from the two above-mentioned avenues of the veins [surrounds the white of the egg ;] and shortly after, the body of the young bird may be distinguished, which at first is very small and white. But the head is very manifest, and the eyes especially are inflated ; and do not till after a long time decrease, and so contract themselves as to have a due proportion with the other parts of the body. At first, also, in the inferior part of the body no member is seen distinct from the rest. But
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 208 But of the two avenues which extend from the heart, the one tends to the membrane which surrounds the white, but the other to the yel low performing as it were the office of a navel. The principle, there fore, of the infant bird is from the white, but its nutriment is derived from the yellow, through the navel. On the tenth day, however, the whole infant bird, and all its parts, become manifest. But it still has the head larger than the rest of the body, and the eyes larger than the head, not as yet possessing sight. The eyes, also, about this time being prominent, are larger than beans, and black ; but if the skin of them is taken off, a white and cold liquor is seen, which is very splendid when exposed to the light, but has nothing of solidity. Such, therefore, is the manner in which the eyes and head are is posed. At the same time, too, the viscera, the belly, and the nature of the intestines, become apparent ; and the veins which are seen to extend to the heart now become situated near the navel. From the navel, also, two veins are extended, one to the membrane which con tains the yellow; and the yellow at this time is liquid, and more so than is natural to it ; but the other vein extends to the membrane which contains the whole membrane in which the infant bird is en closed, and, also, the membrane of the yellow, and the liquid which is between these. For the infant bird gradually increasing, one part of the yellow becomes situated in the superior and the other in the inferior place ; but in the middle the white liquid is situated. The white, however, as at first, is situated under the inferior part of the yellow. But on the tenth day the whole of the white subsides under the yellow, and then the white is in a small quantity, is viscous and thick, and is of a yellowish colour. For each of the parts within the egg is ar ranged after the following manner : In the first and last part of the egg contiguous to the shell there is a twofold membrane, the one native, and conjoined to the shell, the other adventitious, and produced when the infant bird begins to be formed. This second membrane, also, is un der the first, and in it the white is contained, and, also, the infant bird, together with the membrane in which it is enclosed, and which separ- ates
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 209 ates it, lest it should immediately touch the white, or the liquid. Under the infant bird, also, is the yellow, to which one of the before mentioned veins extends, but the other vein tends to the surrounding white. Another membrane, however, contains all these [viz. the in fant bird, the yellow, and the veins,] together with a moisture which is of the nature of lymph. Afterwards, as has been before observed, another membrane surrounds the embryo itself, and separates it from the liquid. And under this is the yellow, involved in another mem brane, to which the navel, originating from the heart and the great vein, extends ; so that the embryo is not in either of the liquids, [i. e. is not in either the white or the yellow.] On the twentieth day, however, the infant bird begins to chirp, and if any one separates the shell and touches it, it will move itself in a small degree. Now, also, when twenty days have elapsed after incubation, and the bird is disclosed, it is covered with soft feathers. But it has its head above the right leg, near the flank ; and the wings are above its head. At this time, also, the chorion, or membrane, which is after the last membrane of the shell, and to which one of the navels extends, becomes apparent ; and in this the infant bird is then wholly situated. In a similar manner, also, the other membrane becomes apparent which surrounds the yellow, and to which the other navel is extended. Each navel, however, originates from the heart and the great vein. At this time, likewise, [i.e. about the twentieth day] the navel, which extends to the membrane that surrounds the white, is loosened from the animal, and falls ; but the other navel, which extends to the yellow, adheres to the infant bird by a thin intestine, and through it much of the yellow passes to the young bird, and a yellow sediment is emitted in the belly. About this time, like- Avise, the young bird discharges its excrement towards the external chorion. And both in the belly of the bird and external to it there is a certain white excrement. But, at length, the yellow always be- coming less is wholly consumed by the bird; so that if it is cut open ten days after it is disclosed, a little of the vellow will be found still remaining in the intestine. The bird, however, is now liberated from the navel, and nothing intervenes; but the whole of the moisture is 2 E consumed
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 210 BOOK VI. consumed. During the before-mentioned time, also, the young bird sleeps, but is sometimes excited from sleep, looks up and chirps ; and the heart is inflated, together with the navel, as if respiring. After this manner, therefore, the generation of birds from an egg subsists. Some birds, also, bring forth unprolific eggs, and these pro duced from copulation. But no bird is generated from these by incu bation. This, however, has been observed particularly to happen with pigeons. Double eggs, however, have two yolks, which sometimes that they may not be confounded are separated by a thin interstice of the white ; and sometimes the two yolks are in contact with each other without this interstice. There are, also, some hens that bring forth all their eggs double, so that in these, also, the above-mentioned circumstance happens respecting the yolk. For a certain hen having brought forth eighteen double eggs, disclosed two chickens from each, those eggs excepted which were unprolific. Two chickens, also, were disclosed from each of the double eggs, but one of the chickens was larger than the other. But the last chicken that was disclosed was a monster. CHAPTER IV. All birds, however, of the genera of pigeons, such, for instance, as the ring-dove and the turtle-dove, bring forth two eggs ; but the most which the turtle and ring-dove bring forth are three eggs. And the pigeon, indeed, brings forth, as we have before observed, at all seasons, but the ring and turtle-dove bring forth in the spring, and not oftener than twice. When the former eggs, likewise, which they have pro- duced
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 211 duced are destroyed, they lay the second eggs ; for many birds destroy their eggs. The ring and turtle-dove, therefore, as I have said, some times bring forth three eggs, yet they never disclose more than two young ones from them ; and sometimes they only disclose one ; but the remaining egg is always unprolific. Most birds, however, that are but one year old generate nothing. But all birds, when they once begin to bring forth, always contain eggs in the womb ; though in some birds the eggs are so small that they can scarcely be seen. The pigeon, also, for the most part, produces a male from one egg, and a female from the other ; and, for the most part, she produces the male prior to the female. Besides this, likewise, after she has brought forth in one day, she omits many days, and again brings forth another egg. The male, however, incubates in a part of the day; but the female at night; and the young bird which was produced from the first of the eggs is disclosed, and flies within twenty days. But pigeons perforate the egg the day before they disclose it ; and both the male and female warm [with their vivific heat] the young for a certain time, in the same manner as they warm their eggs. With respect to rearing the young, also, the female conducts herself with more severity than the male, in the same manner as other animals after delivery. They, likewise, bring forth ten or eleven times in a year ; and in Egypt twelve times. But both the male and female pigeon copulate within the year in which they are born ; for they copulate in six months after their birth. Some, however, say that the ring-dove and the turtle-dove copulate and generate when they are three months old, of which they consider the multitude of them as an indication. Their gestation, likewise, con tinues for fourteen days, and their incubation for the same number of days ; but in another fourteen days the young are covered with fea thers, and fly so much that they cannot easily be caught. It is, also, said, that the ring-dove lives forty years, and partridges more than sixteen years. But the pigeon having hatched her young, brings forth again in the space of thirty days. 2e2 CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 212 CHAPTER V. The vulture, however, buflds her nest in inaccessible rocks ; and on this account the nest and the young of the vulture are but rarely seen. Hence, Herodotus, the father of Brysson the sophist, says, that vultures come from another land, unknown to us ; of which, he says, this is an indication, that no one has seen the nest of the vulture, and that many of them suddenly appear following armies. Though it is difficult, however, to see their nest, yet it has been seen. Vultures, also, bring forth two eggs. All carnivorous birds, therefore, accord in this, that they are not seen to bring forth more than once in a year; except the swallow, which, though a carnivorous bird, builds her nest and brings forth twice in a year. And if any one pierces the eyes of the offspring of swallows while they are yet young, they will after wards be restored to a sane condition, and again possess the power of seeing. 5 ca As.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 213 CHAPTER VI. The eagle, however, brings forth three eggs, but discloses two of these, as it is said in the verses which are ascribed to Musæus : , " Three eggs she lays, two hatches, and one bird she rears." For the most part, therefore, this happens to be the case; yet three young have been known to be disclosed from the eggs of the eagle. But when the two young ones are grown up, the eagle ejects one of them, in consequence of being wearied with their nurture. At this time, also, it is said she remains without food, because she does not then seize the whelps of wild beasts. Her nails, also, are then, distorted for a few days, and her wings become white; so that at that time eagles become cruel to their offspring. But the osprey receives and nurtures the ejected young eagle. The eagle, also, incubates her eggs for thirty days; and as much time as this is, also, spent by other large birds in incubation, as by the goose and the bustard ; but by birds of a middle size, as the kite and the hawk, twenty days are employed in incubation. The kite, how ever, for the most part, brings forth two eggs, and sometimes she dis closes from them three infant birds. But the kite called Aetolius sometimes brings forth four eggs, and discloses four young. The raven, however, not only brings forth two eggs, as some say, but many. She, also, incubates them twenty days, and expels the young from her nest. This very same thing is, likewise, done by other birds. For frequently those birds that bring forth many young expel one of them. All the genera of eagles, however, are wot similarly disposed with respect to their
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 214 their offspring, but the eagle called pygargus ' is cruel, and the black eagle is benevolently disposed, towards her young. For, in short, all birds that have crooked claws expel their young from the nest as soon as they are able to fly, and compel them by blows to depart. Nearly, likewise, most other birds, as we have before observed, do the same thing ; and except the crow, having nourished, take no far ther care of their young. The crow, however, pays attention to them for a certain time ; for she nourishes them even when they are able to fly. CHAPTER VII. With respect to the cuckoo, some are of opinion that this bird is a transformation from the sparrow-hawk, because about the time in which the cuckoo is seen the sparrow-hawk, which resembles the cuckoo, disappears. About the time, however, in which the cuckoo begins to sing, not only the sparrow-hawk is not to be seen, but this is also the case with every other species of hawk ; except that they are only visible for a few days. But the cuckoo is seen for a short time in summer, and disappears in winter. The sparrow-hawk, however, has crooked claws, but the cuckoo has not. Farther still, neither does the head of the cuckoo resemble that of the sparrow-hawk, but both its head and its claws are more similar to those of the pigeon, and it alone resembles the sparrow-hawk in its colour, except that the colour of the latter is variegated like lines, but that of the cuckoo like points. 1 So called from having a white tail. The
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 215 The cuckoo, also, in its magnitude and flying resembles the smallest species of the sparrow-hawk, which, for the most part, is not seen at the time in which the cuckoo appears ; though both of them have been seen at the same time. The cuckoo, also, has been seen to be de voured by the sparrow-hawk ; though no birds of the same kind are known to do this. It is, likewise, said, that no one has ever seen the young of the cuckoo. The cuckoo, however, brings forth, indeed, but does not build a nest ; and sometimes she brings forth in the nest of lesser birds, the eggs of which birds she eats. She more particularly, however, brings forth in the nest of the ring-dove, and eats the eggs •of this bird. For the most part, likewise, she brings forth one egg, but very seldom two. She, also, brings forth in the nest of the hen linnet, who incubates the egg, and nurtures the young of the cuckoo. But the cuckoo at the time in which she brings forth is most fat, and her flesh is sweet as food. The young, likewise, of sparrow-hawks are very fat, and their flesh is very sweet. But there is a certain genus of sparroAv- hawks who build their nest on steep rocks. CHAPTER VIII. A great number of birds, however, incubate, as we have observed concerning pigeons, the males alternately succeeding the females in this employment during the time in which the female is engaged in the search of food. Among geese, however, the females alone incu bate, and when they have begun to do this, continue sitting without intermission. The nests, also, of all birds that live in marshes are constructed
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI ■2\d constructed in swampy and grassy places, on which account, being undisturbed while they incubate, they are able to impart a certain nutriment to their young, and are not entirely without food. Of crows, also, the females alone incubate, and continue sitting on their eggs without intermission. But in the mean time the males nourish the females, bring them food, and feed them with it. With respect to pigeons, however, the female beginning to incubate in the evening continues in this employment the whole night, till the hour of break fast; and the male incubates the remaining time. But partridges make two receptacles of eggs; and in one of these the female, but in the other the male, incubates. Each, also, discloses its young, and as soon as they are disclosed copulate with them. CHAPTER IX. The peacock, however, lives five-and-twenty years, and especially begins to generate at the age of three years ; at which time, also, it receives a variety of plumage ; and discloses its eggs in thirty or a few more days. But it brings forth once only in a year, and lays twelve, or a somewhat less number of eggs. It, likewise, omits two or three days in bringing forth, and does not lay its eggs in an uninterrupted succession; but its first progeny do not consist of more than eight eggs. Peacocks, also, bring forth windy or unprolific eggs. But they copu late in the spring; and bring forth immediately after copulation. They, also, lose their feathers at the same time that the leaves fall from trees, and they again begin to be replumed when the trees are in blos som. Those persons, likewise, that rear peacocks put their eggs under hens
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 217 hens to be incubated, because if the female peacock incubates her own eggs, the male flying on the female breaks them. On this account, also, among certain wild birds, the females, [when the time of bringing forth is near] flying from the males, lay and incubate their eggs [secret ly.] Two eggs, however, alone of the peacock are put under a hen, because the hen can only disclose two eggs of the peacock by incubation. Care, likewise, is taken that there is no intermission in the incubation of the hen, and that for this purpose she is supplied with food. Birds, however, at the time of copulation have their testicles manifestly larger; those, indeed, that are more salacious have them more conspicuously larger, as cocks and partridges ; but those that do not continually copulate have them less manifestly increased. CHAPTER X. After this manner, therefore, the conception and generation of birds subsist. But with respect to fishes, that all of them are not oviparous has been asserted before, for the cartilaginous kind called selache are viviparous. They first, hoAvever, conceive an egg in themselves, and nourish it in themselves, the marine frog excepted. Fishes, also, have different wombs, as we have before observed. For those that are oviparous have wombs situated in the inferior part, and divided into two cavities; but the selache have wombs more similar to the wombs of birds. They differ, however, from those of birds, because birds contain their eggs in the superior part of the womb, i. e. under the transverse septum; but certain of the selache contain their eggs in the 2 p middle
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI 218 middle part of the womb, near the spineof the back; in which place the eggs, when increased, are transferred to another part of the womb. The e^g, likewise, of all fishes is not of a twofold colour, but of one colour only. But it is more white than yellow, both at first and when it contains a young fish. The generation of fishes, however, from an ecrcr differs from that of birds, because fishes have not a second navel [or umbilical chord] extending to the membrane which is under the shell, but they have in the same manner as birds the avenue which extends to the yellow of the egg. But in other respects the generation of fishes from an ego- is similar to the generation of birds. For both birds and fishes are produced in the supreme part of the egg, and the veins in both similarly extend first from the heart; and the head, the eyes, and superior parts are, at first, in both, similarly the largest. As the fœtus, however, increases, the egg always becomes less, and at length disap- pears and enters into the interior parts of the little fish, in the same manner as the whole of the yellow is absorbed by the infant bird. The navel, also, adheres a little below the entrance of the belly. And the navel in fishes while they are young is long, but as they increase it becomes less, and diminishes till at length, as was before observed in birds, it wholly hides itself within the fœtus. Both the embryo, also, and the egg are contained in a common membrane, and under this there is another membrane which particularly contains the embryo ; but between the membranes there is a liquid. The nutriment, also, of the little fishes exists in the belly, in the same manner as the nutriment of infant birds, and is partly white, and partly J yellow. With respect to the figure of the womb, however, the mode of its subsistence must be surveyed from dissections. But there is a difference in the wombs with respect to themselves, as in those of the sea-dogs with respect to each other, and, also, with respect to the wombs of the broad fishes. For in some, as in the little sea-dogs, as we have before observed, the eggs adhere to the middle of the belly, near the spine; * i. e. The nutriment of fishes is white, but of birds yellow. but
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 219 but when increased they are liberated from the place to which they adhere; and as the womb is divided into two cavities, the eggs when liberated descend into each inferior part of the womb, and adhere to the transverse septum. The womb, however, both of these and other sea-dogs, a little below the transverse septum, has, as it were, white mammæ, which are not apparent, except when these animals are preg- nant. The small sea-dogs, therefore, and thornbacks have in their womb certain testaceous substances which contain an egg-formed liquid ; but the figure of this shell resembles the tongue of a flute ; and within the shell there are capillary tubes. In those little sea-dogs, therefore, which some call colts, when the shell bursts and falls the young ones come forth ; but thornbacks bring forth their young enclosed in the shell, and when the shell bursts the young fish emerges. The thorny sea-dog, however, contains its eggs in the superior part of the womb, near the transverse septum, and above the [before-mentioned] mammæ of the womb ; but when the egg descends, and is liberated, then a young one is produced from it. The generation of the sea-fox is, also, effected after the same manner. The sea-dogs, however, that are called smooth have their eggs situated in the middle of the womb, in a manner similar to the small sea-dog ; and afterwards the eggs descend into each of the cavities into which the womb is divided. An animal, also, is then generated, which through the navel adheres to the matrix, so that the egg being con sumed the embryo appears to subsist in a manner similar to that in which quadrupeds are contained in the womb of their mother. But the navel [or umbilical chord] being long, adheres [by one of its extremities] to the inferior part of the matrix, as if depending from an acetabulum, but by the other extremity adheres to the middle of the embryo, or to that part in which the liver is contained. On dissecting the embryo, likewise, nutriment of the nature of an egg will be found, though the egg no longer remains ; but a chorion and peculiar mem branesenvelop each of the embryos, in the same manner as in quadrupeds. The embryos, likewise, have their head at first in the superior part of the womb ; but when they are larger and perfect, they have their head 2 f 2 . in
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI 220 in the inferior part of the womb. Males, however, are generated in the left part of the womb, and females in the right, and sometimes both males and females are generated in the same part. When embryos, also, are dissected, the viscera, such as the liver, Sec. in the same manner as those of quadrupeds, are found to be large and sanguineous. All the selache, however, have a multitude of eggs in the superior part of the womb, near the transverse septum, which eggs in some are larger, and in others less; but in the inferior part of the womb they contain the embryos. Hence fishes of this kind are thought to bring forth and copulate frequently in a month, because they do not bring forth all that they have conceived at once, but frequently, and for a long time ; for while they conceive eggs in the superior part of the womb, the fœtus is matured and arrives at perfection in the inferior part of it. Other sea-dogs, therefoie, and, also, the file, and the torpedo or cramp fish, emit their offspring from themselves, and again receive them into themselves. A large cramp-fish, also, has been seen which contained in itself eighty embryos. But the thorny dog is the only one of the sea-dogs which does not receive its offspring within itself, in con sequence of the thorn [with which the young are armed.] Of the broad fishes, also, neither the pastinaca nor the scate receive their young within themselves, on account of the roughness of their tail. Nor does the marine frog receive its young, on account of their thorns, and the magnitude of their head. For, as we have before observed, the marine frog is the only fish of the cartilaginous kind that is not viviparous. chap.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 221 CHAPTER XI. Such, therefore, is the difference of these fishes with respect to each other, and such is the generation of them from eggs. The males, however, at the time of copulation have their ducts so full of genital seed, that when compressed white seed flows externally from them. But these ducts or avenues are bifidated, and originate from the transverse septum and the great vein. At the time of copulation, therefore, the ducts of the males are manifestly enlarged, though at other times they can scarcely be seen. For in some fishes they some times become entirely immanifest, as we before observed concerning the testicles of birds. The spermatic ducts, however, of the males differ from those pertaining to the womb in females in other respects, and in this, also, that the ducts of the males adhere to the kidneys, but those of the female are easily moved and involved in a thin mem brane. The mode, however, in which the ducts of the males subsist must be surveyed from anatomical descriptions. Superfetation, also, pertains to the selache, and the longest period of their conception is six months. But that sea-dog which is called the star-fish brings forth most frequently ; for it brings forth twice in a month. It, also, begins to copulate in the month of September. Other sea-dogs, however, bring forth twice in a year, the little sea-dog excepted; and this fish brings forth once in a year. All of them, like wise, bring forth in the spring ; but the file-fish brings forth the second time in autumn, towards the setting of the winter pleiades; and the first time, in the spring. Its second progeny, also, is more abundant than
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 222 than the first. But the cramp-fish brings forth in autumn. The se lache, likewise, bring forth on the land, ascending for this purpose from the sea, and the profundities of the sea, both on account of warmth and the greater security of their offspring. With respect to other fishes, therefore, none are seen to copulate with any other than those of their own kind ; but the file-fish and the scate alone appear to do this; for there is a certain fish which is called rinobatus, or the file-scate. For it has the head and anterior parts of the scate, but the posterior parts of the file, as being formed from both these fishes. CHAPTER XIL The sea-dogs, therefore, and those of the same species, such as the dog-fox, the dog properly so called, and those broad fishes, the cramp* fish, the scate, the smooth scate, and the pastinaca, producing an egg within themselves, are after this manner viviparous. The dolphin, also, the whale, and such other cetaceous animals as have not gills, but a pipe through Avhich by respiring they draw the air, are viviparous ; and this is, also, the case with the pristes, and the sea-ox. For no one of these is seen to have eggs, but each has immediately a fœtus, from which when evolved an animal is generated, in the same manner as man and viviparous quadrupeds. The dolphin, however, for the most part, only brings forth one fœtus, and sometimes two ; but the whale, for the most part, and frequently, brings forth either two or one. And the phocæna brings forth similarly with the dolphin ; for it resembles a small dolphin, and is produced in the Pontic sea. The phocæna, how ever, differs from the dolphin ; for its magnitude is less, its back is broader,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS BOOK VI. 223 broader, and it is of an azure colour. Many, also, say that the phocæna is a certain species of the dolphin. All fishes, however, that have a pipe respire ; for they have lungs, and receive the air through the pipe by respiring. And the dolphin has been seen to sleep and snore, with his pipe raised above the water. The dolphin, likewise, and the pho cæna have milk, with which they nourish their young ; and they, also, receive their offspring when little within themselves. But the offsprinc of the dolphin increase rapidly, for in ten years they acquire a perfect magnitude. The female dolphin, also, is pregnant during the space of ten months ; but she brings forth in the summer, and not at any other season. At the rising of the dog-star, however, it happens that dolphins are concealed for thirty days. They, also, follow their young for a long time ; for the dolphin is an animal attached to its offspring. It, likewise, lives many years; for it is certain that some dolphins have lived twenty-five, and others thirty years. For fishermen, having cut off the tails of certain dolphins, have afterwards returned them to the sea, and by this circumstance have been able to ascertain their age. The phoce, however, or sea-calf, is an amphibious animal ; for it does not, indeed, receive water [like fishes], but respires, and sleeps, and brings forth on the land, but near shores, as ranking among the num ber of pedestrious animals. It lives, however, the greatest part of its life in the sea, from which, also, it derives its nutriment ; on which account, it must be considered in conjunction with aquatic animals. The phoce, therefore, immediately conceives an animal in itself, brings it forth enveloped in a chorion, and has milk in the same manner as a sheep. But it brings forth one or two, and at most three, offspring. It, likewise, has two mammæ, and is suckled by its young after the manner of quadrupeds. It brings forth, also, like a woman, at every season of the year, and especially at the time in which goats first bring forth. But about the twelfth day after delivery it brings its offspring to the sea, and this it does frequently every succeeding day, that it may gradually accustom them to that element. The young phoeæ, however, do not walk, because they cannot support themselves on their feet, but they creep along in a prone position. The phoeæ, also, can
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 224 can collect and contract itself, for it is fleshy and soft, and has carti laginous bones. It is, likewise, difficult to kill the phoce violently, unless it is struck on the temple ; for the body of it is fleshy. But it emits a voice resembling that of an ox. The vulva of the female, also, is similar to that of the scate ; and all such animals have a vulva re sembling that of a woman. CHAPTER XIII. After this manner, therefore, aquatic and viviparous animals gener ate, and bring forth their offspring. But oviparous fishes, as we have before observed, have their womb bifidated, and situated in the infe rior part. All fishes, however, that have scales are oviparous; such, for instance, as the wolf, the mullet, the cephalus or pollard, and the etelis; and all those that are called white, together with those that are smooth [because they are without scales], except the eel. Their egg, also, is sandy. It appears, however, to be so, because the whole womb of these fishes is full of eggs, so that in small fishes there appears to be only two eggs ; for the womb in them is immanifest, on account of its smallness and thinness. Concerning the copulation, therefore, of all fishes, we have before spoken. In most fishes, however, there is a distinction of male and female; but it is dubious whether there is this distinction in the roach and chamæ, for all that are caught of these are found to have eggs. Fishes, therefore, that copulate generate eggs from their copulation. But they, also, have eggs without copulation ; and this is evident in some
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: EOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 225 some river fishes. For the phoxini, which are very small, have eg<rS, as I may say, as soon as they are born. All fishes, however, scatter their eggs [through the sea,] and, as it is said, the males devour the greater part of the eggs, and some perish in the water ; and those alone are preserved which are brought forth and deposited in opportune places. For if all the eggs were preserved, fishes of every kind would be too numerous. Many, also, of those' Avhich are preserved are not prolific, but those only' which the male sprinkles with his genital seed. For this purpose, however, the male follows the female ; and when the female has brought forth, the male sprinkles the eggs with his seed. From all such eggs, likewise, as he sprinkles little fishes are produced ; but they are produced from other eggs, just as it may happen. The very same thing, likewise, happens in the mollia. For the male cuttle-fish, when the female brings forth, sprinkles the eggs with his seed ; which, also, may reasonably be sup- posed to happen in the other mollia, but at present is only seen to take place in the cuttle-fish. Fishes, also, bring forth their eggs near the land ; gudgeons, indeed, in the cavities of stones, except the egg which is brought forth is broad and sandy. Other fishes, likewise, bring- forth in a similar manner. For places near the land are warmer, and afford more abundant nutriment ; and the offspring in such places are not so liable to be devoured by the larger fishes. Hence the greater part of fishes in the Pontic sea bring forth near the river Thermodon; for this place is tranquil and warm, and abounds with sweet water. But other oviparous fishes bring forth once in a year, except the small phycis ; and this fish brings forth twice in a year. T he male phycis, however, differs from the female in this, that it is blacker, and has larger scales. Other fishes, therefore, bring forth their eggs through the avenue or mouth of the womb ; but the fish which some call the needle, at the time of bringing forth bursts, and thus the eggs come forth. For this fish has under its belly a certain fissure resembling the fissure of the blind serpent. When the needle-fish, however, has brought forth, it lives, and its belly which was burst again coalesces. 2 g The
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 226 The generation, however, from an egg happens similarly, both in those fishes that produce an egg inwardly and in those that produce it externally. For the fœtus is generated in the summit of the egg, and is enclosed in a membrane, and the eyes, which are large and spheri cal, are the first parts that are manifest; by which it is evident, that fishes are not, as some say, generated in a manner similar to those ani mals which are produced from worms. For, on the contrary, in the latter the inferior parts are at first larger, but the head and the eyes are increased afterwards. When the egg, likewise, bursts the little fish appears, just as the nut of an almond is seen when the shell, is broke. And at first, indeed, the little fish receives no nutriment, but is increased from the moisture produced from the egg. Afterwards, however, it is nourished with river water, till it is sufficiently increased. But when the Politic sea purifies itself, a certain substance is carried into the Hellespont, which they call phucos [or sea-weed,] and which is of a yellow colour. Some, however, say that this is the flower of the phucos, from which a paint is made.. It is, also, produced at the be ginning of the summer. Shell-fish, and the little fishes which live in these places, are, likewise, nourished with it. And some persons that live near the sea say, that the purple-fish derives from this phucos its flower. CHAPTER XIV. The fishes, however, of lakes and rivers, for the most part, as I may say, conceive in the fifth month of their age ; and all of them bring forth within a year. But the females of these, in the same manner
