text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 227 manner as marine fishes, do not emit all their eggs at once, nor do the males discharge the whole of their seed, but the females have always a greater or less number of eggs, and the males a greater or less quan tity of genital seed. The females, also, bring forth in an appropriate season ; the carp, indeed, five or six times in a year, and especially at the rising of certain stars ; but the chalcis brings forth thrice ; and others once in a year. All of them, however, bring forth on the sides of rivers and lakes, and in places abounding with reeds ; as, for instance, the phoxini and perches. But the glanis and the perch bring forth eggs, adhering to each other like a necklace, in the same manner as frogs. So connected, indeed, and entwined are their eggs, that fishermen roll the eggs of the perch round the reed to which their line is fixed. The larger glanii, therefore, bring forth in deep lakes, and some of them in lakes six feet in depth ; but the smaller glanii bring forth in lakes less deep, and especially near the roots of the willow, or some other tree, and, also, among reeds and moss. Sometimes, also, the large glanii copulate with the small, and applying those avenues to each other which some call navels, the female emits eggs, and the male liis genital seed. Such eggs, also, as are mingled with the genital seed immediately become whiter, and, as I may say, in the same day appear to be larger. But in a short time after, the eyes of the little fish are manifest ; for these in all fishes, in the same manner as in other ani mals, are immediately most manifest, and appear to be the largest of all the parts. Those eggs, however, which have not been sprinkled with the seed of the male are useless and unprolific. But when the little fishes are increased from prolific eggs, they are purified as it were from a shell ; and this is a membrane which envelops both the egg and the little fish. When, however, the genital seed is mingled with the egg, the egg becomes very viscous and glutinous, and, therefore, adheres to the roots of herbs or other substances in the places where it is brought forth. Where the greatest number of eggs, also, are laid, the male glanis guards them, in the absence of the female that brought them forth. The increase, however, of the glanii from eggs is most slow, 2 g 2 on
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 228 on which account the male sits as a guardian of the eggs for thirty or forty days, in order that the progeny may not be devoured by fishes that may happen to meet with them. But the generation of the carp is next to that of the glanis in slowness ; and, in a similar manner, its eogs, after they are brought forth, are guarded by the male. The eggs, also, of some smaller fishes so rapidly increase, that in the space of three days they become little fishes. But the eggs which have been sprinkled with the seed of the male receive an increase, both in the day in which they were sprinkled, and, likewise, afterwards. The eggs of the glanis, therefore, increase to the size of the grains of the bitter vetch ; but those of the carp, and such like fishes, to the size of a grain of millet. These fishes, therefore, bring forth and generate after this manner. But the chalcis brings forth its eggs thick, and collected together. And the fish which they call psylon brings forth its eggs near shores, in places exposed to the wind. This fish, also, collects its eggs together in one place. But the carp, the balin, and all other fishes, as I may say, are impelled into shallow water for the purpose of bringing forth ; and frequently thirteen or fourteen males follow one female. But when the female after having brought forth her egg departs, the males sprin- kle it with their genital seed. Most of their eggs, however, perish; for, because the female as she passes through the water lays her eggs, it is necessary that the eggs being dissipated by the stream should perish, except those which adhere to some substance they may meet with. For no fish besides the glanis is a guardian of the eggs of the female except the carp, and this fish only then guards them when it finds them collected into one place. All male fishes, however, have genital seed,. except the eel ; and this fish has neither genital seed, nor an egg. Mullets, therefore, ascend from the sea into lakes and rivers ; but eels,. on the contrary descend from lakes and rivers into the sea. c II a p.

text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 229 CHAPTER XV. Most fishes, therefore, as has been said, are generated from eggs. Some, however, are generated from mud and sand ; and there are some of this description even among those which are produced from copula- tion and eggs, which they say sometimes happens to be the case both in other muddy places and in the pools about Cnidos, which become dry through the heat occasioned by the dog-star, so that even all the mud remains without moisture. These places, however, begin to be filled with water with the first rain that falls, and as soon as the water com- mences, little fishes are generated in it. But these little fishes are a certain species of mullets, which are not produced from copulation, and are of the size of small mœnidia ; but in these there is neither any egg nor genital seed. In the rivers in Asia, also, where they flow into the sea, other small fishes are generated after the same manner as the before-mentioned, of the largest of which they make sauce. Some, however, assert that all mullets are generated spontaneously from putrid matter. [But this is false ;] for the females of them are seen to have eggs, and the males genital seed. There is, however, a certain genus of them which is spontaneously generated from mud and sand. That some fishes, therefore, are generated spontaneously, neither from eggs nor from copulation, is evident from what has been said. All such fishes, however, as are neither oviparous nor viviparous are generated either from mud or sand, or any putrid matter which floats on the surface of the water. Such, for instance, is the fish aphye, which is
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 230 is called foam, and is generated from sandy earth ; and this fish is without increase, and is unprolific. After a long time, also, it perishes, and another is again produced in its stead. Hence, except during a short time, the apkyæ are generated in every other season of the year; for they continue to be formed from the autumnal arcturus to the spring. But there are indications that they are sometimes produced from the earth [which is at the bottom of the sea;] for they are not caught by fishermen if it is cold, but only when it is warm, in conse quence of ascending from the earth at the bottom of the sea, allured by the tepid heat. If the earth, also, at the bottom of the sea is agi tated, it frequently happens that the aphyæ are caught, and are then better and more numerous. But other aphyæ are inferior to these in consequence of receiving a rapid increase. The aphyæ, likewise, are produced in shady and warm places, at those times in which the earth becomes warm through the serenity of the weather. Hence they are produced in Athens, at Salamis, and near that part of the Piræus which bears the name of Themistocles, and in Marathon; for in these places foam is generated. But they are seen in such like places, and during such like serenity of weather. Some times, likewise, they are generated when there happens to be an abun dance of rain, in the foam which is produced by the rain water; and hence they are denominated foam. Sometimes, also, they are borne along on the surface of the sea, when the weather is serene, and then they are involved in the foam from which they are produced, in the same manner as small worms in the dung from which they originate. Hence the aphyæ are borne along to many places together with the sea ; and they are generated and caught in greater abundance when the year happens to be moist and warm. Other aphyæ, however, are the progeny of fishes. For the aphye which is called cobites is produced from small putrid gudgeons, which descend into the earth. But the aphyæ which are called arades are produced from the phalerice. From these, also, the trichides are generated ; and from the trie/tides, the trichiæ. From one aphye, likewise, such as that which is found in tie port of the Athenians, those little fishes are generated
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 231 generated which are called encrasicholi. But there is another aphye, which is the progeny of the mœnides and mullets. The aphye, how ever, which is called foam, and which is unprolific, is moist and continues but for a short time, as was before observed; for at length nothing is left but its head and eyes. But fishermen that they may carry it away with them sprinkle it with salt; for by this means it continues for a longer time. CHAPTER XVL Eels, however, are neither generated from copulation, nor do they bring forth eggs, nor has any eel ever been caught which had either any genital seed or an egg. In the dissection of eels, also, no avenues have ever been found destined to the reception or emission of seed, or to performing the office of a womb; but among sanguineous animals, the whole genus of eels is neither produced from copulation nor from eggs. It is, however, evident that this is the case ; for in some muddy lakes, all the water being exhausted, and the mud extracted, when the rain falls, eels are again generated. But in dry seasons, they are not generated even in perennial lakes ; for they live and are nourished by rain-water. That they are neither generated, therefore, from copulation nor from eggs is evident. To some, however, eels appear to have the power of generating, because small worms are ingenerated in certain eels; for they fancy that eels are generated from these worms. This, however, is not true ; but they are generated from what are called the entrails of the earth ; which are spontaneously formed in mud, and in moist earth. For some eels have been seen proceeding from these entrails
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 232 entrails of the earth, and other have been found in them when dissected. In the sea, also, and in rivers substances of this kind [i. e. such as the entrails of the earth] are generated, especially where there is putrefac tion. They are generated, indeed, in the sea, in places where the phucos is found ; but in rivers and lakes they are generated near the banks ; for in these places the bland heat causes putrefaction. Such, therefore, is the generation of eels. CHAPTER XVII. All fishes, however, do not bring forth at the same time, nor in a similar manner, nor are all of them pregnant for an equal time. Prior to copulation, therefore, shoals of male and female fishes assemble, but at the time of copulation they so join themselves together, that for the most part one male is united to one female. Some of these, also, are pregnant for not more than thirty days ; but others for a less time. All of them, however, continue pregnant during times which may be divided into hebdomads. But those fishes are pregnant the longest time which some call marini. The sargus, indeed, copulates in the month of December; but is pregnant during thirty days ; and among the genera of mullets, that which some call the lip, and, also, the muxon, are pregnant at the same season and during an equal time with the sargus. All fishes, likewise, are in pain during the time of their pregnancy ; hence at this period especially they fall on the land, for they are furiously hurried along towards the shore ; and, in short, at this time they are in continual motion till they bring forth ; and this is especially the case with the mullet. But when they have brought forth they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 233 they are tranquil. Many fishes, however, cease to bring forth when little worms are generated in their belly; for small and animated sub stances are produced in them, which expel the fœtus [before it is perfect, and cause an abortion.] Those fishes, indeed, that are denominated ruades bring forth in the spring ; but most bring forth during the vernal equinox. Others, however, do not bring forth in the same season of the year, but some in the summer, and others during the autumnal equinox. But among fishes of this kind, the first is the arista, or ear-of-corn, which deposits its offspring near the earth ; and the cephalus is the last. This is evident from the progeny of the arista being first seen, and that of the cepha lus being seen the last. The mullet, also, is among the first that bring forth ; but the stock-fish, in most places, brings forth at the beginning of summer, and in some places in autumn. The alopias, also, which they call anthias, brings forth in summer. But after these are the, gold-fish, the wolf, the mormurus, and, in short, those that are called runners. The last, however, of those that live in a shoal are the bar bel, and the coracinus 1 ; and these bring forth in autumn. But the barbel deposits its eggs in mud ; on which account it is late in bring ing forth, for the mud is cold for a long time. The coracinus, how ever, is later than the barbel, and brings forth among sea-weeds, be cause it lives in stony places. It is, also, pregnant for a long time. But the mœnides bring forth after the winter solstice. Most other fishes, however, that dwell in the deep sea bring forth in summer; of which this is an indication, that at this time they are not caught. The mœ.nis, likewise, is the most prolific of fishes ; and of the sc- Jaches the marine frog: but they are rare because they easily perish. For the marine frog brings forth all its eggs at once, and deposits them near the earth. In short, the selache are less prolific [than oviparous fishes], because they are viviparous. But these are especially preserved on account of their magnitude. The fish, also, called the needle is among the number of those that 1 A blackish sea-fish, having a head shining like gold, 2 H are

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 234 are late produced ; and many of them, prior to their bringing forth, are burst by the eggs they contain. The womb, however, of this fish is burst, not so much on account of the number, as on account of the magnitude of the eggs; and the progeny of the needle are scattered round their parent, after the manner of the spipers called phalangia. For as soon as they are brought forth, they adhere to the mother ; and if they are touched, they run away. But the fish called the ear-of com brings forth by rubbing its belly on the sand. The belly of the tunny, likewise, bursts through its fat; of which fishermen conceive this to be an indication, that when the female tun nys fail in one year, the tunnys, also, fail in the following year. The tunny, also, appears to be older by a year than the pelamys*. But the tunny and the scombrus, or mackerel, copulate in the month of February, and bring forth about the beginning of June. The eggs, also, which they bring forth are, as it were, in a sack. But the increase of the tunny is rapid. For when these fishes bring forth in the Pontic sea, what some call scordylæy but the Byzantines auxidæ, are generated from the egg; because they are increased in a few days; and the scor dylæ, indeed, come forth from the Pontic sea, together with the tun ny, in autumn, but return to the sea in spring, being now pelamides. Nearly, indeed, all other fishes receive a rapid increase ; but all in the Pontic sea increase more rapidly. For every day many hamiæ are manifestly increased. In short, it is necessary to think that the same fishes have not in different places the same time of copulating, being pregnant, bringing forth, and receiving increase; since those fishes that are called coracini, in some places, bring forth about the time of get ting in the wheat. In what has been said, however, we have directed our attention to what most usually happens. The conger, also, generates and contains in itself a fœtus ; but this is not in all places similarly manifest; nor is the fœtus very apparent, on account of the fatness of the conger. It contains, however, in its womb eggs connected with each other in an oblong series, in the same manner 1 A fish produced in the Hellespont, of the genus of the tunny. as

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 235 as the eggs of serpents are connected. And though the eggs of the conger cannot be clearly seen on account of the fat in which they are immersed, yet if fire is applied to the fat, the eggs may be sufficiently distinguished. For the satis consumed and evaporates; but the eggs leap, and, being separated, crepitate. The eggs, also, of the conger may be distinguished by the touch. For if any one handles the conger and rubs it with his fingers, he will feel that the suet is smooth, and the eggs rough. Some congers, therefore, have suet alone, but no eggs ; and others, on the contrary, have no suet, but an egg of such a kind as I have just now mentioned. And thus I have nearly considered all other animals that bring forth an egg, as well the aquatic as the winged and terrestrial ; and have, likewise, spoken concerning their copula tion, pregnancy, and generation, and other particulars similar to these. CHAPTER XVIII. Let us now direct our attention to what pertains to such pedestri ous animals as are viviparous, and, also, to man. We have already, therefore, considered what pertains to the copulation of all animals, both peculiarly and in common. But it is common to all animals to be vehemently stimulated by the desire of, and pleasure arising from, coition. Females, therefore, when they have brought forth are at first more ferocious, [through love of their offspring ;] but the males are ferocious at the time of copulation. For horses at this period bite other horses, and throw and pursue their riders ; and wild boars are most ferocious, though at this time they are most imbecil from the effect of copulation. They, also, then fight with each other in a 2 h 2 wonderful
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 236 BOOK VI. wonderful manner, arming themselves for this purpose, and hardening their skin by rubbing it against trees, and frequently defiling them selves with mud, and then suffering it to dry. They, likewise, fight with each other so fiercely, separating themselves from the herd to which they belong, that both the combatants frequently die. After the same manner, also, bulls, rams, and goats are affected. For those among these that at other times feed gregariously in con- cord fight at the time of copulation, becoming discordant with each other. But the male camel at the time of coition is ferocious, whe- ther a man or another camel approaches him ; for he is always hostile to the horse. The like, also, happens to savage animals. For bearsy and wolves, and lions, at this time become more ferocious to those that approach them ; but they are less hostile to each other, because- no animal of this kind is gregarious. The she bear, likewise, becomes more savage from the presence of her young, in the same manner as bitches from the presence of their puppies. Elephants, also, at the time of copulation become fierce and unmanageable. Hence they say, that the Indians do not permit their elephants to copulate. For becoming furious at this time, they throw down the habitations of the Indians, which are badly constructed, and commit other ravages. They say, however, that an abundance of nutriment renders them more mild, and that other elephants are introduced to them who are ordered to strike and tame them. Those quadrupeds, however, that frequently copulate, and not at one season of the year, such for instance as those animals that live with man, as swine and dogs, are less ferocious at the time of copula tion, in consequence of the abundant connexion of the male and females with each other. Female quadrupeds, likewise, are impelled with an ardent desire of copulation, and especially a mare, and in the next place a cow. Mares, therefore, have the hippomania, or an insane desire of coition; hence, also, libidinous women are metaphorically said to have the hippomania. Mares, also, at this time are said to become prolific by the wind ; and hence in Crete they do not separate the stallions from the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 237 the mares. When mares, however, are impelled with this desire of copulation, they run away from the other horses. This passion, also, is that which in some animals is called pruriency [to xclotti^uv'}. But they run neither towards the east nor the west, but towards the north or south. When, also, they are under the influence of this passion, they do not suffer any one to approach them, unless they are either fatigued by labour, or have arrived near the sea; butthen the}7 emita certain humidity which is called hippomanes, in the same manner as that substance which a colt recently born carries in its forehead. And this resembles what is called capria, [or the virus which flows from the genital parts of a sow.] This-, likewise, is especially sought after by all those who are employed in sorcery. At the time of copulation, also, they incline to each other more than before ; they, likewise, move their tail frequently, and neigh in a manner more unusual than at another time. A certain moisture, also, flows from their genital parts resembling seed, but much thinner than the seed of the male ; and some call this hippomanes, though this hippomanes differs from that which is produced in colts. But they say it is difficult to collect this moisture, because it flows gradually. At that time, likewise, mares make water frequently, and sport with each other. And such are the particulars respecting horses. Cows, also, are inflamed with an ardent desire of bulls. But the passion with which they are possessed is so vehement, that cowherds can neither manage them, nor lay hold of them. Both mares, however, and cows plainly show when they are stimulated to copulation ; for at this time the genital parts of cows swell, in the same manner as those of mares. Farther still, cows get on the backs of bulls, and always follow and are present with them. But the younger females both among mares and cows are the first that are impelled to copulation. And when the weather is serene, and their bodies are in a good con dition, they are more impelled than at other times. Mares, therefore, when their hair is cut have less of this impulse to copulation, and become more sad. But male horses know the females with which they associate by their odour, though they began to feed together but a few days prior to copulation. And if other mares should

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 238 should be mingled with the troop, the horses bite and expel them, and each horse feeds with the mare of his choice, separate from the other mares. They, likewise, give to each mare thirty stallions, or a few more. And if another horse approaches, the first horse, running in a circle about his own mares, fights with him ; and if any mare is allured by this other horse, he bites and restrains her. But the bull at the season of copulation feeds with the cows, and fights with the other bulls. At other times, however, they feed with other bulls separate from the cows, which is called a contempt of the herd. For frequently the bulls in Epirus are not seen for three months. And, in short, all savage animals, or the greatest part of them, do not feed together with the females prior to the season of copulation ; but when they become adult, the males are separated, and feed apart from the females. Swine, also, when they are impelled to copulation, which is called subation, attack even men themselves. But a passion of this kind in bitches is called catulition. In the females, likewise, when they are stimulated with lust, the genital parts swell and become wet; but mares at this period distil a certain white moisture. Females, likewise, are subject to the purifications of the menses, yet these purifications are in no female animal so abundant as in women. In sheep and goats, therefore, at the season of copulation, a certain menstrual moisture is seen, which, also, flows for some time after copu lation, and then ceases till they are about to bring forth. But then it again begins to flow, and shepherds know by this token that the time of their parturition is at hand. After delivery, however, an abundant purification follows, which at first is not very sanguineous, but is so afterwards ; and the cow, the she-ass, and the mare emit a greater quantity of this menstrual moisture, on account of their magnitude, yet less in proportion to their bulk than sheep and goats. The cow, therefore, when stimulated to copulation has but a small purification, since she only emits as much menstrual moisture as will fill the half of a cup called cotylus1, or a little more. But the time in which cows ' This cup contained nine ounces. are

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 239 are most adapted to copulation is when they are purified by the emis sion of the menstrual moisture. A mare, however, brings forth the most easily of all quadrupeds, is the most free from menstrual purgations, and emits the least flux of blood, in proportion to the magnitude of her body. But the menses are especially an indication of pregnancy in cows and mares, and they cease for the space of two, four, or six months ; yet the failure of the menstrual flux cannot be known by those who are not very much accustomed to observe them, on which account some are of opinion that mares and cows are deprived of this purgation. Again, the females of mules have not this menstrual moisture, but the urine of the females is thicker than that of the males. In short, therefore, the excrement of the bladder is thicker in quadrupeds than men ; and the females of sheep and goats discharge a urine thicker than that of the males. But, on the contrary, the urine of all she-asses is thinner than that of the males ; and the urine of the ox is more acrid than that of the cow. All quadrupeds, however, after they have brought forth their young emit urine thicker than others that have a more abundant men strual purgation. Animals, also, that begin to have milk at the time of coition, at that period emit a milk which resembles pus, and which is useless; but their milk becomes useful after they have brought forth. Female sheep and goats, likewise, and in a similar manner cows and all other quadrupeds, are more fat, and eat a greater quantity of food when they are pregnant. Moreover, for the most, part, animals are more impelled to copulation in the spring. All of them, however, do not copulate at the same time of the spring, but in times adapted to the nourishment of their offspring. Domestic female swine, therefore, are pregnant during four months, but the greatest number of offspring which they bring forth is twenty ; though when they bring forth many, they are not able to nourish all of them. When they are old, also, they in a similar manner bring forth, but they copulate more slowly. They, likewise, become pregnant from one copulation; but repeatedly copulate, because after copula tion they emit that moisture which is called by some subation. This, therefore.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 240 therefore, happens to all female quadrupeds ; but some females emit together with this seed. But during the gestation of the sow, any one of her offspring that happens to be vitiated and mutilated in the mao-nitude of its body is called melachoiron ; and this may happen in any part of the womb. When the sow, also, has brought forth, she gives her first nipple to her first-born. When sows, likewise, begin to be impelled to coition, they must not be suffered to copulate till their ears are pendant ; for if they are not, they copulate in vain, and do not become pregnant. But sometimes a sow when she copulates, impelled by venereal desire, becomes preg nant, as we have before observed, from one copulation. It is, also, useful to the sow when she is about to copulate with the male swine, to give her barley, and to give her boiled barley after she has brought forth. The first progeny, likewise, of some sows are fine pigs ; but other sows as they are more advanced in age generate a good progeny and fine pigs. But some say that a sow, for the most part, soon dies, if she loses one of her eyes. Most sows, however, live about fifteen years, and the life of some is but a little short of twenty years. CHAPTER XIX. But sheep, and, in a similar manner, she-goats, become pregnant, indeed, in three or four copulations ; yet if it happens to rain after they have copulated, they bring forth immaturely. Most of them, however, bring forth two, sometimes three, and sometimes even four offspring. Both sheep and goats, likewise, are pregnant for five months, and hence in

text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 241 in some places that are warm, and mild, and abound with pasture, they bring forth twice [in the same year.] But the goat lives about eight, and the sheep about ten, years. For the most part, however, they do notlhe so long as this, the leaders of the flock excepted ; for these live fifteen years. For in every flock of sheep there is a leader of the males, who, when the shepherd calls him by his name, precedes the flock. But the shepherds accustom him to do this when he is very young. The sheep, however, in the vicinity of Ethiopia live twelve or thirteen years ; and the goats ten or eleven years. Both the sheep and the goat, likewise, copulate as long as they live. And the females of these species of animals bring forth twins, in con sequence of being well fed, and when either the male or female sheep or goat happens to be a twin. They, also, are generated either males or females from the water which they drink ; for some waters are prolific of females, and others of males. And this, likewise, arises from their copulations. In a similar manner, also, if sheep and goats copulate when the north wind blows they generate males ; but females if the south wind blows. Such, indeed, is the power of the -wind, that it causes those sheep or goats which were naturally accustomed to bring forth females to bring forth males, if they copulate when the north wind blows. It is necessary, however, that the females when they copulate should look to the north. But the sheep which were accus tomed to copulate in the morning will not suffer the rams to copulate with them in the evening. The lambs, also, are white or black, if there are white or black veins under the tongue of the ram ; they are white, indeed, if these veins are white, but black if they are black ; both, if the veins are both black and white ; and red if they are red. But the sheep which drink salter water copulate prior to others that do not. It is necessary, however, that sheep should drink salt-water, not only before they copulate, but, also, before and after they have brought forth, and again in the spring. But shepherds are not accustomed to appoint a leader of goats [as they do of sheep], because goats are naturally unstable, and are quick and alert. With respect to sheep, however, if the elder are impelled 2 i to

CHAPTER XX. Of dogs, however, there are many genera. But the Laconic dogs copulate in the eighth month of their age ; and about this time, some of the males of this species begin to lift their leg when they make water. A bitch, also, becomes pregnant from one copulation ; and this especially becomes evident in those bitches that copulate furtively ; for having once copulated they become pregnant. The Laconic bitch, however, is pregnant during a sixth part of the year; sixty-one or two, or three days at most. And her puppies when they are born are blind for twelve days. Having brought forth, also, she again copulates in the sixth month, and not before. Some bitches, however, are pregnant the fifth part of the year; i. e. seventy-two days. But the puppies of these bitches are blind during fourteen days. And there are some bitches that are pregnant a fourth part of the year; i. e. three whole months; but the puppies of these are blind for seventeen days. Bitches, also, for an equal space of time appear to possess an ardent desire of copulation. They have the menses, likewise, at this period for seven days ; and at the same time it happens that their genital parts swell. At this time, however, they do not suffer the male to copulate with them, but in the seven following days. For they appear for the most part to possess an ardent desire of copulation dur ing the whole fourteen days; and some are under the influence of this passion
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 243 passion for seventeen days. A purification, also, proceeds from the puppies, and the bitches that brought them forth, at one and the same time. But this purification is thick and phlegmatic ; and bitches after delivery are purified in a quantity less than is analogous to the size of their body. Bitches, also, have milk for the most part five days before they brim* forth ; though some have milk seven or four days prior to this period. The milk, likewise, is useful [for the purposes of nutrition] immediately after they are delivered of their young. But the Laconic bitch begins to have milk in thirty days after copulation. The milk, therefore, at first is thick, but in process of time becomes thinner. The milk, also, of bitches is thicker than that of other animals, except that of the sow and the hare. There is, likewise, an indication in bitches when they are of an age adapted to copulation; for in these, in the same manner as in woman, there is a swelling and a cartilaginous hardness in the mammæ. Yet because these indications are obscure, they cannot easily be detected, except by such as are skilful ; for the indication possesses no magni- tude. This, therefore, happens to the females among dogs, but none of these indications happen to the male. The males, also, for the most part, elevate their leg in making Avater when they are six months old ; but some of them do this when they are eight months, or even before they are six months old. For, in short, they do this when they begin to be robust. All bitches, however, make water sitting ; though some have been seen to raise the leg when they made water. Bitches, also, bring forth at most twelve puppies; but generally five or six; and a bitch has been known to bring forth one only. Laconic bitches, how- ever, for the most part bring forth eight. The females and males, likewise, of this species of animals copulate as long as they live. But it happens to be peculiar to Laconic dogs, that when they are exer cised with labours they are more able to copulate than when they are idle. Of Laconic dogs, likewise, the male lives ten years; but the female about twelve years. But of other dogs, the greater part live fourteen 2 i 2 or
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI, 244 or fifteen years ; and some live twenty years. Hence some think that Homer acted rightly in making the dog of Ulysses to die in his twen tieth year. Among Laconic dogs, therefore, because the males labour more than the females, the latter live longer than the former; but in other dogs this is not very manifest; though, at the same time, the males live longer than the females. Dogs, also, do not lose their teeth, except those that are called the canine teeth ; and these both the females and males lose when they are four months old. But in consequenceof dogs losing these teeth only, a difference of opinion has arisen among certain persons. For, because they lose only two teeth, some say that they do not lose any ; for it is difficult to meet with these. But others, when they see these teeth, are, in short, of opinion that they, also, lose other teeth. The ages of dogs, also, are known from their teeth. For those that are young have white and sharp teeth, but those that are older have black and obtuse teeth.. CHAPTER XXL The bull, also, renders the cow pregnant from one copulation, and copulates with so much violence, as to oblige the cow to bend herself. But if the impulse of the bull should be inefficacious, the cow after an interval of twenty days again admits copulation. Older bulls, therefore, do not cover the same cow frequently in the same day, but with some intermission. But younger bulls, in consequence of their vigour, copulate with the same cow frequently, and also with many cows. The bull, however, is less lascivious than other male animals. He, also, copulates after having vanquished other bulls; and it fre- quently
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VT. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 245 quently happens, that the vanquished bull again attacks the victor now debilitated by coition, and subdues him. Bulls and cows, also, begin to copulate, so as to generate in the first year of their age ; but it rarely happens that bulls generate when they are one year, or eight months old. It is, however, acknowledged that they generate when they are two years old. Cows, also, are pregnant during nine months, and bring forth in the tenth month. But some contend that a cow is pregnant ten months, a few days excepted. Whatever fœtus, likewise, is produced before the above-mentioned time is abortive, and does not live long ; for the horns of its feet are soft and imperfect. For the most part, also, the cow brings forth but one calf, and rarely two. She, likewise, copulates and brings forth as long as she lives. " But she lives for the most part about fifteen years; and bulls live for the same number of years, if they are castrated. Some cows, however, live twenty or more years, if they have a good habit of body. The keepers of oxen, also, appoint castrated bulls to be the leaders of the herd, in the same manner as shepherds appoint leaders of a flock of sheep ; and hese leaders of the herd live longer than the rest, because they are exercised by labour, and have better food. Oxen, likewise, are most vigorous when they are five years old; and hence some consider Homer as speaking rightly when he says, The male was five, the ox was nine years old ; for both are capable of effecting the same thing. But the ox loses its teeth in the second year of its age, yet not all of them, but those only which the horse loses. And when they are attacked with the gout, they do not lose the horn of their feet, but the feet only very much swell. Cows, likewise, when they bring forth have useful milk ; but prior to this they are without milk. The milk, also, which is first pro duced, when it is congealed, becomes as hard as a stone ; but this happens when it is not mingled with water. Heifers, likewise, that are not a year old do not copulate, unless something prodigious takes place ;.

text: BOOK VI, THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 246 place ; yet some have been found to copulate when they were but four months old. For the most part, also, they begin to copulate in the months of April and May; though some neither copulate nor are pregnant before autumn. But when many cows are pregnant, and very much admit copulation, it is considered as a sign of tempest and rain. Cows, likewise, have menstrual purgations, in the same manner as mares, but in a less quantity. CHAPTER XXII. With respect to the horse, however, the male begins to copulate, and, also, the female, at the age of two years ; yet it rarely happens that they copulate at this period, and when they do their progeny are smaller and more imbecil. For the most part, however, both male and female begin to copulate at the age of three years ; and their off spring continually become better, till they are twenty years of age. The mare, also, is pregnant eleven months, but brings forth in the twelfth month. The horse, likewise, fills the mare, not in any fixed number of days, but sometimes in one, or twro, or three days, and sometimes in a greater number of days. But the ass more rapidly fills the mare than the horse ; and the copulation of horses is not labori ous, like that of bulls. Both the male and female horse, likewise, are the most lacivious of all animals, after man. Younger horses, how ever, when their nutriment is good, and in abundance, copulate before the usual age. A mare, therefore, is for the most part uniparous; nevertheless, she sometimes brings forth two, but never more. A cer tain mule, also, brought forth two, which was considered as a prodigy. A horse,

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 247 A horse, therefore, copulates in the thirtieth month of his age; yet so that he alone generates colts of a good quality when he has ceased to lose his teeth. Some horses, however, as they say, have been known to fill mares while losing their teeth ; such horses not being naturally unprolific. The horse, therefore, has forty teeth, but loses the four primary teeth in the thirtieth month of his age, viz. two from the upper and two from the lower part. But when another year has elapsed, [i. e. in the forty-second month], he loses four other teeth, after the same manner, two from the upper, and two from the lower part; and again at the expiration of another year, [i. e. about the si sty-fourth month,] he loses four others, after the same manner. But when four years and six months have elapsed, he no longer loses any teeth. It has, however, happened, that a horse when he has lost his first teeth has at the same time lost all of them ; and that he has lost all his teeth at the same time that he has lost his last teeth. But things of this kind happen but rarely ; so that, for the most part, a horse is especially useful for the purposes of generation when he is four years and six months old. Older horses, however, are more prolific, the older than the younger males, and the older than the younger females. Horses, likewise, cover their mothers, and, also, their daughters ; and then the stud appears to be perfect, when they copulate with their own offspring. But the Scy thiansride the pregnant mares, when the embryo more rapidly turns itself in the womb, and they say that this occasions their delivery to be more eas}\ Other quadrupeds, therefore, bring forth lying down, and on this account the embryos of all of them come forth on the side ; but a mare, when the time of her delivery is near, erects herself, and sends her offspring into the light standing. Most horses, likewise, live about eighteen or twenty years, and some live five-and-twenty or thirty years; and if any one pays attention to them, their life may be extended to fifty years. But the longest life of horses is, for the most part, thirty years; and the female generally lives five-and-twenty years ; though some mares have been known to live forty years. The males, however [in general] live a shorter time than

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 248 than the females, on account of copulation [by which the males are de bilitated ;] and those horses that are nurtured privately do not live so lono- as those that are in a stud. The female, therefore, in five years arrives at perfection in length and height; but the male in six years. But in the six following years they increase in bulk, and make a profi ciency till the twentieth year of their age. The females, however, arrive at perfection prior to the males; but in the womb the males are more rapidly perfected than the females, in the same manner as in the human species. The very same thing, also, happens in other ani mals that are multiparous. They, also, relate, that when six months have elapsed the mule no longer sucks from the mammæ of the mare, because if it should suck after this period it would tear and thus produce pain in the teats of the mother ; but they say that a horse sucks his mother for a longer time. The horse and the mule, likewise, are vigorous after the loss of their teeth ; but when they have lost all their teeth, it is not easy to know their age. Hence they say that the age of horses may be known before the loss of their teeth, but not after the loss of them. In short, however, their age may be especially known after the loss of their teeth by the canine tooth. For in those that are seven years old, this tooth is small in consequence of attrition from the bridle; but in those that are not seven years old, this tooth is large, indeed, but more obtuse, and in young horses it is sharp and small. The male, also, copulates in every season of the year, and as long as he lives; and the female, likewise, copulates as long as she lives, and in every season of the year, unless some bond, or any other necessity, prevents her. There is not, indeed, any definite time of the copulation of the male and female; yet they are not able from any casual copula tion to rear the offspring which they have generated. In Opus, there fore, [a city of Locris], a stallion belonging to the stud copulated when he was forty years old ; but it was necessary to assist him by raising his fore legs. Mares, also, begin to copulate in the spring. But a mare, after she has brought forth, is not immediately filled with a new of spring, but some time after; and if three or four years intervene, she is
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 249 is delivered of a better offspring. After delivery, however, it is neces sary that she should abstain from coition for at least one year, and act as if she were young in the business of copulation. A mare, therefore, brings forth by intervals, as we have before observed ; but. a mule con_ tinually. Of mares, likewise, some are entirely without offspring, but others conceive, indeed, yet cannot carry in the womb what they have conceived, so as to educe it with life into light. But they say that an indication of things of this kind is obtained from the embryo ; in which, if it is dissected, other substances resembling the kidneys are found about the kidneys, so as to cause the appearance of four kidneys. When a mare, likewise, brings forth, she immediately devours the chorion, and, also, eats the excrescence which grows on the forehead of the colt, and which is called hippomanes. But the magnitude of this excrescence is less than that of a small fig, and it is of a broad form, round and black. This hippomanes if any one plucks from the colt, the mother excited by the odour of it rises, and is rendered furious by the smell. And hence sorceresses search for and collect this hippo manes. If, however, an ass copulates with a mare, the mare corrupts the inherent embryo. The keepers of studs of horses, likewise, do not constitute anyone horse the leader of the rest, after the manner of a herd of oxen; because the nature of horses is not stable, but ardent and alert. 2 K CHAP.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI, 250 CHAPTER XXIII. Both the male and female ass, also, copulate in the thirtieth month of their age, and at that time lose their first teeth; but they lose their second teeth, and, also, their third and fourth teeth, in the sixth month ; which fourth teeth are called gnoma or gnomons. An ass, how ever, has been known to be pregnant when but one year old, and to bring forth and rear her offspring. After copulation, likewise, she dis charges the seed she had received from the male, by making water, unless she is prevented ; and hence the keepers of asses strike and pursue the females immediately after they have copulated. The ass, also, brings forth in the twelfth month ; and, for the most part, she is delivered of only one fœtus ; for she is naturally uniparous ; but some times she brings forth two. An ass, therefore, by copulating with a mare corrupts, as we have before observed, the seed which she received from the horse ; but the horse does not corrupt the seed of the ass, when a mare has previously had connection with an ass. A pregnant ass, likewise, begins to have milk in the tenth month ; and on the seventh day after her delivery again suffers coition, and on this day especially is filled from the male, and conceives. She is, also, filled, if she co pulates after the seventh day. But if she does not bring forth before she has lost the teeth called gnomons, she no longer becomes filled from the male, nor is she pregnant during the remainder of her life. The ass, likewise, is not willing to bring forth in the sight of man, nor in the light ; and, therefore, the keepers of asses lead them into dark places when
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 251 when they are about to bring forth. She, also, brings forth during the whole of her life, if she brings forth before she has lost the gnompns. But the ass lives more than thirty years, and the female lives longer than the male. When, however, a horse copulates with an ass, or an ass with a horse, they are much more subject to abortion, than when the males and females of the same species mingle with each other, as for instance, a horse with a mare, and a male with a female ass. The time of gestation, also, when a horse and an ass are mingled together is regulated by the male. My meaning is, that the mare is pregnant for the same length of time as the nature of the ass requires to its perfection. But the magnitude, form, and strength of the body are more assimilated to the female than the male. If, also, the males and females of different species continue to copulate without inter ruption, the females become rapidly unprolific. Hence the keepers of these animals do not suffer those of a different species to be mingled with each other without intermission, but after a certain time has elapsed. The mare, likewise, and the she-ass, do not willingly admit a male of another species, unless he has been nourished with the same milk ; and hence their keepers take care, that some of the progeny of the ass may be suckled by the mare, and some of the progeny of the mare by the ass. But asses copulate with mares by violently cover ing them in the place where they feed, in the same manner as horses. 2 b 2 CIMP.
