title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 252 CHAPTER XXIV. The mule, however, covers and copulates with the female after the loss of his first teeth ; and when he is seven years old he, also, fills the female. When he covers a mare, also, he begets a young mule. But afterwards he no longer covers her. The female mule, likewise, some times becomes pregnant, though she is unable to bring the fœtus she has conceived to perfection. The she-mules, however, in Syria, above Phœnicia, both copulate and bring forth ; but this genus of mules is different from those of which we are speaking, though it resembles them. What are, likewise, called ginni are generated from a mare when she is diseased during her pregnancy, in the same manner as dwarfs are produced in women, and that imperfect fœtus which is called metachoiron in sows. The ginni, also, in the same manner as dwarfs, have large genital parts. But the mule lives many years. For a mule has been known to live eighty years ; as was the case writh a mule at Athens, when the temple was building. This mule, though exempt from servitude on account of his age, yet being yoked to a car, used to assist in drawing it ; so that it was decreed, that no one should drive him away when he ap proached to any heap of corn. The female mule, however, grows old more slowly than the male. Some, also, say that the female mule is purified by the discharge of urine, and that the male by the smell of urine becomes more rapidly old. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VL THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 253 CHAPTER XXV. Such, therefore, are the generations of these animals. But those who pay attention to quadrupeds are able to distinguish the young from the old. For if the skin when strips from the lip is quickly re stored, the quadruped is young ; but if it remains for a long time shrivelled, the quadruped is old. CHAPTER XXVI. But the female camel, indeed, is pregnant ten months, and always brings forth only one offspring ; for this animal is uniparous. The keepers, also, of camels separate from them an offspring that is one year old. The camel, likewise, lives a long time ; for it lives more than fifty years. But the female brings forth in the spring, and then has milk till she again becomes pregnant. Both the flesh, also, and the milk of the camel, are more agreeable to the taste than those of other animals. But the milk of the camel is drank by mingling with it a double or triple quantity of water. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: EOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 254 CHAPTER XXVII. With respect to the elephant, however, both the male and female begin to copulate before the twentieth year of their age. But when the female has copulated, she is pregnant, as some say, for a year and six months ; but according to others, for three years. The cause, how ever, of this difference of opinion, with respect to the time of her pregnancy, arises from not surveying the time in which she copulates. But the female is delivered, lowering herself in the posterior part of her body, and with manifest signs of pain. And her young one when it is born sucks with its mouth, and not with its proboscis. It, also, walks and sees as soon as it is born. CHAPTER XXVIII. Female wild boars, also, copulate at the beginning of winter. But they bring forth in the spring, retiring for this purpose into the most inaccessible places, and such as are particularly steep, narrow, and umbrageous. But the male for the most part, associates with the fe- male
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 255 male thirty days. The number, however, of the offspring of the fe male boar, and the time of her pregnancy, are the same as those of domestic swine. To the voice of these, also, their voice is similar, ex cept that the voice of the female boar is more frequently exerted than that of the male ; for the male employs his voice but rarely. Wild boars, likewise, when they are castrated become larger and more fierce, as Homer, also, says : A gelded boar in dreadful woods she rear'd, The top resembling of some woody mount, With umbrage dark ; nor like a corn-fed brute. Boars, also, while they are young, after a manner castrate them selves; for labouring under an itching of the testicles, they destroy their testicles by rubbing them against trees. CHAPTER XXIX. But the female stag copulates, for the most part, retiring under the male, as we have before observed ; for she frequently cannot support the efforts of the male, on account of their vigour. Sometimes, how ever, the females suffer the males to copulate with them after the man ner of sheep ; and when they are impelled with the desire of coition, they decline associating with each other. The male, likewise, is not constant to one female, but after a short time leaves her, and associates with other females. The time, also, in which they copulate is after arcturus, in the months of August and September. Moreover,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VL 256 Moreover, the female is pregnant eight months ; but she becomes pregnant in a sew days, and many females are filled from one male. For the most part, also, they bring forth but one fawn ; though some few have been seen to bring forth two. They, likewise, bring forth near the public roads, through the fear of wild beasts. But the in- crease of the fawns is rapid. The menstrual purgations, also, do not happen to the female stags at other times ; but when they are delivered, they have a phlegmatic purification. They, likewise, accustom the fawns to thickets. But this is a place to which stags retire, and is a steep rock which has only one entrance ; in which place, also, they are accustomed to defend themselves, and repel invaders. With re- spect, however, to the life of the stag, it is fabulously reported to be long, but there does not appear to be any clear evidence in support of this assertion. For neither the gestation of the females, nor the in- crease of the fawns, affords any indications of a long life 1. But in a certain mountain of Asia, which is called Elaphus, in the island Ar- ginussa, where Alcibiades died, all the female stags have a cut ear; so that they are known by this circumstance, if they happen to migrate to another place. The embryo, also, of such stags in the womb have immediately this mark. The female stag, likewise, has four papillae, in the same manner as the cow. When, however, the females are filled, the males are separated from them ; and each from the impulse of venereal desire lives by himself alone, digs cavities in the earth, and produces a fetid smell resembling that of a goat. Their face, also, from the sweat that runs down it at that time, becomes black, like the face of a goat. And in this man ner they live till the rainy season. But after this they return to their accustomed pasture. These things, however, happen to the stag, be cause he is naturally a lascivious and gross animal ; and hence through the heat of lust, their fat is dissolved into that fetid sweat, through 1 For animals which are not a longtime in the womb, and which rapidly increase, do not generally live long. But the period of gestation of female stags is short, and the increase of their young is rapid. which
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 257 which their face becomes black. But they become excessively fat in summer, so that they are not able to run, and are, therefore, in the second or third course caught by those who pursue them on foot. They, likewise, fly to the water, through the heat, and the difficulty of respir ation. But at the time in Avhich they copulate their flesh is bad, and has a fetid smell, in the same manner as the flesh of goats. In the Avinter, therefore, they are thin and feeble ; but in the spring they are especially vigorous in the course. AVhen they fly from their pursuers, also, they sometimes rest, and stop till he who pursues them is near ; and then they again betake themselves to flight. But they appear to do this inconsequence of labouring under an imbecility in the intestines; for they have an intestine so thin and feeble, that it is burst by even gently striking them on the belly, the skin at the same time remaining entire. CHAPTER XXX. Beaus, however, copulate, as was before observed, not by covering, but lying on the ground. But the female bear is pregnant thirty days. She, also, brings forth one or two offspring, but never more than five. The embryo, likewise, which she brings forth is very small in proportion to the magnitude of the body of the mother ; for it is less than a wea sel, but larger than a rat. It is, also, when born, naked and blind, and its legs and most of its members are nearly rude and unformed. Bears, likewise, copulate in the month of December, and the females bring forth at the time in which these animals hide themselves. About this time, therefore, both the female and the male become very fat. But 2 l when
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VL 258 when they have nurtured their cubs for three months, they make their appearance in the spring. The porcupine, also, hides itself, and is pregnant for the same number of days as the bear ; and other particulars respecting it are the same as those which pertain to the bear. The she-bear, likewise, is with difficulty taken when she is pregnant. CHAPTER XXXI. We have already observed that the lion discharges his urine from behind, and, also, copulates with his buttocks against the buttocks of the female. This animal, however, does not copulate and bring forth at every season of the year; but it copulates, indeed, every year, and brings forth in the spring. Generally, likewise, the lioness brings forth two whelps, but the most she brings forth are six, and sometimes she brings forth but one. That, however, which is reported of the lioness, that when she brings forth she at the same time throws away the womb, is a delirious fable, which arose from lions being rare, and the author of the fable being dubious of the cause why they are so. For the genus of lions is rare, and they are not produced in many places; but they are produced in the whole of Europe which is intercepted between the rivers Achelous and Nessus. The lioness, also, brings forth whelps so very small, that they can scarcely walk when they are two months old. The lionesses, however, in Syria bring forth five times during the course of their life. And at first they are delivered of five whelps, and after wards always of one less than the preceding number; but after they have been
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 259 been delivered of these, they no longer bring forth any offspring, but remain unprolific. The lioness, also, has no mane, but the lion has. The lion, likewise, loses those four teeth which are called canine, two from the upper, and two from the lower part; but he loses them when he is six months old. CHAPTER XXXII. The hyæna, indeed, is of the colour of the wolf, but is more hairy, and has hair which extends the whole length of the spine of the back. That, however, which is related of this animal [by Callisthenes the poet, and others] that the male and female have the same genital parts is false. But the genital parts of the male, indeed, resemble those of the wolf and the dog; and the reason why the}' appear to be the same as those of the female, is because the male has under its tail something similar in figure to the private parts of the female ; yet it has not any avenue. Under this, however, is the passage of the excre- ment. But the female hyæna has under her tail, in the same manner as the male, something similar to what is said to be the vulva, and this, also, has no avenue. After this is the avenue of the excrement; and under this is the true vulva. The female hyæna, also, has a womb, in the same manner as other animals who are naturally formed to have this part. The female hyæna, likewise, is rarely caught; for a certain hunter said that he had only found one female out of eleven hyænas that he had taken. 2 l 2 CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI* 260 CHAPTER XXXIII. With respect to hares, however, they copulate from behind, viz. with buttock against buttock ; for they discharge their urine backward. The females, also, copulate and bring forth at all seasons, and after delivery again become pregnant. They are, likewise, subject to super fetation, and bring forth every month. They are not, however, delivered of all their offspring at once, but successively with the interposition of certain days. The female, likewise, has milk before she brings forth ; and immediately after she is delivered copulates, and becomes again pregnant even while she suckles. But her milk in thick ness resembles that of the sow ; and her offspring are born blind, in the same manner as the offspring of most animals that have multifidous feet. CHAPTER XXXIV. The male fox, however, copulates by getting on the female ; and the female brings forth her young in the same manner as the bear, and even still more rude and unformed. But when she is about to bring forth,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 261 forth, she so changes the place of her usual abode, that a pregnant fox is rarely caught. When, however, she is delivered, she licks her offspring with her tongue, and warms and brings it to perfection. But she never brings forth more than four. CHAPTER XXXV. The she-wolf, also, is pregnant and brings forth after the manner of a bitch. For she accords with a bitch in the age in which she copulates, and in the number of the offspring which she brings forth ; and her young, like those of the bitch, are born blind. Wolves, however, copulate at a certain time of the year, and the female is delivered at the commencement of the spring. There is, likewise, a report concern ing the delivery of the she-wolf which harmonizes with a certain fable. For it is said that all wolves bring forth in twelve days of the year. But they fabulously assign the cause of this to be, that Latona, when she was pregnant from Jupiter with Apollo and Diana, being concealed for twelve days under the form of a wolf, through the scar of Juno, was brought from the Hyperborean mountains to the island of Delos. Whether, however, this is the time of their bringing forth, or not, is not yet determined, but is nothing more than an assertion, which does not appear to be true ; as neither is the assertion true, that Avolves only bring forth once in their life. But the cat and ichneumon bring forth the same number of times as bitches, and are nourished with the same food. They, also, live about six years. The
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: ECOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 262 The panther, likewise, brings forth blind offspring, in the same manner as the she- wolf ; and she never brings forth more than four. The female thos, also, is pregnant in a manner similar to the bitch, and brings forth blind offspring. She is, likewise, delivered of two, three, or four in number. But the body of the thos is long towards the tail, and its height is not great. And though its legs are short, it runs remarkably swift. Because, likewise, its body is flexible, it can leap to a great distance. CHAPTER XXXVI. There are, also, in Syria what are called mules, though they are of a different genus from the offspring of an horse and an ass. These mules, likewise, resemble our mules, in the same manner as wrild resem ble tame asses. But as wild asses, so, also, the Syrian mules run with remarkable swiftness. These mules, also, are generated from each other ; of which this is an indication, that there yet remain from among the number of the Syrian mules some which were brought to Phrygia, in the time of Pharnaces, who was the father of Pharnabazus. Three of them, therefore, now remain ; but formerly, as they say, there were nine. c u A p.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: EOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 263 CHAPTER XXXVL The generation, however, of rats, both with respect to their multitude and the celerity with which they are generated, is more admirable than that of other animals. For a female rat having; been shut in a vessel containing millet, on opening the vessel a short time after, there were found in it a hundred and twenty rats. The generation, also, and conception of the rats which cover the surface of the fields are admira- ble. For in many places such an innumerable multitude of field -rats are wont to be generated, that they nearly consume the whole of the corn. The destruction, likewise, occasioned by these animals is so rapid, that some husbandmen, whose agricultural possessions were not very large, having on the preceding day determined to reap, on the following day, when they came with the reapers, have found all the corn consumed by the rats. The disappearing, likewise, of rats is unaccountable. For in a few days they become entirely invisible, though prior to this they baffled all the attempts of men to destroy them, whether by fumigation, or subverting their retreats, or hunting them, or sending swine among them ; for swine destroy the holes in, which they hide themselves. Foxes, also, hunt them, and they are destroyed by wild weasels more than by any thing else, yet these do not prevent their fertility, and their rapid propagation ; nor docs any thing else, except copious showers of rain ; and then they rapidly disappear. But in a certain part of Persia, some embryos of rats being cut open, pregnant female rats were seen
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: 264 THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. seen in them. Some, also, strenuously affirm that female rats by lick ing salt become pregnant without copulation. The Egyptian rats, however, have hard hairs, nearly resembling those of the land hedge-hog. There are, also, other rats who walk upon two feet ; for their fore legs are short, but their hind legs large. These rats, likewise, are very numerous. There are, also, many other genera of rats. THE
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VII. CHAPTER I. IT is now requisite to consider the generation of man, both his first formation in the female, and his posterior generation from his nativity to old age. We have already, indeed, discussed the difference of the male with respect to the female, and the parts pertaining to each. The male, therefore, for the most part, begins to have seed when twice seven years have elapsed from his nativity. At the same time, also, hairs begin to grow about the organs of generation; just as plants, as Alcmæon of Crotona says, are first efflorescent when they are about to bear seed. About this same time, likewise, the voice begins to change into a rougher and more unequal tone, no longer being acute, nor in a certain respect grave, nor wholly equable, but resembling the 2 M slackened
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VII. 266 slackenend rough chords of a musical instrument; which they call a goatish sound. But this mutation of voice is greater in those who endeavour to gratify [at this time] venereal desires ; for the voice of those who have a propensity to such gratifications changes into the voice of a man, but the contrary happens to those who abstain from venery. If, however, attention is paid to the mode of living, in the same manner as it is paid by those who are studions of music, the voice will be longer preserved, and will sustain a very small mutation. The mammæ, also, and the private parts become enlarged, not only, in magnitude, but, likewise, in form. And about this time those who endeavour to procure an emission of tire seed- by friction, not only experience pleasure, but, also, pain from the egress of the seed. About the same time, likewise, the mammæ swell in females, and what are called the menses begin to flow; i. e. blood, which resembles the blood of animals recently slain. But what are called the whites happen to very young girls, and in a greater degree, if they use moist nutriment. They, also, prevent the increase, and extenuate the bodies of girls. The menses, however, in most females begin to flow when the breasts are raised to the altitude of two fingers. About this time, likewise, the voice of girls chanoes to a wraver tone. For, in short, a woman has an acuter voice than a man, but the voice of young is more acute than that of older women, just as the voice of boys is more acute than that of men. The voice, however, of girls is more acute than that of boys; and the wind-pipe of a virgin emits a sharper sound than the wind-pipe of a boy. Boys and girls, likewise, about this time, require that particular attention should be paid to them. For at the time of puberty they are especially impelled to the use of venery; so that if care is taken at this period that they experience no more excitation than what the mutation of the body occasions, and entirely refrain from venery, they are wont to be temperate in this respect during the rest of their life. For girls, if they have connexion with a man when they are very young, become more intemperate in venery ; and this is, also, the casefwith boys, whether they have connexion with each other, or. with those of the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VII. 267 the other sex. For the avenues become enlarged, and cause the humours to flow in greater abundance ; and at the same time, the remembrance of the attendant pleasure produces the desire of its repetition. Some males, however, are from their birth without hairs in the private parts, and are unprolific, in consequence of being injured about the place of fecundity. And this, likewise, happens to women from their birth. Both males and females, likewise, change their habits, with respect to being more healthy and more diseased, and with respect to being more or less corpulent, and in a good condition of body. For, after puberty, some lads from being lean become corpulent, and more healthy ; but the contrary happens to others. Virgins, also, experience a similar change. For such boys and such girls as prior to the age of puberty abound with excrementitious humours, being purified from these after puberty, the former by th e emission of seed, and the latter by the menses, become more healthy, and in a better condition of body, an consequence of being freed from the impediments to their health and nutrition ; but such as do not abound with these humours become through these emissionsmore lean and diseased. For the secretion in this latter case is from nature and parts that are in a good condition; from boys in the seed, and from girls in the menses. Farther still, there is, also, a remarkable difference in the mammæ of virgins, compared with each other. For some have very large, but others very small mammæ. For the most part, however, this happens to such girls as abound with excrements ; since, in consequence of not being yet purified by the menses from a superabundance of moisture, the humours are necessarily elevated till they burst, and then the mammæ become enlarged, and afterwards preserve the magnitude which they have acquired. Males, also, that are of a moist tempera ment, that are smooth and have not large veins, whether they are younger or older, have mammæ more apparent and more feminine ; and this is more particularly the case with men of a dark conplexion, than with such as are white. 2 m 2 The
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 268 The seed, therefore, till thrice seven years is at first unprolific ; but afterwards, it is prolific, indeed, yet the youth of both sexes generate small and imperfect offspring ; which is, likewise, the case with most other animals. Young females, therefore, conceive more rapidly, but when they have conceived, bring forth with difficulty. Their bodies, likewise, become more imperfect, for the most part. Men, also, that are given to venery, and women that bring forth frequently, grow old more rapidly ; for it seems that women, after they have brought forth thrice, admit of no further increase. Such women, however, as are intemperate in venery, become more temperate in this respect, by frequent pregnancy. After thrice seven years, also, women are properly adapted to the propagation of children; but men receive an accession of generative power after this period. Their seed, however, is unprolific ; but the seed is prolific which resembles hail, and males are generated from it more than females; and thin seed, and which is without globules, is prolific of females. About this age, also, [i. e. in the twenty-first year] males begin to* have a beard. CHAPTER II. The menstrual purgation of women, however, takes place at the decrease of the moon ; on which account, it is sophistically said by some that the moon1 is of the female sex, because at one and the same 1 For the reason why the moon was said by ancient wise men to be of the female sex, see the note to page Hi of the Organon. time
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. EOOK VIL 269 time purification happens to women and decrease to the moon ; and, also, repletion to both, after purification and decrease. And some women, indeed, have the menses every third month, though this is rare, but most have them every month. Such women, therefore, as have the menses but for a short time, viz. for two or three days, are liberated from them with ease ; but such as have them for many days, with greater difficulty ; for during these days they are in pain. For in some the purification is effected at once, but in others gradually, and the body of all females labours under an oppression as long as the menses flow. Many, likewise, Avhen the menses begin to Aoav, experience a certain suffocation and tumult in the womb, as long as this effluxion continues. It is natural, therefore, to Avomen to concei\re after the discharge of the menses ; and such as do not, live, for the most part, without offspring. Some Avomen, however, conceive, though they have no menstrual purgation ; and these are such as collect as much of a humid vapour as remains in women that have the menses after their purgations, though it is not in such abundance as to Aoav forth exter nally. Some, also, even conceive during the menses, but not afterwards; because immediately after the emission of the menses the Avomb in such as these is closed. In some women, likewise, after they haAre conceived, the menses still continue to flow, till the time of delivery. It happens, however, to these, that they bring forth an imperfect offspring ; Avhich either cannot be preserved to its increase, or becomes very imbecil. Frequently, also, in some Avomen the Avomb descends, through the want of copulation, either on account of their juvenile age or in consequence of having abstained from venery for a long time ; and the menses frequently flow thrice in a month, till they conceive. But then the Avomb again ascends to its proper place. And sometimes, though the Avomb in other respects is in a good condition, yet happen ing to be moist, it rejects the more humid part of the seed. Women, also, as Ave have before observed, have the most abundant menstrual purgation of all female animals. For animals, indeed, which are not viviparous are entirely deprived of this purgation, because this excrement is in them converted to the nutriment of the body. For some
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VII. 270 some females are larger than the males ; and, farther still, some convert the superfluous moisture into scales of different species, others into a multitude of feathers ; but pedestrious and viviparous animals convert it into hairs, and the whole body ; for man is the only animal that is smooth ; and they, also, convert it into urine. For they emit thicker urine, and in greater abundance ; but in Avomen the excrement, instead of being converted into these, is converted into the menstrual purifica tion. The like, also, takes place in males ; for man, in proportion to the size of his body, emits the most seed of all animals. And of males, such as are naturally more moist, and not very fleshy, emit a greater quantity of seed, and those that are more white than those that are of a dark complexion. This, likewise, happens in Avomen after the same manner ; for in such of these as are corpulent much of the menstrual secretion is converted into the nutriment of the body ; and in venereal connexions, those that are naturally more Avhite evaporate more of this excrement than those that are of a dark complexion. Such connexion, also, is in a greater degree promoted by moist and sharp food. CHAPTER III. An indication, hoAvever, of conception in Avomen is Avhen the place becomes dry immediately after connexion. But if the lips of the vulva are smooth, the conception is difficult; for the seed glides away. The conception, also, is difficult, if the lips of the vulva are thick. But if when touched by the finger they feel rougher and adherent, and are, likewise, thin, then such women are adapted to conception. It is necessary, therefore, in order to conception to be furnished Avith such
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 271 such wombs ; but Avith the contrary, for the purpose of not conceiving. For Avomen the lips of Avhose vulva are smooth do not conceive ; on which account some women, in order that the seed may fall into the matrix, anoint the vulva prior to coition with oil of cedar, or Avith a composition of ceruse, or Avith frankincense diluted with oil. And if the seed remains during seven days it is an indication that conception has taken place ; for what are called effluxions take place in this num ber of days. Some women, therefore, after conception emit certain menstrual purgations ; Avhich, if they have conceived a female, continue for thirty days, but if a male, for about forty days. After delivery, also, the purgations continue for the same number of days ; though the time of their continuance is not accurately the same in all females. But after conception, and the above-mentioned number of days, the purgations cease, and the menstrual moisture is converted to the mam mæ, and milk is produced from it. The first indication, also, of the milk is a certain substance appearing in the mammæ, in a small quantity, and of the consistence of a spider's web. But women,- when they have conceived, perceive that they are preg nant by a swelling in the iliac region and in the groin; for in some these parts become immediately more ; and this happens more ma nifestly in women that are thin. In short, the Avhole genus of testaceous animals resembles plants, Avhen compared with animals that have a progressive motion. And with respect to sense, some of them exhibit no indications of the possession of it; but others indicate it obscurely. The nature, also, of the body of some of them is fleshy; as in Avhat are called tethya, and the genus of sea-nettles; but the sponge perfectly resembles plants. Always, however, the difference is small, according to which some bodies appear to have more of life and motion than others, and this is, also, the case with the actions of life. For the work of such plants as are produced through seed, appears to be nothing else than that of making another being like themselves. The like, also, .takes place in animals;

BOOK VIII. 289 animals ; for of some of these, it is not possible to assign any other Avork than that of generation ; on Avhich account, such actions as these are common to all animals. The lives, however, of those animals, differ with respect to bringing forth and nurturing their offspring, who have a larger portion of sense, and Avho copulate on account of the pleasure Avith Avhich the act of copulation is attended. Some, there- fore, as plants, accomplish at stated times the generation appropriate to their nature; but others labour in the nurture of their offspring, and Avhen their offspring have arrived at perfection separate themselves from and have no longer any communion with them ; and others, Avho are more intelligent, and participate more of memory, conduct them- selves toAvards their offspring in a manner more sociable and political. One part, therefore, of the life of animals consists in the actions Avhich they exercise in the procreation of offspring ; but another part consists in procuring nutriment. For about these two all their attention and life are employed. All kinds of nutriment, however, principally differ according to the matter from which the beings that are nourished are composed ; for the natural increase of every animal is from the same matter as that from Avhich it consists. But that Avhich is according to nature is pleasant; and all animals pursue the pleasure which is adapted to their nature. Animals, also, are divided according to places; for some of them are pedestrious, [i. e. terrestrial,] but others are aquatic. But this difference being predicated in a twofold respect, viz. either from re ceiving air or Avater, some are called pedestrious, and others aquatic. And again, of those animals which do not receive either air or water sufficiently, but are naturally adapted to the temperament of refriger ation, some are called pedestrious, but others aquatic, though they neither respire nor receive the Avater, but derive their nutriment from and live in either of these elements. For many animals, that receive the air and bring forth their young on the land, derive their nutriment from aquatic places, and live the greater part of their time in the Avater; these animals alone, as it seems, partaking of an aquatic and terrestrial nature, and may, therefore, be considered as both pedestrious and aquatic. 2 p CHAP.

No animal, however, Avhich receives the water is either pedestrious, or derives its nutriment from the earth ; but the pedestrious animals Avhich receive the air are many. And some, indeed, receive the air in such a Avay, as not to be able to live Avhen separated from the nature of water; such as the animals Avhich are called marine tortoises, cro codiles, the hippopotamus, and the phoeæ ; and likeAvise smaller ani mals, such as the emys, and the genus of frogs. For all these, unless they respire for a certain time, are suffocated ; and they are accus tomed to bring forth and nurture their young on the dry land, but they live in the Avater. The dolphin, however, is the most extraordinary of all animals; and this is, also, the case Avith every other animal of a similar nature, Avhether it be in the cetaceous or aquatic genus, as the Avhale, and such other animals among these as have a pipe. For it is not easy to rank each of these either among aquatic or terrestrial animals, if those are to be considered as terrestrial Avhich receive the air. and those as naturally aquatic Avhich receive the Avater. For each of these partici- pates both of the aquatic and terrestrial nature ; since they receive the sea and return it through a pipe, and they, likewise, receive the air by their lungs ; for they have this part, and respire through it. Hence the dolphin, when it is caught in nets, is soon suffocated, in consequence of not respiring; though Aut of the water it lives a long time, murmuring and making the same noise as other animals that re spire. The dolphin, likewise, sleeps with his nose raised above the water>

It is, however, absurd, since the divisions are contrary, to arrange these animals in both of them ; but it seems that the aquatic genus must be still further divided. For some of these receive and return the Avater from the same cause through which animals that respire receive the air, viz. for the sake of refrigeration ; but others on account of nutriment. For it is necessary, since they receive their food in Avater, that they should together with it receive the water, and receiving have an organ by which they mav return it. Those animals, therefore, which use Avater in a manner analogous to respiration have gills ; but those sanguineous animals that use water on account of food have a pipe. The like, also, takes place in the mollia, and in crustaceous animals; for these receive water on account of nutriment. After another manner, however, those animals are aquatic, from the temperament of their body and their life, that receive air, indeed, yet live in Avater; but those are pedestrious that receive water and have gills, yet betake themselves to the dry land and derive their nutriment from it. Nevertheless only one animal of this kind is at present known, and this is called the cordylus ; for this animal has no lungs, but has gills, and goes on the dry land, and thence derives its nutriment. It is, however, a quadruped, as being naturally adapted to Avalk. Moreover the nature of all these [ambiguous] animals is, as it Avere, distorted, just as some males participate of female and some females of male characteristics. For animals receiving a difference in the small parts of their body, are seen to differ largely according to the nature of the whoTe body. But this is evident in castrated animals. For in con sequence of a mutilation in a small part the animal is changed into a female ; so that it is evident that in the original formation of animals, from something of the smallest magnitude being changed, if it has but a principal subsistence, one animal becomes a female, but another a male. And, in short, the members being taken away which cause the distinction of the sexes, that Avhich is produced is neither male nor fe male. In a similar manner, therefore, on account of a small corporeal mutation and difference, some animals are terrestrial, and others aqua- 2 p 2 , tir

And some, indeed, do not communicate with both natures, but others do communicate, in consequence of participating something of the matter from which they derive their nutriment in their original formation. For to every animal that which is according to nature is friendly, as we have before observed. But animals being divided into the aquatic and pedestrious triply, viz. by receiving air or water, and by the temperament of their bodies, but, in the third place, by their food, their lives are conformable to these divisions. For some are aquatic or pedestrious according to their temperament and food, and according to their receiving Avater or air; but others from their temperament or their life alone. Of testaceous animals, therefore, those which do not change their place are nourished with potable Avater. For the sea-water is perco lated through dense bodies, and the more attenuated part of it is con cocted, and receives a generation as it were from the beginning. But that sea- water by percolation may become potable is evident ; since this has been ascertained by experiment. For if a vessel made of thin Avax, to Avhich a string is fastened, is dropt into the sea empty, and re mains there for the space of a day and a night, there will be found Avithin it a considerable quantity of potable water. Sea-nettles, hoAvever, are nourished Avith any small fishes they may happen to meet with. But they have a mouth in the middle of their body, Avhich is very apparent in large sea-nettles. They have, likeAvise, in the same manner as oysters, a passage in the superior part of their body, through Avhich they discharge their excrements. For the sea-net tle, in the same manner as the oyster, appears to have a fleshy sub stance internally, and to use a rock as a shell. But the lepas frees it self from the place to which it adheres, and goes in search of nutriment. Of such testaceous animals, hoAvever, as are motive, those, indeed, that are carnivorous, as, for instance, the purple, feed on small fishes ; for this animal is carnivorous, and on this account it is caught by things of this kind ; but others feed on plants that grow in the sea. The marine tortoises, likeAvise, feed on shells ; for they have a body the most robust of all animals. For whatever they take into their mouth,

text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 293 mouth, Avhether it be a stone, or any thing else, they break and de- vour ; and, going on shore, they feed on grass. But they labour and frequently perish, Avhen swimming on the surface of the sea, they are dried by the sun ; for they cannot again easily plunge themselves in the depths of the sea. Crustaceous, also, are nourished after the same manner as testace- ous animals. Thus, for instance, crabs of the rock feed on stones wood, mud, sea-Aveed, and dung; and they are, also, carnivorous. But lobsters vanquish, indeed, large fishes, and a remarkable recipro- cation happens to some of these. For the polypi subdue the lobsters ; so that lobsters Avhen they perceive the polypi near them in the same net die through fear. Lobsters, however, vanquish the congers ; for the latter cannot escape on account of the roughness of the former ; and the congers eat the polypi; for the former, on account of their smooth- ness, cannot be caught and retained by the latter. All the mollia, like- wise, are carnivorous. Lobsters, hoAvever, feed on the little fishes,. which they hunt after near their retreats. For their habitations are in such places of the sea as are rough and stony. And whatever they catch they carry to their mouth Avith a forcipated foot, in the same manner as crabs. Naturally, likeAvise, Avhen they are nor terrified, their progressive motion is to the anterior part, letting fall their horns on their side ; but when they are terrified, they make their retreat backAvard, and extend their horns. They, also, fight Avith each other, in the same manner as rams, Avith their horns, raising these and striking Avith them. They are, likewise, frequently seen with each other in a great number, as if they were a herd. Crustaceous animals, therefore, live after this manner; but of the mollia, the small calamary and the cuttle-fish vanquish large fishes. But the polypi principally collect shell-fish, and extracting the fleshy part feed on it ; on which account, those who hunt for them knoAv their retreats by the shells [which they find in them.] That, however, which some assert, that the polypus eats itself, is false; but some of them have their arms gnaAved by the congers. All fishes, however, at the time in which they bring forth are nou- rished

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIIL 294 rishcd with their own eggs; but with respect to other nutriment, all of them do not use the same. For some of them are carnivorous only, such as the selache, the congers, cockles, the tunny, the wolf, the dentals, the amia, the or phi, and lamprey; but barbels are nourished Avith sea-Aveed, oysters, and mud, and, also, Avith flesh. But the das- cillus feeds on mud and dung; the scarus and melanurus feed on sea- Aveeds ; and the stock-fish on dung and sea-Aveeds. This last, also, eats the prasium; and is the only fish that is hunted with the colocynthe or gourd. All fishes, likewise, devour each other, except the mullet, and this is especially the case with the congers ; but the cephalus and the mullet are, in short, the only fishes that do not feed on flesh; of which this is an indication, that nothing fleshy is ever found in the belly of these fishes, nor do fishermen use the flesh of animals as a bait in catch- ing them, but bread alone. Every mullet, however, feeds on sea Aveed and sand. And the sephalus, indeed, Avhich some call cheilon, or the, thick-lip, lives near shores ; but the other kind of cephalus Avhich is called peræas does not. The peræas, however, is fed Avith its OAvn mu- cus ; on Avhich account it is always empty. But the cephali feed on mud, on Avhich account they are heavy and mucous ; but they do not eat any fishes. In consequence, however, of living in mud, they fre- quently plunge themselves in Avater, that they may Avash off the mud Avith Avhich they are covered. But none of the large fishes devour the young of the cephali, on Avhich account their progeny are very numer- ous. When, however, their young are encreased in size, then they are devoured by other fishes, and especially by the archanus. But the mullet is the most gluttonous and insatiable of all fishes ; on Avhich ac- count its belly is distended, and Avhen it is not hungry it is in a bad condition. When it is terrified, also, it hides its head, as if by so do ing the Avhole of its body was concealed. The dental, likeAvise, is car nivorous, and devours the mollia : and frequently Avhen this fish and the cockles pursue smaller fishes, they throAv their belly out of their mouth, because the belly of fishes is near their mouth, and they have not a stomach. Some fishes, therefore, as we have before observed, are only carnivo- rous,

text: BOOK VIIL THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 295 rous, such as the dolphin, the dental, the gold-fish, the selache, and the mollia ; but others, for the most part, feed on mud, sea-weed, moss, and Avhat is called caulium, and other marine plants ; and these fishes aresuch as the phycis, the gudgeon, and those that live in rocks. But the phycis does not eat any other flesh than that of the squill. Fishes, likeAvise, frequently devour each other, as Ave have before observed, and the larger devour the smaller. This, howeA'er, is an indication that they are carnivorous, that they are caught with baits made from the flesh of animals. And the amia, the tunny, and the wolf, are for the most part carnivorous, but they, also, eat sea-Aveed. But the sar gus feeds on the barbel ; and Avhen the barbel, having stirred the mud, comes forth, (for it is able to excavate the mud), the sargus descends into the mud, there feeds and prevents other fishes weaker than him self from descending together Avith him. AVhat is called the scarus, also, appears to be the only fish that ruminates after the manner of quadrupeds. Other fishes, therefore, hunt such as are smaller than themselves Avith their mouths opposite to their prey, in the same manner as they naturally SAvim ; but the selache, dolphins, and all of the cetaceous kind, seize their prey in a supine position. For they have the mouth beneath ; on Avhich account smaller fishes more easily elude them ; since otherwise very few fishes Avould escape. For the celerity of the dolphin in pursuing it's prey, and the voraciousness with which it de vours them, are Avonderful. Some few eels, likewise, in certain places are nourished with mud, and Avith such eatables as any one may happen to throw to them ; nevertheless the greater part of them is nourished with potable water. And those that nurture eels are particularly careful that the Avater in Avhich they are kept is pure, and that there is a perpetual flux and re flux of it on ground covered with gravel. For they are soon suffocated unless the water is pure ; since they have small gills ; and hence those that fish for them disturb the Avater in which they are contained. And eels, indeed, are caught in the river Strymon about the rising, of the pleiades [i. c. in the month of November], for then the water and the mud

Moreover, eels, when they are dead do not swim on the surface of the water, nor are borne upward, like most other fishes. For they have a small belly », and but few of them are fat. When taken out of the water, likeAvise, they live five or six days ; and they live longer Avhen the north than when the south wind blows. If, also, they are taken out of lakes, and put into fish ponds in summer, they die; but not if they are taken out in Avinter. They, likeAvise, cannot sustain violent mutations. Thus, in summer, if they are plunged into cold Avater, a great number of them frequently perish. But they are suffocated, if they are nourished Avith a small quantity of water. The very same thing, also, happens to other fishes ; for they are snffocated, if they are always kept in the same small quan tity of Avater, in the same manner as animals that respire perish if they are surrounded Avith but little air. Some eels, likewise, live seven or eight years. River fishes, however, feed on each other, and, likewise, on herbs and roots, and other substances which they find in the mud. They, also, feed more by night than by day, and withdraw themselves in the day into deep water. Such, therefore, are the particulars pertaining to the nutriment of fishes. Of birds, however, all such as have crooked claAvs are carnivorous; but they cannot sAvallow corn, even if it is put into their mouth ; as, for instance, all the genera of eagles, kites, and the two species of hawks, viz. the hawk which pursues the ring-dove, and that Avhich at tacks the chaffinch and the buzzard. These two species of haAvks, also, differ very much from each other in magnitude. But the buzzard is as large as the kite, and is seen at all times. Among carnivorous birds, also, are the osprey and the vulture ; but the osprey is larger than the eagle, and its colour resembles that of ashes. With respect to all birds, however, as I may say, some derive their nourishment from the earth, others from rivers and lakes, and others from the sea. But those which obtain their nutriment in water may be distinguished into two kinds, viz. into the palmipedes, or flat-footed, and the fissipedes, or cloven-footed. text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 300 BOOK VIIL Avhat is called the raven, Avhich in magnitude is equal to the stork except that its legs are less. But the raven is flat-footed, swims well, and its colour is black. This bird, also, perches on trees, and is the only bird of this kind Avhich builds its nest in trees. To these may be added the goose, the small goose Avhich goes in a flock, the goose-sox the goat, and the penelops. But the eagle of the sea dwells near the sea, and frequents lakes. Many birds, however, are omnivorous. But those that have crooked claws, not only feed on such other terrestrial and aquatic animals as they are able to vanquish, but, also, on other birds; except that they do not feed on birds of the same species, and in this differ from fishes, who frequently devour those of the same species Avith themselves. The whole genus of birds, likewise, drinks but little ; but those that have crooked claws entirely abstain from drinking, a few expected, and these drink but seldom. This is particularly the case Avith the kestrel. The kite, also, has been seen to drink, though rarely. CHAPTER IV. Animals, also, Avhich are covered Avith a scaly skin, such as the lizard and other quadrupeds, and, likewise, serpents, are omnivorous. For they feed both on flesh and grass. But serpents are the most dainty of animals. These, therefore, drink but little, and such other animals as have spongy lungs. But all animals have spongy lungs that have but little blood, and that are oviparous. Serpents, however, are immoderately fond of wine ; and on this account, some in order to catch vipers place wine in shells on the hedges; for they are caught when

text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 301 Avhen they are intoxicated. But serpents being carnivorous, whatever animal they seize, Avhen they have sucked out the juice of it, they emit the remaining body of the animal by the passage through which they discharge their excrement. Other suchlike animals, also, as, for instance, spiders, do the same; but spiders, when they suck the juice of any animal keep the animal external to themselves, and serpents have the animal Avhich they suck in their belly. A serpent, therefore, seizes and eats Avhatever he may happen to meet Avith ; for he eats birds and beasts, and devours their eggs. But seizing his prey, he raises himself till he is in an upright position ; and afterwards he so gra dually collects and contracts himself, that Avhen he becomes extended that Avhich he devours descends. This endeavour of serpents in devour ing their prey is necessary, because their stomach is long and thin* The spiders called phalangia, also, and serpents can live a long time Avithout food. But this is evident from those serpents and phalangia Avhich are nourished by druggists. CHAPTER V. With respect, however, to quadrupeds and viviparous animals, all such as are savage and have serrated teeth are carnivorous ; except Avolves, who, as they say, are the only savage animals that eat Avhen thev are hungry a certain earth. At another time, however, they do not touch grass ; but when they are ill, in the same manner as dogs, they eat certain herbs, Avhich they vomit, and are purged. But those wolves that search for prey apart from other Avolves more frequently devour men than those that are hunters. The animal, however, Avhich some

THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 302 some call glanus, but others an hyæna, is in magnitude not less than the wolf, but it has a mane like a horse, though its hairs are harder and thicker, and are extended through the whole of its spine. This animal, also, insidiously attacks and hunts after men; and, vomiting in the same manner as men, it seizes and devours dogs. It, likeAvise, digs into sepulchres, through a desire of eating human flesh. But the bear is omnivorous ; for it eats the fruits of trees, which, through the pliability of its body, it climbs. It, also, eats leguminous fruits. Destroying, likeAvise, the hives of bees, it eats their honey, and feeds on crabs and ants; and is carnivorous. For on account of its strength, this animal not only attacks stags, but, also, Avild-boars, if it can invade them latently. It, likewise, attacks bulls. For attacking the bull in front, he falls on his back, and while the bull endeavours to strike him [as he lies in this supine position] the bear throws his arms round the horns of the bull, bites his shoulder, and lays him prostrate. For a short time, likewise, the bear Avalks erect on two feet , and eats every kind of flesh, previously macerating it. The lion, also, is carnivorous, in the same manner as other animals that are savage, and have serrated teeth. But he eats voraciously, and swallows a great quantity of flesh Avithout dividing it. Afterwards, for two or three days he abstains from food; for he is able to do so on account of his excessive repletion. He drinks, howeATer, but little; and rarely emits excrement; for he does not emit it till the third day, or just as it may happen. But his excrements are dry and hard, and resemble the excrements of the dog. He, likewise, emits a very pun gent flatus, and his urine has a fetid smell. Hence dogs [that hunt the lion] smell the trees ; for the lion makes Avater against them, lifting up his leg in the same manner as dogs. His breath, also, produces a strong smell in the food which he eats. For when a lion is dissected, the interior parts of his body produce a strong exhalation. Some savage quadrupeds, however, procure their nutriment about lakes and rivers ; but no quadruped except the sea-calf searches for food about the sea. Sheep and goats, however, feed on grass; and sheep, indeed, feed stably fixed to a certain place, but goats rapidly change their places while they feed, and only crop the top of the grass. Drink, likewise, especially fattens sheep ; and hence, in summer, shepherds give a medimnus of salt every five days to a hundred sheep ; for the leader of the flock becomes by this mean more healthy and fat. Frequently, also, they mingle a great quantity of salt Avith the straw Avhich they give to sheep, in or- that being thirsty they may drink more abundantly; and in autumn they give them a gourd sprinkled Avith salt ; for this produces in them a greater quantity of milk. By Avalking, likeAvise, in mid-day, sheep drink more abundantly in the evening. And those sheep that have had salt in their nutriment, have their breasts Avhen they bring forth more distended. The leaves of the olive, also, both cultivated and Avild, the herb swine-snout, straAV, and grass, fatten sheep; but all these fatten them in a greater degree Avhen they are sprinkled Avith salt. These, likewise, fatten them still more, if prior to eating them they have fasted three days. In autumn, also, northern is better for sheep than southern water, and it is profitable to feed them in the evening. But journeys and labour render them thin. Shepherds, likewise, know strong sheep from those that are Aveak by this, that the former in Avinter have frost upon them, but the latter have not; for sheep that are not strong, by the motion and agitation of their body [in consequence of the cold] shake off the frost. All the actions, however, of animals are conversant about copula tion, the nurture of their young, the means of procuring sufficient nutriment, and providing a habitation Avhich may defend them from the inconveniences arising from heat and cold, and the mutations of the seasons. For all animals have a connascent sense of the mutation according to heat and cold. And as of men, some in Avinter betake them selves into houses, but others, Avho have dominion over a large tract of land, spend the summer in cold and the Avinter in Avarm places; the like, also, happens to animals that are able to change the places of their abode. And some, indeed, find the assistance of Avhich they are in Avant in the places to Avhich they are accustomed ; but others for this purpose migrate ; betaking themselves after the autumnal equinox from Pontus and other cold places, that they may avoid the approach ing winter. After the vernal equinox, however, they migrate from warm to cold places, fearing the heat; some, indeed, departing from neigh bouring places, but others, as cranes, from one extremity of the earth to another. For they migrate from the Scythian plains, to the marshes l above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. But these places [to which the cranes migrate] are inhabited by the Pygmies. For this is no fable, but both the men that inhabit these places and the horses arc, as they are said to be, a small race ; and the men dwell in caverns. Pelicans, likewise, migrate and fly from Stryinon [a river of Thrace] to the Ister [or Danube], and there beget offspring. After the same manner, also, fishes [migrate from one place to another,] some, indeed, from Pontus, but others to Pontus. And some, indeed, in the winter migrate from the sea to the land, in search of Avarmth ; but in the summer migrate from the shore to the sea, avoid ing the heat. More imbecil birds, likewise, [which cannot migrate from one region to another,] in Avinter descend from elevated places to the plains, in search of heat; but in summer ascend to the mountains, in order to avoid the heat. More imbecil animals, however, migrate prior to others, both in excessive heat and cold. Thus, for instance, mackerell migrate prior to the tunny, and quails prior to cranes. For inackcrell and quails begin to migrate in the month of August, but the tunny and cranes in the month of September. But all animals are fat ter, when they migrate from cold than Avhen they migrate from hot places. Thus, for instance, quails arc fatter in autumn than in spring. But it happens that at one and the same time they migrate from cold places and from the season of heat. Animals, also, are more impelled to copulation in the spring season, and Avhen they migrate from Avarm places. Of birds, therefore, cranes, as Ave have before observed, migrate from one extremity of the earth to another; but they fly in the direction of the wind. What is asserted, however, respecting a stone is false. For it is said, that they carry a stone in order to balance them as they fly ; Avhich stone, when it falls, is useful for the purpose of trying gold. The large ring-dove, also, and the stock-dove migrate, and do not stay here during the Avinter ; and this is, likewise, the case with the swallow and the turtle-dove ; but pigeons stay Avith us. In a similar manner quails migrate, except some few quails, and, also, turtle-doves, which winter in places exposed to the sun. But the large ring-dove and the turtle-dove fly in troops, both when they approach to us, and again when the season arrives of their departure. Quails, however, when they fly, if the air is serene or the wind northern, assemble to- gether,

But if the Avind is southern, their journey is difficult, because they are then impeded in their flight; for this Avind is moist and heavy. Of fishes, however, some, as avc have before observed, migrate from the sea to the land, and from the land to the sea, avoiding the excesses of heat and cold. But fishes that live near the shore are better than those that live in the deep sea; for they have more abundant and bet ter nutriment. For the productions of the place Avhich the sun irradi ates with his beams are more abundant, better, and more delicate, as is evident in gardens; and the black algula grows near the shore, but the other species of algula resembles a Avild plant. Farther still, places near the sea-shore are Avell tempered with heat and cold ; on Avhich account the flesh of such like fishes has more consistence ; but the flesh of fishes that live in the deep sea is moist and loose. But the fishes that live near shores are, the dental, the cantharus, the orphus, the gold-fish, the mullet, the barbel, the thrush, the sea-dragon, the calli onymus, the gudgeon, and all those that live in rocks. Those, also, that live in the deep sea are, the pastinaca, the selache, the Avhite con gers, cockles, the roach, and the glaucus. But the pagrus, the scor pion, the black conger, the lamprey, and the cuculus or gurnard, live near shores, and, also, in the deep sea. There are, hoAvever, differ ences of these according to places. Thus, for instance, about Crete, gudgeons and all fishes that live in rocks are fat. But the tunny is better after the rising of arcturus, because at that time it is no longer infested by the marine asilus or gadbee; for in consequence of the molestation which it suffers from this animal in summer, it is not so good. The amiæ, likewise, are produced in Alopeconnesus ; and the greater part of the genera of fishes are to be found in the lake Biston. The greater part, however, of the fishes called collias do not enter the Euxine Pontus, but in summer live in Propontis, and there bring forth, but they winter in the Ægean sea. The tunny, however, the pil cher, and the amiæ, migrate into the Euxine Pontus in spring, and continue there during the summer. But this is, also, the case with nearly most of the fishes called ruades, and most of the gregarious fishes ; and most fishes are gregarious, and those that are so have a leader. All those, hoAvever, migrate into the Euxine Pontus, on account of nutriment; for the food in that sea is better, and more abundant on account of its admixture with potable water; and, also, because this sea is less infest ed with large voracious fishes. For except the phocene and the dol phin, there is no voracious fish in the Euxine Pontus; and the dolphin in this sea is small ; but in the sea which immediately joins with Pon tus there are large dolphins. The tunny, therefore, and other fishes migrate into the Pontus on account of nutriment, and for the sake of their offspring. For there are places in this sea adapted to the delivery of fishes ; and the potable and more sweet water which it contains nourishes the little fishes. When the fishes, however, are delivered, aud their progeny have acquired a larger size, they again swim out of the Pontus after the rising of the pleiades [i. e. in November.] And, indeed, if the winter is southern [i. e. if the southern winds blow dur ing the winter], they migrate from this sea more sloAvly ; but if the win ter is northern, they migrate more rapidly ; because the northern winds are favourable to their egress from the Pontus, and at the time of their egress, the offspring of these fishes, which arc then small, are caught about Byzantium, in consequence of not continuing long in the Pontus. Other fishes, therefore, are seen both when they enter into and when they depart from the Pontus, but the trichiæ alone, are, indeed, caught when they enter into the Pontus, but are not seen when they depart from it. The reason, hoAvever, Avhy the trichiæ alone are not seen to depart from the Pontus, is because after they have entered into it, they are the only fishes that enter into the Danube; and afterwards swim through the Danube, where it is divided into the Adriatic sea; of which this is an indication, that Avhat happens there is contrary to Avhat happens in the Pontus, for Avhen they swim into the Adriatic they are not caught, but when they swim out of it they are caught. But the tunny swim into the Pontus on the right hand, keeping close to the land ; and they swim out of the Pontus on the left hand. They do this, however, as some assert, because they natu rally see more acutely Avith the right eye, but Avith the left eye they do not see acutely. The ruades, therefore, make their voyage in the day, but rest and feed by night, if the moon does not shine ; for if it does, they continue their voyage, and take no rest. But it is said by some of those that dAvell near the sea, that during the Avinter solstice these fishes do not move, but continue quiet in the place Avhere they may happen to be found, till the vernal equinox. The colias, therefore, is caught when it enters into the Pontus ; but is not caught during its egress from that sea. After this manner, therefore, the migrations of fishes are accomplish ed. The very same thing, also, takes place in terrestrial animals, Avith respect to concealing themselves. Some of them, however, are caught about the time of their concealment, as is, also, the case Avith some other fishes that hide themselves, at the time when they betake themselves to Avarm places, or Avhen the fine Aveather is extended to an unusual length ; for they sometimes come forth from their retreats, for nutriment, and especially during the full moon. The primadiæ, hoAvever, conceal themselves in mud ; of Avhich this is an indication, that at that time they are not caught, but are seen to have a great quantity of mud on their back, and their fins ruffled. They begin to move, however, in the spring, and come forth on the land, for the sake of copulating and bringing forth. They are, also, caught when pregnant, and then appear to be seasonable; but the autumnal and Avinter primadiæ are not so good. At the same time, likeAvise, the males are seen to be full of genital seed. While the fœtus, therefore, of the primadiæ are yet small, it is difficult to catch them, but when they are larger they are caught in great abundance, on account of the gad-flies with Avhich they are infested. Some fishes, likewise, hide themselves in sand, but others in mud, having no other part uncovered but their mouth. Most fishes, therefore, hide themselves in Avinter ; but such as are crustaceous, those that live in rocks, the thornback, and the selache, conceal themselves only during more winterly days; but this is evident from their not being caught Avhen it is cold. Some fishes, however, as, for instance, the glaucus, conceal themselves in summer. For this fish hides itself in summer for about sixty days. The fish called the ass, likewise, and the gold-fish, hide themselves. But this appears to be an indication that the ass hides itself for a long time, viz. that for a long time it is not caught. And that some fishes hide themselves in summer appears to be indicated by this, that they are caught during the rising of certain stars, and especially of the dog star. For then the sea is subverted; which is particularly the case in the Bosphorus. For the mud ascends to the surface, and the fishes are carried up with it. But when great rains take place, many animals are seen [in the sea,] Avhich before were either not seen at all, or were not frequently seen. CHAPTER XVI. Many birds, likewise, hide themselves ; nor do all of them, as some fancy, migrate to warmer climates ; but some, indeed, being near to places of this kind in Avhich they perpetually dwell, as, for instance, kites and SAvallows, migrate to them ; and others being more remote from places of this kind, do not migrate, but conceal themselves. For many swallows have been seen in hollow places entirely stript of their feathers, and kites have been seen flying from such like places, when they first appear. Those birds, hoAvever, that have crooked, and those that have straight claws, equally hide themselves. For the stork, the blackbird, the turtle-dove, and the lark conceal themselves. And that the turtle-dove, indeed, hides itself is universally acknowledged. For no One, as I may say, is reported to have seen the turtle-dove any where in Avinter. But this bird Avhen it begins to hide itself is very fat, and though it loses its feathers during its retreat, yet it still continues to be fat. Of ring-doves, however, some hide themselves, but others do not, but migrate together Avith swallows. The thrush and the starling, also, hide themselves, and for a few days, among birds that have crooked claws, the kite and the owl. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 319 CHAPTER XVII. Among viviparous quadrupeds, also, porcupines and bears hide themselves. That savage bears, therefore, hide themselves is evident ; but it is dubious Avhether it is from cold, or some other cause. For both the males and females become about this time very fat, so as to be unwieldy. The female, also, brings forth at this season, and con ceals herself till the period arrives of leading forth the young bears from her retreat. But she does this in the spring, and in the third month after the Avinter solstice. The bear, likewise, is concealed for about forty days at least. And it is said, that for fourteen of these days it does not move at all, but in most of the days after these it is concealed, indeed, yet is in a vigilant state, and in motion. A pregnant bear, hoAvever, has either never been caught by any one, or by very few. It is evident, also, that the bear during the time of its concealment does not eat anything; for it does not come forth from its retreat : but when it is caught, both its belly and intestines are found to be empty. It is, likewise, said, that the intestine of the bear at that time is nearly adherent, and that on this account, as soon as it quits its retreat, it eats a certain herb Avhich is called arus, for the purpose of relaxing and separating the intestine. The dormouse, also, conceals itself in trees, and at that time becomes very fat ; and the white Pontic rat, likewise, hides itself. But of those that hide themselves, some put off what is called their old age. This, however, is their exterior skin, and the covering Avhich they received in their formation. With respect to pedestrious and viviparous
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 320 viviparous animals, therefore, it is dubious Avhy among these the bear hides itself, as Ave have before obser\^ed; but nearly the greater part of those that are covered with scales hide themselves ; and such as have a skin soft, and not of a testaceous nature, as the tortoise, put off their old ao-e. For the tortoise and emys [or aquatic rat] rank among ani mals that have a scaly skin. Thus, for instance, the stellio and the lizard, and especially serpents, divest themselves of their old age in spring, and again in autumn. Vipers, also, put off their old age in spring and autumn; for that which is asserted by some is false, viz. that vipers are the only serpents that do not divest themselves of their old age. When, hoAvever, serpents begin to divest themselves of their old age, they say that it is first drawn off from their eyes, so that they appear to be blind to those Avho do not perceive this circumstance ; but afterwards, it is drawn off from the head, and then from the rest of the body. In a night and a day, also, nearly the whole of their old age is. drawn off, beginning from the head, and ending at the tail. But the inward part of the skin of their old age, Avhen it is drawn off, becomes outward. For it is put off in the same manner as an embryo from the chorion, in Avhich it is enveloped. Such insects, likeAvise, as put off their old age are divested of it after the same manner; as, for instance, the silk-Avorm, the gnat, and those Avhose Avings are enclosed in a sheath, as the beetle. None of them, however, put off their skin, till a new one is formed under it. For as the fœtus of viviparous animals is enveloped in the chorion, thus, also, the fœtus Avhich originate from Avorms are enveloped in a shell, similarly Avith bees and locusts. Grasshoppers, also, when they come forth from their shell sit upon olive-trees and reeds ; but the shell bursting they come forth, leaving but little moisture Avithin it ; and in no long time aftenvards they fly and sing. Of marine animals, also, locusts and lobsters put off the skin of their old age, sometimes, indeed, in the spring, and sometimes in the autumn after the birth of their young. For certain locusts have been caught having the parts about the thorax soft, because the shell was on all sides burst ; but the parts beneath their thorax Avere hard, because the shell in
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 321 in those parts was not yet burst. For they do not divest themselves of the skin of their old age in the same manner as serpents. Locusts, also, hide themselves about five months. Crabs, likeAvise, put off their old age ; confessedly, indeed, such of them as have a softer shell ; and it is said that this is, also, the case with such of them as have a harder shell, as, for instance, Avith the crabs called maiæ. But when they have put off their skin, a very soft shell is formed [in the place of the old ;] and crabs are not very Avell able to Avalk. Animals, likewise, of this kind do not put off their skin once, but frequently. And thus much concern ing animals that hide themselves and put off their old age. CHAPTER XVIII. Animals, hoAvever, do not live prosperously at the same seasons, nor similarly happy in all excesses of heat and cold. Farther still, health and disease vary according to seasons in animals of different genera, and on the Avhole are not the same in all animals. Hot and dry seasons, therefore, are advantageous to birds, both Avith respect to their health and delivery, and especially to ring-doves ; but rain is advantageous to fishes, a very feAV excepted. On the contrary, rainy seasons are disadvantageous to birds, but hot and dry seasons to fishes. For, in short, it is not advantageous towards to drink much. Birds, therefore, Avith crooked claws, as Ave have before observed, live entirely without drink. Hesiod, however, Avas ignorant of this ; for in his narration ot the siege of Ninus, he represents the eagle the assessor of the divination drinking. Other birds, indeed, drink, yet do not drink much. In a similar manner, neither does any other animal drink largely that has 2 t spong.V
