title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIII.. g 322 spongy lungs, or is oviparous. When birds, however, are afflicted Avith any malady, it is indicated by their feathers ; for they are disordered, and are not disposed in the same manner as Avhen they are well. CHAPTER XIX. But of fishes, the greater part, as Ave have before observed, are in a prosperous condition in rainy seasons. For then they not only have more food, but, in short, rain-Avater is advantageous to them, in the same manner as it is to the productions of the earth. For leguminous substances, though they are Avatered, yet make a greater proficiency when irrigated by rain. The very same thing, also, happens to reeds Avhich groAv in lakes; for none of them, as I may say, are increased Avithout rain. That fishes, hoAvever, are delighted with sweet Avater is indicated by this, that most of them migrate into the Euxine Pontus, for the purpose of staying there during the summer ; for on account of the multitude of rivers Avhich flow into the Pontus, the Avater of it is more sweet, and the nutriment it contains more abundant. Farther still, many fishes, such as the amia and the mullet, swim into rivers, and in rivers and lakes are in a prosperous condition. But gudgeons become fat in rivers ; and, in short, places which abound with lakes have the best fishes. With respect to waters* themselves, however, summer rains are more advantageous to most fishes, and, also, spring and autumnal rains; and fishes are benefited by a serene winter. In short, those seasons which are favourable to man, are, also, favourable to the greater part of fishes. But
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOKsVIII. 323 But fishes do not prosper in cold places. And those that have a stone in their head, as the chromis, the wolf, the umbra, and the pagus suffer most in the winter ; for on account of the stone they are congealed by the cold, and fall, deprived of life. To most fishes, therefore, rain is profitable ; but, on the contrary, it is noxious to the mullet, the cepha lus, and the fish Avhich some call murin. For many of them become rapidly blind by rain-Avater, if it falls in great abundance. And the cephalus is more accustomed to this disease of blindness in winter. For the eyes of this fish become Avhite, and at that time it is lean when it is caught ; and at length its eyes are entirely destroyed. It seems, however, that they are not so much affected in this manner by exces sive rain, as by cold. In other places, therefore, and, also, about the Argive Nauplia, near to Tenagos, many of the cephali are caught blind in very cold weather. Many, also, have been caught Avhose eyes Avere Avhite. The gold-fish, likewise, suffers in Avinter; but the acharnas in summer, at which time it becomes thin. The coracinus, however, as I may say, is the only fish that is benefited by more dry seasons, and this because it happens that in dry seasons there is more heat. Such places, likewise, as are naturally near shores are more favour able to the prosperous condition of fishes than those that are in the deep sea ; but such fishes as are amphibious prosper either near shores or in the deep sea. There are, however, peculiar places which are favourable to particular fishes; and, in short, those places are advanta geous to them which abound with weeds. Fishes, therefore, Avhich seed in all various places, are fatter Avhen they are caught in weedy places. For those that feed on weeds have an abundance of nutriment, and those that feed on flesh find a greater number of fishes for their food in Aveedy places. It is, also, of consequence to fishes, whether places are northern or southern. For long fishes are in a better condition in northern places, and, therefore, in summer, more long fishes are caught than broad fishes in northern situations in the same region. But the tunny and the sword-fish are tormented with the gad-fly about the time when the dog star rises ; for then both of these fishes have under their fins a little 2 T 2 Avorm
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIII. 324 Avorm as it were, which is called oistros, and Avhich resembles, indeed, a scorpion, but in magnitude is equal to a spider. These fishes, Iioav ever, suffer so much from this insect, that the sword-fish sometimes through pain leaps no less than the. dolphin ; on Avhich account it frequently falls into ships. The tunny, likeAvise, delights in heat the most of all fishes, and for the sake of heat betakes itself to the sand on the shore, and swims on the surface of the sea that it may become warm. Small fishes, also, are preserved from the tunny and SAvord-fish because they escape their notice ; for large fishes pursue such as are large. A great part, hoAvever, of the eggs and spaAvn of fishes perish on account of heat, [i. e. in consequence of fishes going in search of warmth], for through this they injure whatever they touch. Fishes, likewise, are principally caught before the rising and after the setting of the sun ; and, in short, about the rising and setting of the sun ; for the castings of the nets are then said to be seasonable. Hence fishermen at this time draw up their nets ; for at these periods the sight of fishes is especially deceived. For they rest at night, and see more clearly in proportion as there is more light. Fishes, also, do not appear to be subject to any contagious maladies> such as frequently happen to men, and, among viviparous quadrupeds, to horses and oxen, and to some other animals, both tame and wild. Fishes, hoAvever, appear to be sometimes ill, of which this is con ceived by fishermen to be an indication, tliat some fishes Avhen caught are thin, and resemble animals that are umvell. Their colour, also, is found to differ from that of many others that are caught at the same time, that are fat, and of the same genus. And thus much concerning marine fishes. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 325 CHAPTER XX. With respect, hoAvever, to fishes that live in rivers and lakes, these, also, are not subject to contagious maladies ; but some of them are afflicted Avith peculiar diseases. Thus, for instance, the glanis in con- sequence of swimming on the surface of the Avater is injured by the deadly influence of the dog-star, and is laid asleep by very loud thun- der. Sometimes, likewise, the carp is affected in this manner, but in a less degree. But the glanis perishes Avhen struck in shallow Avater by the serpent called a dragon. In the ballerus and the tillon, however a Avorm is engendered under the dog-star Avhich causes them to rise to the top of the Avater, and renders them Aveak. And when they are raised to the top of the Avater, they are destroyed by the heat. But the chalcis is afflicted with a very violent disease ; for it is destroyed by a great quantity of lice produced under its gills. No other fish, hoAvever, is subject to a disease ofthis kind. Fishes, likewise, die by eating the herb long-Avort ; and hence some fishermen that they may catch fishes infect rivers and lakes with the poison ofthis herb ; but the Phœnicians after this manner catch fishes in the sea. Some, also, adopt two other modes of catching fishes. For because fishes in Avinter avoid the pro- fundities of rivers (and potable or SAveet is colder than salt water), hence fishermen dig a canal in a river, and cover it Avith herbs and stones, thus forming as it Avere a cavern, having its egress from the rivers ; and Avhen it is fiosty Aveather from this canal they catch fishes in a bow net. Another similar mode, also, of catching them is employed by fishermen, both in summer and winter. For in the middle of the river they

text: 326 THE HISTORY T)F ANIMALS. EOOK VIII. they make an enclosure with small branches of trees and stones, so as to leave an avenue, and in this placing a bow-net, the stones beino moved, the fishes are caught, [while they run to the avenue.] Rainy seasons, hoAvever, are advantageous to testaceous animals, except the purples ; of which this is an indication, that if the purples taste of the potable water Avhich runs into the sea, they die on the same day in which they taste it. The purple, likewise, lives after it is caught about fifty days. But these fishes are nourished by each other; for a certain Aveed as it Avere and moss grow on their shells. Fishermen, therefore, throw food to the purples, in order that they may Aveio-h more and sell for a greater price. To other testaceous animals, how ever, dry seasons are disadvantageous, for in these seasons they are of a less size, and of an inferior quality ; and cockles then become more red. In the Pyrrhæan Euripus, however, cockles sometimes fail, not only on account of the instrument with which they are caught by fish ermen, but, also, on account of dry Aveather. But rainy seasons are advantageous to other testaceous animals, because the sea-water then becomes sweeter. Testaceous animals, however, are neither produced in the Euxine Pontus nor in rivers, on account of the cold, except a few of the bivalves ; but the univalves are especially congealed by cold. After this manner, therefore, aquatic animals subsist. CHAPTER XXI. Of quadrupeds, however, swine are subject to three diseases ; one of Avhich, indeed, is called a quincy; in Avhich disease, the jaAvs and throat are principally inflamed. This disease, also, attacks any other part
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK vm. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 327 part of the body ; for it frequently attacks the foot, and sometimes the ear. But the diseased part becomes immediately putrid, and then the part next to this, till the ulcer arrives at the lungs; and then the ani mal dies. This disease, likewise, is rapidly increased ; and swine when they are attacked by it in any part of the body eat nothing. Swine herds, however, cure this disease Avhen they perceive it is but small in no other Avay than by cutting off the whole of the infected part. Swine, also, are subject to two other diseases, both which are called the evil; of Avhich one is a pain and heavinesses the head, with Avhich most SAvine are afflicted ; but the other is a flux of the belly, and this appears to be incurable. The former malady, however, is alleviated by applying Avine to the nostrils, and Avashing them with it. Swine, also, with difficulty escape from this disease ; for it destroys them in three or four days. But swine principally become subject to a sore throat, Avhen the summer supplies them Avith abundance of food, and they are very fat. This malady, however, is remedied by giving them the fruit of the mulberry-tree, by Avashing them abundantly in a hot bath, and by opening a A'ein Avhich is under the tongue. SAvine, likeAvise, Avhose flesh is humid are afflicted Avith a malady resembling hail-stones in their legs, neck, and shoulders, in which parts many hail-stones are formed. And the flesh, indeed, of those swine that have but few hail-stones is sweet ; but the flesh of those that have many becomes very humid and insipid. It may, also, be clearly seen when SAvine have this disease. For they have hail-stones in the infe rior part of the tongue ; their hairs when plucked from their back ap pear bloody ; and, farther still, they cannot stand on their hind feet. While they suck, however, they are not afflicted Avith this malady*. And they are liberated from this disease by that kind of corn which is called tiphe, which is useful for food. But in order to fatten them peas and figs are the best nutriment; and, in short, various and not sim ple food is best calculated for this purpose. For, like other animals, they are delighted with change of food ; and at the same time they say, that by this mean they become partly inflated, partly fleshy, and partly fat. They, also, add, that they willingly eat acorns, but that this
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII; THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 328 this nutriment renders their flesh humid, and that pregnant sows if they eat abundantly of acorns become abortive, in the same manner as sheep ; for sheep are more manifestly thus affected by eating acorns. Swine, also, are the only animals Avith Avhich we are acquainted thai are afflicted with the malady of hail-stones. CHAPTER XXII. Dogs, also, are subject to three diseases ; and these are denomi nated, rage, a sore throat, and gout. But of these, rage produces mad ness; and all animals that are bit by dogs when they have this disease become furious, except man. This disease, also, destroys dogs, and all animals that are bitten by mad dogs, except man '. A sore throat, likeAvise, destroys dogs; and but few of them escape death Avhen at tacked by the gout. Camels, also, are subject to rage. But it is said that elephants are free from other diseases, and that they are afflicted Avith flatulency. 1 As this is not the case at present, perhaps, in the days of Aristotle, a method was known of curing the bite of a mad dog in the human species. CHAP.

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 329 CHAPTER XXIII. Moreover, gregarious oxen are subject to tAvo diseases; of Avhich, one is the gout, but the other is called the evil. In the gout, there fore, the feet of oxen sAvell, but they neither die, nor lose their hoofs ; and they are relieved, by anointing their horns Avith Avarm pitch. But Avhen they have the evil, their respiration is hot and frequent; and Avhat the fever is in men, that the evil is in oxen. Indications, also, that oxen are unwell are, the hanging their ears, and an incapacity of eating. But they die rapidly, and Avhen dissected their lungs are found to be putrid. CHAPTER XXIV. Of horses, hoAvever, those that are gregarious, indeed, are not subject to any other disease than the gout. But Avith this disease they are afflicted, and sometimes through it lose their hoofs; though when they lose them, others immediately groAV in their place ; for the loss of one hoof is accompanied Avith the production of another. The indications, 2 u also,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIII 330 also, of disease in a horse are, the leaping of the right testicle, and a certain hollow and wrinkled substance being formed a little below the nostrils. But horses which feed in stables are subject to many diseases. For [in the first place] they are afflicted with the colick ; Avhich is indicated when they lift their hind to their fore legs, so as that they knock against each other. But if after they have fasted a few days they .become furious, they are relieved by opening a vein, and taking away some blood. They are, likeAvise, subject to a disease called tetanos [or an equable and perpetual convulsion of the whole body ;] Avhich is indicated by a tension of all the veins, and of the head and neck, and by Avalkin<r with their legs stiff. Horses, also, are troubled with puru- lency. And they arc afflicted Avith another malady which is called barley, and Avhich is indicated by the palate becoming soft, and the respiration fervid. But this disease is incurable, unless the horse that is afflicted Avith it becomes spontaneously convalescent. Horses, likeAvise, are subject to another malady, by Avhich they are said to be lympha- tic ; in Avhich disorder it happens that they stand still at the sound of a flute, and bend their head ; and Avhen any one gets on their back, they run with great rapidity till they arc stopped. A horse, also, if he is seized Avith rage, is always sorrowful. But the indications of this malady are the inclining his ears to his mane, and again extending them, fainting away, and breathing short. The following maladies, also, to Avhich horses are subject are incurable. A pain in the heart, an indica- tion of which is a subsidence of the flank. Secondly, a displacing of the bladder, indications of Avhich are the inability of making Avater, and draAving up the hoofs and the hip. Thirdly, the swalloAving the insect staphulinus, which is about the size of a,sphondulc [or book-worm.] The bite, also, of a shrew-mouse is pernicious both to horses and to other cattle ; for it produces pustules. But the bite is more pernicious, if the shrew-mouse happens to be pregnant, for the pustules caused by the bite burst; but this is not the case if the shrew-mouse is not preg nant. The bite, also, of an animal Avhich some call chalcis, and others zyguis, either kills horses, or causes them to suffer great pain. But this animal resembles a small lizard, and its colour is that of the blind serpent.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIII. 331 serpent. In short, those that are skilful say that horses and sheep are nearly subject to the same diseases as men. A horse, likewise, and every beast of burden, are destroyed by the poison of red arsenic. But this poison is given percolated in Avater. The smell, also, of an extin guished lamp causes a pregnant mare to become abortive. And this, likeAvise, happens to be the case with some pregnant Avomen. After this manner, therefore, the diseases of horses subsist. But Avhat is called the hippomanes grows, indeed, as it is said, on the fore head of colts ; and mares, licking and Aviping off the hippomanes, devour it. Other particulars, hoAvever, respecting the hippomanes may be considered as the fables of Avomen and inchanters. But it is acknoAv ledged that mares prior to their delivery emit a liquor Avhich is called polion. Horses, likewise, on hearing, know the voice of the horses with Avhich they happen to fight. But horses delight in meadows and marshes ; for they drink turbid Avater ; and if the Avater happens to be pure and clear, they disturb it Avith their hoofs, and after they have drank wash them selves in it. For, in short, the horse is an animal which loves to wash itself, and is delighted Avith Avater. Hence the nature of the river horse is such that it cannot live Avithout Avater. The ox, howeArer, is in this respect contrary to the horse ; for unless the Avater is pure, and cold, and clear, he is unwilling to drink. CHAPTER XXV. Moreover, asses are principally subject to one disease, which is called melida. But this malady is first produced in the head, and causes 2 u 2 a
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIII. 332 a thick and red phlegm to flow from the nostrils. And if this malady descends to the lungs, the ass dies ; but Avhen it is confined to the head, it is not mortal. The ass, likewise, endures cold Avith very great dif ficulty; and on this account, there are no asses about the Euxine Pontus and Scythia. CHAPTER XXVI. But elephants are subject to flatulent diseases, through which they are rendered incapable of ejecting cither the moist excrement [i. e. urine] or the excrement of the belly. They are, also, diseased if they feed on earth, unless they eat it very frequently ; for then they sustain no injury ; and sometimes they even swallow stones. Elephants, like- Avise, are subject to a flux of the belly ; but Avhen they are afflicted Avith this malady, their keepers cure them by giving them hot Avater to drink, and hay steeped in honey to eat, and each of these stops the complaint. When they are Aveary, likewise, from want of sleep, they are restored to health by rubbing their shoulders Avith salt and oil and Avarm Avater. When, also, they have a pain in their shoulders, their keepers give them the roasted flesh of swine, and by this mean afford them relief. But Avith respect to oil, some elephants drink it, and others do not. If, likeAvise, it should happen that a dart remains in the body of an elephant, it is said that it is ejected if he drinks oil ; but to those elephants that do not drink oil, they give a root boiled in oil. And thus much concerning the diseases of quadrupeds. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 333 CHAPTER XXVII. Of insects, however, the greater part are in a prosperous condition Avhen the temperature of the year resembles the season in which they Were born, viz. Avhen it resembles the spring, being moist and tepid. But in the hives of bees certain animals are produced Avhich injure the hives ; and, also, a Avorm of the nature of a spider, Avhich weaves a web, and is detrimental to the hives. This Avorm is called by some cleros, and by others purauste ; and it produces in the hive an animal resem bling itself, viz. having the form of a spider, and causes the swarm of bees to be diseased. Another insect, also, resembling the butterfly Avhich flies about lamps, is noxious to bees. This insect brings forth a certain substance full of dust, and is not stung by the bees, but is alone expelled by smoke. Caterpillars, also, are produced in hives Avhich they call augers, and Avhich the bees do not attack. But bees are principally subject to diseases Avhen the floAvers of trees are spoiled with rust, and in dry seasons. All insects, likeAvise, perish when rubbed with oil ; but most rapidly Avhen, their head being rubbed Avith oil, they are exposed to the sun. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VIN 334 CHAPTER XXVIII. In short, animals differ according to places. For as in some places certain animals are not at all produced, so in others they are produced, indeed, yet they are smaller, live a shorter time, and are subject to a greater number of maladies. Sometimes, also, there is a difference of this kind in places near to each other. Thus, for instance, there are certain places in Milesia, which border on each other, in some of which grasshoppers are produced, and in others not. In Cephalenia, likeAvise, a river separates certain places, in some of Avhich there are grasshoppers, and in others there are not. In Pordoselene, also, there is a road betAveen two places, in one of Avhich there are Aveasels, but there are none in the other. And in Bceotia, there are many moles about Orcho- menus ; but in the Lebadic vicinity there are none ; and even if they are brought to this place they are umvilling to dig into the earth. But in Ithaca, the hares Avhich are brought thither from other places cannot live, but they are seen dead turned towards the sea through Avhich they entered the island. And in Sicily, indeed, there are no hippomyrmeces, or horse-ants ; but in Cyrene, there Avere formerly no croaking frogs. text: BOOK IX. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 365 CHAPTER XIV. With respect to the halcyon, it is, indeed, not much larger than the sparrow ; but its colour is a mixture of azure, green, and purple. Some of the nests, however, of the halcyon are less than this. The opening, also, of these nests is narrow, and only affords a small entrance; so that the seaAvhen it is impelled to the shore [Avhen the halcyon builds its nest] cannot enter into the nests. But the cavities of the nest resemble those of the sponge. It is, however, doubt ful from Avhat materials the halcyon constructs its nests ; but it seems that it is principally constructed from the thorns of the needle-fish ; for the halcyon lives by eating fishes. The cuckoo, therefore, brings forth one egg, which she does not herself incubate ; but the bird in whose nest she lays it hatches and nourishes it. And, as they say, when the young of the cuckoo is grown, the bird Avhich nourished it ejects her own offspring, and thus they perish. But others assert that the bird Avhich nourishes the young cuckoo kills her own offspring, and gives it to the young cuckoo to eat. For because the offspring of the cuckoo is beautiful, she despises her own. Some persons, therefore, confess that they have been spectators of most of these particulars ; but all do not agree in explaining how the offspring of the bird which nurtures the young cuckoo perishes. For some say that the cuckoo, returning to the nest in which she had deposited her egg, eats the offspring of the bird that received it; but others assert that the offspring of the cuckoo, in con sequence of surpassing in magnitude the offspring of its nurse, devours all the food that is brought into the nest, and thus causes them to die Avith hunger. And others again assert that the young of the cuckoo, as being stronger, kills the young of its nurse. But, however, this may be, the cuckoo appears to conduct, herself prudently with respect to the procreation of her offspring. For, from a consciousness of her timidity, and that she is incapable of defending her young, she gives them to other birds to be nurtured and preserved. For this bird is excessively timid, since she suffers herself to be plucked by small birds, and flies from them. CHAP

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IX, 378 There is, also, another genus of eagle, which is called plangus, and is the second in magnitude and strength. But it dwells in thickets, val- Jies, and lakes, and is called the duck-destroyer and morphnus. It is, also, mentioned by Homer1 in the departure of Priam [from Troy to re- deem the body of Hector.] There is, likewise, another species of eagle of a black colour, and Avhich in magnitude is the least, but is the strongest of all the species of eagles. This eagle, also, flies rapidly, is elegantly formed, is unen- vious and intrepid, warlike and auspicious, and is neither querulous nor clangous. But when the eagle becomes old, the superior part of its beak increases, and always becomes more curved, and at length the eagle dies from hunger. It is, however, fabulously said, that the eagle suffers this punishment, be- cause Avhen he Avas formerly a man he had injured his guest. The eagle, also, reserves for its young the surplus of the nutriment Avhich it does not itself consume. For, because it is not easy for it to supply its young with food every day, it sometimes has not any thing to give them. If, likewise, the eagle finds any one invading its nest, it strikes him Avith its Avings, and lacerates him with its claAvs. But it builds its nest not in plains, but in lofty places, and especially in steep rocks, and, likewise, in trees. Eagles, also, nourish their young till they are able to fly; but then they drive them from the nest, and expel them from the w hole of the region in the vicinity of the nest. For one pair of eagles occupies a great extent of territory, and on this account the pair do not suffer other eagles to dwell near them. Again, eagles hunt after their prey, not from places near to their nest, but from those that are far distant. But Avhen they have hunted and caught their prey, they do not immediately carry it to the nest, but first make trial of its Aveight, and rest themselves. Hares, likewise, are not immediately seized by them, but they suffer them to run into the plain, and they do not directly descend to the ground, but their descent is gradually less and less. The eagle, however, does both these in order that he may be more safe from stratagems. He, also, perches on elevated places, be- cause he is sloAvly elevated from the earth. And he flies high that he may have an extended view; on Avhich account men say, that he is the only bird that is divine. But all birds that have crooked claws perch but very little on rocks, because the hardness of the rock is an impedi- ment to the curvature of their claws. The eagle, also, chases fawns, hares, foxes, and such other animals as he is able to subdue. He, like- wise, lives long; as is evident from the same nest of the eagle always remaining. 3c? CHAP.

For when the eagle expels the young from the nest, the osprey receives and nurtures them ; since the eagle expels her young prematurely, Avhile they are y et in want of food, and incapable of flying. But it seems that the eagle ejects its young through envy; for it is naturally an envious and greedy bird, and, also, rapacious. When it eats, likewise, it devours a great quantity of food. It envies its young, therefore, when they have arrived at maturity, because they are then good to eat, and tears them Avith its claAvs. The young eagles, also, fight with each other for a place in the nest, and for food ; but the mother expels and strikes them. And the young eagles when expelled cry, and the osprey receives them. The sight of the osprey, hoAvever, is imperfect, and its eyes are injured. The sight, however, of the eagle of the sea is most acute, and this bird compels its offspring Avhile they are yet without feathers to look to the sun. She, also, strikes any one of her offspring that is unwilling to do this, and turns it to the sun. She, likewise, kills the young eagle that is the first that weeps, but she nurtures the other. But she dAvells near the sea, and lives, as we have before observed, by hunting the birds that frequent the sea. She, also, attacks them severally, observ ing Avhen they emerge from the sea. When, however, the emerging bird sees the eagle of the sea, it again merges itself through fear, in order that it may at some other time [more opportunely] emerge. CHAPTER XXXVII. After this manner .therefore, the particulars respecting birds sub- sist. In marine animals, also, many indications of sagacity in the lives of each may be surveyed. For the reports which are circulated about the frog called the fisher and the cramp-fish are true. For this frog hides itself in sand or mud, and leaves out of the sand certain ca- pillaments which hang before its eyes, and Avhich are globular in the extremity, and are given to the animal as a bait. The little fishes, therefore, run to the globules of the capillaments [conceiving them to be food ;] and then the frog gradually contracts the capillaments, till he has brought the globules together Avith the little fishes to his mouth. But the cramp-fish numbs the fishes Avhich he intends to subdue, and thus catches and feeds on them. For this purpose, hoAvever, he con- ceals

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IX- 384 ceals himself in sand and mud, and numbing the fishes that swim near him, he makes them his prey ; and of this certain persons have been eye-witnesses. The pastinaca, also, hides itself, yet not in a manner similar to the cramp-fish. That the frog called the fisher and the cramp fish, hoAvever, live after this manner is indicated by mullets being fre quently found in their belly when they are caught, though the mullet is the swiftest, and they are the slowest of fishes. In the next place, the frog when he has no longer little fishes on the globules of his capil laments, is thinner when he is caught ; and men are evidently numbed by the cramp-fish. But the fish called the ass, the frog, the plaice, and the file-fish hide themselves in sand ; and Avhen they have rendered themselves immanifest, they agitate Avhat the fishermen call the rods which they have in their mouth ; but the little fishes run to these as to pieces of sea-Aveed Avith Avhich they are fed. No voracious fish, also, is found where the anthias is seen. Hence those that search for sponges call the anthias a sacred fish. This, however, is merely a casual circumstance; just as it is entirely acci" dental that where there are snails there is neither a swine nor a par tridge. For swine and partridges eat all the snails they find. But the marine serpent resembles in colour, indeed, and the form of its body, the conger, except that it is of a darker hue, and is more robust. If, however, after it is caught it is dismissed, it rapidly hides itself in the sand, which it perforates Avith its nose. Its mouth, also, is more acute than the mouth of land serpents. With respect, however, to Avhat is called the scolopendra, when it has swallowed the fish-hook, it turns its imvard parts outward, till it has thrown up the hook, and afterward again turns them inward. But marine in the same manner as land scolopendræ are attracted by odour. It has, also, been observed that other fishes and the lamia have been Avounded by the amiæ, which they had attacked. Of river-fishes, however, the male glanis pays great attention to its offspring. For the female, indeed, when she has brought forth leaves her eggs ; but the male abides in that place Avhich contains the great est number of the eggs, and stays there as their guardian, affording no other assistance than that of driving aAvay other little fishes, that they may not plunder the eggs ; and he does this for the space of forty or fifty days, till the young ones are so much increased in size, as to be able to fly from other fishes. Fishermen, hoAvever, knoAv where to find the glanis who is the guardian of the eggs ; for Avhile he drives aAvay the little fishes, he leaps and produces a murmuring sound. So great, also, is his attachment to his offspring, that though the fishermen en deavour to bring the eggs from deep to shallow Avater, he does not leave the eggs, but follows them. But if the guardian glanis is young, he is soon caught by the hook, in consequence of seizing the little fishes that approach to the eggs ; but if he is accustomed to danger, and eats the bait from the hook, he does not desert his charge, but Avith the bite of his very hard teeth breaks the hook. All aquatic animals, however, as well those that sAvim as those that are fixed to one place, are fed in the places in Avhich they are produced, or in others similar to these; for the nutriment adapted to each is in these places. But carnivorous fishes Avander more than others, and all of them nearly are carnivorous, a few excepted ; such as the mullet, the stock-fish, the barbel, and the chalcis. Oviparous fishes, however, flourish in the spring, till the time in which they bring forth ; but viviparous fishes flourish in autumn; and besides these, mullets, barbels, and all the rest of a similar kind. But all marine fishes, and those that dwell in the Euripus, bring forth in the Lesbian Euripus. They copulate, therefore, in autumn, but bring forth in the spring. The male and female selache, also, mingling together, copulate in autumn ; but in spring they swim apart from each other, till they bring forth. At the time, however, in Avhich they copulate many of them are caught joined together. But the most crafty of the mollia is the cuttle-fish, Avhich alone em ploys its ink, or black liquor, for the sake of concealing itself, and not only when it is terrified. The polypus, however, and the small cala mary discharge their ink through fear. But none of these animals ever discharge the whole of their ink; and Avhen they discharge it, it is reproduced. The cuttle-fish, however, as Ave have just observed, fre quently uses its ink for the sake of concealment, and Avhen it has pro ceeded out of the ink so as to be visible, it returns into it. Farther still, it not only hunts after little fishes with its long appendices, but, also, after mullets. But the polypus is a stupid animal ; for if a man puts his hand into the water, it walks towards it. It is, hoAvever, economic ; for it collects every thing into the retreat in Avhich it d wells. But when it has consumed Avhatever is most useful to it, it throws away the shells and crusts of crabs and shell-fish, and the thorns of little fishes. Of insects, however, the genus of ants and the genus of bees are nearly the most industrious, Avhen compared with all other animals. Of the phalangia that bite, indeed, there are two genera; one resembling the spiders called wolves, Avhich are small, variegated, quick, and adapted to leap, and these spiders are called psylla ; but the other genus is large, of a black colour, has its fore-legs long, is sIoav in its motions, walks leisurely, is not strong, and does not leap. If, also, any thing falls on the web between the middle of it and the extremities, it first proceeds to the middle as from a principle, and from thence to the substance which fell on the web. But if any one injures the web, it again begins to weave it about the rising or setting of the sun, because at these times especially its prey fall into the web. The female, like wise, weaves and hunts after prey; but the male partakes of the booty. Of elegant spiders, hoAvever, and which Aveave a thick web, there are two genera; the one, indeed, being larger, but the other less. The larger spider, therefore, Avhich has longer legs, hanging under the Aveb, observes the little animals that are his prey, in order that they may not through fear escape him, but may fall on the superior part of the web ; for this spider, on account of its magnitude, cannot Avell conceal itself. But the less spider, whose body possesses more symmetry, conceals itself in a small hole in the superior part of the Aveb. Spiders, likewise, as soon as they are born are able to emit a thread, not from the interior part of their body, as if it were an excrement, as Democritus says it is, but from the external part, as from a rind, or after the manner of the porcupine, who hurls forth his hairs. Spiders, also, circumvent and infold larger animals. For they attack small lizards, and surround them with their threads, so as at length to close their mouth ; after which they approach to and bite them. And such are the particulars respecting these animals. CHAP.

text: BOOK IX. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 391 CHAPTER XL. There is, however, a certain genus of insects which is anonymous by one name, but all the individuals of which have a congeneric form. And these are such insects as construct Avaxen cells ; such as bees, and the insects Avhich resemble them in form. Of these there are nine genera ; of which, indeed, six are gregarious bees, the kings of bees, the drone, which lives among the bees, the annual Avasp, and besides these, the hornet, and the tenthredon, [an insect resembling a Avasp.] But there are three that live alone ; the small siren, Avhich is of a brown colour; the larger siren, Avhich is black and variegated ; and a third, Avhich is called bombylius, and is the largest of these. Ants, therefore, do not hunt any thing, but collect Avhat is made by others ; but spiders neither make any thing, nor collect what is made by others, but only hunt after food. Of the before-mentioned nine genera, hoAvever, Ave shall afterwards speak about the rest; but bees hunt after no prey, but make and deposit honey, Avhich is their food. That it is their food, indeed, is evident from this, that when those that keep bees endeavour to take the honey from the hives by smoking them, the bees who suffer very much from the smoke, at that time eat more honey than usual, but at another time they are not seen to eat any great quantity of it, as reserving and depositing it for the sake of nutriment. They have, also, another food, which some call cerinthus. But this food is inferior to honey, and possesses the SAveetness of figs. For Avhere a pure hive is delivered to them, they construct their cells from different floAvers, and various trees ; such as the willow, the elm, and others that abound Avith rosin. With these, also, they anoint the bottom of their hives, in order to prevent other animals from entering into them ; but the keepers of bees call this work incrustation. If the avenues of the hives, likewise, are broad the bees build near it, [so as to make itnarroAver.] They, also, first fabricate the cells in which the [common] bees are born ; and afterwards the cells in Avhich those that are called the kings and the drones are born. Some of the cells, therefore, they always fabricate ; but they construct the cells of the kings Avhen there is a numerous progeny of bees, and the cells of the drones Avhen there are indications of a great abundance of honey. They, likewise, construct the cells of the kings near the cells of the [common] bees ; and these are small ; but they construct the cells of the drones near the cells of the kings ; and these are less than those of the [common] bees. But they begin the series of their cells from the roof of the hive, and form many series or Avebs of these connected Avith each other in a descending order till they reach the bottom of the hive. The cells, also, in Avhich they deposit their honey, and those in Avhich they bring forth their young, have a double entrance ; for about one basis there are tAvo avenues, after the manner of cups Avith two handles ; the one being internal, and the other exter nal. But the first cells of the honey-comb, Avhich are joined to the hive, are narrow, and void of honey, and consist of two or three circular ranges ; but those cells are fuller of honey which are constructed Avith an abundance of Avax. The first part of the entrance into the hive, likewise, is covered with an ointment called mitys ; but this is suffici ently black, being as it were a certain sediment of Avax, and of an unpleasant smell. This mitys, also, is used as a remedy for Avounds, and such like suppurations. But the matter nexi: to this with which the hive is plastered is called pitch-wax, Avhich emits a less powerful odour, and is a less efficacious remedy than mitys. The magnitude, also, of this genus is double that of the useful bee. But the most excellent bee is small, round, and variegated ; another is long, and resembles the Avasp; and a third, Avhich is called a thief, is black, and has a broad belly. Besides these, likewise, there is the drone; this is the largest of all of them, is without a sting, and is sloth ful. Bees, also, Avhich inhabit cultivated places differ from those that are the inhabitants of mountains. For the bees Avhich dwell in forests are more hairy, are less, more industrious, and more irascible. The good bees, therefore, fashion their hives equable, and render theAvhole of the surface that covers them smooth. They, also, assign different cells to different uses ; as, for instance, the Avhole of one cell is appro priated to honey, another to the young bees, and another to the drones ; and if it should happen that all these are in the same cell, the cell immediately following is found empty. The longer bees, however, construct anomalous hives, and the surface that covers them is tuber ous, and resembles the covering Avhich hornets place over their hives. Besides this, also, they do not dispose in an orderly but in a casual manner either their offspring, or any thing else. From these, likewise, leaders of a bad species are produced, many drones, and those bees that are called thieves ; and they either make a very small quantity of honey, or none at all. Little worms, also, are generated in the corrupted honey-combs, which acquire Avings, and fly away. Bees, likeAvise, are careful to place in an upright position those honey combs that have fallen, and they support them Avith piles, in order that they may be able to enter into them. There is no Avork, however, of the thief and the drone, and they injure the works of the other bees. But when they are caught they are put to death by the bees of the good species. These good bees, also, particularly destroy the leaders when they are numerous, and above all those that are bad, lest the multitude of them should be the cause of dispersing the swarm. But those bees that are called thieves injure their own honey-combs, and if they are able latently enter into other hives ; but if they are caught they are put to death. It is not, however, difficult to take them, since there are guards at the entrance of each hive. But the thief, if he can latently enter any hive, in consequence of immoderate repletion is unable to fly, and rolls himself before the hive, so that it is difficult for him to escape. But the kings themselves are never seen out of the hives, ex cept when they migrate Avith the SAvarm, and then the other bees are seen collected about the king. When, however, the bees are about to migrate, for some days prior to their emigration a certain peculiar voice is heard, and for two or three days a few bees fly about the hive ; but Avhether the king is among these is not yet ascertained, because it is difficult to ascertain it. When, hoAvever, they are collected together, the other bees fly and arrange themselves about their respective kings. And if a few bees happen to be situated near many, the few betake themselves to the many, and destroy the king they have left if he fol lows them. After this manner, therefore, bees quit their hive, and settle in some other place. Different works, also, are assigned to different bees. Thus, for instance, some collect the juice of flowers ; others bring wa ter; and others polish and erect the honey-combs. They, likewise, bring water Avhen they nourish their offspring ; but they do not sit on any flesh, nor eat any thing that is prepared for the table. There is not, however, any definite time in Avhich they begin to work; but if there is a fit opportunity, and they are well, they principally apply themselves to work in summer; and when the Aveather is serene, they labour without intermission. Young bees, also, begin to work on the third day after they are born, if they are not in want of food. And when a swarm stops any where, some of the bees go in search of food, and afterwards re turn to the swarm. The bees, however, that have stung any animal [generally] die, be cause together Avith the sting they lose their intestine ; but they are frequently saved, if the animal that is stung is careful that the bee does not leave its sting behind. Young bees, however, do not sting similarly with the old ones ; and on this account swarms are carried aAvay without danger, for they are composed of young bees. But when honey fails, the keepers of bees expel the drones, and supply the bees Avith figs and other sweet substances. Of bees, hoAvever, those that are older Avork within the hive, and are more hairy, in consequence of remaining within it. A certain swarm, also, being once diseased, some bees came from another hive, fought Avith those that were diseased, vanquished them, and took aAvay their honey. The guardian of the hive, however, killed the foreign bees, and was assisted in so doing by the other bees, who did not sting the man [that revenged the injury they had sustained.] Swarms of bees, likewise, that are in a prosperous condition are princi pally subject to the disease which is called clerus. Bees, like wise, are subject to another disease, which is a kind of lethargy, and then the SAvarm emits a fetid odour. Thyme, also, is the food of bees ; and the white is better than the red thyme. But the place in Avhich they settle is in summer not fer vid, and in Avinter is warm. They are, likewise, principally diseased when they operate on rusty materials. And when there is much wind, they carry with them a stone, as a support against the violence of it. If, likewise, a river is near, they drink out of it, and in no other place, first laying down their burthen; but if a river is not near, they drink elseAvhere, vomit their honey, and immediately proceed to their Avork. For the making of honey, however, there are two seasons, spring and autumn. But the honey which is made in spring is whiter, and, in short, better than the honey which is made in autumn. The honey, also, is better which is made from new wax and neAv plants. But the red honey is not so good, on account of the Avaxen cells in which it is deposited ; for it is corrupted by these, in the same manner as wine by the vessel in Avhich it is kept. Hence it is necessary to dry this viti ated honey. When thyme, however, is in flower, and the cells are full, the honey does not become hard. But the honey which is of a golden colour is good ; and the white honey is not produced from genuine thyme. The Avhite honey, however, is good for the eyes and ulcers. The Aveak part of honey, also, always ascends to the surface, which part must be separated ; but the pure part subsides. When, however, the trees are in floAver, the bees make their wax; on which account the wax must then be taken from the hive, for the bees immediately produce neAv Avax. The plants, also, from Avhich the bees bring their wax are the following : the atractyllis, or wild bastard saffron, the melilote, the asphodelus, or daffodil, the myrtle, the phleus, the Avillow called agnus, and the sparton. But when the bees work upon thyme, they carry water into their cell, before they anoint them. All bees, likewise, emit their ordure, either flying, as we have before observed, or in one of the cells of the hive. The small bees, also,

Bees, also, appear to be delighted Avith a noise ; and hence it is said, that they are collected into the hives by the sound produced from strik ing earthern vessels. It is, however, perfectly immanifest Avhether they hear or not, and Avhether they do this from pleasure or from fear. Bees, likeAvise, expel from their hives both those that are indolent and those that consume too much honey. Every bee, also, as was before observed, is assigned a certain employment. And some, indeed, build the Avaxen cells, others make the honey, and others form the glue for the cement of the hives. Some, also, polish the cells ; others bring water to the cells, and mingle it with honey ; and others betake them selves to Avork out of the hive. But at day-break they are silent, till one of them by humming twice or thrice rouses the rest. Then all of them fly to their work ; and again returning to the hive, at first they are tumultuous, but they gradually become less noisy, till one of them flying round hums, as if signifying that they should go to sleep ; after which they are suddenly silent. The signs, also, by which a swarm is known to be in a good condi tion are, much noise, and the motion of those that are going out of and entering into the hive; for then the younger bees are at work. But they are especially industrious, Avhen the Avinter being elapsed they begin their Avork. And if any one in taking away honey from a hive leaves more than is necessary, the bees become more indolent. It is necessary, therefore, to leave just as much honey in the honey combs as is sufficient for the multitude of bees. But if less honey is left than is sufficient, they labour with less alacrity. They, also, be come more indolent if the hive is very large, as despairing that they shall be able to fill it. One hive, hoAvever, furnishes one measure, or one measure and a half of honey ; but a very full hive furnishes two measures, or two measures and a half ; and rarely three measures. These wasps, therefore, live tAvo years, and are seen in winter to fly from oaks which are cut down. But they live in winter in concealment, and pass their time in the trunks of trees. Of these Avasps, also, some are mothers, and others are labourers, in the same manner as among the milder wasps. But what the nature is of the labouring Avasp, and of the mother, will be evident in Avhat will be said of the milder wasps. For of mild Avasps there are tAvo genera ; some of them, indeed, being leaders, Avhich are called mothers, and others labourers. But the leaders are much larger and more mild than the labourers. And the labourers, indeed, do not live tAvo years, but all of them die at the commencement of the winter. This, however, is evident. For at the commencement of the Avinter, the labouring Avasps become stupid, and about the Avinter solstice they are not at all seen. But the leaders, which are called mothers, are seen during the whole of the Avinter, and conceal themselves under the earth. For many persons that plough and dig the earth in Avinter have seen the mothers, but no one in the winter has seen the labourers. The generation, also, of wasps is as follows : the leaders Avhen they have found an opportune place at the commencement of the summer fashion their honey-combs, and construct what are called small Avasp hives, which have four avenues, or nearly so, and in which the [labour ing] wasps and not the mothers are born. When these young labour ing wasps are increased in bulk, the leaders again construct other larger Avasp-hives, and Avhen the young wasps that are born in them grow larger, they again construct others ; so that at the end of autumn many and the largest Avasp-hives are formed, in which the leader called the mother no longer begets labouring Avasps, but mothers. But these are generated in the superior part of the wasp-hives in the form of large worms, in four or a few more cells connected with each other. And, in a similar manner, the other Avasps are produced in the cells of the honey combs. When, hoAvever, the labouring wasps are produced in the honey-combs, the leaders no longer work, but the labouring wasps bring them

The mother-wasp, hoAvever, is broad and heavy, and is thicker and larger than the labouring wasp. It, likewise, does not possess much strength for flying, and is incapable of flying far : hence, the mother wasps always sit in the Avasp-hives engaged in domestic employments. In most wasp-hives, also, there are what are called the mothers; but it is dubious Avhether they have stings or are without stings. It seems, however, that in this respect they resemble the leaders or kings of bees, who have, indeed, a sting, but who do not employ it in piercing and wounding. But of wasps, some are without stings, in the same manner as the drones, but others have a sting. And some, indeed, call those that have stings males, but those that are without stings females. They are, also, produced under the earth, and they fashion their honey-combs from earth and other materials which they collect together ; each honey-comb being con structed from one principle, as from a root. He is, likewise, by no means of a suspicious dispo sition ; and towards his associates and familiars he is very playful and bland. When he is hunted, also, he never flies if he is seen, nor hides himself through fear ; but if, on account of the multitude of those that hunt him, he is compelled to withdraw himself, he retires slowly step by step, and turns round [and faces his opponents] at every step. And if, indeed, he meets with a thicket, he flies rapidly through it till he comes into a plain; but then, again, he slowly retires. If, however, in plains and open places, he is at any time compelled to fly, through the multitude of his pursuers, he runs in a continued course, and does not leap; so that the continuity of his course resembles that of a dog. But when he pursues his prey, he leaps upon it when he is near to it. What is asserted, likeAvise, of the lion is true, that he is particularly. afraid of fire, as Homer1, also, says: And glowing torches, which, though fierce, he dreads. And, also, that he recognizes the person by Avhom he is struck, and attacks him. If, however, any one strikes, but does not hurt him, the lion if he catches him does him no injury, nor lacerates him with his claws; but shaking and terrifying, he again dismisses him. Lions, also, principally betake themselves to cities, and injure men, when they become old, and are unable through age to hunt, and their teeth are in a bad condition. They, likewise, live many years ; and a lame lion that was caught had a great number of broken teeth ; by which circumstance, some persons conjecture, that the life ot lions is very extended ; for their teeth would not be broken, unless they lived long. Among marine animals, also, many indications are related of the gentleness and mildness of the dolphin ; and, likeAvise, of the love and attachment Avhich it has shown to boys, about Tarentum, Caria, and other places. For a dolphin being caught and Avounded about Caria, a great multitude of dolphins came to the port, and continued there till the fisherman dismissed the dolphin which he had taken; for then all of them at once departed. Some one of the large, likewise, al ways follow the small dolphins, as their guardian. A troop, also, of large and small dolphins has been seen ; and of these, tAvo leaving the rest, were shortly after seen carrying on their back, and raising to the top of the Avater, a small dead dolphin which had fallen to the bottom of the sea, as if influenced by pity, lest it should be devoured by some other fish. Incredible things, also, are related respecting the swiftness of this animal. For it appears to be the swiftest of all animals both aquatic and terrestrial, and to surpass in rapidity the masts of large ships. This, however, particularly happens to be the case with them when they pursue any fish for the sake of food. For then, if the fish flies from them, they follow it to the depths of the sea, impelled by hun ger. But when their return from the bottom of the sea is long, [through the distance] they hold their breath, as if estimating the distance, and turning themselves, they are carried upward with the velocity of an ar row, in order that by their rapidity they may arrive at the place in which they can respire; and in doing this they surpass in velocity the

But it is dubious with respect to them why they rush into the earth ; for it is said that they sometimes do this from no assignable cause. CHAPTER XLIX. As, however, it happens that the actions of all animals are conform- able to their passions, so again their manners change conformably to their actions. This, likewise, is frequently the case with certain parts of the body; as, for instance, in birds. For hens when they vanquish the cocks crow, and imitating the males endeavour to copulate. They likeAvise, raise their crest and their tail, so that it is not easy to know that they are females ; and sometimes hens have certain small spurs. Some males, also, have been seen on the death of the female perform- ing the office of the female in attention to the chickens, by leading them about, and nurturing them, so as no longer either to crow or en- deavour to copulate. Certain male birds, likewise, become so effemi- nate from their birth, as neither any longer to sing, nor endeavour to copulate, but suffer the males that endeavour to copulate Avith them [as if they were females.] Many birds, likeAvise, change both their voice and their colour at certain seasons. Thus, for instance, the blackbird, instead of black has a yellow colour and a various voice. For in the summer it sings, but

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IX. 414 but in the Avinter it makes a stridulous noise, and utters tumultuous sounds. The thrush, also, changes its colour ; for in Avinter it is of an ash colour, but in summer its neck is variegated ; yet it suffers no mu tation in its voice. But the nightingale, indeed, sings continually day and night for fifteen days, during the time in Avhich the mountains are thick with foliage. After this period, likeAvise, she sings, yet no longer without intermission. But as the summer advances, she emits another and no longer an all various voice, nor a rapid and modulated, but a simple voice. She, likewise, changes her colour ; and in Italy, at this season of the year, is called by a different name. She is not, hoAvever, seen for a long time ; for she conceals herself. The robin-red-breast, likeAvise, and what is called the roach, are changed into each other. But the robin-red-breast is a bird of the Avinter; and the roach is a summer bird. They do not, however, at all differ from each other, as I may say, except in colour. In a similar manner, also, the becafigo [a bird like a wheat-ear] and the black-head are changed into each other. But the becafigo makes its appearance about the beginning of autumn, and the black head immediately after autumn. These birds, also, differ in no respect from each other, ex cept in their colour and voice. That the becafigo, however, and the black-head are the same bird is evident from this, that at the time of their change each has something which is the peculiarity of each. Nor is it at all wonderful that these birds change their voice and their colour, since the pigeon, also, is not at all vocal in Avinter, and, therefore, those who are skilled in the manners of birds are surprized if pigeons are vocal when fair Aveather succeeds a very severe winter ; but Avhen the spring commences, then the pigeon begins to be vocal. In short, birds are especially and most frequently vocal at the time of copula tion. The cuckoo, likewise, changes its colour, and its voice is not clear, when it is about to conceal itself. But it disappears when the dog-star rises. It, also, becomes visible at the commencement of the spring, and continues to be so till the rising of the dog-star. But the bird Avhich

But with respect to viviparous and pedestrious animals, the greater part have their testicles externally, and some have them internally ; but all of them have them near the end of the belly. Some birds, however, are castrated near the rump, at the part Avith Avhich they come into contact with the female when they copulate. For if any one burns this part Avith two or three hot irons, if the castrated bird is perfect, its crest will become pale, and it Avill no longer sing nor endeavour to copulate ; but if it is castrated Avhile it is yet young, it Avill never sing, nor copulate, nor have a red crest. The same thing, also, happens to men. For if they are mutilated in their private parts Avhile they are children, they will neither have hairs of posterior origin, nor will they experience a mutation of voice, but their voice will continue to be acute. But if they are castrated af ter puberty, the hairs of posterior origin will fall off, except those which are about the private parts; which, though they will be diminished, yet will not entirely fail. And they erred in the second place, because at different times the same persons have not the same, but different manners. For it sometimes happens that those who are [for the most part] sad pass through the day pleasantly, and assume the manners of one who is cheerful; and on the contrary, those Avho are [for the most part] cheer- ful are [sometimes] sad, so that the manner in the face is changed. Farther still, if any one alone considers the habit of the countenance, he will be able to frame a conjecture of but few passions of the soul, [because there are but feAv Avhich change this habit.] But those that physiognomize from savage animals do not rightly make the selection of signs. For it is not possible by directing our attention to the form of every animal to assert, that the animal Avhose body resembles that of another animal has, also, a similar soul. For, in the first place, in short, no one will find a man thus similar to a Avild beast, but resembling it in a certain respect. And in addition to Avhat has been said, few- animals have peculiar, but many have common signs. Hence when any one resembles a brute, not according to a peculiar, but according to a common sign, in what respect will he be more similar to a lion than to a stag? For it is reasonable that peculiar signs should signify something peculiar; and common signs something common. Common signs, therefore, Avill not manifest any thing to. him avIio physiognomizes. But if any one selects the peculiarities of each savage animal, he wilt not be able to assign the man of whom these are the signs; for it is reasonable that peculiarity should belong to no other animal than that of which it is the peculiarity. No one, however, can assume in his mind the peculiarity of any one of those animals which are the subject of physiognomy. For neither is a lion alone endued with fortitude, but many other animals are brave; nor is a hare alone timid, but an infinite number of other animals. If, therefore, nothing becomes manifest either to him who selects common, or to him who selects peculiar signs, Ave must not in physiognomizing direct our attention to. one genus of animals, but a selection must be made from all of them that suffer the same passion. With respect to voice, indeed, some one directing his attention to passion may think that an acute voice is to be considered as indicative of an irascible disposition, and this for a twofold cause. The lion, indeed, the bull, and the barking dog, and the more animated cocks, emit a grave voice ; but the stag and the hare, an acute voice. text: TO JOHN LA TOUCHE, OF Harristown, in the County os Kildare, Esq. DEAR SIR, TO the feelings of that Gratitude, which a friendship, almost paternal, and, for near thirty years, invariably experienced from you, has engraved upon my heart, you are to attribute this Dedication to you of FEMALE HEROISM. Vanity has, indeed, no part in the step. Both as a Man, and a Writer, I am fully apprized of my defects. Always sensible of the honour your Notice has conferred upon me, I have been equally conscious, that the merits of the Protege could not, in turn, reflect lustre on thc Patron. To suppose then for a moment, that my feeble voice could add any thing to the approbation os the Public ; or that my Penetration could point out to our sellow citizens additional virtues in your Characler, would be to betray a folly and presumption, that, I trust, #re foreign to my own. text: ADVERTISEMENT. THE Tragedy here presented to my Subscribers, was commenced in December, 1793. I had made some progress in it, [having written the First Ad, part of the Second, nearly the entire Third, and a few speeches of the Fifth) when I learned, that I had been anticipated by an English •writer, whose play on the same subject -was represented on the Dublin theatre. I immediately discontinued mine : nor, Jhou'd I ever have resumed it, but that, on a perusal of Mr. Eyre's performance, I found his tragedy not only de fective in form, {consisting only of four AEls) but censurable in other respects. Mr. Eyre has taken an unwarrantable liberty -with the well-known character of Charlotte Corde\ He pourtrays her as a Royalist ; and degrades her conduct, by ascribing to the influence of private resentment an act, really the result of public, tho' mistaken, zeal. To represent her attack of Marat, as originating in despair at the death of a favoured lover, is tofirip her character of the Heroism

text: VI ADVERTISEMENT. that distinguishes it. The merit of her Patriotism consisted in her sacrificing youth, beauty, the endearments of natural affection, and every prospect of happiness, to {whatshe deemed") the interests of her Country. Add to this, that, as a Royalist and avenger of a murdered lover, no motive can be assigned, why Jhe shou'd select Marat for the object of her vengeance : but, -when considered, con formably to fact, as a Republican of the Brijfotinor moderate party ; her detestation of Marat, a leader of the faction of the Mountain and a persecutor of her friends, is naturally accounted for. I must observe further, that Mr. Eyre's drama violates not only Historic truth, but probability itself Thus he makes Charlotte Corde'' {contrary to fact too !) have two in terviews with Marat ; a circumstance highly improbable. Hcr avowal of loyal principles wou'd have prevented the possibility of a second conference. Had Jhe even escaped the guillotine by a miracle, how very unlikely is it, that Marat wou'd a second time have admitted to his presence an En thusiast, who had already threatened his life, and warned him to beware of Cesar's fate ?

Enter Robespierre followed by Marat, Robespierre. \J RGE me no more — Thy zeal is rash, and with its frantic haste Wou'd mar our projects. Have we not our foes Secur'd, and pining in a dungeon's gloom ? There let them groan ; till fit occasion whet Th' avenging axe, and drag to public view Its destin'd victims. Marat. Still I must insist, Delays are hazardous ! Brifsot's at large, And the Departments of the South combin'd Espouse his cause. Marseilles and proud Toulon Their manifestoes issue ; and Calvados Arms openly against us. text: 2 FEMALE HEROsSM, Robespierre. Fear them not ! Firm in its native strength and the support Of our fam'd Jacobins, the Mountain stands Deep-rooted in a grateful Nation's love ; And mocks the malice of its prostrate foes, The ruin'd Girondists: Their puny efforts, Those last weak struggles of expiring faction, Serve but to grace our conquest, and to give A zest more poignant to the joys of vengeance ! Marat. Why not complete those joys ? Blood, blood alone Can purify the State and seal its safety. Robespierre. Thou shalt have blood enough. The Bour- bons soon Shall pour fresh streams of royal gore to fate Thy thirsty soul. Deluded fury still Survives the harmless Tyrant, and pursues Th' ill-fated race. Egalite, and She, The scourge of France in slav'ry's former day, Proud Austria's dame, shall mount the scaffold next And lead a train of victims to the grave ; While despots arm and Pitt conspires in vain ! Marat. I live but in the prospect. How my soul Elate, in thought anticipates the day, The glorious day, that to remorseless death Yields up that Siren ; fated now no more With studied grace of soft persuasive note?, And beauty, still more eloquent, to lure A Nation to its ruin ! When her Art, Her ambufh'd wiles and complicated guilt Rise in my mem'ry, Pity throws a veil O'er her late husband's fault, regrets his doom, And half-absolves the Tyrant that she form'd. Robespierre. Tis true, my friend. Her crimes of blackest die Both justify abhorrence, and provoke The sword of justice : Yet those very crimes Have serv'd our cause. Hence have the Girondists, Whose erring mercy wou'd avert her fate,

text: A TRAGEDY. 3 Become unpopular : And prudence bids us To fan with soft 'ring breath the gen'ral flame Of indignation, till the spreading blaze Devour at once the Austrian and her friends. Maria's death shall thus the prelude prove To Brissot 's final downfal ! Marat. Haste we then T' accelerate the great event and teach To seepter'd pride a mortifying lesson. Well I remember, when this haughty queen Wou'd not have deign'd to notice with a glance Marat or thee : But now the circling hours, Our lots reversing, make her former slaves The sole disposers of her destiny ! I'll to the Jacobins — With them, thou know'st, My int'rest stands unrivall'd — Urg'd by Me, Soon shall their clamours, for her trial, force To prompt decision the Convention's measures, And send her to rejoin her slaughter 'd lord. [Exit.] Robespierre alone. Go, self-plum'd Statesman, go, and idly dream Of pow'r and consequence ! Thou and thy friends, St. Just, Le Gendre, Danton and Bazire, Are but my Jackals ; dull, officious slaves, Whose labours cater for my great revenge ! The prey run down, the lordly lion stalks Forth from his covert, and at leisure feasts ; While his purveyors, at a distance, tremhje Fools ! not to see, that this their forward zeal Seconds my plans, and, pioneer-like, smooths The road to my Ambition. How secure The game I play ! The stake and toil are Theirs, Whilst ali the golden prosit is my own. Like Jove's in darkness wrapt, my hand unseen Guided the storm, and lanc'd the bolts that blasted The giant sons of Aristocracy ! By me too fell their Monarch ; and, ere long, Th' extinction of the Bourbon race and name Shall crown my daring hopes, and leave the reins Of empire, uncontested, in my hands — But soft — who comes here . Fauchet ! in his looks Big with importance, and his haste, I read Some lurking secret. Honied flatt'ry, now Sit on my lips ; and thou, Dissimulation, Moulding each feature, for a while transform me, And hide the wily Serpent in the Dove. Enter Fauchet. Whence, Fauchet, in such haste, and wherefore sits That gloom upon thy features ? Fauchet. Canst thou all- Why, in these times of danger to my Country, Dejection clouds my brow ? Are not my friends Deep in a dungeon's dark recesses plung'd, As traitors to the State ? And I myself, Tho' yet at large, suspected I Doom'd to hold Precarious life and freedom at the will Of rane'rous foes, whose yet-unglutted rage Contempt alone (degrading thought !) suspends. text: 5 A TRAGEDY. Speaks peril nearer, and augments my sears ; Thy smiles are more alarming than thy frowns. Robespierre. Now, by the genius of victorious France, And all the hopes that fire a patriot's breast, My lips but speak the dictates of my heart ! Tho' stil'd by Thee its Chief, far other thoughts From those that animate the Mountain's zeal In secret sway me. Long have I beheld With silent indignation the career Of furious Anarchy ! Why seem For years our steady foe ? Robespierre. Because I fear Th' all-pow'rful Jacobins — Thou know'st, Marat Sways them, and they the people. text: 6 FEMALE HEROISM, Malignant envy, and of civic fame Base jealousy, impel him to destroy The man he seems to cherish : When occasion Favours the blow, he plants th' insidious steel Ev'n in the bosom of his heedless brother Yet warm from his embrace ! Fauchet. The portrait's just In ev'ry feature, and thy vehemence Speaks thee sincere : Thus thinking, I may trust thee With an intelligence thou'lt joy to hear — Destruction hovers o'er Marat ! Robespierre. How! how! [Eagerly.] Said'st thou? Fauchet. This day he dies ! Robespierre. Unfold the means. By poison, or the dagger ? Fauchet. By the last. Robespierre. Th' attempt is far more arduous than thou think'st ; Marat is ever on his guard — In public, Fenc'd by his creatures 'round, and follow'd close By the admiring rabble — When at home, Hard of access, mistrustful, and prepar'd 'Gainst all attacks . His fellow-deputies Themselves are not admitted, 'till they leave Their swords without, and stand a private search. Fauchet. That caution shan't avail him ; for the blow Comes from a quarter he can ne'er suspect : 'Tis from a female's hand his guilt shall meet Its due reward. Robespierre. A female's? Fauchet. Yes — from Normandy This very morning has arriv'dthe Maid Whose poniard shall avenge the wrongs of France. Grac'd with the charms of beauty and of youth, Her country's and her sex's pride, me comes : Possest of courage equal to th'attempt, And virtues meriting a gentler fate.

text: 8 F-EMALE heroism, Regardless hears the summons ! Distance, toil, Danger, and pain, all vanish at the sound ; Or, if appearing, but incentives prove To acts of more exalted enterprise. But say, good Fauchet, has no Patriot's steel Prevented Chariot's ? Lives the monster still, And glories in his yet-unpunished crimes ? Fauchet. As yet France groans beneath th 'ignoble yoke Of him and his associates — Public virtue Sinks overpow'r'd, or languishes in chains ; While licens'd Murder rears its bloody front, And Terror is the order of the day. Charlotte Corde. O that this arm, obedient to my wish, Cou'd blast him with the light'ning's speed ! The dagger Is tardy for the purpose, and each hour, That respites his destruction, proves an age. Fauchet. [Aside. \\ Now, art, assist me — For awhile I'll seem To doubt her prowess, till offended pride Wakes all the sex within her soul, and arms her With firmness more determin'd. text: A TRAGEDY 9 Charlotte Cordi. Wound me no more With those degrading doubts — Behold an arm Steel'd to its purpose, and with inborn vigour Firm as the Vet'ran's nerve ? Th'aspiring soul Is of no Sex ; and, granting that a Female Were ill by Nature fitted for the task, I'm not the first weak instrument os vengeance, That Heav'n selected from our feebler race To blast the triumph of its guilty foes. By Jael's hand the warlike Sifera Inglorious died : Bethulia's honour'd Matron, Ev'n in the midst of his victorious host, Slew Holofernes, and redeem'd her Country ! Marat, a guiltier, tho' a meaner victim, Shall fall by Charlotte's steel. Fauchef. Yet think, what rifle Attends thy purpose — What decided njin Follows the blow — Inevitable death ! Charlotte Corde. True ! I shaU die— Os this assur'd I come _ Prepar'd, with joy, to pay the debt I owe To Nature and to France. Living or dead, My Country shall not blush to own her daughter. Fauchet. How much I honour thy heroic worth, These tears, that mingled love and pity draw, Fair excellence, may witness ! But, alas ! Still must I tremble for the issue ; still Anticipate that moment, when the blaze Of high-wrought zeal expires, and cooler reason Wakes to the horrors that must yet surround thee ; Dragg'd to the scaffold by remorseless ruffians, With ignominy dragg'd : Of hooting crowds The gaze, and by their base licentious taunts Insulted and tradue'd ! text: 10 FEMALE HEROISM, Is highest Honour, and to fuff'ring Virtue The scaffold proves a Throne ! Cou'd all mankind Witness the solemn scene, with conscious pride From the four winds I'd summon them together To mark my parting triumph, and to learn How sweet is death, when suffer'd for our Country ! Fauchet. Exalted Heroine ! No more I strive To check the tow'rings of a foul like thine, Or damp a zeal that Heav'n itself inspires. Go then, avenge thy Country : Go, transcend All that of female excellence proud Greece Or prouder Rome displays ! Go, rival her, Whose sainted mem'ry grateful France adores, Th'immortal Maid of Orleans Like hers, Thy name, enroll 'd in fame's eternal page, Our future sons shall teach their eager babes To lisp with transport ; and to hail the hour, Th'auspicious hour, that blest thy Mother's throes, And gave the Maid of Normandy to France ! [Exeunt."] END OF THE FIRST ACT. ACT II. SCENE, a Walk in the Champs Eitsee^s. Enter Clerville. Clerville. I err'd not surely ! — On this faithful heart Too well has love her matchless charms pourtray'd For Clerville to forget that angel form ! 'Twas she — But why from all her friends remote ? Why, unattended, in this haunt of crimes, This theatre of horrors ? O my Charlotte, Ill-suited to thy purity of mind And gentleness of temper are the scenes Of this deprav'd and blood-stain 'd Capital ! What can thy presence here portend ? Fond heart.

text: A TRAGEDY. 11 Throb not with idle panick thus, nor deem The meeting inauspicious See ! she comes : And ev'ry thought ill-omen'd at her sight Flies, as the mist before the rising fun. Enter Charlotte Corde\ My Charlotte ! my ador'd J Charlotte Corde. Ha ! Clerville here ! Clerville. Why dost thou seem confus'd ? Why coldly meet me With half-averted looks ? Methinks thine eye No longer beams with its accustom'd mildness — A sterner lightning plays in ev'ry glance, And strikes me with an awe unfelt before ! Charlotte Corde. Thy Charlotte is the fame : But, since we parted, The times are alter'd — Guilt, undaunted, rears Its gorgon brow, and Shame has lost her blush : Dejected virtue sickens at the view ! Clerville. Why hast thou sought the Capital ? Why left The calm retirement of that happy vale, Where peace and innocence together dwell ? Charlotte Corde. Enquire not further — 'Tis enough to tell thee That duty call'd me from the blissful scene. Clerville. Thy short mysterious answers — Thy reserve — Each circumstance — [Charlotte Corde' in taking out her handkerchief, drops a dagger.] O all ye Saints, what's this ? A dagger !
