text: 12 FEMALE HEROISM, . Still melted at a tale of woe, whose eye» A sparrow's fate has oft suffus'd with tears, That wears th'assaffin's badge, and boasts a purpose Our sterner sex might shrink from ? Charlotte Corde. Dost thou wonder That woman, apt to feel, more promptly kindles At others' wrongs ? lt is not cruelty, 'Tis pity arms me thus — Who does not bless The well-aim'd shaft, that, in his stoop triumphant, Piercing the Falcon, from his murd'ring pounces Rescues the trembling dove ? Justice herself In mercy bares her glave ; and, while she gives Death to th' oppressor, bids the injur'd live. Let guilt unpitied fall ! Clerville. Oh yet beware Lest, while thy poniard's aim'd at guilt, its point Shall deeper wound thyself. The weight of blood Falls, like a mountain, on the lab 'ring breast, And throws a gloom eternal o'er the mind. How, in the midnight hour, shall trembling fancy Shrink from the writhings of the ghastly victim, More ghastly thro' the retrospective glass Of conscience dimly seen ? Charlotte Corde. Those midnight horrors May scare the slumbers of Revenge, or haunt Ambition's guilty couch — The patriot's foul, Unstain'd by crimes, in retrospection's mirror No other objects views, but grateful Man, Admiring Angels, and approving Heav'n. text: A TRAGEDY. 15 The present, to the suture lifts an eye Of tranquil hope. Queen, [rising] Hope, saidst thou ? Do not mock Our sorrows with the found — When Louis died, Hope died alike to me'. Deep in his grave She lies, for ever buried — What event, What human pow'r may remedy or soothe Our cureless woes ? Not France, with all her millions, Tho' prostrate at our feet, cou'd now repair Mine and my Orphans' losses ! Can her pity Undo that deed of horror, and restore To me an husband, and to them a sire ? Princess Elizabeth. Afflicting truth ! Yet in the widow's feelings Lose not the memory of other ties : Duties, more sacred now, and more endear 'd Ev'n by the loss we both deplore, remain ; Still, in his children, lives your Lord ! Affection Shou'd, in their service, rally all its strength, And call the Mother to the Christian's aid. Queen. Alas, my Children ! When I think of you, Affection only barbs each fatal shaft, And irritates my wounds — Inhuman Frenchmen, Were bars, and locks, and prisons then devis'd For unoffending innocence ! Princess Elizabeth. Suppress These unavailing transports — Rather try T' o'erlook the malice of triumphant foes, And wait with calmness, till the hand of Heav'n In its due time shall interpose its aid, Or Man, relenting, cease to persecute. See, where, in native loveliness array'd, To sooth a mother's wounded heart appears Our interesting charge ! Enter the Princess Royal and the Dauphin. Queen. Come to these arms, [Embracing them.] My all that's left of (hip-wreck'd happiness !

text: 16 PEMALE HEROISM. My only stay on earth ! But wherefore droops My dearest Louis thus ? Dauphin. Oh mother, mother, I'm weary of confinement ! Shall I ever Breathe the pure air at large, and range at pleasure The fields and groves, as I was wont to do _ Queen. I hope thou wilt, and shortly too — That God^ Who loves the good, will yet, I trust, assert Thy cause, my injur'd Child. Dauphin. But tell me, Mother, Was not my father good . Queen. He was ! he was ! Too good for France, and far too good for Me ! Dauphin. Why then did God, who loves the good, permit Those wicked Men to take my Father's life ? Queen. Ah ! why indeed ? [Aside.] My love, God suffer'd it, Because your Father merited a crown Brighter than That he wore. Remov'd to Heav'n, He reigns, a martyr'd faint, in glory there ! Dauphin. I wish, dear Mother, we were with him now— Na}', weep pot thus, or I shall cry myself; And tears, I've oft been told, are most unmanly. Queen. He wrings my heart — That sweet simplicity And strong affection for his parents, wound, Ev'n while they soothe my bosom, O thou Pow'r [Kneel}. Supreme in goodness, tho' in wisdom still Inscrutable by man ; let not my sins Untimely blast the promise of his youth, Or call thy thunders on his guiltless head ! On me, me only may they aU descend ; But on my children ever gracious fall The dew of thy benevolence. To Thee, And thy paternal wisdom, I commit Their destiny, resign'd! Howe'er obseure

text: A TRAGEDY. 17 Their lot, thy favour can ennoble it : The Christian's birth-right far transcends the King's ! Enter abruptly Robespierre. Ha ! Who art thou, whose forward rudeness thus Intrudes upon our grief? Robespierre The Nation's friend — And thence a foe to Thee, and to the Bourbons ! If more thou wou'dst enquire ; instinctive awe, Methinks, might whisper to thee, that my name Is Robespierre ; a name not more abhorr'd Than fear'd by princes! Queen. I have heard thc name, But never fear'd it yet. [Scornfully.] Robespierre. Art thou to learn My arm dethron'd thy husband, and my voice Doom'd him to death ? Behold this handkerchief — [Shews a bloody handkerchief.] Know'st thou, whose blood distains it ? 'Tis thy Lord's ! Queen. Oh execrable Monster — God of Heav'n, Shall guilt so black provoke thy bolts in vain ? To wound anew this lacerated bosom, And with a father's blood thus blast the sight Of his ill-fated offspring ! text: A TRAGEDY. 19 The theme of death my fav'rite thought, when sleep Fled from these burning eye-lids ; and had arm'd My soul against its terrors : But this stretch Of cruelty resin'd what mother's breast Cou'd e'er anticipate ? — It weighs me down — It drinks my blood — It preys upon my spirits, And withers my contracted heart — Princess Royal. text: 20 FEMALE HEROISM, Divide us not, but let a duteous child Wait still upon her Mother, share her sorrows, And chear a dungeon's melancholy gloom. Queen. text: A TRAGEDY. 21 Each avenue to mercy, and possess My ev'ry ser.se; that not one genial ray Of pity, thro' their frozen ducts, may pierce To thaw th' unyielding winter of my soul ! [Exit.] 5ND OF THE SECOND ACT. ACT III. SCENE a Chamber iu Marat's house. Enter Marat and Robespierre. Marat. At length the Nation's vengeance is arous'd, And fate's inextricable toils epclose The trembling Austrian. Our Convention, wak'd From its late apathy, decrees her trial ; And over her devoted head the axe Already gleams. Let me but see it fall, And, fortune, I'll forgive thy future malice ! Robespierre. Didst thou behold her present miseries, Thou wou'd'st recall thy wish, and deem the axe Her only hope — Horrors beset her round ! Stretch 'd on the pavement of a narrow cell In earth deep-funk, and by the chearing eye Of day, and zephyr's all-reviving breath Alike unvisited : with dripping dews All-dank, and fetid with unwholsome vapours. There, to the vultures of remorse a prey, Lies the once proud aspiring Queen of France, Thc Circe of her day ; whose witching smiles And cup of magic potency transsorm'd To worse than brutes the Nobles ofa Court, And made a Nation glory in her chains. Marat. With such a master's hand thou draw'st her suff- 'rings

text: 22 FEMALE HEROISM, As wakes desire to witness them ! Methinks It were no vulgar luxury to hear And count her groans ; to talk of the Bastile, And ask her, can (he image now its pains ? By heav'n, 'tis greatly thought, and I'm resolv'd To try her Firmness : By the night's approach That glorious taunt shall wound her inmost soul. Robespierre. [Aside.] Shall it indeed ? — Fool ! ere the night arrives, Thou and thy projects shall together perish.! Enter a Servant. Servant. A female citizen below, Marat, Requests admittance. Robespierre. Nay then, it is time To take my leave — Adieu, and may thine heart Reap all th' advantage from this fair-one's visit That friendstiip, true as mine, must wish thee ! [Exit. J Marat. Ha ! [Aside. What mean his parting words ? If raillery ; 'Tis couch'd in terms equivocal and dark.] [To the Servant.] Say, hast thou seen this visitant before ? If not — describe her person and appearance. Servant. Unknown to me her features ; but her mien And dress bespeak her of no vulgar rank : She seems a Maiden, young, and grac'd with beauty. Marat. Beauteous and young ? Admit her — but be sure To place, within my call, a trusty guard To wait my orders. [Exit Servant.] Some unwonted impulse Warns me, th' occasion may require their aid, And seems to hint that danger is at hand — Fie, fie, Marat ! Dismiss these idle fears, The weak suggestions of a mind diseas'd, Harrass'd with business, and by vigils worn. Woman, all-charming Woman, shou'd excite Far different emotions : Form'd by Heav'n To scatter roses o'er the path of life,

text: A TSACEDY. 23 To solace with her sprightly wit our toil, And with her radiant smiles dispel our care. Enter Charlotte Corde\ Charhtte Corde. Forgive a stranger's boldness! — Thi? intrusion, My age and sex consider 'd, may appear A mark'd departure from establish'd forms. Marat. Your sex can ne'er intrude. Say then, to whom I owe the honour I receive. Charlotte Corde. My name Is Charlotte Cord_, and from Norman race My lineage is deriv'd. I come, deputed From the department of Calvados to thee, On matter of high import. Marat. Give it utt'rance. So fair a messenger ensures respect, And adds importance to their embassy. Charlotte Corde. I come to tell thee, what thy flatt'rers dare not ! To tell thee, that thy sanguinary genius Alike from safety and from glory leads Thy unsuspecting Country. Where are now Those promis'd blessings, for whose distant joys Thro' four long years deluded France has paid, Profusely paid, in treasure and in blood ? Marat. Where, dost thou ask ? In what sequester'd nook, Obscure and unobserving, hast thou liv'd, If yet a stranger to thy Country's triumphs ? Look round, and own them ! See, where the Bastile Whelm'd slav'ry in its ruins! See the yoke Of the proud Nobles from th' indignant neck Of freemen burst : See, crush 'd beneath their feet The Tyrant's sceptre, and his throne o'erturn'd ; While, on its wreck firm-rising, a Republic To Grecian arts, to Grecian fame aspires, And Roman virtues ! Walks not Man at length
name: West, Matthew

text: 24 FEMALE HEROISM, Bold and erect, with undegraded mien, As Nature form'd him ? Conscious of his rights, And proudly claiming for his unborn issue The first great Charter of Equality ! Charlotte Corde. Vain this parade of unsubstantial boasts, And vainer still delusive theories, When stubborn facts refute them ! — Roman virtues ? Where shall I hail them ? Where shall I attest These triumphs of regenerated France With filial joy ? Alas ! a Patriot's eye Vainly, thro' all our provinces, in quest, In anxious quest, of peace and order strays And law's mild government. Like Noah's dove, It finds no spot to rest on. Still around One scene of horror to the sight presents The sorest evils, and the blackest crimes : Sedition, insurrection, civil war, Rapine, and rage, and wide-extended Massacre ! What worse from scepter 'd tyranny can spring ? Marat. What worse ? Fond maid, thy inexperienc'd mind. In narrow views concenter'd, idly mourns A transient evil ; nor discerns the End, The glorious End, that consecrates the means. 'Tis thus the tempest to the bounded ken Of abject souls bears only on its wing Ruin and terror, while th' enlighten'd eye Hails radiant hope amid the deep'ning gloom ; And sees Disease, with all her train of Ills, Fly, fear'd, before the salutary blast. Know, that these wild commotions of the State With wholesome violence shall purify The atmosphere of freedom, and disperse Each lurking taint. Thus present evils teem With future benefits ; and, rightly fcann'd, Are blessings in disguise. Charlotte Corde. Think'st thou, Marat, With sophistry thus gross to warp the heart, Or cloud the understanding ? 'Tis a plea

text: A TRAGEDY. 25 That villains ever urge, and fools alone Can listen to with temper. Who, but fools, Wou'd buy contingent and precarious good With certain evil ? Yet this weak pretext, This hacknied argument of knaves, is wanting To more than half thy measures. What advantage From Capet's death, for instance Marat. How ! what mean'st thou ! Dar'st thou to censure those illustrious Patriots, Who led, amid their Country's just applause, The Tyrant to the axe ? Charlotte Corde. I dare ! the deed With blood unnecessary stain'd the land. Unscepter'd once, the Bourbons had a claim To pardon. Why disgrace a righteous cause With useless horrors? — When assembled France Abjur'd a Monarchy, her solemn act Stood not in need of Capet's death to give it The seal and sanction of Validity. The punishment was bootless, when example Cou'd warn no future despot. Even Justice Oppos'd his doom ! In yielding up his crown He paid the mulct of antecedent crimes Or real, or imputed. Self-defence Bids us indeed disarm th' assailant's hand, But sanctions not revenge : The conflict o'er, True courage scorns to stab a prostrate foe, And mercy spares her unresisting suppliant. Marat. I know thee now ! This splenetic attack Of the fam'd Mountain and its godlike chiefs Speaks thee the tool of those designing traitors, Rolland and his confed'rates. Yes ! I mark The lurking Royalist beneath the veil, The flimsy veil, thy politics assume, Of moderation. Thou'rt a Brissotin And Girondist ! Charlotte Corde. I glory in the name ! 1 glory, that the friends my heart approves i

text: 26 FXMALE HEROISM. Are objects of his base envenom'd malice, Whose praise were infamy — Nay, colour not With rising rage ; nor think, with scowling brow And glance expressive of a demon's hate, T' appall this soul : for know, my fear of Thee Is less than ev'n my love ! Marat. Presumptuous woman, 'Gainst whom is levell'd this thy wild abuse ? Is't not Marat ? Marat, the people's friend ? The leading Architect, to whose design Th' immortal fabric of our Commonwealth Owes its first rise ? Yes ! Insolent, I tell thee That millions, yet unborn, shall hail Marat Their friend and benefactor ; the prime source Of all the blessings that sliall crown his country ; Of peace and freedom ! Charlotte Corde. Thou, the people's friend ? Thou art the enemy of human kind, The fell defacer of the Maker's image, Whose trade is Murder, and whose joy is Blood ! Thou give thy Country peace and freedom ? Thou ? How dar'st thou with those foul polluted lips Usurp and violate the hallow'd sounds ? The peace and freedom thou wou'dst give to France Are such as reign amid the pathless Wild ; Where desolation only meets the eye, And not one sound is heard, unless the howl Of famish'd monsters, savage as the scene ! Marat. Thy Sex has long been privileg'd to rail, Aud I wou'd listen to thy declamation With calm disdain, did not a Patriot's duty Forbid all converse with a Girondist : As such, henceforth I shall avoid thee, Charlotte ; Yet note my parting words — Some secret impulse. Like pity, or like love, I know not which, Prompts me to save thee from th' impending fate That soon sliall burst, tremendous, on the heads Of Brissot's guilty faction : Hie thee hence
name: West, Matthew

text: A TRAGEDY. 27 To Normandy ; and there, in safety, hear The distant ruin : study to forget Thy dang'rous tenets ; or, by prudence fway'd, Ev'n from thy dearest intimates conceal them. Tliis is a friend's advice ! Charlotte Corde. It is a counsel Worthy the giver's soul. Guilt and Marat May hide the head and tremble : but to fear Charlotte is yet a stranger ! Conscious worth Disdains alike retreat or mean disguise, And meets the danger with a brow erect. There's not a wish, there's not a thought of mine But I am ready to proclaim aloud To France, to all the World ! — If impious men, Amid the fury of the waves that toss The State's frail vessel, with unhallow'd hands Have seiz'd the helm ; it is my firm resolve To perish in the storm that wrecks my Country, And not survive her glories — How ! what means That vacancy of look ? What studied wile Lurks in thy fraudful breast, and waits the gloss Of that designing tongue ? Marat. Her ev'ry word, [Aside.] Her ev'ry glance betrays an energy That awes, and yet attracts. Two adverse feelings Divide my soul — I love and hate at once ! This moment I cou'd clasp her in my arms : The next, devote her to the axe — And both, Both passions shall, ere long, be gratisied. Charlotte Corde. What, silent still ? Shall female vanity Dream of Marat's conversion ? Marat. Yes, fair Maid — Beauty, like thine, can work far greater wonders! I am thy Proselyte — but 'tis in love — Be mine in Politics, and share at once The heart, the hopes, and greatness of Marat. Thus let me sue ! [Kneels and attempt. In take her hand.] Charlotte Corde. Away, thou miscreant — E 2
name: West, Matthew

text: 28 FEMALE HEROISM. Thy love is insult, and thy touch pollution ! Avaunt, before my kindling rage shall quench In thy own pois'nous blood thy flame impure. Marat. I laugh at woman's menaces— but thou, Rash fool, shou'dst dread my pow'r ! Hast thou not heard My will is fate, and with a single word Sweeps Nobles to the grave ? — But hence all threats On either side ; 'Tis happiness I offer, Nor thou reject the gift : Come, come, be kind ; Dismiss this virgin coyness, that belies Thy secret wissies and retards our bliss — Come, let me lead thee to yon couch — [Laying hold on her.] Charlotte Corde. First take This greeting from my hand — [Stabs him.] Die, nor pollute The Land, that bore thee, longer with thy crimes ! Marat. Help, hoa ! I'm slain — V/ho waits there ? [Enter an Officer, and party of National Guards.] Seize the traitress— My lifeblood choaks me— Oh untimely fate- Lost — lost — for ever — [Dies.] Officer. Rash, unhappy Maid, What hast thou done ! Charlotte Corde. Aveng'd an injur'd realm ! Shades of my mangled Countrymen, whose blood Yon tiger's thirst insatiate drain'd, look down Complacent on the scene ! Behold him here Stretch'd at my feet, the victim of his crimes : And own, that Heav'n's offended justice nerv'd This arm, and guided to his heart the blow ! On me too deign to bend an eye ! On me, A self-devoted sacrifice for France : And oh ! amid the trials that await My closing hours, sustain a woman's Weakness With fortitude transfus'd ! Let steady zeal. Meek patience, and collected dignity, Attest the motive that unflieath'd my steel, Grace my last sigh, and vindicate my fame !
name: West, Matthew

text: A TRAGEDY. 29 Enter haslily Clerville; he starts hack on feeing Marat's body. Clerville. Oh horror— I'm too late — The deed is done, And hope's last gleam is vanish'd — Charlotte Corde. Thou too here ! [To Clerville.] This is indeed the bitterness of death ! To witness thy distress were agony— In pity leave me ! Clerville. Cruel, cruel Charlotte— Wou'dst thou deny then to despair like mine The last sad interchange of looks and tears ? Yet what can these avail me ! — What resource, What hope, what mitigation for a wound Incurable as this ! Was't not enough To whelm in ruin unforeseen my peace, But deepest horrors must attend the blow ? Oh ! had th' inexorable Tyrant worn A milder form ; had accident or sickness Snatch 'd my heart's treasure from these fost'ring arms, I cou'd have borne it ! But — to lose her thus — Madness is in the thought ! Charlotte Corde. O shame to manhood ! Where is thy fortitude ? The saints can witness, A love as fervent animates thy Charlotte : And now, when, standing on the verge extreme Of life, I take a last and ling'ring view Of all its joys ; thy dear, thy cherish'd image Excites regret alone, and makes this heart Dissolve with more than female tenderness. Yet see — with calmness I resign thee, Clerville — Then learn from me composure ! Check those wild, Those frantic bursts of anguish ; nor condemn My feebler sex to bear a double burthen, Thy sorrows, and my own. Clerville. And is it thus Thou'd'st comfort me and all thy weeping friends
name: West, Matthew

text: JO FEMALE HEROISM. By proving what an Angel we shall lose ? Ah ! what a task is mine ! How shall I e'er Revisit love's too well-remember'd scenes ? Scenes, that my Charlotte shall adorn no more ! How shall these trembling lips disclose thy fate To thy fond father's ear ? Charlotte Corde. There— There indeed This heart is wrung with anguish — O my father, Who now shall watch o'er thy declining years, Beguile th' infirmities and cares of age, And gently smooth thy passage to the grave ? Farewell the hope I once so fondly cherish'd, That I, myself, with tender hand ssiou'd close Those honour'd eyes, and see thee duly laid Beside the sacred dust of her who bore me ! Now strangers shall perform that pious office ! Now far, far distant from those lov'd remains Shall rest thy luckless child !— Assist me, Heav'n, Nor let regret and unavailing softness Turn from her glorious fate a Patriot's eye : My Country's bosom shall receive this frame, And gratitude embalm it with her tears — For thee, my Clerville — Clerville. Anguish and despair — I cannot save thee, Charlotte — All that fate Allows me, is to join thee in the grave ! This sword — Charlotte Corde. Hold, cruel and unthinking mau Let me not blush for love, mistaken choice; Compell d to own, that partial fancy drew The worth this bosom idoliz'd so long. Renounce thy selfish purpose. Know 'tis treason In times so arduous to desert that Country Who claims, and shou'd receive, her offspring's aid. If thou wou'd'st have thy Charlotte meet serene The axe's terrors, live, I charge thee, Clerville : Live — to defend from obloquy her fame ! She dies not wholly, while thy faithful love

text: A TRAGEDY. 31 Preserves her image — Take this last embrace From thy betroth'd and best belov'd — Farewell — Farewell — Be blest — Be virtuous, and — Be Free ! [Exit guarded.] Clerville alone. «* Be free !" Ah Charlotte, what to me were freedom Thus purchas'd with thy loss ? The common joy Wou'd but enhance my sorrow ! Each return Of public triumph only ope my wound, And bid it bleed afresh — The earth I tread, Yon light of Heav'n, the vital air I breathe, Henceforth alike are odious in these eyes ! What's life without thee ! Yet I'm doom'd to live — Thy parting pray'r, thy last command enjoin'd it ; And I must yield obedience Yes ! most dear, And first of Women, for thy fake alone Will I endure existence : for thy fake In faithful service consecrate my life To that lov'd Country thou hast fall'n to save. Awake then, Clerville, to the glorious task 1 With kindling energy pursue her steps, And emulate her fame ! Like her, disdain The mean pursuits of selfish bliss, and live Alone for Others : Live, to shew the World Clerville was worthy of his Charlotte's love. [Exit.] END OF THE THIRD ACT.
name: West, Matthew

text: 32 female heroism, ACT IV. SCENE, Robespierre's Lodgings. Enter Robespierre and Fauchet. Robespierre. Your tale amazes me ! To triumph thus O'er faction's rage, and into softness melt The flinty bosoms ofthe populace ! What potent charm cou'd thus transform their nature ? Fauchet. The charm of virtue. Oh ! had'st thou beheld The sweet composure of th' angelic Maid, By dignity ennobled ; Had'st thou mark'd The fire that sparkled in her eye, and spoke A Roman soul, submitting to its fate,' Yet still unconquer'd ; Thou had'st join'd to curse The ruthless axe, whose undiscerning edge Robb'd France of such a daughter! Robespierre. Well — She's gone, And grief avails not — Dry your tears — A statesman Shou'd scorn to play a puling woman's part : Revenge is nobler, and befits the times. Fauchet. You counsel right — And here I claim your pro- mise Of aiding my opprest but virtuous friends : Marat's no more ; And in his well-tim'd death I've crown'd your wishes. Robespierre. Thou hast serv'd me well : And now — receive my thanks. Within there, hoa ! [Enter a Guard.] I do arrest thee, Traitor, in the name Of thy much-injur'd Sovereign, the People : Thou base assassin of their faithful friend, The brave Marat !
name: West, Matthew

text: A TRAGEDY. 33 of thy Fauchet. O monstrous perfidy ! Am I then made at once the wretched tool And victim of thy dark designs ? — But down My swelling rage — Why shou'd a villain, stain'd By crimes like mine, complain of treachery ? 'Tis strictest justice ! Yes, my Monarch's wrongs At length o'ertake me, and avenging Heav'n Makes thee, the base accomplice of my crimes, Its minister to scourge disloyalty ! From Capet's brow, with impious hand, I join'd To rend his crown, with sliameless front denied His royal virtues, and aspers'd his fame ; Taught his misguided subjects to believe The best of Kings a Tyrant ; basely lent The sanction os a Christian prelate's name To foul conspiracy, and thus enabled Still blacker villains to atchieve a deed My soul revolted from — They stew their King- But I — had first dethron'd him ! Robespierre. Thy own lips Proclaim the justice of thy doom. Then perish Thou half-soul 'd traitor, coward in thy crimes, And fool no less than villain ! To the chains He merits, bear him hence. Fauchet. Hold — ere I go To meet the vengeance I too well deserve ; Hear thou, [To Robespierre] what Heav'n, prophetic fate, Announces by my voice. Insult my fall With poor unmanly triumph ; bid thy minions Deride my fuss' rings, and with art excite The rabble to disturb my dying hour : Gaze on the scene with transport ; catch my blood While streaming from the scaffold ; feast thine eyes With these convuls'd and agonizing features : Yet know — My ruin but precedes thine own ! The fame fad fate awaits thee ! The fame axe Shall from those slioulders lop that guilty head : f

text: FEMALE HEROISM, 34 And, ere it falls, the fame inhuman taunts, The fame vile hootings of the savage crowd Shall wound thine hearing, and embitter death. [Exit guarded.] Robespierre alone. What means this strange disorder in my frame 'Till now unfelt ? A coH and clammy sweat Bedews my temples ; and this throbbing heart Seems bursting thro' my breast : My trembling knees Scarcely support their wonted weight. What pow'r Has thus unmann'd me ! Shall his idle threats, The weak, wild ravings of despair, appall The soul of Robespierre ? — Methought his voice Seem'd more than human, and, in thunder, bore Heav'n's sentence to my ear ! Oh coward guilt 1 To start at visionary dangers. Rouse, Rouse, my Ambition, gaze with eagle-eye On empire's fun ; wing thy aspiring flight Upward amidst its dazzling blaze, and scorn All thoughts of peril If I fall, ev'n foes Shall praise my courage ! TeU me not of scaffolds And hooting crowds : The public curse but proves The public terror : and the axe but rids The trembling dastards of the Man they fear'd. Enter St. Just hastily. How now, St. Just ! Whence are that quiv'ring lip And bloodless countenance ? What luckless tale Is written in thy looks ? St. Just. All's lost— success Favours our foes, and France upon the verge Of ruin trembles. Each successive post Comes wing'd with new disasters — Even now The fall of Valenciennes — Robespierre. How ! Valenciennes . Have we lost that too ?

text: A TRAGEDY. 35 ] St. Just. The intelligence This moment is arriv'd. The disaffected With triumph ill-disguis'd insult the grief That clouds each patriot's brow. What steps, my friend, Shall we in this emergency pursue To steel with constancy the public mind, And guard our lov'd Republic from th' attacks Of foes external and domestic traitors ? Robespierre. The juncture's critical, and loudly calls For morc than common counsels — Ha ! a plan This instant strikes me, that may yet avert Th' impending evils — Shou'd it fail, our hopes Of safety must arise from scorning safety, And boldly plunging into deeper guilt. Say, is not this th' appointed day, that cites The Austrian to her trial ? St. Just. 'Tis. Robespierre. Then hie thee To Herman, chief of that illustrious Court, Before whose bar degraded Majesty Must soon appear : Bid him select, and summon For his assessors, citizens of zeal And principles approv'd ; staunch to the cause Of freedom, cold, remorseless, steel'd alike 'Gainst pity, and that secret nameless influence That waits on beauty's tears. Thus, shou'd the weal Of France require it, shall Maria's death Involve us all in one distinguifh'd guilt, And nerve to prowess ev'ry Gallic arm. [Exeun. SCENE changes to the Conciergerie. Enter the Keepek of that Prison, and Clertille. The latter disguised as an Officer of the National Guard. Keeper. Away, nor tempt me thus — Dost thou presume Upon my former kindness ? text: 36 FEMALE HEROISM, A And admiration of thy Charlotte's worth, Relax'd the rigour of official duty In favour of two hapless lovers ; think'st thou A feeling bosom must, of course, conceal A traitor to his trust ? Clerville. Mistake me not — My civism is as pure, my zeal as warm In the Republic's service as thine own ! For ever may that hallow'd structure stand For which my Charlotte died ! Yet unprofaij'd By wanton cruelty, unstain'd by blood, Th' asylum, not the dungeon, of the good ! She, whom I plead for- Keeper. Merits well the fate Thy folly pities. Was she not a Queen ? Did not her wild profusion beggar France, And mock a Nation's mis'ry ? Clerville. Grant it did Misfortunes shou'd disarm a gen'rous Nation ! She claims no crown, nor can her woes advance The cause of freedom. Let republicans, For milder virtues fam'd, their seepter'd foes Transcend no less in clemency than arms. 'Tis not the Queen, 'tis the defenceless female, The widow, weeping o'er her murder'd lord, The halF-distracted mother, basely torn From the dear pledges of connubial love, That now implores thee ! Cou'dst thou hear unmov Those claims, thy bosom wou'd indeed " conceal A traitor to his trust," deaf to the call Of yearning Nature, and of nature's God ; That God, who gave it utt'rance in a voice Confest by all his works : which ev'ry heart Untutor'd owns, and with instinctive throbs Responsive greets ! Keeper. Why wilt thou urge me thus To pity unavailing ? Know'st thou not My pow'r is limited ? That ev'ry week

text: A TRAGEDY. 37 The guard is chang'd, and not a centinel A second time is station 'd here ? — Nor force, Nor fraud can e'er unbar the pris'ner's cell, Dark, silent, fad, unop'ning as the grave ! Know'st thou not too, that licens'd spies beset Each hour my steps, and note my ev'ry look ? Ev'n thy disguise but ill protects us both From jealousy's enquiring eye. Clerville. Full well I know at what a risk thy steady kindness Grants me access here : yet permit my stay For some few hours longer. Keeper. What, alas ! Can the indulgence profit or Thyself, Or Her, the object of thy gen'rous care ? Clerville. I know not. From despondency alone The wish, resistless, springs within my breast. When most despair'd of, thro' condensing clouds A ray may break ; and, like the Phenix, hope From its own ashes spring. This day decides Our pris'ner's destiny : and something here [Putting his hand on his breast.] Whispers that Cleryille sliall together triumph, Or perish with her. Keeper. Then obtain thy wish, And may th' event prove fortunate to both ! Retire now for the present — I expect Each minute Robespierre's arrival — Hence, Nor risk an interview : That eye of his Seems form'd, with penetrating glance, to search Man's inmost soul — He must not find thee here. [Exeunt severally.]

text: 38 FEMALE HEROISM, SCENE, the Queen's Cell. She is discovered stretched on a wretched Bed upon the Floor. She rises and comes forward. Queen. Can slumber, that, in palaces, so oft Flies from the down and canopies of state, Thus, in a dungeon, visit with its sweets The pris'ner's flinty couch ! All-gracious God, Blest be thy Mercy, that has gently lull'd, In rest unhop'd for, sorrow's weary frame, And with celestial visions sooth'd my mind ! This inward calm, these thought-composing dreams, Are earnests surely of approaching peace, And ope glad prospects to my fainting soul. I see the distant port, expanding wide Its hospitable bosom to receive My (hatter'd bark ; long, long, the wretched sport Of winds and waves ! Welcome, thou friendly Pow'r, Mifnam'd the king of terrors : thou to me Wearest an angel's smile, and thy dread call, That bursts in thunder on the guilty ear, To mine wafts accents more harmonious far Than all the vernal music of the grove ! Enter Robespierre, preceded by the Keeper, who, after stewing him in, retires. Robespierre. Well, haughty dame, has solitude's restraint Taught thee aright to measure thy condition ? Has that imprisonment, which tames the gaunt And hungry lioness, subdu'd the pride That swell'd within thy breast when last we met ? Or art thou still unconquer'd, and must new And greater rigours bend thee to our will ? Queen. Read in my looks my answer ; and confess How vain the hope that calls those rigours forth [

text: 39 A TRAGEDY. The body may be fetter'd ; but the soul, Active and unconsin'd, defies at once Tu' immuring dungeon and the galling chain, Unclogg'd by guilt, no mortal pow'r can cramp Its native energies : borne on the wing Of pray'r, it seeks the presence of its God, And pours its sorrows in a father's bosom : Hence, heav'n-sustain'd, it calmly waits the hour Of final freedom, and, with dignity, Looks down meanwhile on prisons, whips, and racks, And — savages like Thee ! Robespierre. By Heav'n, this firmness Is worthy of a nobler cause than thine ! What constancy must arm the patriot's soul, When strength of mind like this can animate A tyrant's wife ? Queen. A tyrant's ? Wretch, thou know'st Too well the falshood of that odious charge ! Had Lewis been a tyrant, slaves like thee Had, at an awful distance, kneel'd before him, And trembled at his nod ; still had the crown Of his forefathers grac'd his brow : and She, Who now, a captive, meets th' ignoble taunts Of upstart power, still had mov'd a Queen, The mistress of thy fate ! Ah no ! his heart, Of penetrable mould and milky nature, For all his subjects, as his children, felt, And sought their weal, regardless of his own. Yes ! thou dear Saint, thy unsuspecting virtues, Leagued with the crimes of traitors, have undone Thy family and France ! Robespierre. Beware, rasli woman, Nor in recriminations, false and useless, Express a rage ill-suited to thy state. Thou hast no flatt'rers now with servile gaze To watch thy looks, no rival parasites To catch the word, half-utter'd, from thy lip?, And consecrate thy follies : wholesome truth
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 40 FEMALE HEROISM. Alone, with sounds unpalatable, greets thee, And freemen now, not slaves, surround thy steps. Think'st thou, Republicans will bend the knee To fallen greatness and degraded pow'r ? Queen. I ask no homage. To domestic woe And private sorrows some respect is due : The sacredness of grief is all I urge. Kings and republicans alike shou'd own The ties of nature : Man is born to suffer, And all alike are vulnerable there ! Robespierre. 'Tis well that humbler feelings tame the pride Of pamper'd Royalty, and make the foes Of Man to moralize on Man's condition ! Submission, duly shewn, can best avert The Nation's rage, and mitigate thy doom. Queen. My doom ? 'Tis fixt — 'Tis irreversible — France cannot aggravate, or sooth its horrors — Vain is her pity ! Impotent her rage ! Robespierre. Hast thou not friends, hast thou not children left? And dost thou not their valued safety prize, Tho' reckless of thine own ? Queen. Oh yes ! — my children — Dear pledges of a murder'd husband's love ! Sweet solace of my woes ! Still do ye here Entwine around my heart ! Still do I feel Your tender pressure, into genial flow Warming its languid current ! Still for you I live, tho' dead to all the world beside ! Robespierre. Learn, that thy children's safety is the end And motive of my visit. Tell me truly, Dost thou not long to see them, and once more Indulge the raptures of o'erfiowing love ? Queen. Oh ! canst thou ask it ! Robespierre. What then, if I come Commission-, to restore them to thine arms, And heal a Mother's sorrows ?
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY ♦« Queen. Can it be? In pity speak, and calm this heart's wild throbbing, Divided 'twixt its wishes, and its scars ! Robespierre. Then hear, and let attention rouse thy foul. Deputed by the National Convention I bear proposals to thee, that concern Thy private int'rest and the weal of France. The war, which Capet's secret arts and thine Against this realm excited, rages still With violence encreas'd. This very week Th' allies, by treach'ry or by force triumphant, Have enter'd Valenciennes Queen. Have they indeed ? [Interrupting him eagerly.] Oh crown with conquest still their righteous arms, All-gracious God, and give them to restore The rights usurp'd of violated Nature And Heav'n blasphem'd ! On this devoted head Empty the vials of thy wrath alone, And bless the great avengers of Mankind. Robespierre. Ha ! Is it thus thou com'st prepar'd to meet The nation's clemency ? Perfidious woman, The gall of bitterness is black within thee, And, spite of struggling fraud, thy ranc'rous heart Escapes still to thy lips : but know, thy curses And pray'rs alike are impotent. The pow'r To wound and torture thee is wholly ours — Thy children's deaths — Queen. Oh spare them — rack this frame — Tear out this tongue, if it provokes — but spare, Oh spare my unoffending Innocents ! Robespierre. 'Tis thine alone to doom them, or to save. Queen. Tell, tell me how, be quick, disclose the means, And my last breath sliall bless thee ! Robespierre. To thy nephew Write such a letter as the State shall dictate. Bid him withdraw his troops, restore to France His sev'ral conquests, and dissolve the league Ambition and resentment form'd against us. G
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 42 FEMALE HEROISM, That conduct, on his side, engag'd for ; France Will to thy relatives, uninjur'd, send Thee and thy children : Nay, with gen'rous care Will make provision for your future wants, And grant such dowry as your ancient rank Was once entitled to. Say, is not this A lib'ral offer ? Queen. I accept it gladly ; And tho' my prompt compliance may be deem'd A mean desertion of another's rights Robespierre. Hold — one condition yet remains unmention'd. Thou must, besides, in clear explicit terms Confess, and with thy signature annex'd, The royal treasons that at length provok'd To arms the nation, and o'erturn'd the throne : Thou must own further the Convention's justice In dooming to the axe — Queen. How ! stain my fame ? And, dearer still, the mem'ry of my Lord i Complete the triumph of insulting vice, By bowing down th' unconquer'd soul before The body's tyrants ? Stamp on blackest treason The hallow'd name of Patriotism ? Stile The parricide's and rebel's impious dagger The sword of justice ? — No ! — 'midst all the horrors And degradations of her ruin'd state, 'Midst all the woes that yet await her, still Teresa's daughter (hall assert her race, Reject dishonor in the garb of safety, And prove her former by her present worth ! Robespierre. Is then the jingle of a sounding name Preferr'd to life's substantial joys ? Thou rasli And cruel Mother, wilt thou thus consign Thy children to destruction ? Queen. Will I ? Yes- Dear tho' ye are, my Children ; dear beyond The crimson tide that warms this heart, your honor Is dearer to your Mother stiU ! No act
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY. 43 Of hers shall basely stain with infamy The source from whence ye sprung. So highly born, Unblemish'd fame is all the legacy A sainted father left you : Oh ! for ever Sacred be that bequest ! Still may it grace Your lives, howe'er obscure ; and, unresign'd, Bloom with unfading honors o'er your grave ! Robespierre. Is this your final resolution ? Queen. 'Tis. Robespierre. Yet pause a moment, ere you seal their fate. Repentance must, ere long, awake. I see A tear yet trembling in your eye. Queen. That drop Was the last weakness of a Mother's heart—* Go, tell the ruthless men who sent you here, I scorn alike their mercy and their rage ! Cou'd I submit t'implore a boon from those Whose fiend-like cruelty denied their King The respite of a day, my only pray'r Were instant death. In prison, or at large, Alike the world's a solitude to me, Bereft of all that made it joy to live ! Go — tell them this : and rid me of thy presence Robespierre. I go, to spring the mine that (hall o'erwhelm thee ! Tremble, if life be dear ; or wounded pride Shrink from a death of public infamy : That death, from which not all the arms combin'd Of Europe, nor domestic treason's arts, Nor ev'n thy own repentance now shall save thee ! [Exit.] Queen alone. Deluded man, thy menaces are vain, And only soothe, where they were meant to wound ! Come, gentle slumber, image of that rest Which soon sliall (eal these woe-worn lids for ever ; Come, steep once more in thy Lethean dews These throbbing brows, that renovated strength C 2
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: _}4 FEMALE HEROISM. And new-brac'd nerves may aid th' unyielding soul To tow'r above the malice of its foes Triumphant. Let the proud philosopher, Th'o'erweening Jacobin, be taught by me, That tho' his impious phrensy may profane Religion's temples, and o'erturn her ssirines ; No arm can reach her altars in the heart, No woes degrade the Christian sufferer, Or intercept her commerce with the Skies ! [She stretches herself on the Bed, and the Curtain falls.] END OF THE FOURTH ACT. ACT V. SCENE, a Street. Enter St. Just and Robespierre meeting. St, Just. Why hast thou loiter'd thus ? The Court already Is seated, and thy foe arraign'd. Methinks The certainty of triumph, which shou'd wing Thy hatred, has relax'd its eagerness : Dost thou at length relent, and pity her ? Robespierre. Ay, as the tiger does the prostrate deer Panting beneath his fangs. 'Twas active hate That caus'd my absence. All things are prepar'd, Thanks to my caution, to prevent th' escape Or rescue of our pris'ner : Nay, ssiou'd pity Disarm her judges, they'll absolve in vain ! She dies — So vow the Patriots — So decree The Mountain's leaders St. Just. Yet a woman's death Can add but little to our party's strength, And must exasperate our foreign foes.
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY. 45 Robespierre. Agreed ! and for that reason 'tis (he dies ! St. Just. How ? Shou'd not rather policy incline To spare her as the hostage of our safety ? Robespierre. Tho' nurtur'd in a court, thou'rt yet, it seems, A shallow statesman. When the sword is drawn 'Gainst kings, 'tis wise to throw away the sheath. Her blood must flesh us in the common cause, Enhance our guilt, and thus cement more firmly Our union by our danger : But we waste The time in trifling — Let us haste, my friend, To witness and applaud a deed of courage That ssiall immortalize our Country's fame. [Exeunt.] SCENE changes to the Court of the Revolutionary Tribunal. The President and Members are seated, the Officers ofthe Court attending, as also military guards, the Queen standing at the bar.- and near her, Tin r ille, the public Accuser. Enter to them, Robespierre and St. Just. Tinville. Illustrious members of this high Tribunal, Avengers of the Nation, dread vicegerents Of Heav'n, whose sentence on that haughty race, Which scorn'd responsibility, and trod Beneath its feet the Maker's sacred image, Your hallow'd lips pronounce ; much-injur'd France With confidence awaits your just decision Between her, and this guilty dame, th' accomplice Of our late Tyrant. Ye have heard her charg'd With treason 'gainst the Nation's majesty ; Have heard the evidence, and the pris'ner's plea The charge rebutting : It remains alone, That your collected suffrages sliall find Her innocence or guilt A verdict then In justice both to her and France, I call for ; And may its tendency be such, as best,
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 46 FEMALE HEROISM, In the event, your credit ssiall advance, The Nation's welfare, and the Nation's fame! [After having conferred with the other Members] President. We find the charge against the pris'ner prov'd; Unanimously find so ! She is guilty Of treason 'gainst the Nation's majesty, Its laws, its liberties, and dearest rights. Tinville. Then in the Nation's name, whose voice I am, I now demand the sentence of the Court On the unhappy object at your bar. President. Widow of Capet, ere th' offended Law Borrows my voice to fix the doom of guilt, What hast thou yet, amidst this awful pause, To offer in arrest of judgment ? Queen. Nothing ! * I was a Queen ! And from the throne I fill'd Your treason hurl'd me to a dungeon's gloom ! I was a Wise ! And from the best of hussiands Your blood-stain'd hands for ever have divorc'd me ? I was — a Mother too ! And from these arms, These widow'd arms, your last consummate cruelty Tore my devoted Innocents ! — What more Can Austria's daughter, Bourbon's widow give To glut your rage ? My blood alone remains ! Take it, unfeeling Tyrants ! Sate your thirst With the rich stream that royal veins ssiall yield — Yet know, I smile upon that pow'rless hate That can no longer wound — All that of torture Ye cou'd inflict, already have I borne, And your last vengeance is — unwilling Mercy! President. Obdurate Woman ! Wilt thou brave its wrath Thus to the Nation's face, nor own thy crimes ? Queen. What ssiou'd I own? That I was born a Princess? 'Twas my misfortune, not my crime — That France With erring kindness plac'd me on a throne, And judg'd me worthy of her Bourbon's hand ? • This speech was really spoken by the Queen, and is taken from .he French Papers.
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY. 47 awards Blame her discernment then, but blame not Me ! Her partial fondness was, perhaps, misplac'd : So is her present rage — I lov'd the Nation ; I lov'd its courtesy, its martial fire, Its fense of honour, and its thirst of glory : Nor are its former benefits forgot By Her, whom once a gen'rous Public blest ! Aiks France my life ? To forward her repose, I'll lay it down, with transport, at her feet, And, with it, all its blessings : All, save one, One dear, inestimable gem, my fame 1 To sully this by any false avowal No pray'r ssiall win me, and no force compel : That more than suicide I'll ne'er commit, But, to the last, assert my unstain'd honour, And die at once the Christian arid the Queen ! President. Then hear the sentence which thc Law Against thy treasons — Death ! and by the Axe Upon the public scaffold ! There to justice Yield up thy forfeit head, and with thee die The hopes of traitors and of foes to France. Queen. Misjudging Man ! This country's enemies Are they, who first depriv'd me of her love, And taught her to believe her Queen a foe ! Tlieir hopes, instead of dying, will derive New life, and ssioot more vig'rous from my grave Yet, witness Heav'n, with pity more than anger I mark that unrelenting Cruelty, Which thus pursues me to the verge of being ! Yes! I forgive you : and, resign 'd, contemplate The contrast 'twixt your fortunes, and my own ! You go to triumph hence, and I to die ! I envy not that triumph, nor wou'd change Conditions with you. He, whose sov'reign will Can, with a look, arrest the tempest's wing, Vex'd Ocean's rage, and the still wilder fury Of frantic Nations ; in his own good time Will calm tht phrenfy of deluded France,
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 48 FEMALE HEROISM, Dispel this cloud of prejudice, unveil The truth, and from disgrace redeem my name ! [Exit guarded.] [The Court breaks up, and all withdraw, except Robespierre, Tinville, and St. Just.] Robespierre. [To Tinville.] Well didst thou, Citizen, sus- tain thy task ! Thy talents grac'd it, and thy Country owes thee — > Tinville. More than thou'rt yet aware of — Read this note, [Gives him a paper.] And learn, how near escaping was our victim ! Robespierre, reads. " Unhappy relict of a murder'd prince, " Not innocence will here avail to save thee ; " Thy condemnation is decreed — Yet fear not : " Heav'n watches o'er thy fate ! Thy guards are gain'd ; " And, ere an hour elapses after sentence, " Thou'lt owe thy life and liberty to Him " Who signs himself, with truth, thy steady friend, " But still no Royalist." — Audacious traitor ! Thinks he the task so easy then to foil The vigilance of freemen ? By what means [To Tinville.] Didst thou obtain this ? Tinville. While the witnesses Engag'd th' attention of the crowded court, One ofthe pris'ner's guards, whose restlessness Had fix'd, before, my notice ; near her stole, And strove by signs to catch her eye : I watch'd him ; And, as the traitor from his bosom drew The billet, with a sudden spring I seiz'd it, And call'd out to arrest him : but in vain ! The tumult of th' assembly drown'd my voice ; And, mixing with the crowd, th' affrighted slave Eluded apprehension. Robespierre. If the writer Declares the truth, accursed treachery Taints ev'n republicans — But vain th' attempt !
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY. 49 Not treason's arts can save her — Well convinc'd The effort wou'd be made, my care provided Against th' effects of bribery — By this The guards and all the centinels are chang'd. St. Just. Then disappointment blasts the traitor's hope. Robespierre. Not disappointment only, but destruction Awaits the wretch. Yes ! let him idly boast That Heav'n is watching o'er her fate. Ere long He'll find, that Heav'n has only watch'd for Me ! Tinville. When dies Maria ? Robespierre. Speedily — Th' attempt To save her ssiall accelerate her doom. [To St. Just.] Haste thou to Henriot — Bid him instantly Draw forth the Horse and Foot he held prepar'd To march upon my orders ; and with speed Invest the Austrian's prison. [Exit St. Just.] Shine out bright Thou fun, and gild imperial Freedom's triumph O'er trembling Royalty : Let not a cloud Obscure the pomp of that distinguissi'd scene, Where beauty, birth, and station ssiall bow down Before the majesty of France, and grace The victim offer'd to a Nation's wrongs. [Exeunt.] *tfs,o>L_.s_^ SCENE changes to the Queen's Cell. She appears lying on the ground. Queen. Why, cruel Mem'ry, thus recall the past With restless ingenuity ? Why point The finger still at our departed joys ? Are not the present Ills severe enough, Unless enhanc'd by contrast ? O the mis'ry Of such a retrospect ! When dwelling on it, My brain turns giddy, and my fever'd reason, Bereft of its discriminating pow'rs, H
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 50 FEMALE heroism, Begins to deem reality illusion : Events seem links of incoherent horrors, By hag-rid fancy, in some monstrous dream, Forg'd to torment the sleeping Wretch — Alas i My former fortunes were indeed a dream ! My present are more faithfully a sketch Of life, and its vicissitudes Then welcome Th' approaching hour, that terminates this scene Of instability, and gently lays O'er-labour'd nature in eternal rest ! Enter Clerville. Clerville. Thus far success is mine — Yes ! there ssie lies ! How chang'd, alas ! from Her, upon whose steps Applauding millions waited, and whose smile Spread happiness around and blest a kingdom ! Queen. What gentle voice, in pity's soothing notes, Breaks on the sullen silence of my dungeon ? Who art thou, stranger ? Clerville. A republican, Yet friend to thy misfortunes ; One, who pities The woman, and reveres the heroine : Who, 'mid this dark eclipse, beholds thee greater, Than when admiring Nations, bowing low, Hail'd thy meridian glories ! Queen. Think'st thou then I still can relissi flattery ? Ah no — Misfortunes have thus far befriended me, I know myself at last ! [stghs.] Clerville. Thou wrong'st my zeal. Wert thou encircled by thy former court, I ssiou'd not seek thee out — 'Tis not thy rank, 'Tis thy unconquer'd foul that I admire ! 'Tis the august Unfortunate I'd serve ! Queen. Thy kind intentions claim my warmest thanks— But wissies, Youth, are all that Thou canst offer, Or I accept — Soon, soon within the grave
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY. -■' Shall mis'ry rest ; alike beyond the reach Of pity or of insult ! Clerville. Say not so ! Heav'n yet extends a friendly hand to save thee — I've won thy keeper and thy guards : Arise, And, guided by me, from these horrid walls Escape to life, to liberty, and bliss ! Queen. You urge me vainly. For a wretch like me Life has no charms. Who'd quit the ssielt'ring port, Again to combat with the winds and waves? Clerville. If life presents thee with no joys, yet life Has sacred duties to enchain thy stay ! Dear are its ties yet — Think upon thy children ! Queen. My children, saidst thou? Oh ! thou hast struck at last The chord, to which this bosom's strongest feelings Responsive vibrate ! Shall I see them yet ? [Eagerly.] Shall I embrace them, ere I die ? Yes ! lead, Lead where thou wilt. For them I'll strive to live ! Clerville. Haste then — Each moment's precious — Let my arm Raise thee from earth, and aid thy trembling limbs — [As Clerville is affifling the Queen to rife, Enter Robespierre behind them, with his sword drawn.] Robespierre. Turn thee, vile traitor — Quit that wretch proserib'd, And meet the lightning of a freeman's sword ! Queen. That monster here ? Then farewel ev'ry hope ! Clerville. Am I betray'd at last ? Robespierre. Thou art — and death Marks his devoted victim — Yield thee, traitor. Clerville. No— ere I fall, this heav'n-directed arm Sliall yet avenge my Country and my Charlotte ! [They stght — Robespierre is thrown and disarmed.] Robespierre. Thou hast th' advantage — Use it like a Man, And spare a vanquish'd foe. H 2
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 52 FEMALE HEROISM, Clerville. Take thy life then — Take thy sword with it, and from earth arise, A better man, to thank my mercy. [As Clerville is stooping over him to raise him up, Robespierre draws a concealed dagger and stabs him.] Robespierre. Thus I thank that mercy ! Clerville. Base, insidious coward ! [Falls .] Bessirew this hand, that nail'd not to the ground The brute, whose nature thus belies his form. Much-injur'd Queen, farewel — I will not mourn Thy fate's approach : for who wou'd bear to live In such a land as this, and breathe an air Polluted by such monsters ? — O my Charlotte— I come — receive me — for this soul with joy — Takes its last flight — to join thee in a world — Where all is [Dies.'] Robespierre. There a traitor's spirit fled ! Queen. Assassin, no ! There died the good and brave ; The victim of his own too gen'rous heart, And thy infernal perfidy ! Robespierre. Rail on, While thou hast breath to curse ; Shortly that axe, Whose stroke consign'd the Tyrant to the grave, Shall fall upon the neck of his Accomplice. Ere it descends, bethink thee of his fate, And let fear'd fancy tell thy guilty conscience, That the same scaffold, which thy blood ssiall stain, Drank h'<s before ! Queen. Inhuman ! — Yet in vain Thou aim'st the wound — That very thought sustains My soul, and arms it 'gainst approaching fate. Yes ! my beloved Lord, with looks serene And steps unssirinking, on the path I'll enter In which thy Innocence before me trod : That block, which late thy sacred head sustain'd,
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 53 A TRAGEDY. Shall pillow mine in death, and the same steel Alike release me from insulting foes. [The beat of muffled drums is heard at a distance.] Robespierre. Hark ! my long-wissi'd for triumph is at hand ! Hear'st thou those drums ? They beat for thy destruction. Queen. 'Tis false — Those drums are harbingers of peace — More welcome to my soul their solemn sounds, Than choral symphonies, the cannon's thunder, Sky rending ssiouts of popular applause, And all the flatt'ries lavissi'd on my youth ! O Thou, [kneels] the widow's comforter and friend, God of my fathers, whose sustaining hand, Thro' life's perplexing wilderness, has led Thy weary pilgrim to this hour of rest ; Accept my heartfelt gratitude and praise For all thy dispensations : Ev'n for those That wrung this bleeding breast — To thee, great God, In humble trust my Orphans I bequeath ! Be thou their Sire and Guardian ! Thro' that world, Whose stormy surge their h-pless Parents wreck 'd, Guide thou, in safety, their unfriended youth: Or, if thy will denies this ; Oh ! dispose them, Like me, to bless that will, and with tlieir last, Their dying accents murmur out thy praise ! [ The drums are heard louder and nearer ; A[t length enter St. Just, a municipal Officer in his Scarf, &c. the Executioner and guards to escort the Queen.] Officer. [To the Queen.] Excuse the tidings which im- perious duty Requires me, tho' reluctant, to announce ; Your fated hour is come, and all arrang'd For the last dread procession : Henriot Without attends to guard you to the scaffold. Qiiecn. One moment yet indulge me ! For myself I live no longer — All resentment dies Within my breast, and tenderness alone
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: 54 FEMALE HEROISM, Pays its last tribute to the world I leave. France, thou lov'd source of all my youthful joys, And late of all my sorrows : Tho' unjust, Still priz'd; and, tho' thus cruel, still most dear ! Take my forgiveness, and my parting pray'rs — Ne'er may this blood in judgment rise against thee, And cry to Heav'n for vengeance ! In my grave For ever buried be my wrongs ! May peace Close soon the gaping wounds of civil war : And oh ! whatever form of Government Thy sons ssiall fancy, may their future chiefs Restore the blessings of a Christian faith, And, in their God at least, confess a King ! Now lead me where you please — Henceforth on Heav'n My looks and wissies fix— There, there, my soul, Lies all thy treasure : There, in thought, ascend, And taste the bliss that ssiortly must be Thine ! [She goes out, escorted by the soldiers, and followed by thii* municipal Officer and Executioner. ] Robespierre and St. Just remain — The latter weeps. Robespierre. For ssiame, St. Just ! What ! turn a Woman thus, While, in thy sight, with such heroic strength This Austrian tow'rs above her sex ? St. Just. Forgive The tear her suff'rings claim — * Bred in the court She grac'd so long, and honour'd with her notice, I can't forget the gracious Queen I scrv'd. But oh ! my friend, this constancy of hers Alarms me too ! Such unexampled firmness Can spring alone from confidence of bliss Immortal in a future state ! If that Persuasion be well-founded, what are we, And what the cause our guilty toils sustain ? * St. Just had been a Nobleman, Marquis of Fontvielle, and was a very young Man when thc Queen suffered.
name: West, Matthew

title: Female Heroism, a tragedy in five acts [and in verse] founded on revolutionary events that occurred in France in ... 1793
text: A TRAGEDY. 55 Robespierre. Already wav'ring ? Fool ! — if Heav'n pre- sides, Speaks it not in our favour? And if chance, Blind chance alone decides the lot of Man, Tis ours to make the most of all its blunders: Sure, that no After-reck'ning ssiall arrive ! St. Just. Vain Sophistry ! The voice of Heav'n within me Refutes it in the feelings of my heart — It tells me, that success awhile may crown Th' aspiring villain, whose triumphant crimes Scourge a deluded Nation : That the Good May seem deserted by eternal Justice, And one dark Cloud involve the ways of Heav'n ; Yet, soon or late, ssiall Retribution poise Th' unerring Scales, dispense to All the meed Deserv'd, and, with resistless evidence, To erring Mortals vindicate their God. — THE END.

text: POSTSCRIPT. IT may, perhaps, be objected to me, that I have fallen into the very error I censure in Mr. Eyre ; having made Robespierre conscious to, and secretly favouring, the assassina tion of Marat. To this I reply, that to invent and to falsify are two very different things. The latter is a liberty never conceded in historic dramas of recent slory ; The first, if dis creetly used, consistently tuith probability, and the discriminat ing features of a character, is allowable. That Robespierre, during the preponderance of the Briffbtin party in the Con vention, patronized and protested not only Marat, but his ether associates, is well known : But 'tis no less certain, that, after the suppression of the Girondists, he secretly undermined, and successively led to the scaffold the co-partner s and rivals of his power. This the fate of Danton, Fabre d' Eglantine, Anacharfs Cloots, &c. &c. abundantly testifies. .4 4F 54 / wish I cou'd justify as well, to rigid Chronologers, the liberty I have taken of mis-dating the capture of Valenciennes. I have supposed the intelligence of that event to arrive on the day ofthe fjfhteen's trial : more than twa months after it was first bwwn. To make the interval of time between the Fourth and Fifth Aft more consistent with probability and dramatic representation, was my motive, and must be my apology.

text: PREFACE BY THE EDITOR. kJF the Author of the subsequent Poems, whose lot it was, with genius, learning, and morals, to pass a life of almost total obscurity, few bio graphical memorials could be expected. Such as have been obtained, together with some account of the circumstances attending the present publication, will, doubtless, be acceptable to the reader. Henry Moore was born on March 30, 1732, at Plymouth, where his father, a man of extensive learning and merit, was minister to a con gregation of Dissenters. His mother was the daughter of William Bellew, Esq. of Stockleigh-court, in the same county. He received his grammar-education under Mr. Bedford, afterwards vicar of Charles parish, in Plymouth. The conversation and instruction of his father could not fail to contribute farther to his early improvement. In the year 1749 he was entered at the academy of Dr. Doddridge at Northampton ; and he was a member of it at the time of that eminent tutor's decease. On this occasion, Mr. Moore paid a tribute of respect and veneration in a poem to his memory, to the publication of which he gave his consent, but not to the many alterations which were made without his knowledge, and with which he was much displeased. The poem was dedicated to Mrs. Doddridge, and was justly admired as a production of elegant fancy and warm affection. He finished his academical course under Dr. Ash worth; and in 1755 or 1756, was elected minister to a dissenting con gregation at Dulverton in Somersetshire. In these long periods of life he appears to have been almost totally lost from the notice of the world ; recollected, perhaps, by some of his fellow-students as a youth of promise ; known by a few brother ministers as a man of learning and critical talents ; but probably scarcely recognised by two or three individuals for the splendid and cultivated genius, capable of shining in the highest ranks of literature, had fortune produced him upon a theatre suited to his powers. How he appeared in the latter portion of this narrow course, to an intimate friend who was able properly to estimate him, will best be shewn in that friend's own words. " He was probably led to adopt his " retjred and obscure mode of life, partly from the weakness of his " constitution, the original infirmity of which was distressingly increased " by his studious and sedentary habits ; partly from the singular modesty " and diffidence of his disposition. Notwithstanding, however, he thus " voluntarily withdrew from general society, when in company with any " one with whom he felt himself at ease, his conversation was most " agreeable and entertaining, enlivened with sprightly sallies and sea " sonable anecdotes. Although there was so little in his situation that " seemed calculated to produce contentment and thankfulness, and " although he had long suffered under painful and complicated bodily u complaints, yet he was perfectly free from any disposition to repine. " I never heard him utter a querulous expression. The composure and " resignation of his mind seemed always undisturbed. His manners were " singularly mild and gentle. He appeared utterly unconscious of pos " sessing any extraordinary powers : indeed, his behaviour indicated a " greater degree of humility and distrust than I almost ever witnessed." I shall add, that both the trials he underwent, and the sources of his con solation, are strongly marked in his poems ; in perusing which, we cannot but feel, that though he suffered much, he was nobly supported. M. are by his hand. These pieces obtained for the author the character of a very learned, ingenious, and useful critic, from such judges a.? the late Dr, Geddes, and Michael Dodson, Esq. Mr. Moore was the author of an anonymous letter, in which the doc trines of Mr. Madan's Thelypthora are attacked with much humour and vivacity. At the solicitation of his nephew, who was a very intelligent surgeon at Plymouth, he printed, in 1795, a short poem entitled, "Private Life, " a Moral Rhapsody." This, though a performance of much poetical and sentimental beauty, yet appearing from a country press, and with no advantages of publication, seems to have attracted little notice. Its merit, however, did not pass unobserved by one of the periodical critics. During the last summer, Mr. Moore put into the hands of the friend above referred to, a volume of MS. poems, which, with singular mo desty, he requested him to shew to some person sufficiently conversant with productions of the kind, to judge of their fitness for the public eye. I was applied to on the occasion ; and I trust the readers of these pieces will be convinced that I could not hesitate in giving a decided opinion in their favour. In reality, I scarcely ever experienced a greater and more agreeable surprize, than on the discovery of so rich a mine of poetry, where I had not the least intimation of its existence. That the author should have passed seventy years of life almost totally unknown, was a circumstance that excited the interest of all to whom the poems were communicated; and we were impatient that, however late, he should enjoy those rewards of merit which had so long been withheld. text: VI mean time he was attacked with a severe stroke of the palsy, which, while it left his intellects free, incapacitated him for every exertion. There was now no time to be lost. My offer of taking upon myself the whole care of the editorship was thankfully accepted ; and a subscription was set on foot, which met with the warm support of many, who were desirous that all possible comfort should be supplied to cheer the helpless decline of such a man. But the progress of debility anticipated these well-intended efforts. Pie sunk tranquilly under his disease on Nov. 2. 1802, having, however, lived to enjoy some satisfaction from the know ledge that there were persons whom he had never seen, who could regard him with cordial esteem and friendship. As he lived in celibacy, and had no dependent relatives, no other object remained for a subscription than that of bringing forward his posthumous work in an advantageous manner, secure both from loss and neglect. It is now committed to a liberal and discerning public,in the confidence that the Author will obtain no mean place among those who have contributed to elevate the minds, purify the morals, and gratify the noblest tastes of their countrymen. Stoke Newington, Jan. 1, 1803. J. AIKIN,

text: 2 j Maya's rosy fingers now Cull the fairest flowers that blow, And ev'ry balmy sweet combine To form the wreath divine, And consecrate the gift at Nature's sacred shrine. The mighty Mother, bending from her throne, Receives the fragrant boon, And bids it her refulgent brows infold, And breathe perfume around her locks of gold. Hence, Sadness then, with sullen brow, And gloomy thoughts, that feed on woe ! Hence Discontent's corroded breast, With all Heav'n's blessings still unblest! While hill, and .dale, and stream supply, Whate'er can charm the ear, or eye, Scenes where enthusiast Fancy strays, Lost in wild Rapture's magic maze, Indulge the genial hour, and taste The thousand sweets of Nature's feast. Let Cheerfulness with golden ray Beam ev'ry cloud of care away; Let warm Benevolence expand the mind, And Nature's kindness teach us to be kind. The Fairy-tribes, as village legends fay, From silent haunts of dale, and hill, And pebbled fount, and rush-clad rill, And tangled copse, and forest hoar, Where Winter winds have ceas'd to roar Now hold their yearly holy-day.

text: 4 CharmM are the passions, harmoniz'd the mind, Calm as the glassy seas, while sleeps the wind. O'er-wearied Labour feels no more his toils : Dew-ey'd Sorrow, rous'd to hear, Wipes away the starting tear : Woe-worn Melancholy smiles, And grim Despair, that beat her madding breast, Forgets awhile that she was e'er unblest. But when of dawn the rosy dyes Brighten o'er the blushing skies, And the gray clouds their robes unfold, Streak'd with purple, edg'd with gold, And their blended colours throw On the glitt'ring lake below, See ! Health, the blooming village-Maid, Her cheek in native red array'd, Her tresses gracefully -untied, Which shame the artful hand of Pride, Sprightly o'er the spangled lawn Comes tripping like the nimble fawn! Then at her work, the streams along, Rudely trills the rural song ! Content, that lightens ev'ry care, Sits smiling in her chearful eye ; While Luxury with languid air Leans on pale Envy pining by. text: 5 Spontaneous Graces catch the ravifh'd view, Scenes ever varying, beauties ever new. The hills rejoice around, the vallies sing, And e'en rough mountains gratulate the Spring, While the gay quires, that haunt the shelt'ring shade, Their untaught music mix, to glad the groves, Where Contemplation, sweetly-pensive Maid, With Peace and Rapture roves. Rejoicing in the good, his hands bestow, Th' Almighty Father looks well-pleas'd below ; But chief, his fav'rite work to fee, The pious, grateful, social Soul, Where tun'd to Nature's harmony The softest, sweetest passions roll ; That throbs in sympathy with woe, That flames with friendship's holy glow, That swells with wishes unconfin'd To scatter blessings o'er Mankind, And, in divine resembling lines imprest, Loves his own image on the gen'rous breast.

In full-orb'd glory move majestic on, And shed a sober, a religious ray ; O'er the gloomy front of Night Cast a sweetly-solemn grace, Show'r o'er her fable plumes thy pearly light, And kindle into smiles her awful face. Here, musing in the secret glade, While beneath the waving ssiade Dance on the chequer'd ground thy quiv'ring beams Or play bright-sparkling on the trembling streams, O'er the smooth lake a softer lustre throw, And the hill tops seem tipp'd with silver snow, From Folly's laugh, from Splendor's idle glare, The routs of Riot, and the toils of Care, My foul to Solitude, to Silence, flies, To Contemplation's pure, and placid joys ; O let her here a calm asylum find, And leave the Busy, and the Gay behind ! Hail heav'nly Contemplation ! meek-ey'd Maid ! Fair Hermit ! born beneath th' embow'ring shade, And nurs'd by Silence, daughter of the Night, Conversing in thy native wood With holy Genii, guardians of the Good, Wisdom serene, and Rational Delight ;

text: 7 Receive the fugitive — my cares asswage, And bid the swelling passions cease to rage ! I long to hear the whisper'd sounds, that flow From thy lov'd lips to chear the lonely hours, Mild as th' ambrosial gales of heav'n, that blow O'er amaranthine flow'rs. O come ! and beaming full on Fancy's eyes Bid Virtue's sacred glories rife, Such as beside Ilyssus' streams Blest her Plato's hallow'd dreams, Whence his warm transported thought Its high ecstatic spirit caught ! Bid me with awful pleasure trace Each mental charm, each moral grace, In all their fair attractions drest, The Sage's thought, the Patriot's flame, The pure desire, the gen'rous aim, And the bright ardor of the godlike breast ! The friendly heart, the social glow, The melting soul of tenderness, The tear by Pity taught to flow, To sooth the pangs of keen distress; The firm resolve, that dares defy The lightning of the Tyrant's eye, And, spite of flattery, or force, Holds on unmov'd its honest course ! Thus let me view the mind-ennobling Maid, In mingled majesty and grace array'd, 'Till in my breast her thrilling pow'r inspires Her own divine delights, her own immortal fires

text: 10 Nor for this world alone, a transient scene, Form'st thou the Soul — Some instinct from within, Thine inspiration, wings her wish sublime Beyond the bounds of nature, and of time. The strong and restless energy of Mind, That roves the fields of Science unconsin'd, That spreads its darting plumes from pole to pole, Wherever tempests rage, or oceans roll, Explores the secrets of the realms on high, Draws the red lightning from the low'ring sky, Bids seven-fold light its magic dyes display, The blended glories of the golden day, Treads the bright path the circling planets run, Sports in the living splendors of the fun, Or far outflies the comet's blazing race, And seeks new systems thro' the wilds of space — Immense designs, Immortal hopes, and unextinguisiVd fires, Exalt her vast aspiring thought to Thee, And only find a bound in thine Infinity. But when, forgetful of her heav'nly birth, She drops her idle plumes, and sinks to earth, When lost to Virtue's sacred charms, Her vigour melts in Pleasure's arms, Her grace and beauties by degrees decay, And mists of error cloud her mental ray ; Slaves to a tyrant lust, divine no more, Her towring faculties no longer soar; Her nobler pow'rs in wild confusion tost By furious passions, or in languor lost, Lie drear and waste, like once a beauteous World Dash'd into ruin, and in Chaos hurl'd.

text: 11 ODE ON CONTENTMENT. Behold those haughty hills, that heav'n invade, And o'er the vales extend their awful shade! Sublime upon his icy throne, There tyrant Winter reigns alone, In sullen majesty ; while vapours hoar And rainy clouds involve his gloomy brow; Beneath his feet the chilling tempests roar, And down the mountain drive th' incessant snow; Beat by the hollow blast the rocking woods Wave their brown horrors, howling o'er the floods. Here seems old Chaos to maintain The relics of his ancient reign, When yet the rude materials of the world Were all in wild confusion hurl'd; Ere yet the Sov'reign Mind In friendly league the jarring atoms join'd, Poliih'd the rugged form of Nature's face, Mix'd strength with elegance, with grandeur grace, And pour'd those beauties o'er the blended Whole, Which charm the sight and elevate the foul. And is there ought of bliss 'mid scenes so dear? And can Contentment fix her dwelling here ? text: 12 And scatters with a sparing hand His treasures o'er the barren land, Yet, while in studious quiet blest, Beneath my humble roof I rest, I envy not the happier skies, Where brighter funs unclouded rise To gild Hesperia's flow'ry vales; Where Beauty wreath' d by Love with roses In the myrtle bower reposes, Her bosom cool'd by fragrant gales ; And vernal Hours display their purple pride On broider'd Arno's blushing side. True Bliss is not to place confin'd, But stays, or travels with the Mind ; Nor luxury, nor pomp impart Her genuine rapture to the heart. Those vaunt her favours most, who least obtain, The Great, the Proud, the Vicious, and the Vain. Coy Beauty and reserv'd, she flies The croud's applause, the public eye, Loud-laughing Folly's idle joys, And Grandeur's childish pageantry ; Deep in the breast retir'd she sits unseen, Still sought without and over-look'd within. When Dionysius crown'd the purple bowl, Bid round the board the tides of pleasure roll, And call'd her to the feast, he call'd in vain; She fled the noisy banquet with disdain, And swift her downy pinions spread To Plato in his Academic shade,

text: 13 While by Ilyssus' bank with transport high His foul enjoy 'd her immortality. In Pleasure's blooming walks and fragrant bow'rs, Where Venus waves her golden hair, Beneath the shades, among the flow'rs Lurks the fly deceiver Care : While Admiration gazing counts The trophies in long triumph born, Aloft the Victor's gilded car she mounts, And with the wreathing laurel twines her thorn; And while " a God ! a God !" — resound the skies, The sighing heart the loud acclaim belies. Her gloomy front she dares intrude Upon the Tyrant's solitude ; Nor can the bravest guards, that round him wait, Drive the fell harpy from his chairs of state. The found of titles, and the soothing strain Of servile flatt'ry charm remorse in vain, To the sore mind like music idly play'd To Mothers, on an infant's bier Shedding the pathetic tear; Or to the fond and faithful Maid, With a breaking heart that hangs O'er a dying Lover's pangs. Guilt o'er his bosom throws infernal night; There the grim ghosts of ancient crimes affright; Now Vengeance flames before, now frowns behind ; Vengeance he hears in ev'ry whistling wind :

text: 16 THE VANITY OF FAME. As vapours from the marsh's miry bed Ascend, and gath'ring on the mountain head, Spread their long train in splendid pomp on high . Now o'er the vales in awful grandeur lour ; Now flashing, thund'ring down the trembling sky, Rive the tough oak, or dash th' aspiring tow'r ; Then melting down in rain Drop to their base original again ; Thus earth-born Heroes, the proud sons of praise, Awhile on Fortune's airy summit blaze, The world's fair peace confound, And deal dismay, and death, and ruin round, Then back to earth these Idols of an hour Sink on a sudden, and are known no more, Where is each boasted Favourite of Fame, Whose wide expanded name Fill'd the loud echoes of the world around, While shore to shore return'd the lengthen'd sound? The Warriors where, who, in triumphal pride, With weeping Freedom to the chariot tied, To Glory's Capitolian temple rode ? In undistinguish'd dust together trod. Victors and vanquish'd mingle in the grave; Worms prey upon the mould'ring God, Nor know a Cæsar from his slave ;
