text: OF THE EAST. 45 This thought might well alarm, and fear create, Not for myself, but for my followers' fate. 'Tis true, I might with ease, if so dispos'd, Your schemes have baffled, and your hopes fore-clos'd ; Might, with a word, have caus'd my sire to fall, And burn up actors, audience, house, and all ! Not even yourself, my fury could withstand, Had I unbar'd my dread, avenging hand ! But, scorning to employ such magic force, I left your play to take its natural course. Well, then, I saw your play, and must declare I found my fears were vain, and light as air! Found, what your bills a comedy proclaim, Had nothing of Thalia, but the name. No point, no force, no humour could I trace, To raise a smile, and dimple o'er the face. Some lame attempts, indeed, at wit you tried; But lame they were, and nerveless turn'd aside. No

It ap peared interesting to myself, and to those friends who urged the publication : I hope it may prove equally so to the (public, and especially to those to whom it is more peculiarly addressed. And if it should be the cause of saving the lives of any of my fellow creatures, or of producing other narratives equally interesting and authentia, the object will be answered. I never saw the Malays kiss each other, or their children, but they would smile upon them. The parents, however, often played with their children when young. When a chief or rajah dies, the body is con veyed immediately to the longar, or great house of public business, and on its way the people sing and throw stones before it, carrying at the same time all their instruments of war; and every person possessed of a palempore, which is a co vering of a bed, like our coverlids, hang it round the longar so as to cover it completely. They also make fans of white cloth, at the dead man's expense. Four girls sit on one side of the corpse, and four on the other, fanning it, for the space of two days and one night. Two lamps are kept burning near the corpse. By this time the corpse becomes offensive : it is 'therefore put into a coffin, which it generally is the custom for the rajahs to furnish themselves with in their lifetime. If not, a canoe is made use of ; in which, after cutting off both its ends, the body is placed.

The head priest then sits down by the side of the grave, the priest next in rank to him standing at his left hand, and the next to that priest on his left hand : the three next in rank stand behind these three, and then three behind them ; and so on in rotation. text: 120 The Malays manufacture very good and strong cotton cloth with mixed colours. Their cotton is remarkably fine and well picked, and they clear it by a kind of jenny. They understand the art of dyeing, and are very fond of gaudy colours. Their proas are from about five to thirty tons in size, are sharp at both ends, and much resemble our whale-boats. At the after-part of the proa they build a kind of house or cabin*. They use wooden anchors, which are large and strong. Their cables are made of braided rattan, and are strong, but not very pliable. Their sails are pe xuliarly light and strong, and made from the skin of a certain leaf, which is cured in the sun, knot ted together, and woven. The rope for the sail is made from the bark of a tree, and is pliable and strong, but not equal to what the sails are made of. The proas are constructed for rowing as well as for sailing ; they are used for fishing, trading, carrying provisions, or for privateering, and are fitted out and managed accordingly. The proa belongs to the captain, and, if a merchant- proa, is manned by about twelve hands, which consist of the captain, who is called an accord- er ; the mate, jere mode; boatswain, jere bot too: and nine sailors, ourari. The men have no wages, bring their own provisions, and divide their earn ings. * Vide plate, No. 3.

They have plenty of gum, of which they make what they call dama, to pay the seams of their proas with, instead of pitch. The canoes are navigated by three or four hands, and sometimes up to twenty. At Otaheite ten of these men were found; and the ship, in the pursuit of her voyage, struck on a reef of rocks* on the 2Sth of August, 1791. Ninety-nine men were saved out of the wreck, including the ten prisoners. The whole number embarked in four boats belonging to the ship ; viz. a pinnace of eight oars, two six-oared yawls, and one launch. The ship got off the reef a few hours after she struck, and was brought to an anchor; but, filling with water, sunk about sun-rise on the 2yth. The boats were directed to rendezvous at Coupang in the island of Timor. The two yawls separated from Captain Edwards in the pinnace, who arrived at that place on the 16th of September by their account, or the 1 7th by the account of time at that place. Each man's allowance was about three ounces of biscuit per day for the first three days : it was afterwards reduced to two ounces per day, and three small glasses of water or wine. There was no meat saved from the wreck — at least not enough to admit of a mouthful to each person. With this scanty proportion of sustenance, it was re marked that their great sufferings arose more from deficiency of^ drink than the want of food. text: REMARKS ON THE BEST METHOD OF PREVENTING DOWER. BOWER is that estate which the law gives the widow for life, of or in the third part •of such lands, tenements, and hereditaments as her husband was seized of, of an absolute estate of inheritance in fee simple or in fee tail in possession, at any time during the coverture, and which estates the issue of the widow would possibly have inherited. An estate for one's own life, or even an estate pour autre vie, which i,_ a less estate, are both denominated freeholds, as being able to support contingent remainders, &c. But though this is the case, and though the latter in particular is usually limited to the heirs ofthe cestuique use, yet there being no estate of inheritance, there cannot be any dower out of those estates. By accepting a jointure before marriage, or even a yearly sum of money, though not char- b2

As to the several circumstances which must concur to render a jointure a legal bar of dow er, see Co. Lit. Chap. Dower. If, however, the wife is an infant at the time of the marriage, the provision made for her must be in the nature of a jointure, so as to take effect in point of benefit immediately on the death of the husband. See Carruthers v. Carruthers, 4 Brown, C. C. 500. Where the Avife has not been barred of dow er by a settlement executed by her previous to marriage, the moment the husband becomes seized of any estate of inheritance, his wife's dower attaches, or, in other words, she has a title of dower. A perfect conveyance, or marketable title, cannot, in such case, be made to a purchaser without the concurrence of the vendor's wife, and her joining in levying a fine or suffering a recovery. Hence the difference between dower and free bench, which is the widow's customary estate in copyhold premises. In the latter the widow can only claim in respect of those copyhold lands of which her husband died seized ; and even an equitable alienation by the husband will defeat the wife's title to free bench. See Hinton v. Hinton, in Vesey's Reports. Where the value ofthe estate is small, it is sometimes the practice, in order to save the expence of levying a fine, to take a bond of

But as the present remarks are to be prin cipally confined to the consideration of the most effectual mode of barring dower, or pre venting it from attaching, I shall pass on to the more immediate object of this essay. Terms, then, it appears, are not to be im plicitly relied on ; so that it may be prudent, where they exist, not only to take an assign ment of them, but to look out for some more effectual method of barring the purchaser's wife's dower. Where terms do not exist, the neces sity of doing the latter is rendered the more imperious. By considering what it is that gives a wife a title to her dower or thirds, we shall more ea sily discover the best method of preventing it from attaching. Before a widow can claim dower out of her deceased husband's estates, it must appear 1st, that he was possessed of an es tate of inheritance in fee simple or fee tail in possession. 2dly, That he was solely seized of such an estate ; and 3dly, That he was so sei zed in possession. Dower may therefore be barred or prevented three ways : first, by crea ting a trust ; secondly, by conveying the estate to the purchaser and a trustee jointly, thereby creating a joint tenancy ; or, thirdly, by put ting the fee in remainder or reversion. Any form of limitation, therefore, that embraces ei ther of those objects may be deemed safe, and they will be more or less desirable or approv ed of, as they meet the wishes of the parties interested, and agree with their ideas of con venience. This accounts for the variety of the forms of limitation which are analyzed in the ensu-

Perhaps either of those forms, would answer the grand end, that of preventing the wife's claim of dower, but some of them may be pronounced the most eligible, on account of their general utility. I shall therefore examine the merits of such as I have met with, and pronounce according to the best of my judgment, which has been matured by sixteen years practice. Mr. Powell's method of preventing dower was (according to a form lately put into my hands as settled by him, see form A in appendix) by making the habendum to a trustee, his heirs and assigns, to the uses after mentioned, viz. to the use of such person, &c. as the purcha ser, by deed or will, should appoint, and sub ject to such appointment, to the use of the purchaser, his heirs and assigns, for ever. This form, besides the common objection, that the purchaser cannot sell or mortgage without the concurrence of his trustee, has been said to be open to a more serious one, namely, that there being no intervening limi tation between the power of appointment and the use of the fee, the husband is seized of the fee immediately, subject to his power of ap pointment, and it is questionable whether the exercise of the power of appointment will de feat the wife's title of dower. The reason is, that, in the one case, the person can only dispose of the land as owner, in the other he acts instnuuentally only, according to his pow er or authority, and his appointee does not come in as under him or deriving the estate from him, but under a title paramount, namely under that conveyance by which the power of appointment was reserved : just in the same manner (as to tlie point now under consider ation) as if the use had been declared to such appointee in such conveyance itself, instead of awaiting the interposition of the appointment by the person to whom such power was re served. This is thc doctrine upon which the great question in the case of Sir Edward Cleere, above cited, was decided, and which has been since confirmed and established by a variety of authorities ; and this is the true reason that an appointment, under such power as that in the present cane, prevents the wife's dower; be cause the appointee, under tlie execution of such power, does not derive his title from the husband or from or out of the estate that he was seized of at the time of the appointment, but comes in directly under the uses of the original conveyance, by which such power was reserved, and the uses to be declared by such * He may vest the use of thc fee, but not the legal fee, that being in his trustee, who cannot be divested of it, but by his own act.

The husband cannot, in my mind, be fairly said to be actually possessed of more than a life estate*; or, in other words, the limitation to him for his life gives him only the present right to the possession and to the rents, &c. though I grant he has the complete and abso lute fee at his disposal. His estate is similar to an estate of fee tail in possession, as in the latter he can cut off the intail by suffering a recovery, so in the former he can exclude his heir by ex ecuting an appointment. If indeed he be ac tuairy tenant in fee-tail in possession, (a widow b:ing dou able out of such an estate) his wife, of course, would not be barred of dower, un less the deed expressly says she shall be ; for wr.ich reason it is safer to insert those words in the limitation. At the same time he has all the advantages which he could have, if the estate was granted to him in fee in the first place ; especially if the words without impeach ment of or for any manner of waste, are introduc ed in the limitation of the estate to him for life : and even greater, because his wife's dow er does not attach, and because he can dispose of all his estate and interest in the premises by a simple instrument of appointment, and likewise because in case of forfeiture he does not lose the benefit of his life estate. But I apprehend Mr. Fearne's answer relative to the appointee, (see the above opinion) applies with greater force to the heir at law, namely, that " he does not derive his title from the husband, or from or out of the estate that he was seized of at the time of his decease," " but comes in directly under the uses of the original convey ance." The appointee (says Mr. Fearne) does so, as much as if he had been named in such original conveyance. How much stronger does this apply to the heir ? For he is virtually named, inasmuch as the original conveyance de clares, that, if the husband makes no appoint ment, the heir shall have the fee. If it did not so declare, I think his heir at law could not claim it, but, that it would revert (for want of that limitation of the ultimate remainder) to the heir of the settler or vendor, that is, in case the purchaser had not disposed thereof by deed or will. This, perhaps, is a novel opinion, but, it should always be recollected, that as antiquity cannot privilege a mistake, neither can novelty prejudice truth. It should be kept in mind, that the convey ance under consideration is a conveyance to uses, and not a conveyance in fee in the fast instance, and will operate the same in respect to the appointee and heir at law, as if it was a settle ment made merely for a good consideration (na tural love and affection.) or for a nominal valu able consideration, and the estate was thereby

In both cases the legal fee is in a trustee, and in the for mer case it is declared to be so vested in him for the express purpose of preventing the wife from being entitled to her dower. Fearne, in his form of limitation above in serted, and also B r, in the method latterly adopted by him, (see form D in appendix) make the habendum to the purchaser only, and do not give the legal estate to the trustee, but in the event of the determination of the pur chaser's life-estate, in his life-time, which, by the bye, cannot happen where the words with out impeachment are introduced in the limitation of his life-estate, unless in cases of forfeiture to the crown ; and I see no reason why a man may not be Aw own trustee, if I may be allowed that phrase. The settler, for in that light I consider the vender, where he merely executes a conveyance to uses, says, I shall hold the estate in trust to convey to whom I please, or to enjoy the same for my life, and suffer it to descend to my heirs, but it shall not be subject to ■my wife's dower. And cannot the same power that gives it me, by parity of reasoning, ex clude my wife from a participation thereof? I hold the estate, it is true, but I hold it in trust for myself, my appointees and heirs, and it cannot be held upon any other terms, till I ex ecute an appointment: therefore I have, as

Another form of limitation to prevent dow er, and which is much less objectionable than many now in use, is to limit the estate to a trustee during the joint-lives of the purchaser and his wife, remainder to the purchaser in fee ; thus not only vesting the legal fee in a trustee, but creating a trust to last as long as the wife shall live, and thereby completely cut ting her off from claiming dower. The only objection to this form is, that, on a mortgage or sale, the trustee's concurrence is requisite to pass the estate of freehold in him. Numerous are the methods of limitation to prevent a wife's dower from attaching. Mr. Watkins, in his work before quoted, mentions several, and I have in my possession, many more beside those above mentioned, which, I believe, have never been printed. But the best way, (says Mr. Watkins) is to limit the estate to such uses as thc husband shall appoint, which gives him the power over the whole fee, so that he may pass it to a purchaser, without any fine or concurrence of the wife or others, and the purchaser, on the execution of the power, " shall be in from the original conveyance, and so paramount the claims of the wife," (these are exactly Mr. Fearn's words in his opinion above stated) and in default of execution to the husband for life, with remainder to

This form of limitation I most cordially ap prove of, except that I would, for the reasons above quoted from Mr. Watkins, have the li mitation to the trustee, his executors and admi nistrators, and not to him and his heirs. There are four limitations or clauses in the last men tioned form, each of which is material. The first is the power of appointment. By means of this power the purchaser may dispose of and pass the whole fee by executing a mere instru ment. The second is the limitation to the pur chaser for his life ; this gives him the present right to the possession of the estate, and the perception of the rents and profits. The third

This intervening estate of freeliold keeps the purchaser's estate for life distinct from the inheritance mfce simple, and this pre vents even the attachment of any title of dow er. The fourth is, the limitation of the fee-simple to the heirs and assigns of thc purchaser. By this limitation, if the purchaser dies without mak ing any appointment or disposing of the pre mises by his will, the inheritance will vest in his heirs, unaffected by any title of dower in his widow, and without any estate in his trus tee, since that estate, if it ever commences, will determine by the death of the purchaser. The last mentioned form of limitation, therefore, seems, upon the whole, free from objection, that is, admitting that the husband is a good trustee for himself, which I think is clear, from the arguments I have before stat ed. If, however, the contrary should be pro ved, 1^ know of no form of limitation which would prevent dower and yet leave the legal fee in the purchaser, so as to enable him to sell or mortgage without the concurrence of his trustee. To those who are willing to submit to that inconvenience, I would recommend to limit the estate to the purchaser and his trus tee jointly, (it being certaiu that a wife cannot claim dower out of a joint estate) and to the heirs and assigns of the trustee only, and not of the purchaser ; otherwise, if the trustee should die in the life-time of the purchaser, the estate would survive to the latter, and thereby his wife become dowable out of the premises.

text: sa BEST METHOD OI A FEW REMARKS ON THE BEST METHOD OF Preventing an Husband from having an Estate by the Curtesy. CURTESY is that estate which the law gives the husband for life, in those lands of which his wife is solely seized, of an estate of freehold and inheritance', similar in some re spects to. the estate of dower, which the wife is intitled to out of the husband's real property, though in other respects differing therefrom, as will be seen in the following brief remarks. The circumstances that must concur to give a husband a title of curtesy, out of his wife's es tates are as follow. First, a sole and actual seizin by the Avife, of the freehold and inheritance, without any in tervening or contingent estate of freehold or inheritance. Secondly, the birth of a child, which might inherit or become intitled to the estate of which the wife is seized. See Bacon's Abridg-. ment, Comyns's Digest, " Estates," and Pres-? ton on Estates.
